The paper argues that continual operation without forgetting is a prerequisite for continual learning, and that this ability must be supplied by the surrounding harness, not the model weights.
AI.method: The authors derive seven bottlenecks from the long-horizon setting and address them with a hierarchical architecture of three parts: (i) levels indexed by time scale, each maintaining a bounded file summarising the level below; (ii) a clocked tick serving as the unit of autonomous action; and (iii) cascaded intelligence, where work is escalated to a more capable model only after failing review. The approach is evaluated through a ten-day autonomous campaign.
AI.result: In a ten-day campaign, an agent built on this architecture reproduced a published reinforcement-learning result with a human attending only once per day. The agent kept the thread across every context reset and session boundary, operating knowledge written early changed later behaviour with no change to model weights, and the authors identify where learned components would enter such a system.
AI.conclusion: Continual learning for long-horizon agents requires a substrate that outlives every context and process, and the checks the harness already runs are the natural place for a learner to reside.

title: Dynamic-LIVO: A Dynamic-Aware LiDAR-Inertial-Visual Odometry System Using Spatio-Temporal Normals
summary: This paper proposes Dynamic-LIVO, a dynamic-aware LiDAR-Inertial-Visual Odometry (LIVO) system for robust state estimation and static colored mapping in dynamic environments. Dynamic-LIVO employs Spatio-Temporal (S-T) normal analysis to identify dynamic LiDAR points and propagates the resulting classification to both LiDAR-inertial and visual-inertial updates, preventing dynamic LiDAR measurements and their associated visual observations from affecting state estimation and mapping. However, S-T normal estimation can be unreliable in newly observed and spatially sparse regions due to insufficient spatio-temporal observations. To address this issue, we introduce a time-delayed S-T normal estimation strategy that defers the classification of insufficiently constrained points and re-evaluates them as additional observations become available. This strategy improves dynamic classification reliability while preserving valid static points for map construction. Extensive experiments on public and self-collected datasets with diverse sensor configurations demonstrate that Dynamic-LIVO improves localization accuracy and produces cleaner static colored maps in challenging dynamic environments. The source code and self-collected dataset will be publicly released upon acceptance.

AI.tldr: Dynamic-LIVO is a dynamic-aware LiDAR-Inertial-Visual Odometry system that uses Spatio-Temporal normal analysis with a time-delayed estimation strategy to achieve robust state estimation and clean static colored mapping in dynamic environments.
AI.motivation: Conventional LIVO systems degrade in dynamic environments because dynamic LiDAR points and their associated visual observations corrupt state estimation and mapping. S-T normal analysis can identify dynamic points, but its estimation is unreliable in newly observed and spatially sparse regions due to insufficient spatio-temporal observations.
AI.method: The method employs Spatio-Temporal (S-T) normal analysis to classify dynamic LiDAR points, then propagates this classification to both LiDAR-inertial and visual-inertial updates to prevent dynamic measurements from affecting estimation. To handle unreliable classifications in sparse/new regions, a time-delayed S-T normal estimation strategy defers classification of insufficiently constrained points and re-evaluates them once more observations are available.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on public and self-collected datasets with diverse sensor configurations show improved localization accuracy and cleaner static colored maps in challenging dynamic environments.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic-LIVO achieves robust state estimation and static colored mapping in dynamic scenes. The time-delayed strategy enhances dynamic classification reliability while preserving valid static points for mapping. Source code and dataset will be released upon acceptance.

title: EconSkills: Studying Skill Transfer and Retrieval for Web Agents on Live Economic Data
summary: Web agents often revisit the same sites, yet most evaluations discard the procedures learned in earlier successful interactions. We introduce EconSkills, a skill library and evaluation framework that distills verified EconWebArena trajectories into parameterized standard operating procedures for retrieving live economic data. Each skill records its scope, navigation procedure, site-specific guidance, verification checks, and recovery steps while replacing source-instance values with placeholders. EconSkills separates two questions: whether a known relevant procedure transfers to a held-out task, and whether an agent can retain that benefit when selecting from a library. In controlled transfer, matched skills improve success over no-skill prompting and require fewer steps on paired successes, while abstraction is substantially more effective than replaying raw trajectories. At library scale, retrieval is competitive with the no-skill baseline overall and performs best on directly covered tasks; coverage-stratified outcomes show that approximate matches on uncovered tasks offset these gains. Browser trajectories further identify when procedural guidance shortens portal-specific navigation and when semantic verification remains necessary. These results establish that reusable economic web procedures can transfer across task instances and provide a concrete design target for coverage-aware selection and context delivery.

AI.tldr: EconSkills distills verified EconWebArena trajectories into parameterized standard operating procedures for live economic data retrieval, showing that abstracted skills transfer to held-out tasks and improve efficiency, while library-scale retrieval is competitive overall and strongest on covered tasks.
AI.motivation: Web agents repeatedly revisit the same sites, but most evaluations discard procedures learned from earlier successful interactions, wasting accumulated procedural knowledge. The paper aims to test whether such procedures can be reused and transferred.
AI.method: The authors introduce EconSkills, a skill library and evaluation framework that converts verified EconWebArena trajectories into parameterized skills. Each skill captures scope, navigation procedure, site-specific guidance, verification checks, and recovery steps, with source-instance values replaced by placeholders. Two questions are separated: transfer of a known relevant procedure to a held-out task, and agent retention of that benefit when selecting from a library. Controlled transfer and library-scale retrieval experiments are conducted, including coverage-stratified analysis and browser trajectory inspection.
AI.result: In controlled transfer, matched skills improve success over no-skill prompting and require fewer steps on paired successes; abstraction substantially outperforms replaying raw trajectories. At library scale, retrieval is competitive with the no-skill baseline overall and performs best on directly covered tasks, with coverage-stratified outcomes showing that approximate matches on uncovered tasks offset these gains. Browser trajectories identify when procedural guidance shortens portal-specific navigation and when semantic verification remains necessary.
AI.conclusion: Reusable economic web procedures transfer across task instances, providing a concrete design target for coverage-aware selection and context delivery.

title: ViLoMan: Learning Visual-Proprioceptive Whole-Body Loco-Manipulation Skills for Humanoid Robots
summary: Humanoid loco-manipulation requires adaptive whole-body coordination to seamlessly integrate locomotion and physical interaction. Despite recent advances, learning autonomous loco-manipulation remains challenging due to the scarcity of diverse, physically executable robot-object interaction data and the difficulty of learning unified whole-body control directly from onboard observations. We present ViLoMan, a scalable framework for autonomous humanoid loco-manipulation. ViLoMan first transforms partial kinematic demonstrations of human-object interactions into complete, physically executable robot trajectories. It then leverages these trajectories within a teacher-student distillation framework to learn a unified policy that maps egocentric depth observations and proprioceptive measurements directly to joint-level whole-body actions. During deployment, the policy requires neither reference motions nor intermediate commands. We evaluate ViLoMan on door-closing tasks across diverse door configurations and robot initial conditions in both simulation and the real world. Experimental results demonstrate that a single policy enables a Unitree G1 humanoid to complete the full task using only onboard depth sensing and proprioception, while generalizing robustly across task variations and transferring effectively from simulation to reality. Project page: viloman-anonymous.pages.dev.

AI.tldr: ViLoMan is a scalable framework that turns partial human-object interaction demos into physically executable humanoid trajectories, then uses teacher-student distillation to learn a unified egocentric whole-body loco-manipulation policy, validated on real-world door-closing with a Unitree G1.
AI.motivation: Autonomous humanoid loco-manipulation is hard due to scarce, diverse, physically executable robot-object interaction data and the difficulty of learning unified whole-body control directly from onboard observations.
AI.method: ViLoMan transforms partial kinematic human-object interaction demonstrations into complete, physically executable robot trajectories, then leverages them in a teacher-student distillation framework to train a unified policy mapping egocentric depth plus proprioception directly to joint-level whole-body actions; deployment needs no reference motions or intermediate commands.
AI.result: On door-closing tasks across varied door configurations and initial conditions in simulation and reality, a single policy lets a Unitree G1 complete the full task using only onboard depth sensing and proprioception, generalizing across task variations and transferring effectively sim-to-real.
AI.conclusion: The results indicate that scalable trajectory completion combined with teacher-student distillation can yield a single onboard, reference-free whole-body loco-manipulation policy that generalizes and transfers to real humanoid hardware.

title: A Unified Evaluation Framework for Trustworthy Large Language Models, Agentic AI, and Multimodal Systems
summary: Benchmark scores alone provide an incomplete basis for assessing the trustworthiness of modern artificial intelligence systems. Large language models (LLMs), agentic systems, and multimodal models (MLLMs) require different forms of assessment, yet their evaluation evidence must remain interpretable for development and oversight. We propose a unified framework that connects output-level, trajectory-level, and cross-modal assessment through eight trustworthiness dimensions: capability, robustness, safety, fairness, transparency, governance, oversight, and efficiency. The framework preserves system-specific metrics while mapping native measurements to common performance bands, accompanied by uncertainty estimates and traceable evidence. A meta-evaluation layer examines the validity, reliability, and reproducibility of the evaluation itself. Multidimensional profiles expose strengths and weaknesses, while safety-critical overrides prevent aggregate scores from masking critical failures. Mappings to governance frameworks, international standards, and European Union regulatory requirements connect technical assessment with oversight needs. The framework provides a structured basis for assessing both system performance and the credibility of the evidence supporting it, with empirical validation across deployment contexts remaining an essential next step.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a unified trustworthiness-assessment framework spanning output, trajectory, and cross-modal evaluation across eight dimensions, augmented by a meta-evaluation layer and safety-critical overrides, with governance/regulatory mappings.
AI.motivation: Benchmark scores alone are insufficient to assess the trustworthiness of modern AI systems (LLMs, agentic systems, MLLMs), which need diverse forms of assessment while keeping evaluation evidence interpretable for development and oversight.
AI.method: A unified framework linking output-level, trajectory-level, and cross-modal assessment via eight trustworthiness dimensions (capability, robustness, safety, fairness, transparency, governance, oversight, efficiency). It preserves system-specific metrics while mapping native measurements to common performance bands with uncertainty estimates and traceable evidence; a meta-evaluation layer checks validity, reliability, and reproducibility; multidimensional profiles and safety-critical overrides are included, plus mappings to governance frameworks, international standards, and EU regulatory requirements.
AI.result: The framework yields multidimensional profiles exposing strengths and weaknesses, prevents aggregate scores from masking critical failures via safety-critical overrides, and connects technical assessment with oversight needs through standards and regulatory mappings.
AI.conclusion: The framework offers a structured basis for assessing both system performance and the credibility of its supporting evidence. Empirical validation across deployment contexts remains an essential next step.

title: Kinematics-Grounded Agentic AI for Robotic Additive Manufacturing Process Planning
summary: Robotic additive manufacturing (AM) extends material-extrusion printing beyond gantry kinematics but makes process planning robot-dependent. A slicer-generated plan that appears favorable in part coordinates can become infeasible or robotically unfavorable on a manipulator because slicer-process decisions and part orientation determine the generated path, while part orientation and workspace placement affect its kinematic realization. Existing AM tools, large language model (LLM)-based decision-support methods, and digital-shadow systems do not provide integrated pre-execution evaluation of these coupled decisions. This paper presents agentic robotic additive manufacturing (A-RAM), an agent-specialist-tool framework that converts user intent and a part file into traceable, execution-ready plans. The LLM interprets manufacturing objectives and constraints, identifies prescribed and searchable planning variables, and encodes this reasoning in a schema-constrained request; a deterministic Planning Agent instantiates the corresponding search workflow, while domain tools compute quantitative evidence for slicing, placement, inverse kinematics, trajectory timing, Joint-6 jerk, and extrusion. The framework is evaluated on a six-axis robotic-arm AM cell through three case studies covering expert-specified planning, goal-only planning, objective-dependent infill screening, and geometry-dependent orientation-placement selection. Across the evaluated candidate sets, selected plans achieve up to 53.5% lower maximum Joint-6 jerk and 48.3% lower mean absolute Joint-6 jerk than the least favorable valid candidates, while objective-specific infill screening yields motion-plan completion times up to 40.1% shorter and extrusion paths up to 12.7% shorter than the corresponding least favorable screened patterns.

AI.tldr: This paper presents A-RAM, an agent-specialist-tool framework that integrates LLM-based reasoning with deterministic planning and domain tools to generate traceable, execution-ready plans for robotic additive manufacturing, and evaluates it on a six-axis arm across three case studies.
AI.motivation: Robotic AM extends material-extrusion printing beyond gantry kinematics but makes process planning robot-dependent. A slicer-generated plan that looks favorable in part coordinates can become infeasible or robotically unfavorable on a manipulator, because slicer-process decisions and part orientation determine the generated path, while part orientation and workspace placement affect its kinematic realization. Existing AM tools, LLM-based decision-support methods, and digital-shadow systems lack integrated pre-execution evaluation of these coupled decisions.
AI.method: The proposed A-RAM framework converts user intent and a part file into traceable, execution-ready plans. An LLM interprets manufacturing objectives and constraints, identifies prescribed and searchable planning variables, and encodes this reasoning in a schema-constrained request. A deterministic Planning Agent instantiates the corresponding search workflow, while domain tools compute quantitative evidence for slicing, placement, inverse kinematics, trajectory timing, Joint-6 jerk, and extrusion.
AI.result: Evaluated on a six-axis robotic-arm AM cell through three case studies covering expert-specified planning, goal-only planning, objective-dependent infill screening, and geometry-dependent orientation-placement selection. Across the evaluated candidate sets, selected plans achieve up to 53.5% lower maximum Joint-6 jerk and 48.3% lower mean absolute Joint-6 jerk than the least favorable valid candidates. Objective-specific infill screening yields motion-plan completion times up to 40.1% shorter and extrusion paths up to 12.7% shorter than the corresponding least favorable screened patterns.
AI.conclusion: A-RAM enables integrated pre-execution evaluation of coupled slicer-process, orientation, and placement decisions for robotic AM, producing traceable plans with measurably improved kinematic and extrusion performance.

title: Self Improvement via Fast Tree-search
summary: Coding agents can recursively modify their own implementations, forming a loop of self-improvement. While prior work shows this can boost performance on coding benchmarks, existing approaches are costly and compute-intensive. We introduce a simple, sample-efficient self-improvement framework that significantly improves coding performance under strict budget constraints. We identify evaluation of candidate self-modifications as the main runtime bottleneck since prior approaches estimate their effectiveness by re-running a subset of benchmark tasks with the modified agent, which is time-consuming. We introduce Recursive Self Improvement via Fast Tree-search (SIFT), which augments these downstream task evaluations with an LLM-as-a-judge signal that performs pairwise comparisons between candidate patches, where the win-loss record is aggregated with a regularized Bradley-Terry model, and the resulting strength scores drive rank-based parent sampling inside a lightweight disaggregated tree search. Expensive downstream task evaluations are reserved only for the most promising nodes. Using a fully disaggregated tree search pipeline, the judge scores provide intermediate signal to guide exploration on promising candidate patches without being bottlenecked by slow evaluation runs. SIFT outperforms existing tree-search based self-evolution frameworks on the full Polyglot benchmark with significantly lower resource requirements in terms of CPU hours, wall clock time, and API cost.

AI.tldr: SIFT is a sample-efficient self-improvement framework for coding agents that replaces slow task-based evaluation with an LLM-as-a-judge signal aggregated via a regularized Bradley-Terry model, then drives rank-based parent sampling in a disaggregated tree search over candidate self-modifications.
AI.motivation: Coding agents can recursively modify their own implementations to self-improve, but prior approaches are costly and compute-intensive. The main bottleneck is evaluating candidate self-modifications, since prior methods re-run a subset of benchmark tasks with the modified agent, which is slow and time-consuming.
AI.method: SIFT augments downstream task evaluations with an LLM-as-a-judge signal performing pairwise comparisons between candidate patches. Win-loss records are aggregated with a regularized Bradley-Terry model, producing strength scores that drive rank-based parent sampling inside a lightweight disaggregated tree search. Expensive downstream task evaluations are reserved only for the most promising nodes, and the judge scores provide intermediate exploration guidance via a fully disaggregated pipeline.
AI.result: SIFT outperforms existing tree-search-based self-evolution frameworks on the full Polyglot benchmark with significantly lower resource requirements in CPU hours, wall clock time, and API cost.
AI.conclusion: A simple, sample-efficient self-improvement framework using judge-guided tree search can substantially improve coding performance under strict budget constraints, reducing resource use while surpassing prior tree-search self-evolution methods.

title: Design and Experimental Validation of a 3D Printed Torsional Series Elastic Actuator for Safe Human Robot Interaction
summary: Ensuring intrinsic safety in physical human robot interaction (pHRI) is a critical requirement for social and service robots. While Series Elastic Actuators (SEAs) offer hardware based compliance, traditional metallic designs often require complex, multi part assemblies. This paper presents the design, finite element analysis (FEA), and experimental validation of a low stiffness, torsional spring for SEAs, manufactured via 3D printed thermoplastic polyurethane (TPU). The compliant element exhibits a highly linear torque deformation response (Ks = 0.066 Nm/degree), matching numerical predictions with under 3% deviation, a variance attributed to FDM structural anisotropy. To accommodate external interactions using standard position limited servomotors, a hybrid position controller with torque threshold switching was implemented. Experimental evaluations demonstrate the system ability to accurately track non stationary trajectories and safely yield to external disturbances. Furthermore, the inherent material damping of the TPU acts as a passive low pass filter, preventing high frequency oscillations during control mode transitions. The proposed architecture offers a cost effective, reliable, and easily manufacturable solution for safe pHRI.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a 3D-printed TPU torsional spring for Series Elastic Actuators that achieves a linear torque-deformation response (Ks = 0.066 Nm/degree) with under 3% deviation from FEA predictions, and validates it in a hybrid position/torque-threshold control scheme for safe physical human-robot interaction.
AI.motivation: Ensuring intrinsic safety in physical human-robot interaction is a critical requirement for social and service robots. Although Series Elastic Actuators provide hardware-based compliance, traditional metallic designs require complex, multi-part assemblies, creating a need for a simpler, cost-effective compliant element.
AI.method: The authors designed and manufactured a low-stiffness torsional spring for SEAs via FDM 3D printing of thermoplastic polyurethane. They performed finite element analysis and experimental validation of the torque-deformation response. To work with standard position-limited servomotors, they implemented a hybrid position controller with torque-threshold switching.
AI.result: The compliant element exhibits a highly linear torque-deformation response (Ks = 0.066 Nm/degree), matching numerical predictions with under 3% deviation, attributed to FDM structural anisotropy. The system accurately tracks non-stationary trajectories and safely yields to external disturbances. The inherent material damping of TPU acts as a passive low-pass filter, preventing high-frequency oscillations during control mode transitions.
AI.conclusion: The proposed architecture offers a cost-effective, reliable, and easily manufacturable solution for safe physical human-robot interaction.

title: When Hiring Becomes Agent-Mediated: Evaluating Access and Recurrence in Two-Agent Résumé Screening
comment: 9 pages, 5 tables, 1 figure. Accepted to the REALM Workshop at EMNLP 2026
summary: Hiring is bilateral: employers assess fit, while candidates present and defend evidence of their qualifications. Yet résumé screening, the first gate, is commonly automated as a static, one-call judgment over a résumé-job pair. We study a two-agent alternative in which employer-side and candidate-side agents represent these roles, exchange evidence, and update their judgments before deciding who advances. We compare procedures on 600 constructed résumé-job pairs using GPT-5.5 and Claude Opus 4.7. Two-agent screening advances more applications (33.3% to 39.3% for GPT-5.5; 34.0% to 35.5% for Opus 4.7). Across three runs on the common 191-pair borderline pool, pass-instance rates rise from 4.5% to 26.2% and from 6.5% to 16.1%, respectively. This is not a uniform relaxation: two-agent screening rejects applications one-call advances, changing decisions in both directions. At similar pass volumes, the procedures advance different applications, and no one-call threshold recovers applications consistently selected by two-agent screening. Among discovery-selected cases re-executed in fresh runs, two-agent-only selections recur less often than shared selections, clearly under GPT-5.5 and less certainly under Opus 4.7, while a separate one-call follow-up shows no comparable decline. As hiring becomes agent-mediated on both sides, the screening procedure, not only the model behind it, shapes who reaches human review and how reliably that access recurs.

AI.tldr: The paper reframes résumé screening from a static one-call judgment into a two-agent procedure where employer-side and candidate-side agents exchange evidence and update judgments; this procedure changes both who advances and how reliably that advancement recurs.
AI.motivation: Hiring is bilateral in reality—employers assess fit while candidates present and defend qualifications—yet automated résumé screening, the first gate, is typically modeled as a static, one-call judgment over a résumé-job pair. The authors argue that this mismatch means the screening procedure itself, not only the underlying model, may shape who reaches human review and how reproducibly that access occurs.
AI.method: The authors compare a two-agent procedure (employer-side and candidate-side agents that exchange evidence and update judgments before deciding who advances) against one-call screening. They evaluate on 600 constructed résumé-job pairs using GPT-5.5 and Claude Opus 4.7, including three runs on a common 191-pair borderline pool, re-execution of discovery-selected cases in fresh runs, and a separate one-call follow-up for comparison.
AI.result: Two-agent screening advances more applications (33.3%→39.3% for GPT-5.5; 34.0%→35.5% for Opus 4.7). On the 191-pair borderline pool across three runs, pass-instance rates rise from 4.5%→26.2% and 6.5%→16.1%. The shift is not uniform relaxation: two-agent screening also rejects applications that one-call advances, changing decisions in both directions. At similar pass volumes, the procedures advance different applications, and no one-call threshold recovers the applications consistently selected by two-agent screening. Among discovery-selected cases re-executed in fresh runs, two-agent-only selections recur less often than shared selections (clearly under GPT-5.5, less certainly under Opus 4.7), whereas the separate one-call follow-up shows no comparable decline.
AI.conclusion: As hiring becomes agent-mediated on both sides, the screening procedure—not just the model behind it—determines who reaches human review and how reliably that access recurs. Two-agent screening alters decision composition and bidirectional outcomes, and its uniquely selected cases show weaker reproducibility, raising concerns about the stability of procedure-driven access to human review.

title: Enhancing the Perception of Safety and Comfort during Physical Human-Robot Handshake Interactions by Integrating Flexible Elements into a Robotic Arm
summary: Safety and comfort in human-robot physical in-teractions are essential aspects in the development of social technologies, where natural gestures, such as handshakes, represent a challenge due to their direct physical contact. The implementation of series elastic actuators (SEA) to absorb impacts is proposed as a design strategy that favors safer interactions. This paper presents an experimental study aimed at evaluating how the incorporation of SEAs in robotic arms influences perceived safety and the interaction experience dur-ing handshaking. The design allows a direct comparison of the effect of rigidity versus the incorporation of elastic elements, in order to identify the advantages of SEAs in improving the physical safety and social acceptance of robotic systems in everyday contexts. The experiment was carried out with 10 volunteers (6 men and 4 women), who performed two interactions with each robotic arm: one with rigid joints and the other with flexible joints using SEA. During testing, objective data on end-effector trajectories were collected, as well as subjective information through a perception survey focused on safety, naturalness, and confidence during the handshake. The survey results show increased perceptions of safety and comfort with the SEA-equipped arm, supporting its potential to facilitate safer and more socially accepted human-robot interactions.

AI.tldr: This study experimentally evaluates whether series elastic actuators (SEAs) in robotic arms improve perceived safety and interaction quality during handshaking compared to rigid joints. Results from 10 volunteers indicate higher perceived safety and comfort with SEA-equipped arms.
AI.motivation: Physical safety and comfort in human-robot physical interactions are critical for social technologies. Natural gestures like handshakes pose challenges due to direct physical contact, motivating the use of series elastic actuators (SEAs) to absorb impacts as a design strategy for safer interactions.
AI.method: An experimental study directly comparing rigid versus elastic (SEA) joints in robotic arms during handshaking. Ten volunteers (6 men, 4 women) each performed two interactions—one with rigid joints and one with SEA-flexible joints. Objective end-effector trajectory data were collected, alongside subjective perception surveys assessing safety, naturalness, and confidence.
AI.result: Survey results showed increased perceptions of safety and comfort with the SEA-equipped arm compared to the rigid configuration, supporting SEAs' potential to facilitate safer and more socially accepted human-robot interactions.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating SEAs into robotic arms enhances perceived safety and comfort during handshaking, demonstrating their advantage over rigid joints for improving physical safety and social acceptance in everyday human-robot contexts.

title: Agentic AI Networking for Heterogeneous Unmanned Aerial Systems in Low-Altitude Wireless Networks
summary: Low-altitude wireless networks (LAWNs) are emerging as a key infrastructure for heterogeneous unmanned aerial systems that support concurrent services within a shared three-dimensional airspace. Their coexistence creates strong coupling among mobility, connectivity, and shared network resources, while heterogeneous services impose distinct and time-varying requirements. These interactions naturally form a dynamic non-cooperative game in which both operating conditions and coordination objectives evolve over time. Conventional optimization and learning-based controllers typically rely on predefined objectives, limiting their ability to adapt autonomously to changing service requirements and resource priorities. To address this challenge, we propose a hierarchical hybrid large language model (LLM)- multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) architecture organized as a dual-loop structure. Specifically, an outer adaptation loop employs LLM-assisted game orchestration to interpret service requirements and operator intent, and reconfigure objectives and resource priorities, while an inner loop executes decentralized, parameter-conditioned MARL policies under the configured game. A logistics-monitoring case study illustrates how the proposed framework facilitates coordinated coexistence among heterogeneous services, adapting to evolving operating conditions without retraining the underlying MARL policies. Finally, we discuss key challenges and research directions toward scalable, trustworthy, and adaptive agentic LAWNs.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a hierarchical hybrid LLM-MARL architecture with a dual-loop structure to enable adaptive coordination in low-altitude wireless networks (LAWNs), where LLMs handle game orchestration and MARL executes decentralized policies.
AI.motivation: LAWNs support heterogeneous unmanned aerial systems sharing a 3D airspace, creating tight coupling among mobility, connectivity, and shared resources. Heterogeneous services impose distinct, time-varying requirements, forming a dynamic non-cooperative game. Conventional optimization and learning-based controllers rely on predefined objectives, limiting autonomous adaptation to changing service requirements and resource priorities.
AI.method: A hierarchical hybrid large language model (LLM)-multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) architecture organized as a dual-loop structure. An outer adaptation loop uses LLM-assisted game orchestration to interpret service requirements and operator intent and to reconfigure objectives and resource priorities. An inner loop executes decentralized, parameter-conditioned MARL policies under the configured game.
AI.result: A logistics-monitoring case study demonstrates that the framework facilitates coordinated coexistence among heterogeneous services and adapts to evolving operating conditions without retraining the underlying MARL policies.
AI.conclusion: The paper outlines key challenges and research directions toward scalable, trustworthy, and adaptive agentic LAWNs.

title: Task-Oriented Active Learning of Residual Dynamics for Model Predictive Path Integral Control
summary: Online residual learning can reduce model mismatch in predictive control, but passive data collection may fail to adequately cover states that become important later in the task. Task-agnostic active learning targets uncertain or informative regions, but information acquired in such regions does not necessarily improve task performance. This paper introduces Task-Oriented Information Acquisition (ToIA), an active-learning criterion for model predictive path integral control (MPPI) with online Gaussian process (GP) residual learning. For each sampled control sequence, ToIA estimates how much an observation obtained early in the rollout would reduce predictive uncertainty at later states on the same rollout, and weights this reduction by the rollout's relevance to the task. The score is evaluated over the existing MPPI rollout batch without sampling future observations or re-optimizing control under hypothetical posterior updates. In simulated off-road navigation across held-out maps with heterogeneous terrain, ToIA improved the goal-reaching success rate over passive GP learning by 19.3 and 27.4 percentage points and outperformed task-agnostic active-learning baselines across dense and sparse online-learning intervals. An ablation study indicates that task relevance is particularly important under sparse model updates. The implementation supports online control at 20 Hz on an NVIDIA RTX 2080 Ti.

AI.tldr: ToIA is an active-learning criterion for MPPI with online GP residual learning that scores each existing rollout by how much an early observation would reduce predictive uncertainty at later states, weighted by task relevance, improving off-road navigation success by up to 27.4 percentage points while running online at 20 Hz.
AI.motivation: Online residual learning reduces model mismatch in predictive control, but passive data collection may fail to cover states that become important later in the task. Task-agnostic active learning targets uncertain or informative regions, yet information gained there does not necessarily improve task performance. The work therefore seeks a task-oriented acquisition criterion that focuses learning on states relevant to the control objective.
AI.method: The paper introduces Task-Oriented Information Acquisition (ToIA), an active-learning criterion for model predictive path integral control (MPPI) with online Gaussian process (GP) residual learning. For each sampled control sequence, ToIA estimates how much an observation obtained early in the rollout would reduce predictive uncertainty at later states on the same rollout, and weights this reduction by the rollout's relevance to the task. The score is computed over the existing MPPI rollout batch without sampling future observations or re-optimizing control under hypothetical posterior updates. An ablation examines the contribution of task relevance under dense versus sparse model updates. The implementation supports online control at 20 Hz on an NVIDIA RTX 2080 Ti.
AI.result: In simulated off-road navigation across held-out maps with heterogeneous terrain, ToIA improved goal-reaching success rate over passive GP learning by 19.3 and 27.4 percentage points and outperformed task-agnostic active-learning baselines across both dense and sparse online-learning intervals. The ablation indicates task relevance is particularly important under sparse model updates. Online control runs at 20 Hz on an NVIDIA RTX 2080 Ti.
AI.conclusion: Weighting information acquisition by task relevance yields substantial gains in goal-reaching success for MPPI with online GP residual learning, with the benefit most pronounced when model updates are sparse, while remaining computationally feasible for real-time control.

title: Continual Enterprise World Model Discovery in Dynamic Systems
summary: In an enterprise system, updating one field can set another, create a record, or start an approval. These effects are produced by business rules that are not built into the platform but written by each organization and revised over time. An agent working in such a system cannot predict the result of its own actions without knowing these rules. We study continual enterprise world model discovery, where an agent starts without knowledge of these business rules and discovers them by interacting with records and observing the outcomes. From those observations it builds a world model, which it revises as the rules change. To evaluate this, we introduce EnterpriseWorldShift, built on a live ServiceNow environment with nine tables, 25 hidden rules and 600 evaluation actions. It presents four versions of the same enterprise world, with the tables and records held fixed while a rule is modified, then added, then removed, so that discovery, revision, extension and retirement are each tested in turn. Our Continual Discovery Agent (CDA) builds such a model and carries it from one world to the next. It predicts the effects of the hidden rules more accurately than looking them up for each question, the approach taken by prior work, by up to 8.98 IoU points, and it answers from its own model without querying the running system.

AI.tldr: This paper studies continual enterprise world model discovery: an agent with no prior knowledge of an organization's business rules interacts with records to discover them, builds a world model, and revises it as rules change. It introduces EnterpriseWorldShift (a live ServiceNow benchmark with nine tables, 25 hidden rules, 600 evaluation actions, and four world versions testing discovery, revision, extension, and retirement) and a Continual Discovery Agent (CDA) that carries its model across worlds, outperforming per-question lookup by up to 8.98 IoU points while answering from its own model without querying the running system.
AI.motivation: In enterprise systems, updating one field can trigger cascading effects (setting another field, creating a record, starting an approval) that are governed by organization-specific business rules not built into the platform and continuously revised. An agent cannot predict the outcome of its own actions without knowing these rules, and prior approaches that look rules up per question fail to capture and maintain such knowledge over time.
AI.method: The authors formalize continual enterprise world model discovery, where an agent starts with no knowledge of hidden business rules and learns them through interaction with records and observation of outcomes, then revises the resulting world model as rules change. They build EnterpriseWorldShift on a live ServiceNow environment with nine tables, 25 hidden rules, and 600 evaluation actions, spanning four versions of the same enterprise world: tables and records stay fixed while a rule is modified, then added, then removed, separately testing discovery, revision, extension, and retirement. Their Continual Discovery Agent (CDA) constructs a world model and carries it from one world to the next.
AI.result: CDA predicts the effects of hidden rules more accurately than the prior per-question lookup approach by up to 8.98 IoU points, and it answers from its own model without querying the running system.
AI.conclusion: Continual world model discovery is a viable and effective paradigm for agents operating in enterprise systems: maintaining and carrying a discovered model across changing rule regimes outperforms stateless per-question lookup and removes the need to query the live system at answer time.

title: From Rollout to Reset: A Graph-Based Harness for Autonomous Long-Horizon Manipulation Evaluation
summary: Robot manipulation policies are improving quickly, and real-robot evaluation remains the standard evidence for that progress. It still relies on a human to reset the scene between rollouts, which consumes operator time and leaves the initial state distribution unspecified, so results reproduce poorly. A recent system, AutoEval, automates both reset and scoring, but only for single-step tasks, because a long-horizon rollout can terminate in combinatorially many configurations that no single learned reset policy covers. We present HALTER, a Harness for Autonomous Long-horizon Task Evaluation and Reset, which restores the scene by planning over a library of learned atomic reset skills, so demonstration cost scales with the size of that library rather than with the number of terminal states. HALTER builds a spatial scene graph online from point clouds and vision foundation models, and an LLM reasons over this graph to score the rollout, plan the reset, and verify that the reset succeeded, without collecting labeled success images for any task. On four long-horizon tasks on a Franka arm, HALTER restores the scene in 76% of episodes, against 52% for AutoEval and 65% for a motion-planning reset, and it estimates the completed-skill fraction correctly in 90% of episodes, against 76%. Its reset-verification verdict is correct in 91% of episodes, compared with 78% for AutoEval. It also cuts the operator time of an evaluation campaign by 72% relative to manual reset. We further measure compositional generalization on three held-out tasks, where HALTER resets 74.7% of episodes against 1.3% for a per-task reset policy, and we ablate the scene representation and the graph update rate.

AI.tldr: HALTER is a harness for autonomous long-horizon task evaluation and reset that plans over a library of learned atomic reset skills, using an online spatial scene graph built from point clouds and vision foundation models that an LLM reasons over to score, plan, and verify resets without labeled success images.
AI.motivation: Real-robot evaluation of manipulation policies still depends on humans to reset scenes between rollouts, consuming operator time and leaving the initial state distribution unspecified, hurting reproducibility. AutoEval automates reset and scoring but only for single-step tasks, since long-horizon rollouts can terminate in combinatorially many configurations no single learned reset policy covers.
AI.method: HALTER restores the scene by planning over a library of learned atomic reset skills, so demonstration cost scales with library size rather than the number of terminal states. It builds a spatial scene graph online from point clouds and vision foundation models, and an LLM reasons over this graph to score the rollout, plan the reset, and verify reset success, without collecting labeled success images for any task.
AI.result: On four long-horizon tasks on a Franka arm, HALTER restores the scene in 76% of episodes versus 52% for AutoEval and 65% for a motion-planning reset; it estimates completed-skill fraction correctly in 90% versus 76% of episodes; its reset-verification verdict is correct in 91% versus 78% for AutoEval; and it cuts operator time by 72% relative to manual reset. On three held-out tasks, HALTER resets 74.7% of episodes versus 1.3% for a per-task reset policy.
AI.conclusion: HALTER enables fully autonomous long-horizon robot task evaluation and reset with strong restore, scoring, and verification accuracy, substantial operator-time savings, and markedly better compositional generalization than per-task reset policies; scene representation and graph update rate are ablated.

title: SIMLIFE: Pattern Understanding for Long-Horizon Human-Agent Partnership
comment: COLM 2026 Learning from Situated and Embodied Interaction Workshop
summary: Understanding humans over long horizons requires agents to infer not only what people need in the moment, but also how routines form, why they repeat, and when they change. We introduce SimLife, a scalable platform for simulating long-term household life with rich visual observations, ground-truth action logs, and synthetic dialogues with audio. Built on SimLife, SimLife-BP evaluates long-context pattern understanding: the ability to infer latent behavioral rules from weeks or months of everyday observations. The benchmark contains 106 episodes averaging 15.49 hours and 38.57 in-game days, and 1,439 question-answer pairs. Each task probes direct, counterfactual, noisy, and inverse reasoning under different levels of rule hints. Evaluating frontier models and architectures, we find that current models often achieve surface-level prediction without comprehensive rule understanding, rely on frequency-based heuristics rather than if-then reasoning over evidence, and struggle to adapt when behavioral patterns change. These findings suggest that long-context pattern understanding remains a major bottleneck for future embodied agents, while SimLife opens a broader space for studying memory, personalization, adaptation, and long-horizon planning in everyday human-AI interaction.

AI.tldr: SimLife is a scalable platform for simulating long-term household life with visual observations, action logs, and synthetic audio dialogues; SimLife-BP benchmarks long-context pattern understanding, revealing that frontier models rely on frequency-based heuristics rather than true if-then reasoning and fail to adapt when routines change.
AI.motivation: Understanding humans over long horizons requires agents to infer not only immediate needs but also how routines form, why they repeat, and when they change. Existing benchmarks do not adequately evaluate this long-context pattern understanding from weeks or months of everyday observations.
AI.method: The authors introduce SimLife, a scalable platform for simulating long-term household life with rich visual observations, ground-truth action logs, and synthetic dialogues with audio. Built on it, SimLife-BP evaluates long-context pattern understanding via 106 episodes averaging 15.49 hours and 38.57 in-game days, containing 1,439 QA pairs. Each task probes direct, counterfactual, noisy, and inverse reasoning under varying levels of rule hints. Frontier models and architectures are then evaluated.
AI.result: Current models often achieve surface-level prediction without comprehensive rule understanding, rely on frequency-based heuristics rather than if-then reasoning over evidence, and struggle to adapt when behavioral patterns change.
AI.conclusion: Long-context pattern understanding remains a major bottleneck for future embodied agents, while SimLife opens a broader space for studying memory, personalization, adaptation, and long-horizon planning in everyday human-AI interaction.

title: Predict Before You Deploy: Offline Prediction of Quantization-Induced Task Degradation for World Action Models
summary: World action models (WAMs) rely on video-generation backbones, requiring substantial memory and compute for deployment. Post-training quantization reduces memory and can accelerate inference, but bit width, grouping, and quantizer choice define a large configuration space. Identifying configurations that preserve task performance through exhaustive closed-loop evaluation is costly. We propose PreDE (Predict Before You Deploy), a policy-calibrated framework for predicting quantization-induced task degradation from offline action deviations. Using closed-loop outcomes from a small development set, PreDE calibrates two thresholds and accepts, rejects, or defers new configurations using a fixed observation log. Under a within-setting label-ordering hypothesis, the rule issues decisions where all thresholds consistent with the development labels agree. Across five WAMs and four benchmark settings, quantization produces configuration-dependent task losses that cannot be explained by bit width alone or a shared deviation threshold. Across 28 held-out configurations from two policies, PreDE issued 21 decisions before observing closed-loop outcomes (75% coverage), all matching the observed acceptable or degraded labels. Deferred candidates included both acceptable outcomes and a 33-percentage-point loss. In 450 Franka Research 3 trials across two independently fine-tuned policies, all configurations assigned to high-deviation groups before testing showed significant degradation, while low-deviation comparisons showed no statistically significant degradation. On the real robot, W4A4 achieved a 1.37x action-query speedup and approximately 44% lower peak memory. These results support policy-specific behavioral calibration for quantization configuration selection while identifying candidates that require closed-loop evaluation. The code is available at https://github.com/jiuyixu25/PreDE.

AI.tldr: PreDE predicts quantization-induced task degradation in World Action Models from offline action deviations, using policy-calibrated thresholds to accept, reject, or defer configurations before costly closed-loop evaluation.
AI.motivation: World action models based on video-generation backbones demand substantial memory and compute. Post-training quantization can reduce this burden, but bit width, grouping, and quantizer choices create a large configuration space, and exhaustively evaluating which configurations preserve task performance via closed-loop testing is prohibitively expensive.
AI.method: PreDE is a policy-calibrated framework that predicts quantization-induced task degradation from offline action deviations. Using closed-loop outcomes on a small development set, it calibrates two thresholds and then accepts, rejects, or defers new configurations based on a fixed observation log. Under a within-setting label-ordering hypothesis, decisions are issued only where all thresholds consistent with development labels agree.
AI.result: Across five WAMs and four benchmark settings, task losses were configuration-dependent and not explained by bit width alone or a shared deviation threshold. For 28 held-out configurations from two policies, PreDE issued 21 decisions before closed-loop outcomes (75% coverage), all matching observed acceptable/degraded labels; deferred cases included both acceptable outcomes and a 33-percentage-point loss. In 450 Franka Research 3 trials, high-deviation groups all showed significant degradation, while low-deviation comparisons showed none. On the real robot, W4A4 yielded 1.37x action-query speedup and ~44% lower peak memory.
AI.conclusion: Policy-specific behavioral calibration can support quantization configuration selection and identify candidates requiring closed-loop evaluation. Code is available at https://github.com/jiuyixu25/PreDE.

title: From Intent to Action: Benchmarking LLM Safety in Vehicle Voice Command Authorization
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into vehicle voice assistants. But linking natural-language requests to vehicle functions creates a safety-critical authorization problem. Before executing a command, the system must choose whether to execute, refuse, clarify, require confirmation, defer to manual control, trigger an emergency response, or make no tool call. To our knowledge, prior evaluations do not isolate this pre-action decision across speaker role, authentication status, vehicle state, and tool availability. We introduce a 202-scenario benchmark with Reference Decisions under a seven-class taxonomy. We evaluate two local open-weight models and three API-based LLMs using Decision Alignment and safety-specific error metrics. Alignment ranges from 40.1% for Llama 3.2 3B to 89.1% for Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview. The API-based models score between 83.2% and 89.1%, with no statistically significant differences among them. Even these models produce two to three False Executes among 161 non-execution scenarios, and persistent errors remain in confirmation and manual-control decisions. A controlled Llama 3.2 3B ablation increases alignment to 40.1% under the structured authorization policy, versus 28.2-29.2% under schema-only and generic-safety baselines, but it does not eliminate False Executes. Structured LLM decisions are therefore insufficient as a standalone safety mechanism, and deployment requires an independent enforcement layer that verifies tool permissions and vehicle-state constraints before invoking any vehicle function.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a 202-scenario benchmark with a seven-class reference-decision taxonomy to evaluate how LLMs in vehicle voice assistants decide among execute, refuse, clarify, confirm, defer-to-manual, emergency, or no-tool-call, finding that even top API models reach only 83.2-89.1% alignment and still produce occasional False Executes, so structured LLM decisions are insufficient as a standalone safety mechanism and require an independent enforcement layer.
AI.motivation: Integrating LLMs into vehicle voice assistants turns natural-language requests into a safety-critical authorization problem: before acting, the system must decide whether to execute, refuse, clarify, require confirmation, defer to manual control, trigger emergency response, or make no tool call. Prior evaluations do not isolate this pre-action decision across speaker role, authentication status, vehicle state, and tool availability.
AI.method: The authors build a 202-scenario benchmark with Reference Decisions under a seven-class taxonomy and evaluate two local open-weight models plus three API-based LLMs using Decision Alignment and safety-specific error metrics. They also run a controlled Llama 3.2 3B ablation comparing a structured authorization policy against schema-only and generic-safety baselines.
AI.result: Alignment ranges from 40.1% (Llama 3.2 3B) to 89.1% (Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview); API-based models score 83.2-89.1% with no statistically significant differences among them. Even these models yield two to three False Executes across 161 non-execution scenarios, with persistent confirmation and manual-control errors. The Llama 3.2 3B ablation reaches 40.1% under the structured authorization policy versus 28.2-29.2% for schema-only and generic-safety baselines, without eliminating False Executes.
AI.conclusion: Structured LLM decisions are insufficient as a standalone safety mechanism. Deployment requires an independent enforcement layer that verifies tool permissions and vehicle-state constraints before invoking any vehicle function.

title: From Wizard-of-Oz Human-Robot Dialogue Collection to a Taxonomy of Robot Response Decisions: A Retrospective Analysis of Assistive Pilot Interactions
comment: Accepted at the Human-Robot Dialogue (HRD) Workshop, held by the 2026 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS 2026)
summary: Robots that follow natural-language instructions in everyday indoor environments must act on incomplete human utterances. Instructions often omit essential information, such as the identity of an out-of-view object, an intended destination, or the user's goal. Existing datasets contain little real-world situated dialogue and provide few practice-grounded criteria for deciding when a robot should act, confirm, clarify, or refuse. We retrospectively analyze a pilot Wizard-of-Oz study in which five participants performed everyday indoor tasks, including door opening, drawer opening, feeding, drinking, and cleaning, with a wheelchair-mounted mobile manipulator while the wizard responded without a formal communication policy. This preserved authentic user behavior but produced inconsistent robot-side decisions, motivating an explicit decision scheme. From 40 episodes, we derived a hierarchical taxonomy of six response modes (ANSWER, REPORT_DONE, REFUSE, CONFIRM, CLARIFY, ACT) and four ambiguity types (intent, referential, spatial, intelligibility). Two human annotators and an AI annotator applied the scheme to the pilot data. Clean-label rates were 91% and 89%, and Cohen's ranged from 0.72 to 0.95 across decision-point, mode, and ambiguity levels for both human-human and human-AI comparisons. Fine-tuning LLaVA-1.6-7B on taxonomy-derived labels for ACT and CLARIFY indicates the feasibility of training vision-language models using annotations from our taxonomy. Remaining boundary cases in decision-point identification and REPORT_DONE motivate a constrained protocol for more consistent dialogue collection.

AI.tldr: A retrospective analysis of a Wizard-of-Oz study with a wheelchair-mounted manipulator yields a hierarchical taxonomy of six robot response modes and four ambiguity types; the scheme demonstrates high inter-annotator agreement (Cohen's κ 0.72–0.95) and supports fine-tuning LLaVA-1.6-7B for ACT and CLARIFY decisions.
AI.motivation: Robots following natural-language instructions in everyday indoor settings must act on incomplete human utterances that often omit essential information (out-of-view object identity, intended destination, user goal). Existing datasets contain little real-world situated dialogue and provide few practice-grounded criteria for deciding when a robot should act, confirm, clarify, or refuse.
AI.method: Retrospective analysis of a pilot Wizard-of-Oz study: five participants performed everyday indoor tasks (door opening, drawer opening, feeding, drinking, cleaning) with a wheelchair-mounted mobile manipulator while the wizard responded without a formal communication policy. From 40 episodes, the authors derived a hierarchical taxonomy of six response modes (ANSWER, REPORT_DONE, REFUSE, CONFIRM, CLARIFY, ACT) and four ambiguity types (intent, referential, spatial, intelligibility). Two human annotators and an AI annotator applied the scheme to the pilot data. LLaVA-1.6-7B was fine-tuned on taxonomy-derived labels for ACT and CLARIFY.
AI.result: Clean-label rates were 91% and 89%. Cohen's κ ranged from 0.72 to 0.95 across decision-point, mode, and ambiguity levels for both human-human and human-AI comparisons. Fine-tuning LLaVA-1.6-7B on taxonomy-derived labels for ACT and CLARIFY indicates the feasibility of training vision-language models using annotations from the taxonomy. Remaining boundary cases in decision-point identification and REPORT_DONE were observed.
AI.conclusion: Inconsistent robot-side decisions under an absent formal communication policy motivate an explicit decision scheme. The proposed taxonomy offers practice-grounded criteria for robot action, confirmation, clarification, or refusal, and its labels can train vision-language models. Remaining boundary cases motivate a constrained protocol for more consistent dialogue collection.

title: Reach or Solve? Attributing Agentic RL Gains with Checkpoint Handoffs
summary: Reinforcement learning now trains language-model agents that act over dozens of steps in live environments. The gains are large, and they are read as better decision-making. An agent in a closed loop writes its own inputs. Each observation follows from its own earlier actions, so the states it meets late in an episode are partly of its own making. An SFT checkpoint and an RL checkpoint are then scored from different states, even on identical tasks. Endpoint success mixes two changes: where the agent arrives, and what it does once it is there. Restricting the comparison to states both policies reach does not separate them. That restriction selects on an outcome, and in our data it flips the sign of the effect. We introduce checkpoint handoff, an evaluation protocol that clones a state one released checkpoint reached and hands it to another, with no retraining. Crossing a reacher role and a solver role over SFT and RL splits an endpoint gain into REACH and SOLVE. REACH is how often a policy arrives at a state the environment confirms is a fixed number of actions from success. SOLVE is how often it finishes from an identical cloned state. Across two benchmarks and two independently released pipelines, the reacher by solver interaction is positive in all five conditions. An RL history is worth more to an RL solver than the same history is to an SFT solver. On ALFWorld, RL improves both terms, and the SFT solver never succeeds where the RL solver fails. Independent REACH and SOLVE gaps predict the aggregate interaction. Handoff asks only that one checkpoint's history can be replayed under another, so long-horizon evaluation can report arrival and completion beside endpoint success.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces checkpoint handoff, an evaluation protocol that clones a state reached by one released checkpoint and hands it to another without retraining, thereby decomposing an agent's end-to-end RL gain into REACH (arriving at a state a fixed number of actions from success) and SOLVE (finishing from an identical cloned state).
AI.motivation: RL-trained language-model agents show large endpoint gains over SFT checkpoints, but these gains are naively read as better decision-making. Because an agent in a closed loop writes its own inputs, each observation follows from its own earlier actions, so late-episode states are partly self-generated. An SFT and an RL checkpoint are thus scored from different states even on identical tasks, and endpoint success conflates two distinct changes: where the agent arrives and what it does once there. Restricting comparison to states both policies reach fails to separate them, because that restriction selects on an outcome and, in the authors' data, even flips the sign of the effect.
AI.method: Checkpoint handoff: an evaluation protocol that clones a state one released checkpoint reached and hands it to another with no retraining. Crossing a reacher role and a solver role over SFT and RL splits an endpoint gain into REACH (how often a policy arrives at a state the environment confirms is a fixed number of actions from success) and SOLVE (how often it finishes from an identical cloned state).
AI.result: Across two benchmarks and two independently released pipelines, the reacher-by-solver interaction is positive in all five conditions: an RL history is worth more to an RL solver than the same history is to an SFT solver. On ALFWorld, RL improves both terms, and the SFT solver never succeeds where the RL solver fails. Independent REACH and SOLVE gaps predict the aggregate interaction.
AI.conclusion: Handoff requires only that one checkpoint's history can be replayed under another, so long-horizon evaluation can report arrival and completion alongside endpoint success.

title: Winning a Won Game: Strict Reach-Avoid-Stay Control Barrier Functions for High-Dimensional Black-Box Systems
comment: 9 pages, 2 figures. This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication
summary: Robots must complete their tasks and maintain the achieved outcomes while avoiding safety failures at all times. Strict reach-avoid-stay (sRAS) formalizes this requirement: safely reaching a target and remaining there indefinitely after first entry. We propose an sRAS Q-control barrier function (CBF) safety filter for high-dimensional black-box systems under bounded uncertainty. Our construction combines a stay value encoding safe permanent residence in a target subset with a reach-avoid value encoding safe reachability of this subset while avoiding target states from which safe permanent residence cannot be guaranteed. We prove that these values jointly yield a valid robust discrete-time CBF and lift them to state-action Q-functions for runtime intervention. For exact values and under a measure-zero condition, our filter preserves sRAS feasibility from almost every winnable initial state and keeps the system safely within the target after first entry, against all admissible uncertainty realizations. We adopt reachability-based adversarial reinforcement learning for scalable value approximation using only black-box interactions. Notably, neither synthesis nor deployment of our filter requires known dynamics, affine structure, value derivatives, or hand-designed barriers. We validate our framework in quadruped gap jumping in simulation and hardware, where the robot crosses the gap, lands safely, and remains safe afterward. Simulated F1TENTH races further demonstrate safe overtaking and lead retention.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces an sRAS Q-CBF safety filter for high-dimensional black-box systems under bounded uncertainty, combining stay and reach-avoid values to form a robust discrete-time CBF, learned via adversarial RL, and validated on quadruped gap jumping and F1TENTH racing.
AI.motivation: Robots must complete tasks while maintaining achieved outcomes and avoiding safety failures at all times. This is formalized as strict reach-avoid-stay (sRAS), requiring safely reaching a target and remaining there indefinitely after first entry. Existing safety filters typically do not jointly guarantee reaching, staying, and robust safety for black-box high-dimensional systems.
AI.method: The authors construct an sRAS Q-control barrier function (CBF) safety filter. The construction combines a stay value encoding safe permanent residence in a target subset with a reach-avoid value encoding safe reachability of this subset while avoiding target states from which safe permanent residence cannot be guaranteed. These values are proved to jointly yield a valid robust discrete-time CBF, then lifted to state-action Q-functions for runtime intervention. Reachability-based adversarial reinforcement learning is adopted for scalable value approximation using only black-box interactions, requiring no known dynamics, affine structure, value derivatives, or hand-designed barriers.
AI.result: For exact values and under a measure-zero condition, the filter preserves sRAS feasibility from almost every winnable initial state and keeps the system safely within the target after first entry, against all admissible uncertainty realizations. Validation in quadruped gap jumping in simulation and hardware shows the robot crosses the gap, lands safely, and remains safe afterward. Simulated F1TENTH races show safe overtaking and lead retention.
AI.conclusion: The proposed sRAS Q-CBF safety filter provides robust, scalable safety guarantees for high-dimensional black-box systems. It jointly ensures safe reachability and permanent safe residence without requiring dynamics knowledge, and is demonstrated in both hardware quadruped locomotion and simulated racing scenarios.

title: ScientistTwo: Pioneering the Human Knowledge Frontier with Autonomous AI
summary: Scientific discovery is defined by the ability to identify the boundaries of existing knowledge and venture into unexplored territory. The ultimate vision for AI in science is problem-driven autonomous research: given a fundamental challenge by a human expert, the AI independently navigates the scientific landscape, uncovers theoretical and empirical bottlenecks, and systematically expands the frontier of knowledge. In this paper, we introduce ScientistTwo, a fully autonomous multi-agent framework designed to realize this vision. Specifically, ScientistTwo takes an initial problem as input, establishes state-of-the-art baselines, formulates novel hypotheses, and coordinates specialized agents to orchestrate an end-to-end discovery cycle without human intervention. Moreover, the framework rigorously conducts experiments using diverse datasets and metrics, refines methodologies through automated ablation studies, and validates research findings via a closed-loop simulated peer-review rebuttal engine. To evaluate ScientistTwo's capabilities against the highest standards of human scientific achievement, we benchmark it across papers accepted at top-tier conferences such as ICLR, ICML, and NeurIPS. As a result, ScientistTwo autonomously generates expert-level, publishable papers and fully verified, executable codebases. Its solutions consistently outperform human state-of-the-art models, and achieve higher average review ratings than human-authored papers under automated AI review agents. These results show that ScientistTwo is not merely an assistive tool but an autonomous scientific pioneer capable of pushing the frontiers of human discovery. Project website: https://scientist-two.github.io/

AI.tldr: ScientistTwo is a fully autonomous multi-agent framework that takes a fundamental problem as input and independently produces expert-level, publishable papers with executable code, outperforming human state-of-the-art models.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to realize problem-driven autonomous research, where AI, given a fundamental challenge, independently navigates the scientific landscape, identifies theoretical and empirical bottlenecks, and systematically expands the frontier of knowledge without human intervention.
AI.method: ScientistTwo takes an initial problem, establishes state-of-the-art baselines, formulates novel hypotheses, and coordinates specialized agents to orchestrate an end-to-end discovery cycle. It conducts experiments across diverse datasets and metrics, refines methodologies via automated ablation studies, and validates findings through a closed-loop simulated peer-review rebuttal engine.
AI.result: Benchmarked against papers accepted at top-tier conferences (ICLR, ICML, NeurIPS), ScientistTwo autonomously generates expert-level, publishable papers and fully verified, executable codebases. Its solutions consistently outperform human state-of-the-art models and achieve higher average review ratings than human-authored papers under automated AI review agents.
AI.conclusion: ScientistTwo is not merely an assistive tool but an autonomous scientific pioneer capable of pushing the frontiers of human discovery.

title: GLAMDRING: Gait Learning And Morphology co-Design via Reinforcement LearnING of CPGs
summary: Robots are moving out of the structured factory floor and into unstructured environments such as disaster sites, planetary surfaces, and agricultural fields, for which the right robot often does not yet exist. We present GLAMDRING, a framework that synthesizes the optimal robot for a locomotion task and, jointly, learns the controller that drives it. For the given specifications of forward-velocity bounds, a per-actuator power budget, an actuator library, and a payload requirement, GLAMDRING returns a matched quadruped morphology (link geometry and per-joint actuators) and a Hopf-oscillator Central Pattern Generator (CPG) gait policy. We rank feasible designs against a target design objective, viz., maximum speed, minimum Cost of Transport (CoT), or max Payload Margin. Because body and locomotion are coupled, the optimal morphology dictates how a robot is driven, while optimal gait depends on the physical body. We train a small number of CPG policies by reinforcement learning across the space of candidate morphologies, co-learning the gait with the underlying robot hardware. Link lengths and actuators are then resolved post-hoc from the policy's logged operating envelope, reducing synthesis cost to a small, fixed number of reinforcement-learning runs instead of one per candidate. Our experiments show three key findings: co-designing body and gait is necessary to satisfy locomotion constraints; actuator-envelope feasibility, rather than locomotion success alone, determines realizable payload capacity; and canonical animal gaits emerge naturally in most designs from morphology and constraints alone. A real-world demonstration further highlights the efficacy of our work.

AI.tldr: GLAMDRING is a co-design framework that jointly synthesizes an optimal quadruped morphology and its locomotion controller for unstructured-terrain tasks, using a small fixed number of RL-trained Hopf-oscillator CPG policies and post-hoc resolution of link geometry and actuators.
AI.motivation: Robots are leaving structured factory floors for unstructured environments (disaster sites, planetary surfaces, agricultural fields), where an appropriate robot often does not yet exist. Body and locomotion are tightly coupled, so the optimal morphology dictates how a robot is driven and vice versa; designing them separately is insufficient.
AI.method: Given specifications—forward-velocity bounds, per-actuator power budget, actuator library, and payload requirement—GLAMDRING ranks feasible designs against a target objective (maximum speed, minimum Cost of Transport, or maximum Payload Margin). It trains a small number of Hopf-oscillator CPG gait policies via reinforcement learning across the space of candidate morphologies, co-learning gait with the underlying hardware, then resolves link lengths and actuators post-hoc from the policy's logged operating envelope.
AI.result: Three key findings: (1) co-designing body and gait is necessary to satisfy locomotion constraints; (2) actuator-envelope feasibility, rather than locomotion success alone, determines realizable payload capacity; (3) canonical animal gaits emerge naturally in most designs from morphology and constraints alone. A real-world demonstration further highlights the efficacy of the work.
AI.conclusion: By co-learning morphology and CPG-based gait policy, GLAMDRING reduces synthesis cost to a small, fixed number of reinforcement-learning runs instead of one per candidate design, yielding matched quadruped bodies and controllers that satisfy task specifications and transfer to real-world demonstration.

title: Replan, Repair, or Edit? A Unified Empirical Evaluation of Travel Agents for Itinerary Revision under Resource Disruptions
summary: Travel-planning agents generate itineraries that may become infeasible after acceptance because of flight cancellations, hotel unavailability, or attraction closures. Revising these itineraries involves full replanning, classical plan repair, and LLM-based travel-agent revision, whose differing task formulations and evaluation protocols hinder comparison. We conduct a systematic empirical study using two TREK-derived benchmark sets: 500 single-disruption cases, including feasible and infeasible instances, and 200 feasible simultaneous compound-disruption cases. We compare LLM-Z3 full replanning, IPyHOPPER hierarchical repair, and an iTIMO local-revision adapter across effectiveness, plan stability, and computational cost. LLM-Z3 with Gemini achieved the highest observed compound-disruption success. IPyHOPPER nearly matched that configuration's single-disruption overall success, while preserving substantially more of the accepted itinerary on successful repairs. Successful hierarchical and local repairs made fewer edits and retained more accepted commitments than full replanning. Computational profiles differed: IPyHOPPER used no LLM inference, the evaluated LLM-Z3 adapter used compact one-call inference, and the iTIMO adapter consumed substantially more tokens. The study provides practical guidelines for balancing feasibility recovery, commitment preservation, and computational cost within evaluated settings.

AI.tldr: This empirical study benchmarks three itinerary-revision approaches—LLM-Z3 full replanning, IPyHOPPER hierarchical repair, and an iTIMO local-revision adapter—on TREK-derived benchmarks (500 single-disruption and 200 compound-disruption cases), comparing success, plan stability, and computational cost.
AI.motivation: Accepted travel itineraries can become infeasible due to flight cancellations, hotel unavailability, or attraction closures. Existing revision approaches—full replanning, classical plan repair, and LLM-based travel-agent revision—use differing task formulations and evaluation protocols, which prevents fair comparison.
AI.method: A systematic empirical study using two TREK-derived benchmark sets: 500 single-disruption cases (feasible and infeasible) and 200 feasible simultaneous compound-disruption cases. The study compares LLM-Z3 full replanning, IPyHOPPER hierarchical repair, and an iTIMO local-revision adapter across three dimensions: effectiveness, plan stability, and computational cost.
AI.result: LLM-Z3 with Gemini achieved the highest compound-disruption success. IPyHOPPER nearly matched that configuration's single-disruption overall success while preserving substantially more of the accepted itinerary on successful repairs. Successful hierarchical and local repairs made fewer edits and retained more accepted commitments than full replanning. Computational profiles differed: IPyHOPPER used no LLM inference, LLM-Z3 used compact one-call inference, and iTIMO consumed substantially more tokens.
AI.conclusion: The study provides practical guidelines for balancing feasibility recovery, commitment preservation, and computational cost within the evaluated settings, offering a unified comparison of replanning, hierarchical repair, and local-revision approaches for travel itinerary disruption recovery.

title: Pose-aware Legged Robot Semantic Exploration with Omnidirectional Perception in Confined Unknown Environments
summary: Semantic exploration in confined environments requires both environment mapping and detailed observation of target objects. For ground robots, limited sensor vertical fields of view and restricted standoff distances can leave upper object surfaces unobserved from planar viewpoints. Body tilting can improve coverage, but additional observations and posture transitions increase mission time. To address this trade-off, we present POSE, a pose-aware semantic exploration system that exploits a legged robot's intrinsic body pitch and roll with omnidirectional camera-LiDAR perception. The proposed pose-aware viewpoint sampling module selects body postures from partial object maps according to expected coverage gain, while aim-aligned execution reduces unnecessary body reorientation.
