Further, we introduce an object-centric viewpoint pruning strategy assisted by a vision-language model (VLM), which uses persistent observation history and bird's-eye-view (BEV) maps to reduce redundant inspection visits. The resulting semantic viewpoints are combined with geometric exploration viewpoints in a global exploration planner. Simulations show that POSE improves final target-surface coverage by 8-10 percentage points over the planar planning baseline while reducing exploration time by 17-32%, and achieves the highest mean object coverage AUC among the evaluated baselines. Real-world experiments with a legged robot carrying an omnidirectional camera-LiDAR suite in a machine shop further demonstrate the system's applicability. These results support adaptive body-posture planning for improving the coverage-efficiency trade-off in legged robot semantic exploration. We plan to release the code for community benefit in the future.

AI.tldr: POSE is a pose-aware semantic exploration system for legged robots that leverages intrinsic body pitch/roll and omnidirectional camera-LiDAR perception to balance target object coverage and exploration efficiency in confined environments.
AI.motivation: In confined environments, ground robots with limited sensor vertical field of view and restricted standoff distance cannot observe upper surfaces of target objects from planar viewpoints. Body tilting can improve coverage, but the extra observations and posture transitions increase mission time, creating a coverage-efficiency trade-off.
AI.method: POSE combines three components: (1) a pose-aware viewpoint sampling module selecting body postures from partial object maps based on expected coverage gain; (2) aim-aligned execution to reduce unnecessary body reorientation; and (3) an object-centric viewpoint pruning strategy using a vision-language model (VLM) with persistent observation history and bird's-eye-view (BEV) maps to reduce redundant inspection visits. Semantic viewpoints are integrated with geometric exploration viewpoints in a global exploration planner.
AI.result: Simulations show POSE improves final target-surface coverage by 8-10 percentage points over a planar planning baseline, reduces exploration time by 17-32%, and achieves the highest mean object coverage AUC among baselines. Real-world experiments with a legged robot carrying an omnidirectional camera-LiDAR suite in a machine shop validate applicability.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive body-posture planning effectively improves the coverage-efficiency trade-off in legged robot semantic exploration. Code is planned for future release.

title: When2Think: Learning Difficulty-Aware Length Control for Efficient Hybrid Reasoning Models
summary: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) achieve strong performance on complex tasks but exhibit systematic inefficiency: they often overthink easy problems and underthink hard ones. Existing approaches based on uniform length penalties or rigid routing incur an efficiency tax, trading reduced computation on easy instances for accuracy loss on hard instances. We formulate efficient reasoning as an instance-adaptive computation allocation problem and propose When2Think, a post-training framework for hybrid reasoning that dynamically allocates computation based on problem difficulty. Our method introduces Instance-level Difficulty-Aware Control (IDAC), a reward-shaping mechanism that leverages pre-computed reference statistics (accuracy and token usage) to regulate reasoning depth. Combined with verifier-based rewards and batch-wise standardized advantages, IDAC enables stable critic-free optimization without learned reward models or online reference-model queries. When2Think encourages direct answering on easy instances while preserving extended reasoning on hard instances, thereby learning when to use System 1 (NoThink) versus System 2 (Think). Experiments on mathematical benchmarks demonstrate improved accuracy-efficiency trade-offs: on AIME24, Pass@3 increases by 10.0% while token usage is reduced by 27.9% relative to the base model, and on AIME25, When2Think achieves 40.0% Pass@3, outperforming compression and routing-only baselines.

AI.tldr: When2Think is a post-training framework for hybrid reasoning that allocates computation adaptively per instance, improving accuracy-efficiency trade-offs on math benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Large Reasoning Models suffer systematic inefficiency: they overthink easy problems and underthink hard ones. Existing uniform length penalties or rigid routing trade accuracy on hard instances for reduced computation on easy ones, imposing an "efficiency tax."
AI.method: The paper formulates efficient reasoning as an instance-adaptive computation allocation problem. It proposes When2Think, which introduces Instance-level Difficulty-Aware Control (IDAC), a reward-shaping mechanism using pre-computed reference statistics (accuracy and token usage) to regulate reasoning depth. Combined with verifier-based rewards and batch-wise standardized advantages, IDAC enables stable critic-free optimization without learned reward models or online reference-model queries, learning when to use System 1 (NoThink) vs System 2 (Think).
AI.result: On AIME24, Pass@3 increases by 10.0% while token usage drops 27.9% versus the base model; on AIME25, it achieves 40.0% Pass@3, outperforming compression and routing-only baselines.
AI.conclusion: When2Think improves accuracy-efficiency trade-offs by encouraging direct answering on easy instances while preserving extended reasoning on hard ones, demonstrating effective instance-adaptive computation allocation.

title: FASA: Feedback-Aware Sampling Adaptation for Efficient Diffusion-Based VLA Models
comment: Accepted by the 18th International Conference on Networking, Architecture, and Storage (NAS 2026)
summary: Diffusion-based Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models achieve strong performance in embodied tasks, but their iterative sampling imposes heavy computational and memory-access cost, blocking real-time deployment on edge platforms. Existing acceleration methods either require expensive training (e.g., distillation, flow matching) or degrade perception via statically scheduled pruning and caching, ignoring the dynamic workload variance of robotic interactions. This paper presents FASA (Feedback-Aware Sampling Adaptation), a training-free runtime framework that treats real-time multimodal feedback as a control signal for the denoising pipeline: an interaction-driven range adaptor modulates the global sampling-step budget based on visual and gripper-force feedback, and a proprioception-aware step adaptor pinpoints the optimized step within the adapted range. This co-designed framework allows the underlying hardware architecture to adaptively match the workload demands of different execution phases. Comparative evaluations across several benchmarks show that the inference speed can be increased by up to 1.45$\times$ while maintaining competitive success rates, providing a novel dynamic runtime architecture paradigm for deploying heavy generative embodied AI workloads onto resource-constrained computing platforms.

AI.tldr: FASA is a training-free runtime framework that accelerates Diffusion-based Vision-Language-Action models by using multimodal feedback to dynamically adapt the denoising sampling budget, achieving up to 1.45x inference speedup on edge platforms.
AI.motivation: Diffusion-based VLA models perform well in embodied tasks but suffer from heavy computational and memory-access costs due to iterative sampling, blocking real-time edge deployment. Existing acceleration methods are either training-expensive (distillation, flow matching) or degrade perception via statically scheduled pruning and caching that ignore the dynamic workload variance of robotic interactions.
AI.method: FASA (Feedback-Aware Sampling Adaptation) is a training-free runtime framework treating real-time multimodal feedback as a control signal for the denoising pipeline. It comprises an interaction-driven range adaptor that modulates the global sampling-step budget based on visual and gripper-force feedback, and a proprioception-aware step adaptor that pinpoints the optimized step within the adapted range, allowing hardware architecture to adaptively match workload demands across execution phases.
AI.result: Comparative evaluations across several benchmarks show inference speed can be increased by up to 1.45x while maintaining competitive success rates.
AI.conclusion: FASA provides a novel dynamic runtime architecture paradigm for deploying heavy generative embodied AI workloads onto resource-constrained computing platforms.

title: FINSKILLOPS: A Self-Evolving Multi-Agent System for SEC Filing QA
summary: Financial QA systems are typically improved before deployment through better retrieval, prompting, or agent coordination, leaving their reliability behavior fixed thereafter. In practice, new SEC-filing questions repeatedly expose heterogeneous errors in period, entity, evidence use, and calculation. Existing self-improvement methods can turn failures into new behaviors, but offer limited control over where a correction should apply or which previously correct answers it may break. We therefore frame post-deployment improvement as controlled behavioral maintenance: recurring failures should become scoped skill patches, and each patch should earn deployment with- out introducing regressions. We instantiate this view in FINSKILLOPS, a multi-agent system for SEC filing QA. FINSKILLOPS derives reusable skills from evidence-grounded, typed failure diagnoses and governs them through targeted validation, protected-case regression checks, negative controls, and versioned replacement or retirement. Across six financial QA benchmarks, a single frozen skill registry achieves the highest verdict-weighted correctness and reference consistency among the evaluated systems. Evolved skills raise correctness from 3.70 to 4.55 on our enhanced benchmark. In a separate 12-round operational study, only six of 33 proposed skills are promoted, while the monitoring non-correct rate falls from 20.0% to 12.5%. These results establish controlled skill scope, admission, and lifecycle management as the foundation for reliable self-improvement.

AI.tldr: The paper reframes post-deployment improvement of financial QA systems as controlled behavioral maintenance, where recurring failures become scoped skill patches that must pass validation and regression checks before deployment. The proposed multi-agent system FINSKILLOPS, built on evidence-grounded typed failure diagnoses and a frozen skill registry, achieves the highest verdict-weighted correctness and reference consistency across six financial QA benchmarks, raising correctness from 3.70 to 4.55, while its 12-round operational study promotes only 6 of 33 proposed skills and reduces the monitoring non-correct rate from 20.0% to 12.5%.
AI.motivation: Financial QA systems are typically improved before deployment via better retrieval, prompting, or agent coordination, leaving their reliability behavior fixed afterward. In practice, new SEC-filing questions repeatedly expose heterogeneous errors in period, entity, evidence use, and calculation. Existing self-improvement methods can turn failures into new behaviors but offer limited control over where a correction applies or which previously correct answers it may break.
AI.method: The paper frames post-deployment improvement as controlled behavioral maintenance, requiring recurring failures to become scoped skill patches and each patch to earn deployment without introducing regressions. This is instantiated in FINSKILLOPS, a multi-agent SEC filing QA system that derives reusable skills from evidence-grounded, typed failure diagnoses and governs them through targeted validation, protected-case regression checks, negative controls, and versioned replacement or retirement.
AI.result: Across six financial QA benchmarks, a single frozen skill registry achieves the highest verdict-weighted correctness and reference consistency among evaluated systems. Evolved skills raise correctness from 3.70 to 4.55 on the enhanced benchmark. In a separate 12-round operational study, only six of 33 proposed skills are promoted, while the monitoring non-correct rate falls from 20.0% to 12.5%.
AI.conclusion: The results establish controlled skill scope, admission, and lifecycle management as the foundation for reliable self-improvement in financial QA systems.

title: Self-excited actuation enables adaptive and resilient flapping-wing flight
summary: The muscles that power insect flight fall into one of two categories: 1) synchronous muscles that contract under direct control from the nervous system, and 2) asynchronous muscles which have an intrinsic stretch activation response that spontaneously generates wingbeats without the need for signaling from the brain. It is thought that the emergent nature of asynchronous wingbeats provides both adaptive and responsive capabilities for flight control. To date, most flying robots use synchronous actuation. In this paper we develop the first flight-capable flapping wing robot that uses asynchronous actuation. We demonstrate that asynchronous actuation allows wings to respond to changes in the resonant mechanics of the body without control input, and wings can react instantaneously to collisions with obstacles with no extrinsic sensing needed. Flight tests within cluttered environments demonstrate that asynchronous actuation significantly improves stability and performance when compared to synchronous actuation. In total this work demonstrates that a flapping wing robot actuation strategy that emulates the asynchronous muscles of flying insects can provide fast, reactive actuation responses before a control system would need to intervene. This partitioning of embodied control to both the low-level actuation dynamics and and high-level sensorimotor system provides a compelling blueprint for new flying robots.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the first flight-capable flapping wing robot using asynchronous actuation, whose intrinsic stretch-activation enables instantaneous, sensor-free responses to resonant changes and collisions, improving stability and performance in cluttered environments versus synchronous actuation.
AI.motivation: Insect flight muscles are either synchronous (neurally controlled) or asynchronous (self-oscillating via intrinsic stretch activation). The emergent nature of asynchronous wingbeats is hypothesized to provide adaptive and responsive flight-control capabilities. However, most flying robots rely on synchronous actuation, leaving this bio-inspired strategy unexploited in flight-capable hardware.
AI.method: The authors developed a flight-capable flapping wing robot that employs asynchronous actuation, emulating the stretch-activation response of asynchronous insect flight muscles, and conducted flight tests in cluttered environments to compare asynchronous against synchronous actuation.
AI.result: Asynchronous actuation let the wings respond to changes in the body's resonant mechanics without control input and react instantaneously to collisions with obstacles without any extrinsic sensing. In cluttered-environment flight tests, it significantly improved stability and performance relative to synchronous actuation.
AI.conclusion: An actuation strategy emulating asynchronous insect flight muscles provides fast, reactive responses before a control system would need to intervene. Partitioning embodied control between low-level actuation dynamics and a high-level sensorimotor system offers a compelling blueprint for new flying robots.

title: LearnActCoder: Role-Aware Error Memory for Adaptive Clinical Coding Agents
summary: Clinical coding agents repeatedly encounter the same failure modes, including unsupported codes, missed documented conditions, specificity errors, and procedure-coding convention mismatches. We introduce Learn-Then-Act, an inference-time adaptation framework that converts errors from a small labeled LEARN batch into a structured Mistake Knowledge Database (MistakeKDB). False-negative lessons are routed to a recall-oriented Coder, while false-positive lessons are routed to a precision-oriented Judge. We instantiate the framework in LearnActCoder, a Coder-Judge clinical coding pipeline with lookup-table grounding where available. On 150 matched MIMIC-III notes, structured MistakeKDB improves CPT F1 by 5.9 percentage points, while raw-example and reflection-style memories remain near the no-memory baseline; the ICD-9 improvement is not significant. On a matched MIMIC-IV cohort, memory shifts ICD-10 coding toward higher precision at a recall cost, leaving F1 statistically unchanged. Applying the same memory to 1,000 held-out MIMIC-III notes maintains a stable ICD operating point, providing scale/stability evidence. Overall, the results are consistent with structured, feedback-derived error memory being useful for adapting clinical coding behavior across cases without weight updates or changes to the underlying workflow. Absolute CPT/HCPCS performance remains low, and the system is evaluated retrospectively rather than in clinical deployment.

AI.tldr: Learn-Then-Act adapts clinical coding agents at inference time by converting errors from a small labeled batch into a structured Mistake Knowledge Database that routes false negatives to a Coder and false positives to a Judge, yielding a 5.9-point CPT F1 gain on MIMIC-III.
AI.motivation: Clinical coding agents suffer recurring failure modes: unsupported codes, missed documented conditions, specificity errors, and procedure-coding convention mismatches. The paper seeks a way to adapt coding behavior to these recurring errors without weight updates or workflow changes.
AI.method: Learn-Then-Act is an inference-time adaptation framework that distills errors from a small labeled LEARN batch into a structured Mistake Knowledge Database. False-negative lessons route to a recall-oriented Coder; false-positive lessons route to a precision-oriented Judge. It is instantiated as LearnActCoder, a Coder-Judge pipeline with lookup-table grounding where available.
AI.result: On 150 matched MIMIC-III notes, the structured MistakeKDB raises CPT F1 by 5.9 points, whereas raw-example and reflection-style memories stay near the no-memory baseline; ICD-9 gains are non-significant. On a matched MIMIC-IV cohort, memory shifts ICD-10 coding toward higher precision at a recall cost, leaving F1 statistically unchanged. Applying the memory to 1,000 held-out MIMIC-III notes preserves a stable ICD operating point, giving scale/stability evidence.
AI.conclusion: Structured, feedback-derived error memory appears useful for adapting clinical coding behavior across cases without weight updates or workflow changes, though absolute CPT/HCPCS performance remains low and evaluation is retrospective rather than deployment-based.

title: PIVOT: Perception-aware Independent Viewpoint Online Optimization
comment: 9 pages, 9 figures, 3 tables. Yuyang Chen and Shekoufeh Sadeghi contributed equally to this work. Submitted to IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters (RA-L)
summary: A fundamental assumption in robotic perception is that the sensor's field of view (FoV) is fixed relative to the robot body. Motion-decoupled sensors, such as gimbal-mounted cameras and MEMS-based LiDARs, instead allow sensing direction to be controlled independently at runtime. This freedom creates a computational challenge: efficiently selecting useful viewing directions online in feature-dense environments. We propose PIVOT, a lightweight iterative method that optimizes sensor viewing direction along a fixed translation trajectory to maximize feature visibility. Under a conical FoV model, visibility depends only on the optical axis, yielding a two-degree-of-freedom optimization on the viewing sphere $S^2$. Coordinate-free $SO(3)$ exponential-map updates enable efficient continuous optimization without explicit angular parameterizations or exhaustive viewing-sphere search. Monte Carlo evaluations retain 98.1--99.6% of brute-force visibility with a 76--85x speedup. Photorealistic simulation and real-world experiments further demonstrate improved visual localization robustness and practical viewpoint control on a quadruped robot.

AI.tldr: PIVOT is a lightweight iterative method that optimizes the viewing direction of motion-decoupled sensors along a translation trajectory to maximize feature visibility, using coordinate-free SO(3) updates on the viewing sphere S^2.
AI.motivation: Robotic perception typically assumes fixed sensor FoV relative to the robot body, but motion-decoupled sensors (gimbal cameras, MEMS LiDARs) can control sensing direction at runtime. This freedom creates a computational challenge: efficiently selecting useful viewing directions online in feature-dense environments, which existing approaches handle poorly due to parameterization and search inefficiency.
AI.method: Under a conical FoV model, visibility depends only on the optical axis, reducing the problem to a two-degree-of-freedom optimization on the viewing sphere S^2. Coordinate-free SO(3) exponential-map updates are used for efficient continuous optimization, avoiding explicit angular parameterizations or exhaustive viewing-sphere search.
AI.result: Monte Carlo evaluations retain 98.1–99.6% of brute-force visibility while achieving a 76–85x speedup. Photorealistic simulation and real-world experiments show improved visual localization robustness and practical viewpoint control on a quadruped robot.
AI.conclusion: PIVOT provides an efficient, parameterization-free solution for online viewing-direction optimization of motion-decoupled sensors, validated in simulation and on real hardware with strong robustness and speed improvements.

title: AutoData: Agentic Search for Pre-training Data Selection
summary: LLM agents have recently shown promise in automating machine learning engineering by editing model and training code under execution feedback. Data, however, remains largely outside this agentic optimisation loop. We frame pre-training data selection as heuristic engineering over per-document features, i.e., lexical statistics, categorical labels, and perplexity. We introduce AutoData, an agent that searches directly over executable selection algorithms. Unlike prior data mixture methods that optimise weights over a fixed set of domains, AutoData searches a richer program space of scoring, stratification, and stochastic selection rules, discovering feature interactions automatically by iteratively refining algorithms with validation feedback from a proxy model. Within an overnight search, AutoData discovers a selection algorithm that outperforms existing human-designed curation pipelines. Despite being searched only on this small proxy, the discovered recipe transfers to larger scales and improves the downstream metric CORE. These results suggest that data engineering can be treated as an agentic machine learning problem, extending autonomous research from model and training-code optimization to the data.

AI.tldr: AutoData frames pre-training data selection as heuristic engineering over per-document features and uses an LLM agent to search executable selection algorithms, discovering a recipe that outperforms human-designed curation pipelines and transfers to larger scales.
AI.motivation: Prior LLM agents automate machine learning engineering by editing model and training code under execution feedback, but data remains largely outside this agentic optimisation loop. Existing data mixture methods only optimise weights over a fixed set of domains, leaving a richer space of selection rules unexplored. The authors aim to extend autonomous research from model and training-code optimization to the data itself.
AI.method: The authors frame pre-training data selection as heuristic engineering over per-document features (lexical statistics, categorical labels, and perplexity). They introduce AutoData, an agent that searches directly over executable selection algorithms, covering a richer program space of scoring, stratification, and stochastic selection rules. Feature interactions are discovered automatically by iteratively refining algorithms using validation feedback from a proxy model.
AI.result: Within an overnight search, AutoData discovers a selection algorithm that outperforms existing human-designed curation pipelines. Although searched only on a small proxy, the discovered recipe transfers to larger scales and improves the downstream metric CORE.
AI.conclusion: Data engineering can be treated as an agentic machine learning problem, extending autonomous research from model and training-code optimization to the data.

title: CoreSense: Traceable Failure Recall and Conflict-Aware Belief Gating for Auditable Robot Decisions
summary: Robots can recall prior failures without knowing whether recalled evidence remains valid, conflicts with current observations, or is sufficient to guide a decision. We present CoreSense, a robot-system integration architecture that combines traceable episodic evidence with a conflict-aware belief gate and bounded, auditable recommendations. The gate checks scope, provenance, time, contradiction, and support before it permits PROCEED, requests re-observation, abstains, or escalates. Evaluation follows three complementary layers without commanding a physical robot: offline public real-robot data, a frozen signal-level simulation, and a live cloud deployment path. On CableTrace-120 and BotFails-200, belief gating reduces protocol-defined unsafe proceeds from 20% and 40% to 0%. A disjointly calibrated raw-video policy also reaches 0% unsafe proceed, but overblocks every nominal episode. On public data, a ViFailback-BotFails visual detector reaches 0.778 AUROC yet remains all-blocking, whereas cycle-disjoint UR3 telemetry for protective stops yields 0% unsafe proceed, 36.1% overblocking, and 61.9% coverage; grip-loss transfer remains a negative result. Controlled physical corroboration yields 3.3%, 0%, and 42.0%, while conflict-aware fusion yields 4.7%, 0%, and 42.8%. Finally, 20/20 cloud recalls validate a CockroachDB Cloud-Amazon Bedrock deployment path. The evidence supports an auditable integration pattern, not autonomous recovery or certified safety.

AI.tldr: CoreSense is a robot-system integration architecture that couples traceable episodic evidence with a conflict-aware belief gate, showing 0% unsafe proceeds on benchmark and telemetry tasks while remaining a pattern for auditable integration rather than certified safety.
AI.motivation: Robots can recall prior failures but cannot tell whether the recalled evidence is still valid, conflicts with current observations, or is sufficient to guide a decision; an integration mechanism is needed to gate such evidence before action.
AI.method: CoreSense combines traceable episodic evidence with a conflict-aware belief gate that checks scope, provenance, time, contradiction, and support before permitting PROCEED, requesting re-observation, abstaining, or escalating, plus bounded auditable recommendations. Evaluation uses three layers without commanding a physical robot: offline public real-robot data, a frozen signal-level simulation, and a live cloud deployment path.
AI.result: Belief gating cuts protocol-defined unsafe proceeds from 20% and 40% to 0% on CableTrace-120 and BotFails-200; a raw-video policy also reaches 0% but overblocks all nominal episodes. On public data, ViFailback-BotFails reaches 0.778 AUROC but stays all-blocking, while cycle-disjoint UR3 telemetry for protective stops gives 0% unsafe proceed, 36.1% overblocking, and 61.9% coverage, with grip-loss transfer a negative result. Controlled physical corroboration gives 3.3%, 0%, 42.0%; conflict-aware fusion gives 4.7%, 0%, 42.8%. 20/20 cloud recalls validate a CockroachDB Cloud-Amazon Bedrock deployment path.
AI.conclusion: The evidence supports an auditable integration pattern, not autonomous recovery or certified safety.

title: Rethinking Multi-Agent Collaboration: When More Is Less
summary: The rapid advancement of large language models and single-agent harnesses has reshaped the landscape of autonomous systems, raising a critical question of when multi-agent collaboration offers genuine value. As individual agent capabilities continue to scale, multi-agent collaboration faces diminishing returns while incurring growing context overhead. Through systematic analysis, we delineate the capability boundaries of multi-agent collaboration relative to single-agent alternatives, showing that it confers systematic benefits specifically in long-horizon tasks with sparse dependencies, while single-agent harnesses remain superior in tightly coupled, sequential workflows. Building on these insights, we propose SAIGE, a lightweight multi-agent collaboration mechanism based on Semantic-Aware Incremental Graph Evolution. SAIGE models collaboration as a dynamically evolving graph, where nodes are agent instances spawned on demand and edges encode semantic dependencies established through content-based information retrieval. Experiments on long-horizon, complex task benchmarks show that SAIGE achieves a favorable trade-off between context efficiency and task performance, and that scaling the agent pool or deepening the recursion level does not consistently improve outcomes. Our findings suggest that multi-agent superiority is bounded by task structure rather than universal, and that more agents do not necessarily make a system more intelligent.

AI.tldr: Multi-agent collaboration only helps for long-horizon, sparsely-dependent tasks; the authors propose SAIGE, a semantic-aware incremental graph evolution mechanism that dynamically spawns agents and links them by content-based retrieval.
AI.motivation: As LLMs and single-agent harnesses scale, the marginal value of multi-agent collaboration is unclear while context overhead grows. The paper asks when multi-agent collaboration genuinely benefits over single-agent alternatives.
AI.method: Systematic analysis delineates capability boundaries between multi-agent collaboration and single-agent harnesses. Based on these insights, SAIGE models collaboration as a dynamically evolving graph: nodes are agent instances spawned on demand; edges encode semantic dependencies established via content-based information retrieval.
AI.result: On long-horizon, complex task benchmarks, SAIGE achieves a favorable trade-off between context efficiency and task performance. Scaling the agent pool or deepening recursion does not consistently improve outcomes.
AI.conclusion: Multi-agent superiority is bounded by task structure rather than universal: it benefits long-horizon, sparsely-dependent tasks, while single agents remain superior in tightly coupled, sequential workflows. More agents do not necessarily make a system more intelligent.

title: AURORA: A Natural Language-Driven Agentic Framework for Understanding, Reasoning, and Orchestrating Reliable Air-Ground Co-Simulation
summary: Air-ground transportation research increasingly relies on co-simulation, yet constructing scenarios remains labor-intensive and difficult to validate. More importantly, a generated scenario may execute successfully while failing to realize the spatial, temporal, communication, or behavioral relationships requested by the user. This paper presents AURORA, a natural-language-driven agentic framework that treats air-ground scenario generation as a process of compilation with verification. Central to AURORA is the Air-Ground Scenario Graph (AGSG), a typed intermediate representation that explicitly connects agents, aerial missions, events, communication links, success conditions, and their cross-domain dependencies. This shared representation enables simulator-grounded parsing, joint road-airspace grounding, temporal planning, pre-execution feasibility checking, trace-based runtime verification, failure localization, and bounded repair within a unified workflow. We further introduce AURORA-Bench to evaluate not only whether generated scenarios execute, but whether they faithfully realize the requested interactions. Experiments across multiple language models show that structured execution substantially improves reliability, while runtime verification exposes silent failures that completion-based evaluation overlooks. Localized repair further resolves many violations without regenerating the entire scenario. The results show that reliable scenario generation requires verifying realized behavior, not merely executable code, and demonstrate the value of explicit intermediate representations for verifiable and repairable language-driven co-simulation.

AI.tldr: AURORA is a natural-language-driven agentic framework that treats air-ground co-simulation scenario generation as compilation with verification, using a typed intermediate representation (AGSG) to enable grounded parsing, feasibility checking, runtime verification, and bounded repair.
AI.motivation: Air-ground transportation research increasingly relies on co-simulation, but constructing scenarios is labor-intensive and hard to validate. A generated scenario may execute successfully yet fail to realize the spatial, temporal, communication, or behavioral relationships the user requested—i.e., silent failures that executable-code evaluation misses.
AI.method: The framework centers on the Air-Ground Scenario Graph (AGSG), a typed intermediate representation explicitly linking agents, aerial missions, events, communication links, success conditions, and cross-domain dependencies. This shared representation supports simulator-grounded parsing, joint road-airspace grounding, temporal planning, pre-execution feasibility checking, trace-based runtime verification, failure localization, and bounded repair in a unified workflow. The authors also introduce AURORA-Bench to assess whether generated scenarios faithfully realize requested interactions, not merely whether they execute.
AI.result: Across multiple language models, structured execution substantially improves reliability; runtime verification exposes silent failures that completion-based evaluation overlooks; and localized repair resolves many violations without regenerating the entire scenario.
AI.conclusion: Reliable scenario generation requires verifying realized behavior rather than merely executable code, and explicit intermediate representations are valuable for verifiable and repairable language-driven co-simulation.

title: TorchCraft: Unified binder design by inverting an all-atom structure predictor
summary: All-atom structure predictors model diverse molecular interactions, but using their learned structural priors for binder design remains challenging. Here we present TorchCraft, a unified binder-design framework that optimizes sequence logits through a frozen all-atom predictor. Implemented in TorchFold, TorchCraft combines confidence, contact, geometric, and sequence-prior objectives within a shared optimization procedure for minibinders, framework-conditioned VHHs, cyclic peptides, and ligand-binding proteins. Using pretrained AlphaFold 3 weights, TorchCraft generated representative minibinders and VHHs with experimentally measured binding across four targets in each format, without post hoc sequence redesign. Computational benchmarks further demonstrated the framework's applicability to cyclic peptides and ligand-conditioned pocket design. TorchCraft extends predictor inversion to multiple binder formats and molecular contexts, providing a common framework for reusing all-atom structural priors in design.

AI.tldr: TorchCraft is a unified binder-design framework that inverts a frozen all-atom structure predictor (AlphaFold 3) by optimizing sequence logits with combined confidence, contact, geometric, and sequence-prior objectives, yielding experimentally validated minibinders and VHHs across multiple targets.
AI.motivation: All-atom structure predictors capture diverse molecular interactions, but exploiting their learned structural priors for binder design remains challenging; existing approaches are limited in the range of binder formats and molecular contexts they can handle.
AI.method: TorchCraft, implemented in TorchFold, optimizes sequence logits through a frozen all-atom predictor. It integrates confidence, contact, geometric, and sequence-prior objectives into a shared optimization procedure, supporting minibinders, framework-conditioned VHHs, cyclic peptides, and ligand-binding proteins. Using pretrained AlphaFold 3 weights, no post hoc sequence redesign was required.
AI.result: Experimentally measured binding was achieved for representative minibinders and VHHs across four targets in each format. Computational benchmarks further demonstrated applicability to cyclic peptides and ligand-conditioned pocket design.
AI.conclusion: TorchCraft extends predictor inversion to multiple binder formats and molecular contexts, offering a common framework for reusing all-atom structural priors in design.

title: SLAMSqueezeBench: Comparing SLAM Systems under Resource Constraints
comment: 8 pages, 2 figures, 7 tables. This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication
summary: Simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) is one of the services running on an autonomous robot. It is typically run to assist other tasks such as planning, manipulation, etc. All these tasks are run on edge hardware and are subject to severe resource constraints. However, most SLAM systems are built and tested in isolation, and their performance is reported as if they are the only task running on a system. We observe that existing benchmarks lack a common mechanism for comparing SLAM systems under realistic resource constraints. To address this limitation, we have developed SLAMSqueezeBench, a framework that allows testing of SLAM systems under realistic workloads on edge hardware. It does so by imposing constraints on compute and memory resources available for the SLAM system during execution. It also simulates realistic camera frame acquisition with frame drops when a finite buffer is full. Using SLAMSqueezeBench, we compare nine SLAM systems spanning classical systems, learning-based systems, and approaches for Gaussian splatting. Our testing framework will be available for use by the community upon publication.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces SLAMSqueezeBench, a framework that benchmarks SLAM systems under realistic edge-hardware resource constraints (compute, memory, and camera frame drops), addressing the lack of a common mechanism for such comparisons, and uses it to evaluate nine SLAM systems spanning classical, learning-based, and Gaussian splatting approaches.
AI.motivation: SLAM typically runs on resource-constrained edge hardware alongside other tasks, but most SLAM systems are built and tested in isolation with performance reported as if they were the sole workload. Existing benchmarks lack a common mechanism for comparing SLAM systems under realistic resource constraints.
AI.method: The authors developed SLAMSqueezeBench, a framework that tests SLAM systems under realistic workloads on edge hardware. It imposes constraints on compute and memory resources available to the SLAM system during execution and simulates realistic camera frame acquisition with frame drops when a finite buffer is full.
AI.result: Using SLAMSqueezeBench, the authors compared nine SLAM systems spanning classical systems, learning-based systems, and approaches for Gaussian splatting.
AI.conclusion: SLAMSqueezeBench provides a common mechanism for evaluating SLAM systems under realistic resource constraints, and the testing framework will be made available to the community upon publication.

title: Integrating knowledge from case reports: a medical ontology based multimodal information system with structured summary
summary: Published medical case reports serve as a crucial medical information carrier, documenting discoveries in rare diseases, diagnostic methods, and innovative treatments. Despite the wealth of clinical knowledge in millions of case reports in the public medicine literature database (PubMed), accessing relevant information efficiently is hindered by the limitations of traditional keyword-based retrieval tools on unstructured and diverse case reports. To address the above issues, we introduce a comprehensive multimodal information system for case reports integrating structured clinical summaries of patients including medical images and biomedical named entities from 52949 open-access case reports published from 2000 to 2021. The multimodal essential information is organized in a well-structured medical ontology. Also, a powerful interface for searching and browsing case reports is designed to assist junior clinicians in retrieving cases effectively and improving the identification and diagnosis of rare diseases.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a multimodal information system for 52,949 open-access medical case reports (2000–2021) from PubMed, organizing structured clinical summaries, medical images, and biomedical named entities within a medical ontology and providing an interface for efficient case search and browsing.
AI.motivation: Medical case reports are a crucial carrier of clinical knowledge on rare diseases, diagnostic methods, and innovative treatments. However, millions of case reports in PubMed are unstructured and diverse, and traditional keyword-based retrieval tools limit efficient access to relevant information.
AI.method: The authors build a comprehensive multimodal information system for case reports, extracting structured clinical patient summaries, medical images, and biomedical named entities from 52,949 open-access case reports published between 2000 and 2021. This multimodal essential information is organized using a well-structured medical ontology, and a powerful interface for searching and browsing case reports is designed.
AI.result: The system integrates structured clinical summaries, medical images, and biomedical named entities from 52,949 open-access case reports, organized in a well-structured medical ontology, with a dedicated search-and-browse interface.
AI.conclusion: The proposed system assists junior clinicians in retrieving cases effectively and improves the identification and diagnosis of rare diseases.

title: Navigate or Relocate? Planning Among Movable Obstacles in Unknown Environments
summary: Conventional robot planning methods seek collision-free paths to a goal but fail when all paths are blocked. In these cases, the robot must determine which objects to relocate, in what order, and where to place them to clear a path---a problem known as Navigation Among Movable Obstacles (NAMO). Most NAMO planners assume a known environment, while existing approaches for unknown environments typically reason locally about relocations and cannot plan interdependent relocation sequences. We consider NAMO in unknown environments revealed through onboard sensing, where the robot must decide whether a blocked route requires relocation or a feasible path may exist through unexplored space. We propose an online framework that addresses this ambiguity by selecting between navigation and relocation using shortest paths that treat discovered movable objects as obstacles or as removable. Navigation relies on existing motion planners, while relocation uses a sampling-based approach that, unlike existing approaches for unknown environments, searches over \textit{interdependent} relocation sequences and uses an LLM to bias sampling. Numerical experiments demonstrate scalability to cluttered environments requiring interdependent relocations and improved plan quality over existing baselines.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an online NAMO framework for unknown environments that resolves the navigation-vs-relocation ambiguity via shortest paths treating movable objects as obstacles or removable, combining existing motion planners for navigation with a sampling-based planner over interdependent relocation sequences biased by an LLM.
AI.motivation: Conventional robot planning finds collision-free paths to a goal but fails when all paths are blocked; the robot must then decide which objects to relocate, in what order, and where to place them (NAMO). Most NAMO planners assume a known environment, and existing unknown-environment approaches reason only locally about relocations and cannot plan interdependent relocation sequences.
AI.method: An online framework for NAMO in unknown environments revealed through onboard sensing. It addresses the ambiguity of whether a blocked route needs relocation or a feasible path exists through unexplored space by selecting between navigation and relocation using shortest paths that treat discovered movable objects either as obstacles or as removable. Navigation leverages existing motion planners; relocation uses a sampling-based approach that searches over interdependent relocation sequences and employs an LLM to bias sampling.
AI.result: Numerical experiments show scalability to cluttered environments requiring interdependent relocations and improved plan quality over existing baselines.
AI.conclusion: The proposed online framework enables NAMO in unknown environments by jointly reasoning about navigation and interdependent relocations, outperforming existing unknown-environment baselines and scaling to cluttered settings.

title: Contagion on the Trading Floor: How Adversarial Signals Spread in Multi-Agent Trading Systems
comment: Published in ECML PKDD 2026. 25 pages, including 7 pages of supplementary material
summary: Multi-agent trading systems built on large language models (LLMs) are beginning to appear in quantitative finance, yet their robustness to adversarial inputs is largely unknown. We study the vulnerability of LLM trading stacks to black-box, input-only attacks that enter solely via admissible social-media feeds. We introduce the Generic Multi-Agent Trading System (GMATS), a framework that captures modern multiagent trading architectures and instantiate a class of black-box poisoning attackers that treat an LLM as a post generator and inject budget-constrained, plausibly benign social-media content into the analyst's evidence stream. We define contagion metrics that trace how adversarial content propagates through the stack, including belief-shift scores at analyst and coordinator layers and attack-clean deltas on standard backtest metrics. Experiments on a safe offline benchmark with historical market and social data show that even simple input-only attackers can materially degrade risk-return profiles, sharply reducing Sharpe ratios. At the same time, we find that suitably designed multi-agent topologies and coordinator prompts can dampen adversarial shocks and improve average robustness under identical poisoning budgets.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces GMATS, a framework modeling multi-agent LLM trading architectures, and studies their vulnerability to black-box, input-only poisoning attacks delivered through admissible social-media feeds, finding that even simple attackers materially degrade risk-return profiles while certain multi-agent topologies and coordinator prompts improve robustness.
AI.motivation: Multi-agent LLM trading systems are emerging in quantitative finance, but their robustness to adversarial inputs remains largely unknown. The authors aim to characterize this vulnerability surface, specifically for attacks entering only through legitimate social-media channels.
AI.method: The authors propose GMATS (Generic Multi-Agent Trading System), a framework capturing modern multi-agent trading architectures. They instantiate a class of black-box poisoning attackers that use an LLM as a post generator and inject budget-constrained, plausibly benign social-media content into the analyst's evidence stream. Contagion metrics are defined to trace adversarial content propagation, including belief-shift scores at analyst and coordinator layers and attack-clean deltas on standard backtest metrics.
AI.result: Experiments on a safe offline benchmark with historical market and social data show that even simple input-only attackers can materially degrade risk-return profiles and sharply reduce Sharpe ratios. Conversely, suitably designed multi-agent topologies and coordinator prompts dampen adversarial shocks and improve average robustness under identical poisoning budgets.
AI.conclusion: Multi-agent LLM trading stacks are vulnerable to low-cost, input-only poisoning via social-media feeds, but architectural design choices such as topology and coordinator prompting offer a viable robustness defense under fixed attack budgets.

title: VABench: Measuring Embodied Spatial Intelligence through Visual Demonstrations, Active Perception, and Metric Control
summary: Spatial intelligence requires more than describing object locations. Under incomplete observation, models must identify and acquire missing evidence, interpret it in a common spatial frame, and act on it. We introduce VA-Bench to evaluate the complete observe-reason-act-revise loop. General-purpose MLLMs learn procedural context from RGB-only demonstrations, actively select camera viewpoints, issue metric Cartesian commands, and revise them from execution feedback. Models receive no privileged object poses, oracle trajectories, or learned action heads. A fixed model-agnostic controller executes only model-specified targets. VA-Bench contains 14 base task families (11 single-arm and three dual-arm), seven held-out geometry/layout variants, and a long-horizon five-object composition track. We evaluate 12 primary model conditions in three independent runs over the same 20 physically verified seeds per base task, reporting terminal success, nine trajectory-level behavioral diagnostics, and subtask progress. First, the best-performing model scores 100.0% on target localization and 78.9% on spatial relations in the annotated run. Its three-run macro-average task success is only 53.93+/-3.17%. Second, active camera control significantly improves task success over passive multi-view observation. In one matched comparison, success rises from 27.86% to 57.50%. Third, held-out geometric transfer can reduce task success by over 30 percentage points. No model completes a strict long-horizon episode, despite substantial partial progress. VA-Bench thus tests whether general-purpose MLLMs can turn visual demonstrations and actively acquired evidence into successful embodied action.

AI.tldr: VA-Bench is introduced to evaluate the full observe-reason-act-revise loop in spatial intelligence, requiring general-purpose MLLMs to learn from RGB-only demonstrations, actively select viewpoints, issue metric commands, and revise based on feedback, without privileged poses or learned action heads. It spans 14 base task families, 7 held-out variants, and a long-horizon composition track, testing 12 model conditions over 3 runs and 20 seeds. Best models reach 100% localization and 78.9% spatial-relation accuracy but only 53.93±3.17% macro-average success; active camera control raises success from 27.86% to 57.50%, geometric transfer drops success by >30 points, and no model completes the long-horizon episode.
AI.motivation: Spatial intelligence requires more than describing object locations: under incomplete observation, models must identify and acquire missing evidence, interpret it in a common spatial frame, and act on it. Existing evaluations likely do not test this complete loop.
AI.method: VA-Bench evaluates the complete observe-reason-act-revise loop. General-purpose MLLMs learn procedural context from RGB-only demonstrations, actively select camera viewpoints, issue metric Cartesian commands, and revise them from execution feedback. Models receive no privileged object poses, oracle trajectories, or learned action heads; a fixed model-agnostic controller executes only model-specified targets. The benchmark includes 14 base task families (11 single-arm, 3 dual-arm), 7 held-out geometry/layout variants, and a long-horizon five-object composition track. Evaluation covers 12 primary model conditions in 3 independent runs over the same 20 physically verified seeds per base task, reporting terminal success, nine trajectory-level behavioral diagnostics, and subtask progress.
AI.result: The best-performing model scores 100.0% on target localization and 78.9% on spatial relations in the annotated run, but its three-run macro-average task success is only 53.93±3.17%. Active camera control significantly improves task success over passive multi-view observation, rising from 27.86% to 57.50% in one matched comparison. Held-out geometric transfer can reduce task success by over 30 percentage points. No model completes a strict long-horizon episode, despite substantial partial progress.
AI.conclusion: VA-Bench tests whether general-purpose MLLMs can turn visual demonstrations and actively acquired evidence into successful embodied action, and current results show substantial gaps, especially in active evidence acquisition, geometric transfer, and long-horizon execution.

title: Steering Equilibrium Selection in Regularized Self-Play via the Reference Policy
comment: 17 pages, 8 figures, 4 tables. Companion to arXiv:2606.28308 and arXiv:2607.17543. Fully reproducible: a single self-contained notebook regenerates every number, table, and figure
summary: Regularized self-play -- the family behind DeepNash's Stratego play -- drives a two-player zero-sum policy to a Nash equilibrium by best-responding to a slowly moving, entropy-regularized reference policy $ρ$. When the game has a polytope of value-equivalent equilibria, the regularizer silently breaks the tie: with a uniform reference it selects the maximum-entropy member, the I-projection of $ρ$ onto the Nash set. Can the reference be used to choose the equilibrium on purpose? On five exactly solvable games plus a 2-D polytope, with exact best responses and equivalence tests over independent seeds, anchoring the reference at a target member and refining steers self-play to that member with mean coordinate error 0.007 at median exploitability $5\times10^{-5}$, TOST-equivalent to the request within $\pm0.05$; the anchoring persists through refinement and follows the reference, not the initialization. Selection follows the reach-weighted I-projection (slope 0.969 [0.950, 0.987]). We report with equal emphasis where the story breaks: fixed off-manifold references cost 0.08-0.25 exploitability; stiff or flat families require a smaller mirror step, set by a pre-registered rule; boundary targets undershoot; curvature predicts where boundary saturation bites (rank correlation 0.90, p=0.037) while interior precision is curvature-independent. Table and MLP steering maps are equivalent within $\pm0.03$ at every target (30 seeds); matched control arms show attention's robust signature is excess seed variance, any systematic shift bounded at 0.018 and not significant. Against a best response the selection-robustness trade-off is degenerate: steering matters only against fixed, non-equilibrium opponents. The recipe -- anchor the reference at the desired member and refine -- reinterprets the KL anchor of RLHF-style RL as a selection knob, not only a stability leash.

AI.tldr: Regularized self-play can be steered to select a specific Nash equilibrium by anchoring the entropy-regularized reference policy at a target member; the anchoring persists through refinement and follows the reference rather than the initialization, though it degrades at boundaries and against best-response opponents.
AI.motivation: In two-player zero-sum games with a polytope of value-equivalent Nash equilibria, the entropy regularizer implicitly breaks ties (e.g., selecting the maximum-entropy member under a uniform reference). The authors ask whether the reference policy can be used deliberately to select a desired equilibrium rather than leaving the choice to the regularizer's default.
AI.method: Experiments on five exactly solvable games plus a 2-D polytope, using exact best responses and equivalence tests over independent seeds. They anchor the reference at a target equilibrium member and refine self-play, testing whether selection follows the reference or the initialization, and measure coordinate error, exploitability, and TOST equivalence. They compare table and MLP steering maps, examine fixed off-manifold references, stiff/flat families, boundary targets, and curvature effects, with matched control arms.
AI.result: Anchoring the reference at a target member steers self-play to that member with mean coordinate error 0.007 at median exploitability 5e-5, TOST-equivalent within ±0.05. Selection follows the reach-weighted I-projection (slope 0.969 [0.950, 0.987]). Fixed off-manifold references cost 0.08-0.25 exploitability; stiff or flat families need a smaller mirror step; boundary targets undershoot; curvature predicts boundary saturation (rank correlation 0.90, p=0.037) while interior precision is curvature-independent. Table and MLP steering maps are equivalent within ±0.03 across 30 seeds.
AI.conclusion: The recipe of anchoring the reference at the desired equilibrium and refining successfully selects that member, reinterpreting the KL anchor of RLHF-style RL as a selection knob rather than only a stability leash. However, the selection-robustness trade-off is degenerate: steering matters only against fixed, non-equilibrium opponents, and the approach has limitations at boundaries, off-manifold references, and stiff/flat families.

title: Tele-Traversability: Rethinking Traversability for Teleoperated Ground Robots in Terrain Navigation
summary: Teleoperation, a human-in-the-loop control scheme, allows a human operator to remotely command and guide a mobile robot to navigate in off-road environments, yet fluent and user-friendly tele-navigation requires an alignment of traversability evaluation between human and robot. In the teleoperation system, the human operator typically utilizes off-site incomplete and delayed feedback via a human-machine interface to make a judgment of traversability, while the robot makes such an evaluation based on in situ onboard sensory information, which could cause divergent traversability estimation and thus generate mismatched decisions and actions. Existing approaches for traversability modeling, estimation, and prediction are mainly derived from the view of robots, i.e., robot-centric, and are practically suitable for fully autonomous mobile robots, but neglect the influence of human operators. To address this problem, this paper extends the concept of traversability from robot-centric to human-centric by accounting for the operator's cognitive states, such as attention, workload, and risk tolerance or awareness, termed tele-traversability. We first revisit the definitions and roles of traversability in robotics and then extend them to teleoperation settings. Finally, we highlight future trends and open challenges of tele-traversability toward human-centric teleoperation systems.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes extending the concept of traversability from robot-centric to human-centric by incorporating the operator's cognitive states, coining the term "tele-traversability" for teleoperation systems.
AI.motivation: In teleoperation, human operators rely on off-site, incomplete, and delayed feedback via a human-machine interface to judge traversability, while robots evaluate traversability using in situ onboard sensors. This discrepancy can cause divergent traversability estimation, leading to mismatched decisions and actions. Existing traversability modeling, estimation, and prediction approaches are robot-centric and suited for fully autonomous robots, neglecting the human operator's influence.
AI.method: The paper extends the concept of traversability from robot-centric to human-centric by accounting for the operator's cognitive states—such as attention, workload, and risk tolerance or awareness—and introduces the notion of "tele-traversability." It revisits the definitions and roles of traversability in robotics and then extends them to teleoperation settings.
AI.result: The paper redefines and reframes traversability for teleoperation contexts, establishing tele-traversability as a human-centric concept that integrates operator cognitive states.
AI.conclusion: The paper highlights future trends and open challenges of tele-traversability toward human-centric teleoperation systems, aiming to align traversability evaluation between human and robot for fluent and user-friendly tele-navigation.

title: Dual-Axis Policy Optimization for LLM Agents: Bayesian Feedback Attribution and Trajectory Mass Normalization
summary: Reinforcement learning for LLM agents involves two distinct optimization di- mensions: how environment feedback is exploited within a trajectory, and how complete trajectories are aggregated across a batch. We formulate these dimen- sions as Intra-Trajectory Feedback Attribution and Inter-Trajectory Objec- tive Aggregation, and introduce BATON (Bayesian Attribution and Trajectory Objective Normalization), a dual-axis policy optimization framework. BATON instantiates the first axis with Bayesian Feedback Attribution, which constructs a feedback-conditioned posterior over sampled actions, and the second with Trajec- tory Mass Normalization (TMN), which assigns equal optimization mass to com- plete trajectories. Experiments with GRPO and GiGPO on ALFWorld, WebShop, and SearchQA show that both axes provide independent gains and that their combi- nation consistently achieves the strongest overall performance across model scales.

AI.tldr: The paper decomposes RL for LLM agents into two optimization axes—intra-trajectory feedback attribution and inter-trajectory objective aggregation—and proposes BATON, combining Bayesian Feedback Attribution with Trajectory Mass Normalization, yielding independent and combined gains over GRPO/GiGPO on ALFWorld, WebShop, and SearchQA.
AI.motivation: RL for LLM agents involves two distinct optimization dimensions: how environment feedback is exploited within a trajectory, and how complete trajectories are aggregated across a batch. These are formalized as Intra-Trajectory Feedback Attribution and Inter-Trajectory Objective Aggregation, motivating a dual-axis framework.
AI.method: BATON (Bayesian Attribution and Trajectory Objective Normalization) is a dual-axis policy optimization framework. Axis one, Bayesian Feedback Attribution, constructs a feedback-conditioned posterior over sampled actions. Axis two, Trajectory Mass Normalization (TMN), assigns equal optimization mass to complete trajectories.
AI.result: Experiments with GRPO and GiGPO on ALFWorld, WebShop, and SearchQA show that both axes provide independent gains and that their combination consistently achieves the strongest overall performance across model scales.
AI.conclusion: Formulating RL for LLM agents along two orthogonal axes and addressing each with Bayesian Feedback Attribution and Trajectory Mass Normalization yields independently effective and complementary improvements, with BATON delivering the best overall performance.

title: Recovering Aggressively Pruned Vision-Language-Action Models with Offline Hidden-State Distillation
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models let robots follow language instructions, but their language backbones of several billion parameters are the main obstacle to running them on robot hardware. Structured pruning reduces that backbone, and removing 63% of it from OpenVLA-OFT drops LIBERO-Long success from 93.2% to 0.8%. A recent approach restores such a model with supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning, which needs online rollouts and hundreds of GPU-hours. We recover most of the lost success entirely offline. Width pruning narrows the blocks but keeps the residual stream at its original size, so teacher and student hidden states have the same shape and are matched directly, without a projector. Training against a cache built in one teacher pass lifts the 63%-reduced student to within 3.5 points of the teacher in about 8 GPU-hours. A sweep over nine ratios locates where the recovery objective starts to matter. Up to 45% reduction the two do not differ significantly on OpenVLA-OFT. Hidden-state distillation then adds +2.1 to +4.5 points there between 63% and 87%, and +9.4 to +22.1 points on CogACT from 63% onward. At 81% on CogACT, a tripled recovery budget narrows the distilled student's gap to the teacher to 3.9 points on average, while supervised recovery stays more than 20 points below. At matched compression, width pruning yields higher success and depth pruning lower latency. On a 6-DoF manipulator, the distilled student at 72% reduction reaches 77.5% success against 59.5% for supervised recovery, runs 2.23x faster on-board than the teacher, and uses 62% less memory.

AI.tldr: The paper recovers structured-pruned VLA models almost fully offline via width pruning plus hidden-state distillation, avoiding costly RL rollouts and cutting recovery to ~8 GPU-hours.
AI.motivation: Billion-parameter language backbones prevent VLA models from running on robot hardware. Structured pruning removes much of the backbone, but at 63% reduction OpenVLA-OFT drops from 93.2% to 0.8% LIBERO-Long success. Existing recovery uses supervised fine-tuning plus reinforcement learning, requiring online rollouts and hundreds of GPU-hours—impractical. The paper seeks an entirely offline recovery that restores most lost success cheaply.
AI.method: Width pruning is used: it narrows transformer blocks while keeping the residual stream at original size, so teacher and student hidden states share the same shape and can be matched directly without a projector. Training proceeds offline against a hidden-state cache built in a single teacher forward pass (hidden-state distillation). The recovery objective is swept across nine compression ratios, and compared against supervised recovery. Recovery-budget scaling is also tested, along with width vs. depth pruning trade-offs.
AI.result: A 63%-reduced student reaches within 3.5 points of the teacher in about 8 GPU-hours. Up to 45% reduction, distillation and supervised recovery do not differ significantly on OpenVLA-OFT. From 63% to 87%, distillation adds +2.1 to +4.5 points on OpenVLA-OFT, and from 63% onward +9.4 to +22.1 points on CogACT. At 81% on CogACT, tripling the recovery budget brings the distilled student within 3.9 points of the teacher on average, while supervised recovery stays >20 points below. At matched compression, width pruning gives higher success and depth pruning lower latency. On a 6-DoF manipulator, the 72%-reduced distilled student reaches 77.5% success vs. 59.5% for supervised recovery, runs 2.23x faster on-board than the teacher, and uses 62% less memory.
AI.conclusion: Offline hidden-state distillation with width pruning can restore heavily pruned VLA models far more cheaply than online RL-based recovery, and its advantage grows with compression ratio. Width pruning favors success, depth pruning favors latency, and the resulting compact students run faster and use less memory on real robot hardware.

title: MetaRTL: Meta-path Attention Enhanced Relational Table Learning
summary: Relational table learning has gained increasing attention with the widespread use of relational databases. Existing methods typically rely on deep GNN or HGNN stacks, leading to high computational costs and limited performance on large real-world databases. We propose MetaRTL, a two-stage framework for scalable and expressive relational table learning. In the first stage, MetaRTL obtains initial table embeddings via lightweight pre-training. In the second stage, it performs non-parametric message passing to derive meta-path features, which are then aggregated by an attention module, MetaAttn. By shifting computation from deep message passing to efficient meta-path aggregation, MetaRTL captures rich relational semantics while maintaining high efficiency. Experiments on 10 real-world datasets across 24 tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

AI.tldr: MetaRTL is a two-stage framework for relational table learning that replaces deep GNN/HGNN stacks with lightweight pre-training plus non-parametric meta-path message passing and attention-based aggregation (MetaAttn), achieving scalability and expressiveness validated on 10 real-world datasets across 24 tasks.
AI.motivation: Relational table learning is increasingly important due to the ubiquity of relational databases, but existing methods depend on deep GNN or HGNN stacks, which incur high computational cost and show limited performance on large real-world databases. There is a need for a method that is both scalable and expressive.
AI.method: MetaRTL is a two-stage framework. Stage 1 obtains initial table embeddings through lightweight pre-training. Stage 2 performs non-parametric message passing to derive meta-path features, which are then aggregated by an attention module named MetaAttn. This design shifts computation from deep message passing to efficient meta-path aggregation.
AI.result: Experiments on 10 real-world datasets covering 24 tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.
AI.conclusion: By moving computation from deep message passing to efficient meta-path aggregation, MetaRTL captures rich relational semantics while maintaining high efficiency, offering a scalable and expressive solution for relational table learning.

title: OmniCalib: Target-Free, Task-Structured Self-Calibration for Humanoid Robots
summary: Assembly, wear, and component replacement perturb the sensor extrinsics and joint zeros encoded by a humanoid CAD model. Existing procedures calibrate one sensor pair or require external fiducials. Using only robot-native motion and onboard sensing, we present OmniCalib, a target-free workflow that calibrates the full upper limbs---all 14 arm joint zeros and the extrinsics of both wrist and chest cameras---as well as lower limbs and the multi-camera head rig. Each module matches a robot-native task to a parameter block, checks observability, and writes only supported corrections to the CAD model. Our depth ICP method recovers all 14 arm joint zeros and calibrates all RGB-D camera extrinsics without any calibration target. Relative to CAD, the estimated extrinsic corrections are 10.56 mm and 1.74 degrees for the left wrist, 6.33 mm and 1.25 degrees for the right wrist, and 9.81 mm and 0.929 degrees for the chest RGB-D camera. ICP point-to-plane residual is 2.09 mm. On the same injected offsets, ICP and ArUco recover all 14 joint zeros below the 0.1-degree encoder-resolution reference. On an AGIBOT A3 Ultra humanoid, four static double-support stances recover all 12 lower-limb joint-zero offsets injected with an RMS error of 0.063 degrees. The head module combines multi-camera visual odometry with legged odometry and dynamic compensation through the live ROS transform tree. Using only planar walking, it attains a mean SO(3) error of 1.061 degrees across three sequences. The best sequence reaches 0.775 degrees, competitive with iKalibr at 0.902 degrees from rich 6-DOF excitation. Rig-relative angles repeat within 0.140 degrees. Injection recovery and held-out tests validate each observable block.

AI.tldr: OmniCalib is a target-free, robot-native calibration workflow that simultaneously estimates all 14 upper-limb joint zeros, wrist and chest RGB-D extrinsics, 12 lower-limb joint zeros, and multi-camera head-rig extrinsics on a humanoid, validated by injection-recovery and held-out tests.
AI.motivation: Assembly, wear, and component replacement perturb the sensor extrinsics and joint zeros encoded in a humanoid CAD model, so the nominal CAD parameters become inaccurate. Existing calibration procedures typically calibrate only one sensor pair or require external fiducials, which limits coverage and practicality.
AI.method: OmniCalib uses only robot-native motion and onboard sensing with no calibration target. Each module pairs a robot-native task with a specific parameter block, verifies observability, and applies only supported corrections to the CAD model. A depth ICP method with point-to-plane residuals recovers the 14 arm joint zeros and all RGB-D camera extrinsics; four static double-support stances recover the 12 lower-limb joint-zero offsets; and the head module fuses multi-camera visual odometry, legged odometry, and dynamic compensation via the live ROS transform tree.
AI.result: Relative to CAD, estimated extrinsic corrections are 10.56 mm / 1.74 deg (left wrist), 6.33 mm / 1.25 deg (right wrist), and 9.81 mm / 0.929 deg (chest RGB-D), with a 2.09 mm ICP point-to-plane residual. ICP and ArUco both recover all 14 joint zeros below the 0.1-degree encoder-resolution reference under the same injected offsets. On an AGIBOT A3 Ultra, four stances recover all 12 lower-limb offsets with 0.063 deg RMS error. The head module attains 1.061 deg mean SO(3) error over three sequences using only planar walking, with the best sequence at 0.775 deg, competitive with iKalibr's 0.902 deg from rich 6-DOF excitation; rig-relative angles repeat within 0.140 deg.
AI.conclusion: OmniCalib provides a unified, target-free calibration framework covering upper limbs, lower limbs, and the multi-camera head rig. Injection-recovery and held-out tests validate each observable block, demonstrating accuracy competitive with fiducial-based methods while relying solely on robot-native motion and onboard sensing.

title: A Dual-Process Perspective on Nudge Susceptibility in LLM-Based GUI Agents
comment: Preprint of a manuscript completed in November, 2025
summary: LLM-based GUI agents increasingly act on behalf of users in digital environments that were designed with human users in mind. These graphical user interfaces were designed to support, but also deliberately steer, the behaviour and decisions of users. While behavioural biases in the textual outputs of LLMs are well-documented, far less is known about how such influence operates when models act as agents that perceive interfaces and execute decisions---and, in particular, whether the reasoning capabilities increasingly built into these agents make them more robust to it. Drawing on Dual-Process Theory, we empirically investigate whether LLM-based GUI agents are susceptible to automatic (Type 1) and reflective (Type 2) digital nudges, and how their reasoning configuration moderates this susceptibility. In a randomized online shopping experiment with 3,600 agents and a total of 21,600 simulations across six frontier models from three providers, we found that agents were vulnerable to both nudge types. Crucially, the reasoning configuration moderated these effects in opposing directions, reducing susceptibility to automatic default nudges while heightening it to reflective social influence nudges. Extensive reasoning therefore did not make agents more robust but redirected the route through which choice architecture takes effect. Exploratory analysis further showed this redirection to be systematically structured by model scale. Beyond establishing nudge susceptibility as a behavioural property of agentic AI, the study positions interface design as a governance concern for organizations that delegate decisions to autonomous agents.

AI.tldr: Across 21,600 simulations with 3,600 LLM-based GUI shopping agents from six frontier models, agents were vulnerable to both automatic and reflective digital nudges; extensive reasoning reduced susceptibility to default nudges but increased it to social influence nudges, showing reasoning redirects rather than removes the influence of choice architecture.
AI.motivation: GUI agents increasingly act on behalf of users in interfaces explicitly designed to steer human behaviour, yet little is known about how such influence operates when LLMs perceive interfaces as agents, and whether added reasoning capabilities make them more robust. The paper draws on Dual-Process Theory to test this gap.
AI.method: A randomized online shopping experiment with 3,600 LLM-based GUI agents and 21,600 total simulations, covering six frontier models from three providers. Agents were exposed to automatic (Type 1) default nudges and reflective (Type 2) social influence nudges, with reasoning configuration varied as a moderator; exploratory analysis examined moderation by model scale.
AI.result: Agents were susceptible to both nudge types. Reasoning configuration moderated effects in opposing directions: it reduced susceptibility to automatic default nudges while heightening susceptibility to reflective social influence nudges. Exploratory analysis showed the redirection was systematically structured by model scale.
AI.conclusion: Reasoning does not make LLM-based GUI agents more robust to digital nudges; instead it redirects the pathway through which choice architecture takes effect. Nudge susceptibility is established as a behavioural property of agentic AI, positioning interface design as a governance concern for organizations delegating decisions to autonomous agents.

title: Quantifying Mechanical Intelligence in Legged Robots with Information Theory
comment: 8 pages, 6 figures, 1 table, submitted to IEEE ICRA 2027 for publication
summary: Mechanical intelligence, loosely defined as the reduction in control burden afforded by a robot's physical form, has become a prominent concept in robotics, with instantiations in bioinspired robotics, soft robotics, robotic swarms, and many other areas. However, rigorous theoretical understanding and quantitative measures of mechanical intelligence have lagged behind the engineering systems that the community has developed. In this work, using modern legged robots as a benchmark and exemplar, we propose several information-theoretic metrics for quantifying mechanical intelligence. By viewing body dynamics as both a computational process and a communication channel, we show that several prior insights in legged-robot engineering can be described using information theory, and we quantify how bits are processed by mechanical modes and across robot coordinates. Specifically, we examine the trade-off between explicitly incorporating compliance through series-elastic actuation and using so-called proprioceptive, low-gear-ratio transmissions, and we explore how these mechanisms interact with control policies during locomotion. We develop these results on systems of increasing complexity: a simplified linear model of a robot-leg transmission, a nonlinear single-leg simulation, and simulated quadruped robots controlled by a learned policy while navigating challenging terrain. These results lay the groundwork for broader study of robot mechanisms and their role in embodied computation.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes information-theoretic metrics to quantify "mechanical intelligence"—the control burden reduced by a robot's physical form—using legged robots as a benchmark, and applies them across three systems of increasing complexity.
AI.motivation: Mechanical intelligence is a prominent concept in robotics (bioinspired, soft, swarm robotics), but rigorous theoretical understanding and quantitative measures lag behind the engineering systems developed. A principled framework is needed to formalize and measure it.
AI.method: Viewing body dynamics as both a computational process and a communication channel, the authors propose information-theoretic metrics for mechanical intelligence. They quantify how bits are processed by mechanical modes and across robot coordinates.
