They examine the trade-off between explicit compliance via series-elastic actuation and proprioceptive, low-gear-ratio transmissions, and how these interact with control policies during locomotion. The framework is developed on a simplified linear robot-leg transmission model, a nonlinear single-leg simulation, and simulated quadruped robots with a learned policy on challenging terrain.
AI.result: The information-theoretic framework can describe several prior insights in legged-robot engineering, and it quantifies the bits processed by mechanical modes and across robot coordinates, revealing the trade-off between series-elastic actuation and low-gear-ratio proprioceptive transmissions and their interaction with control policies during locomotion.
AI.conclusion: The results lay the groundwork for broader study of robot mechanisms and their role in embodied computation.

title: Constraint-Safe Graph-Context Scoring for Stable Point-Feature Labels Under Text-Width and Accessibility-Inspired Profiles
summary: Point-feature label placement on interactive maps must reconcile geometric validity, display yield, local placement utility, and stability across camera motion. Accessibility and multilingual requirements further change label dimensions, yet algorithmic evaluations often collapse these concerns into overlap counts. We present LABELSENSE-Pilot, a reproducible prototype that generates eight compass candidates per feature, scores candidates with a multilayer perceptron over graph-context summaries, adds a previous-placement bonus, and selects a layout through mixed-integer optimization. The executed scorer is deliberately not described as a graph transformer. Every returned layout is checked for viewport containment, per-feature uniqueness, and pairwise clearance. Experiments use 2,500 airport coordinates and names spanning 155 countries, with country-grouped splits and generated density, camera, text-suffix, preference, and enlarged-font stressors. Across five seeds, LABELSENSE-Pilot displayed 85.62 percent of labels with 2.09 percent flicker and zero collisions. Versus a handcrafted-utility integer program, LABELSENSE-Pilot sacrificed 1.43 percentage points of display while reducing flicker by 12.04 points. Enlarged-box-aware layouts produced zero proxy violations, whereas standard geometry reevaluated at 1.5x violated 52.57 percent of selected placements. These results establish an auditable engineering trade-off, not human accessibility, multilingual usability, or preference. Official recent baselines and participant evidence remain required before submission.

AI.tldr: LABELSENSE-Pilot is a reproducible prototype for point-feature label placement that generates eight compass candidates per feature, scores them with an MLP over graph-context summaries, adds a previous-placement bonus, and selects layouts via mixed-integer optimization, achieving 85.62% display, 2.09% flicker, and zero collisions across five seeds.
AI.motivation: Label placement on interactive maps must reconcile geometric validity, display yield, local placement utility, and stability under camera motion. Accessibility and multilingual requirements alter label dimensions, yet algorithmic evaluations often reduce these concerns to overlap counts, so a reproducible, auditable trade-off analysis is needed.
AI.method: Eight compass candidates are generated per feature. Candidates are scored by a multilayer perceptron over graph-context summaries, with a previous-placement bonus for stability. Layout is selected through mixed-integer optimization. Every returned layout is validated for viewport containment, per-feature uniqueness, and pairwise clearance. Experiments use 2,500 airport coordinates and names across 155 countries with country-grouped splits and generated density, camera, text-suffix, preference, and enlarged-font stressors. The scorer is deliberately not characterized as a graph transformer.
AI.result: Across five seeds, LABELSENSE-Pilot displayed 85.62% of labels with 2.09% flicker and zero collisions. Against a handcrafted-utility integer program, it sacrificed 1.43 percentage points of display while reducing flicker by 12.04 points. Enlarged-box-aware layouts produced zero proxy violations, whereas standard geometry reevaluated at 1.5x violated 52.57% of selected placements.
AI.conclusion: The results establish an auditable engineering trade-off, not human accessibility, multilingual usability, or preference. Official recent baselines and participant evidence remain required before submission.

title: WorldContact: A Contact-Centric World Model for Scalable Robot Learning
summary: Adapting robots to new objects and tasks requires interaction experience that can be costly to obtain. We present WorldContact, a contact-centric world model for deformable-object manipulation, constructed from a limited set of high-quality trajectories to generate additional training data efficiently. It predicts object dynamics using larger time steps than the source numerical simulator, which requires small integration steps to resolve rapid motion and prevent interpenetration. We evaluate WorldContact across 16 shopping-bag manipulation tasks. State-rollout measurements on a single H100 GPU show a $10\times$ speedup over the source simulator, excluding rendering and disk I/O. We use the generated data to fine-tune an existing vision-language-action policy and deploy it directly on a real robot. In bag lifting, the same policy achieves 65% single-attempt success when fine-tuned on source simulation data alone, compared with 95% when fine-tuned on the dataset expanded with WorldContact. These results support efficient data generation with WorldContact for robot policy adaptation.

AI.tldr: WorldContact is a contact-centric world model for deformable-object manipulation that generates extra training data from few high-quality trajectories, achieving a 10x speedup over the source simulator and boosting real-robot bag-lifting success from 65% to 95% after policy fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: Adapting robots to new objects and tasks requires interaction experience, but collecting such experience is costly.
AI.method: Build a contact-centric world model from a limited set of high-quality trajectories to efficiently generate additional training data. It predicts object dynamics using larger time steps than the source numerical simulator, which needs small integration steps to resolve rapid motion and prevent interpenetration.
AI.result: Evaluated across 16 shopping-bag manipulation tasks; state-rollout on a single H100 GPU shows a 10x speedup over the source simulator (excluding rendering and disk I/O). Fine-tuning an existing vision-language-action policy with the expanded data yields 95% single-attempt success in bag lifting versus 65% with source simulation data alone, deployed directly on a real robot.
AI.conclusion: These results support efficient data generation with WorldContact for robot policy adaptation.

title: Reproducibility is not construct validity: LLM measurement of institutionally situated communication
summary: High annotation reproducibility does not necessarily imply that an LLM-inferred measure captures the construct it is intended to measure. We test this distinction using a dataset from the European Commission's AI Act consultation, linking structured survey responses to free-text consultation submissions from the same stakeholders. LLM annotations of consultation submissions are highly reproducible (intraclass correlations > 0.99), yet show limited convergence with survey-reported measures of the nominal construct they were intended to approximate. Divergence between survey-and LLM-inferred text-based measures varies systematically across stakeholder groups: business associations express greater concern about AI risks in text-based consultations than in survey responses ({g} = +1.0), whereas public authorities and several nonbusiness groups show smaller or negative divergences. Divergences between scores suggest positive spatial autocorrelation across European countries (Moran's I = 0.347, p = 0.036), indicating that stakeholders from neighboring countries tend toward more similar text-based stances towards AI safety concerns. Despite divergence, survey-reported concerns remain strongly associated with support for explainability across all divergence levels. These results demonstrate that LLM annotation reproducibility can coexist with poor construct correspondence and motivate validation procedures that distinguish reproducibility, construct validity, and communication context variation when LLMs are used as measurement instruments.

AI.tldr: High LLM annotation reproducibility (ICC > 0.99) does not guarantee construct validity: LLM-inferred text measures of AI-risk concern diverge systematically from survey responses across stakeholder groups and EU countries.
AI.motivation: Reproducibility is often treated as sufficient evidence of measurement quality, but an LLM-inferred measure may be reproducible yet fail to capture the intended construct. This paper tests whether reproducibility and construct correspondence can diverge when LLMs are used as measurement instruments.
AI.method: Links structured survey responses to free-text submissions from the same stakeholders in the European Commission's AI Act consultation. LLM annotations of the free-text submissions are compared with survey-reported measures of the nominal construct, with divergence examined across stakeholder groups, across European countries via spatial autocorrelation (Moran's I), and against support for explainability.
AI.result: LLM annotations are highly reproducible (intraclass correlations > 0.99) but converge only limitedly with survey measures. Divergence varies systematically by stakeholder group: business associations show greater text-based than survey-reported AI-risk concern (g = +1.0), while public authorities and several non-business groups show smaller or negative divergence. Divergence scores exhibit positive spatial autocorrelation across European countries (Moran's I = 0.347, p = 0.036). Survey-reported concerns remain strongly associated with support for explainability at all divergence levels.
AI.conclusion: LLM annotation reproducibility can coexist with poor construct correspondence. Validation procedures should distinguish reproducibility, construct validity, and communication-context variation when LLMs serve as measurement instruments.

title: TacSushi: Tactile-Grounded World-Action Modeling for Dexterous Sushi Manipulation
summary: Dexterous food manipulation requires control under deformation, occlusion, and uncertain contact. We present TacSushi, a tactile-grounded, Cosmos3-based world-action policy that learns from recorded future consequences while acting on current observations. The backbone encodes current RGB, language, and hand state, and feature-wise gated fusion incorporates fingertip tactile features into the action representation. During training, a decoder conditioned on demonstrated action chunks predicts logged future visual observations, task progress, relative contact risk, and tactile summaries; this decoder is removed at deployment. Failed trials provide consequence supervision, but their actions are excluded from imitation. We train TacSushi on 340 successful and 50 failed real-robot trials and compare six methods in 600 separate rollouts across three in-distribution tasks and two out-of-distribution ingredient variants. To assess food quality beyond a single geometric threshold, we score terminal outcomes using an anchored visual-quality protocol that equally weights five human ratings and three vision-language-model ratings per rollout. Full TacSushi achieves 68.3% average in-distribution success and 37.5% out-of-distribution success, compared with 36.7%/10.0% without future-consequence supervision and 25.0%/17.5% with direct tactile concatenation in place of gated fusion. These comparisons support complementary benefits of feature-wise gated tactile fusion and training-only predictive supervision.

AI.tldr: TacSushi is a tactile-grounded, Cosmos3-based world-action policy for dexterous food manipulation that trains a removed-at-deployment future-consequence decoder on both successful and failed trials, and uses feature-wise gated fusion of fingertip tactile into the action representation, reaching 68.3% in-distribution and 37.5% out-of-distribution success.
AI.motivation: Dexterous food manipulation must be controlled under object deformation, occlusion, and uncertain contact. Standard imitation learning exploits only demonstrated actions and ignores the rich information contained in observed future consequences and in failed trials, and naive tactile integration may not optimally condition the action representation.
AI.method: A Cosmos3-based world-action policy encodes current RGB, language, and hand state, with feature-wise gated fusion injecting fingertip tactile features into the action representation. During training, an auxiliary decoder conditioned on demonstrated action chunks predicts logged future visual observations, task progress, relative contact risk, and tactile summaries; this decoder is discarded at deployment. Failed trials supply consequence supervision while their actions are excluded from imitation. Trained on 340 successful and 50 failed real-robot trials, evaluated in 600 rollouts over three in-distribution tasks and two out-of-distribution ingredient variants, with terminal outcomes scored by an anchored visual-quality protocol equally weighting five human and three vision-language-model ratings.
AI.result: Full TacSushi achieves 68.3% average in-distribution success and 37.5% out-of-distribution success, versus 36.7%/10.0% without future-consequence supervision and 25.0%/17.5% when direct tactile concatenation replaces gated fusion.
AI.conclusion: Feature-wise gated tactile fusion and training-only predictive consequence supervision provide complementary benefits; leveraging failed-trial consequences for supervision without imitating their actions improves control under deformation, occlusion, and uncertain contact.

title: Physical knowledge on historical data matters more than enforcing physical constraints on the forecast
summary: Time series forecasting has seen signicant advancements with the emergence of new deep learning models. However, forecasting time series in applications involving physical processes remains a major challenge. Despite the apparition of Physics Informed Neural Networks (PINN), recent models do not estimate unobservable intermediate physical variables, which are important for domain experts to understand the target behavior. To this end, we propose a Physics Informed Recurrent Neural Network (PIRNN) which predicts, along the target, unobservable variables on both historic data and forecast target. This approach enhances the model robustness and results interpretation using domain knowledge. Our method is easily adaptable to any physical model using several equations, each having its own set of unobservable variables, to describe it-self. As a case study, we incorporate physical equations used for groundwater levels predictions by the physical model called Gardenia. This model uses transfers equations between reservoirs, optimized with data assimilation, to simulate the evolution of groundwater levels. Evaluation includes several well known neural network models and the Gardenia model compared on twelve real world datasets. In addition, we study the impact of each component through an ablation study. Our model outperforms other models on ve out of the twelve datasets and our ablation study underlines the importance of having a physical background in our time series forecasting task. Finally, the coherence of the physical variables predicted by our neural network is assessed by a domain expert.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a Physics Informed Recurrent Neural Network (PIRNN) that forecasts target time series while simultaneously predicting unobservable intermediate physical variables, demonstrated on groundwater level prediction using Gardenia transfer equations, outperforming baselines on 5 of 12 datasets.
AI.motivation: Deep learning has advanced time series forecasting, but forecasting physical processes remains challenging. Existing Physics Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) do not estimate unobservable intermediate physical variables, which domain experts need to interpret target behavior. The authors aim to improve robustness and interpretability by embedding domain knowledge.
AI.method: A Physics Informed Recurrent Neural Network (PIRNN) predicts the target along with unobservable variables, on both historical data and forecast horizon. The approach is generalizable to any physical model described by several equations, each with its own set of unobservable variables. As a case study, it incorporates Gardenia's physical equations for groundwater levels, which use transfers equations between reservoirs optimized via data assimilation.
AI.result: Evaluation compares several well-known neural network models and the Gardenia model on twelve real-world datasets. PIRNN outperforms other models on five of twelve datasets, and an ablation study highlights the importance of the physical background. A domain expert assessed the coherence of the predicted physical variables.
AI.conclusion: Embedding physical equations and estimating unobservable intermediate variables improves forecasting performance, robustness, and interpretability, with domain-expert validation confirming the physical coherence of the predictions.

title: EmbodiedMind: Adaptive Data Curation and Prefix-Tree Reinforcement Learning for Efficient Embodied Intelligence
summary: Training embodied foundation models typically requires massive-scale datasets and extensive computational resources, yet often suffers from three critical limitations: (1) inefficient sample utilization due to low-informative samples; (2) imbalanced gradient contributions across heterogeneous tasks; and (3) severe credit assignment problem in long-horizon planning, where trajectory-level rewards indiscriminately penalize all tokens. To address these issues, we propose an efficient training paradigm that achieves state-of-the-art average performance through strategic data selection and hierarchical policy optimization. Our approach consists of three synergistic stages. First, Rejection Sampling-based Fine-Tuning (RSFT) filters out low-informative samples to establish robust behavioral priors while preventing distributional collapse. Second, Iterative Rejection GRPO (IR-GRPO) employs task-specific queues stratified by difficulty to keep datasets balanced across reinforcement learning iterations, coupled with a hybrid reward mechanism for precise cross-task feedback. Third, to enhance long-horizon task planning, we introduce Trie-GRPO, a novel reinforcement learning algorithm based on action prefix trees, which enables step-level advantage estimation. This resolves the credit assignment problem by isolating intermediate correct decisions from downstream errors, while effectively balancing exploration efficiency and depth compared to conventional search trees. As a result, EmbodiedMind achieves a state-of-the-art average performance of 70.02% across 18 benchmarks, and significantly outperforms other embodied foundation models in long-horizon task planning accuracy. Our project will be released for reproducibility.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an efficient training paradigm for embodied foundation models with three stages—RSFT, IR-GRPO, and Trie-GRPO—that tackles low-informative samples, imbalanced task gradients, and credit assignment, achieving 70.02% average performance across 18 benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Training embodied foundation models requires massive datasets and compute but suffers from three limitations: inefficient sample utilization due to low-informative samples, imbalanced gradient contributions across heterogeneous tasks, and severe credit assignment problems in long-horizon planning where trajectory-level rewards penalize all tokens indiscriminately.
AI.method: A three-stage synergistic training paradigm: (1) Rejection Sampling-based Fine-Tuning (RSFT) filters low-informative samples to build robust behavioral priors while preventing distributional collapse; (2) Iterative Rejection GRPO (IR-GRPO) uses task-specific queues stratified by difficulty to balance datasets across RL iterations, with a hybrid reward mechanism for cross-task feedback; (3) Trie-GRPO, a reinforcement learning algorithm based on action prefix trees, enables step-level advantage estimation to isolate intermediate correct decisions from downstream errors while balancing exploration efficiency and depth.
AI.result: EmbodiedMind achieves state-of-the-art average performance of 70.02% across 18 benchmarks and significantly outperforms other embodied foundation models in long-horizon task planning accuracy.
AI.conclusion: The proposed strategic data selection and hierarchical policy optimization paradigm effectively addresses the three critical limitations, with the project to be released for reproducibility.

title: TRACE: Accountable Agentic Retrieval for Source Discovery in Digital Archives
summary: Historical archives pose a difficult retrieval problem for retrievalaugmented generation systems: documents are OCR-degraded, heterogeneous across genres and sources, and require strong source traceability for scholarly and institutional use. We introduce TRACE, a training-free agentic retrieval framework designed for accountable source discovery over historical corpora. The system was developed in the context of DECIDON, an interdisciplinary project on the circulation of political discourse between parliamentary debates and the press during the French Third Republic, involving digitised historical collections and institutional use cases. The prototype is currently deployed internally within the project and accessible to 24 researchers across six partner institutions. We evaluate TRACE on HistoriQA-ThirdRepublic, a benchmark of 1,752 French historical questions over parliamentary debates and newspapers from 1887, with documents derived from Biblioth{è}que nationale de France digitised collections. TRACE achieves R@10 = 0.856 and MRR = 0.653, outperforming sparse, dense, graph-based, and agentic RAG baselines, with the largest gains on multi-hop and cross-corpus questions. At approximately $0.02 per question under the default hosted inference configuration, TRACE also remains economically feasible for heritage institutions, laboratories or companies that cannot rely on costly local GPU infrastructure. These results suggest that, for large digital libraries and archives, retrieval accountability and corpus-aware agent design can provide a practical alternative to heavier training-based or graph-construction approaches.

AI.tldr: TRACE is a training-free agentic retrieval framework for accountable source discovery over OCR-degraded, heterogeneous historical archives, achieving strong retrieval performance at low cost in the DECIDON project context.
AI.motivation: Historical archives present a difficult retrieval problem for retrieval-augmented generation: documents are OCR-degraded, heterogeneous across genres and sources, and demand strong source traceability for scholarly and institutional use. Existing training-based or graph-construction approaches are heavy and costly. The work is motivated by the DECIDON project on political discourse circulation between parliamentary debates and the press during the French Third Republic, requiring accountable, practical retrieval.
AI.method: The authors introduce TRACE, a training-free agentic retrieval framework designed for accountable source discovery over historical corpora. It was developed within DECIDON and is deployed internally for 24 researchers across six partner institutions. Evaluation uses HistoriQA-ThirdRepublic, a benchmark of 1,752 French historical questions over parliamentary debates and newspapers from 1887, with documents from Bibliothèque nationale de France digitised collections. TRACE is compared against sparse, dense, graph-based, and agentic RAG baselines.
AI.result: TRACE achieves R@10 = 0.856 and MRR = 0.653, outperforming sparse, dense, graph-based, and agentic RAG baselines, with the largest gains on multi-hop and cross-corpus questions. It costs approximately $0.02 per question under the default hosted inference configuration, remaining economically feasible for institutions without costly local GPU infrastructure.
AI.conclusion: For large digital libraries and archives, retrieval accountability and corpus-aware agent design can provide a practical alternative to heavier training-based or graph-construction approaches, as demonstrated by TRACE's strong performance and low cost in the DECIDON historical setting.

title: ReShoot: Generative Visual Domain Randomization of Recorded Robot Demonstrations for Visuomotor Policy Learning
summary: Imitation-learned robot policies are frequently overfit to the visual conditions present in their training demonstrations. Consequently, variations in object color or background appearance often induce substantial performance degradation. A common mitigation strategy is to acquire additional demonstrations in each novel visual context; however, this approach is resource-intensive, requiring repeated access to a robot, a controlled environment, and human operation for every appearance condition to be covered. We introduce ReShoot, a framework that synthesizes visual diversity by re-rendering previously recorded demonstrations under altered appearances, thereby shifting the burden from data collection to generation. A vision-language model captions the scene, edits a targeted attribute (e.g., background, object color, or material), and an edge-conditioned video generator re-renders both camera views to match. The instruction is updated accordingly. The action sequence and proprioceptive trajectory are copied verbatim without relabeling, so each generated episode retains the recorded action and proprioceptive labels. On LIBERO, a policy trained on an equal mixture of recorded and re-rendered demonstrations matches the performance of recorded-only training (96.5% vs. 96.9%). Moreover, the mixed training set improves robustness to scene perturbations on LIBERO-Plus (85.5% vs. 82.3%). Across two physical robotic platforms, deploying ReShoot with 43 and 100 pre-collected demonstrations increased the success rate on recolored objects from 0.0% to 42.9% and 47.5%, respectively, while maintaining performance under the original recorded appearance.

AI.tldr: ReShoot re-renders recorded robot demonstrations under altered visual appearances using a VLM and an edge-conditioned video generator, shifting visual-diversity augmentation from data collection to generation while preserving action and proprioceptive labels.
AI.motivation: Imitation-learned robot policies overfit to the visual conditions of their training demonstrations, so changes in object color or background cause substantial performance degradation. The standard remedy—collecting new demonstrations in each novel visual context—is resource-intensive, requiring repeated robot access, a controlled environment, and human operation for every appearance condition.
AI.method: ReShoot synthesizes visual diversity by re-rendering previously recorded demonstrations under altered appearances. A vision-language model captions the scene and edits a targeted attribute (background, object color, or material); an edge-conditioned video generator then re-renders both camera views to match, and the language instruction is updated accordingly. The action sequence and proprioceptive trajectory are copied verbatim without relabeling, so each generated episode retains the recorded action and proprioceptive labels.
AI.result: On LIBERO, a policy trained on an equal mixture of recorded and re-rendered demonstrations matches recorded-only training (96.5% vs. 96.9%). The mixed set improves robustness to scene perturbations on LIBERO-Plus (85.5% vs. 82.3%). On two physical robotic platforms, ReShoot with 43 and 100 pre-collected demonstrations raised success on recolored objects from 0.0% to 42.9% and 47.5%, respectively, while maintaining performance under the original recorded appearance.
AI.conclusion: ReShoot offers a generation-based alternative to costly visual-context data collection, obtaining robustness to appearance perturbations without additional robot demonstrations and without sacrificing in-distribution performance.

title: From "Who Is This User?" to "What Does This Purchase Mean?": A Deployed Pipeline for Semantic User Profiling at Bank Scale
comment: 10 pages, 3 figures, IEEE International Conference on Data Mining 2026 (ICDM)
summary: Per-user LLM inference on transaction histories binds the inference budget linearly to user count, which becomes prohibitive at applied scale. We re-cast attribute inference from per-user to per-transaction-pattern. The pipeline runs in three phases: Resolve abstracts item names with optional web grounding, Profile infers attributes for each frequent pattern, and Tag clusters free-text attributes into a queryable database. In Profile, a single LLM call per pattern emits predefined categorical labels, free-text attributes, and per-attribute prevalence estimates. Because inference runs over patterns rather than users, the budget grows with the pattern count rather than the user count. On the public Open e-commerce corpus, the database is statistically indistinguishable from an LLM that reads each user's raw history directly in AUC across the evaluated attributes, and the prevalence estimates carry discriminative signal between positive and negative users. The pipeline is deployed at a major Japanese bank profiling on the order of tens of millions of users, with close to a three-order-of-magnitude reduction in LLM inference targets versus a per-user pipeline. The code is publicly available on https://github.com/CyberAgentAILab/profiling-agent-open-ecommerce.

AI.tldr: The paper replaces per-user LLM inference for attribute inference with a per-transaction-pattern approach, using a three-phase pipeline (Resolve, Profile, Tag) that reduces inference cost from scaling with user count to scaling with pattern count. On the Open e-commerce corpus, the resulting database matches a per-user LLM baseline in AUC across evaluated attributes, with prevalence estimates showing discriminative signal, and is deployed at a major Japanese bank profiling tens of millions of users with roughly a 1,000x reduction in inference targets.
AI.motivation: Per-user LLM inference on transaction histories scales the inference budget linearly with the number of users, which becomes prohibitively expensive at applied scale (tens of millions of users).
AI.method: A three-phase pipeline: Resolve abstracts item names with optional web grounding; Profile infers attributes for each frequent pattern, where a single LLM call per pattern emits predefined categorical labels, free-text attributes, and per-attribute prevalence estimates; Tag clusters free-text attributes into a queryable database. Inference thus runs over transaction patterns instead of users.
AI.result: On the public Open e-commerce corpus, the database is statistically indistinguishable from an LLM reading each user's raw history directly in AUC across evaluated attributes, and prevalence estimates carry discriminative signal between positive and negative users. Deployed at a major Japanese bank profiling on the order of tens of millions of users, with close to a three-order-of-magnitude reduction in LLM inference targets versus a per-user pipeline.
AI.conclusion: Re-casting attribute inference from per-user to per-transaction-pattern inference achieves comparable accuracy to per-user LLM inference while dramatically reducing inference cost at production scale; code is publicly available.

title: Runtime Safety Filtering for Two-Terminal Hazards in Robotic Battery Recycling
summary: Runtime safety filters for learned manipulation policies typically define unsafe states as unions of object-wise keep-out regions. This representation can be unnecessarily restrictive for hazards that depend on a joint spatial relation, such as battery recycling, where a conductive payload can short a charged cell only when it approaches both terminals simultaneously. We study runtime filtering for this two-terminal hazard in LIBERO using frozen OpenVLA policies. We factor a runtime filter into three design choices: the predicate structure, its geometric margin, and the fallback action applied when a commanded action is rejected. We compare a conjunctive predicate, a conventional two-site keep-out, and a composite of the two. For each predicate, we vary its margin to obtain a frontier between task success and residual hazard. We then compare four fallback strategies at matched operating points: holding, retreat, sampled search, and a continuous-action barrier projection. Across three workcells, the three predicate families trace nearly identical safety--utility frontiers once each is evaluated over its own margin. In contrast, the fallback strategy has a substantially larger effect: holding reduces task success by up to 0.302 relative to retreat without reducing hazard, while both minimally invasive fallbacks leave substantially more residual hazard. This ordering transfers to a second policy and task suite, while retreat-based filtering remains effective under standing errors in the clearances available to the filter, although correlated error in the estimated payload size is more damaging than larger independent errors in terminal position. These results show that, for proximity-defined manipulation hazards, margin selection and fallback strategy can matter more than predicate structure in determining the safety--utility trade-off of a runtime filter.

AI.tldr: For proximity-defined manipulation hazards, the choice of fallback action and geometric margin matters more than the predicate structure in shaping the safety-utility trade-off of a runtime filter.
AI.motivation: Runtime safety filters for learned manipulation policies usually define unsafe states as unions of object-wise keep-out regions. This is overly restrictive for hazards that depend on a joint spatial relation, such as battery recycling, where a conductive payload shorts a charged cell only when near both terminals at once. The paper investigates whether predicate structure, margin, or fallback action dominates the resulting safety-utility trade-off.
AI.method: The authors study runtime filtering for a two-terminal hazard in LIBERO with frozen OpenVLA policies. They decompose the filter into three design choices: predicate structure (conjunctive predicate, conventional two-site keep-out, and a composite), geometric margin, and fallback action applied on action rejection. For each predicate they sweep the margin to trace a safety-utility frontier, then compare four fallback strategies at matched operating points: hold, retreat, sampled search, and continuous-action barrier projection. They test across three workcells, a second policy and task suite, and under standing errors in clearances.
AI.result: Across three workcells, the three predicate families trace nearly identical safety-utility frontiers when each is evaluated over its own margin. Fallback strategy has a much larger effect: holding reduces task success by up to 0.302 relative to retreat without reducing hazard, while both minimally invasive fallbacks leave substantially more residual hazard. This ordering transfers to a second policy and task suite. Retreat-based filtering remains effective under standing errors in available clearances, though correlated error in estimated payload size is more damaging than larger independent errors in terminal position.
AI.conclusion: For proximity-defined manipulation hazards, margin selection and fallback strategy can matter more than predicate structure in determining a runtime filter's safety-utility trade-off. Conventional keep-out unions may therefore be adequate when margins are tuned and fallbacks chosen carefully.

title: Beyond Depth Truncation: Controlled Evaluation of Depth Utilization in Recursive Language Models
summary:
Depth-recurrent language models iteratively apply a small layer stack, decoupling per-token compute from distinct parameter count. To determine whether such a model genuinely utilizes its depth, both recurrence and layer-pruning literatures rely on a shared evaluation: truncating depth at inference time, plotting quality against retained depth fraction, and reading off the slope. While cheap and training-free, this metric suffers from an unexamined flaw: it extracts a single scalar from an intervention that alters multiple model properties simultaneously. Depth truncation concurrently reduces the number of block applications, decreases the volume of distinct computation performed, and pushes the readout head onto an out-of-distribution residual stream. The observed slope conflates all three factors, yet is conventionally interpreted as reflecting solely the second.
  We propose the Depth Control Protocol (DCP), a diagnostic suite that disentangles these three quantities. DCP comprises three positive controls that isolate each factor while varying the others, a negative control applying the identical interventions to dense transformers to ensure the effect is not an artifact of the measurement protocol, and a controlled training intervention to verify causality. The linchpin control, running the full budget of block applications while executing only a single distinct iteration, is strictly realizable only in depth-wise weight-sharing architectures, since in a dense network repeating a layer yields an entirely different model rather than the same model in an alternative configuration.

AI.tldr: The paper critiques the standard depth-truncation slope metric used to assess depth utilization in depth-recurrent language models, arguing it conflates three distinct effects, and proposes the Depth Control Protocol (DCP) to disentangle them.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations of depth utilization in depth-recurrent language models—both in recurrence and layer-pruning work—infer depth use from the slope of quality versus retained depth fraction under inference-time truncation. This metric is cheap and training-free, but it extracts a single scalar from an intervention that simultaneously alters multiple model properties, so its interpretation is unexamined and potentially confounded.
AI.method: The authors identify three concurrent effects of depth truncation: reduced number of block applications, decreased volume of distinct computation, and an out-of-distribution residual stream at the readout head. They propose DCP, comprising three positive controls that isolate each factor while varying the others, a negative control applying identical interventions to dense transformers, and a controlled training intervention to establish causality. The key control runs the full block-application budget while executing only a single distinct iteration, which is strictly realizable only in depth-wise weight-sharing architectures.
AI.result: The abstract does not report empirical results; it presents a conceptual diagnosis of the confound and a proposed protocol. The central finding is that the conventional truncation slope conflates three factors while being interpreted as reflecting only distinct computation, and that the linchpin control is feasible only in weight-shared depth-recurrent models, not dense ones.
AI.conclusion: Depth-truncation slopes are an unreliable measure of genuine depth utilization in depth-recurrent models. DCP offers a principled diagnostic suite that separates block-application count, distinct computation volume, and readout distribution shift, with the single-distinct-iteration control uniquely enabled by depth-wise weight sharing.

title: Towards High-DoF Dexterous Manipulation through VLA Post-Training
summary: Imitation-learned vision--language--action (VLA) foundation models acquire broad manipulation capabilities by scaling robot data across tasks and embodiments, but reliable deployment on a specific downstream task and hardware platform still requires post-training. Dexterous hands make this adaptation particularly difficult: their broad behavioural repertoire and high degree of freedom create a large and structured action space. Three obstacles are central: open-source VLAs do not natively provide an action interface for high-DoF hands; gesture mismatch during human-gated DAgger takeover creates command discontinuities and contaminates corrective trajectories; and reinforcement learning in the raw joint space is sample-inefficient. We present a unified four-step post-training pipeline comprising a learned temporal hand-action codec, supervised fine-tuning, DAgger, and real-world residual reinforcement learning. The codec adapts a pretrained VLA to absolute dexterous-hand commands. Buffered rollback, pose alignment, and smooth command blending enable continuous, task-relevant DAgger corrections, while latent residual RL confines exploration to coordinated hand motions captured by the codec. We evaluate the pipeline on five diverse real-world tasks spanning bimanual transfer, in-hand reorientation, and tool use. Within the reported post-training budgets, the resulting policies achieve 100\% success on every evaluated task over 20 trials per task. These results provide a practical path for adapting VLA foundation models to reliable real-world dexterous manipulation.

AI.tldr: A four-step post-training pipeline adapts pretrained VLAs to high-DoF dexterous hands, achieving 100% success on five real-world tasks within the reported budgets.
AI.motivation: Imitation-learned VLA foundation models gain broad manipulation ability by scaling robot data, but reliable deployment on a specific downstream task and hardware still requires post-training. Dexterous hands are especially hard because their high-DoF, broad behavioral repertoire forms a large structured action space. Three obstacles: open-source VLAs lack a native action interface for high-DoF hands; gesture mismatch during human-gated DAgger takeover causes command discontinuities and contaminates corrective trajectories; and RL in raw joint space is sample-inefficient.
AI.method: A unified four-step post-training pipeline: (1) a learned temporal hand-action codec, (2) supervised fine-tuning, (3) DAgger, and (4) real-world residual reinforcement learning. The codec adapts a pretrained VLA to absolute dexterous-hand commands. Buffered rollback, pose alignment, and smooth command blending enable continuous, task-relevant DAgger corrections, while latent residual RL confines exploration to coordinated hand motions captured by the codec.
AI.result: Evaluated on five diverse real-world tasks spanning bimanual transfer, in-hand reorientation, and tool use. Within the reported post-training budgets, the resulting policies achieve 100% success on every evaluated task over 20 trials per task.
AI.conclusion: The pipeline provides a practical path for adapting VLA foundation models to reliable real-world dexterous manipulation.

title: MaSCoD: A Multi-Agent Framework for Structural-Context-Guided Candidate Causal Graph Generation
comment: 31 pages, 4 figures, 18 tables. The first two authors contributed equally
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have been applied to causal discovery, but candidate-graph generation rarely treats premature omission of potentially relevant causal relations as an explicit design objective. We propose MaSCoD, a multi-agent framework that organizes candidate third variables and local structural patterns before direct-edge judgment. We evaluate MaSCoD on Auto-MPG, DWD, and Sachs using GPT-5.4 as the primary backbone and GPT-4o for replication. MaSCoD exhibits a dataset- and backbone-dependent retention-selectivity profile rather than uniform superiority. Across all six dataset-backbone settings, Full, which supplies structural hypotheses before direct-edge judgment, achieved higher mean Recall and F1 than No Phase 1, which instead constructs them within the judgment procedure, while also increasing false-positive rates. Additional reference-edge retention over all evaluated baselines was observed on DWD with GPT-5.4 and on Sachs with GPT-4o, rather than uniformly across settings. Partial ablations showed that supplying both information components did not always outperform supplying only one. For GPT-5.4, stage-wise analysis showed that the Full-No Phase 1 retention gap was already present after direct-edge judgment, while reconciliation introduced additional reference-edge loss for Full on Sachs. These findings support structural pre-organization as an explicit design and evaluation target for omission control and motivate evaluating context construction jointly with its utilization in judgment.

AI.tldr: MaSCoD is a multi-agent framework for LLM-based causal discovery that pre-organizes candidate third variables and local structures before direct-edge judgment, trading higher recall/F1 for more false positives and showing dataset/backbone-dependent retention benefits.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based causal discovery methods rarely treat the premature omission of potentially relevant causal relations as an explicit design objective, prompting the need for a framework that controls information omission during candidate-graph generation.
AI.method: MaSCoD organizes candidate third variables and local structural patterns before direct-edge judgment within a multi-agent setup. It is evaluated on Auto-MPG, DWD, and Sachs with GPT-5.4 as primary backbone and GPT-4o for replication, comparing Full (structural hypotheses supplied before judgment) against No Phase 1 (hypotheses built within judgment), plus partial ablations and stage-wise analyses.
AI.result: MaSCoD showed a dataset- and backbone-dependent retention-selectivity profile rather than uniform superiority. Full achieved higher mean recall and F1 than No Phase 1 across all six dataset-backbone settings, but also increased false positives. Extra reference-edge retention over baselines appeared only on DWD (GPT-5.4) and Sachs (GPT-4o). Partial ablations showed both information components together did not always beat supplying only one. For GPT-5.4, the Full–No Phase 1 retention gap was already present after direct-edge judgment, and reconciliation added reference-edge loss for Full on Sachs.
AI.conclusion: Structural pre-organization should be an explicit design and evaluation target for omission control, and context construction should be evaluated jointly with its utilization in judgment.

title: VAST: V2X/Dynamic Map-Aware Autonomous Driving Systems Validation Toolchain
summary: Cooperative autonomous driving in the IoT-to-Edge-to-Cloud continuum requires system-level validation across vehicles, infrastructure sensors, edge-side Dynamic Map services, and in-vehicle autonomous-driving stacks. This paper presents VAST, a V2X/Dynamic Map-aware validation toolchain that connects Scenic, Scenario Simulator v2, AWSIM, Autoware, and SIM-LDM. VAST does not introduce a new search algorithm; instead, it addresses interoperability challenges, including Lanelet2-to-Scenic mapping, ROS 2-based co-simulation through SS2, Dynamic Map object injection into Autoware, and collection of TTC, PET, collision, timeout, and performance measurements. In occluded-intersection scenarios, Lanelet2-compatible constrained sampling increases the edge-case discovery rate from 40.0% to 80.0% and reduces the average time per discovered edge case from 259.7 s to 110.4 s. Under the same generated scenario distribution, Dynamic Map availability reduces the collision rate from 78.0% to 40.0% and increases non-collision outcomes from 22.0% to 60.0%, with statistically significant TTC/PET shifts. A throughput study with 1-16 NPCs shows that sampling remains below 0.1 s, whereas AWSIM/Autoware execution and restart overhead dominate runtime. These results position VAST as a practical validation infrastructure for cooperative autonomous-driving CPSs.

AI.tldr: VAST is a V2X/Dynamic Map-aware validation toolchain integrating Scenic, Scenario Simulator v2, AWSIM, Autoware, and SIM-LDM to validate cooperative autonomous driving across the IoT-to-Edge-to-Cloud continuum, improving edge-case discovery and collision outcomes without introducing a new search algorithm.
AI.motivation: Cooperative autonomous driving across the IoT-to-Edge-to-Cloud continuum requires system-level validation spanning vehicles, infrastructure sensors, edge-side Dynamic Map services, and in-vehicle autonomous-driving stacks. Existing tools lack interoperability across these components, so a practical validation infrastructure is needed.
AI.method: VAST is a V2X/Dynamic Map-aware validation toolchain connecting Scenic, Scenario Simulator v2, AWSIM, Autoware, and SIM-LDM. Rather than proposing a new search algorithm, it addresses interoperability challenges: Lanelet2-to-Scenic mapping, ROS 2-based co-simulation through SS2, Dynamic Map object injection into Autoware, and collection of TTC, PET, collision, timeout, and performance measurements. Evaluation uses occluded-intersection scenarios and a 1-16 NPC throughput study.
AI.result: In occluded-intersection scenarios, Lanelet2-compatible constrained sampling raises the edge-case discovery rate from 40.0% to 80.0% and cuts average time per discovered edge case from 259.7 s to 110.4 s. With the same scenario distribution, Dynamic Map availability lowers collision rate from 78.0% to 40.0% and raises non-collision outcomes from 22.0% to 60.0%, with statistically significant TTC/PET shifts. Sampling stays below 0.1 s for 1-16 NPCs, while AWSIM/Autoware execution and restart overhead dominate runtime.
AI.conclusion: VAST serves as a practical validation infrastructure for cooperative autonomous-driving CPSs, overcoming interoperability barriers and improving both edge-case discovery efficiency and safety-relevant outcomes.

title: Not All AI Agents Are Equal: Characterizing Resource and Performance Dynamics
summary: LLM-based AI agents process user requests through iterative reasoning and tool execution, often involving the invocation of remote LLM APIs with local tool containers. This execution model can make the optimization of agent serving difficult because latency, local resource demand, and container bottlenecks inter-mix across requests. However, the current agent ecosystem runs without much consideration of resource dynamics, which results in significant waste of the precious resources. This paper analyzes the resource inter-mix of AI agents for three representative tasks: retrieval-augmented question answering, web search, and software coding. To this end, we characterize the latency with respect to the resource dynamics of processing multiple requests and tasks concurrently. Our measurements show that agents have a wide range of behaviors depending on tasks, so that even the same tool can differ substantially in resource dynamics. We also find that running multiple requests concurrently exposes task-dependent bottlenecks in resource dynamics such as CPU, disk I/O, and memory. Furthermore, we uncover that faster LLM responses or more CPU cores do not always accelerate agents. Based on these observations, we demonstrate new optimization opportunities that exploit the resource dynamics of tasks: CPU-aware tool admission and task-aware CPU allocation. Our results show that the latency of CPU-sensitive agent tasks improves $\sim$5.4$\times$, and the average latency across multiple tasks is reduced $\sim$32% compared to native agents.

AI.tldr: This paper measures the resource dynamics of LLM-based AI agents across three tasks and shows that same tools behave differently by task, with task-dependent CPU, disk I/O, and memory bottlenecks that motivate CPU-aware tool admission and task-aware CPU allocation.
AI.motivation: LLM-based AI agents iteratively reason and execute tools, often calling remote LLM APIs alongside local tool containers. This mixed execution makes agent serving optimization hard because latency, local resource demand, and container bottlenecks interleave across requests. Yet the current agent ecosystem largely ignores resource dynamics, wasting precious resources.
AI.method: The authors analyze the resource inter-mix of AI agents for three representative tasks: retrieval-augmented question answering, web search, and software coding. They characterize latency with respect to resource dynamics when multiple requests and tasks run concurrently, then propose optimizations exploiting observed dynamics: CPU-aware tool admission and task-aware CPU allocation.
AI.result: Measurements reveal a wide range of agent behaviors depending on task, such that even the same tool can differ substantially in resource dynamics. Concurrent requests expose task-dependent bottlenecks in CPU, disk I/O, and memory. Faster LLM responses or more CPU cores do not always accelerate agents. With CPU-aware tool admission and task-aware CPU allocation, CPU-sensitive agent task latency improves ~5.4x, and average latency across multiple tasks drops ~32% versus native agents.
AI.conclusion: Resource dynamics of LLM-based AI agents are strongly task-dependent, and treating agents as resource-agnostic wastes resources and limits performance. Exploiting these dynamics through tool admission and CPU allocation yields substantial latency gains, indicating that resource-aware agent serving is a promising optimization direction.

title: LYRIC: Language-Driven Physics-Based Character Control for Contact-Rich Whole-Body Object Interaction
summary: We present LYRIC, a generative flow-matching controller for language-driven physics-based contact-rich interaction control, that enables simulated characters to perform contact-rich whole-body object interactions from a free-form language instruction and a sparse terminal object goal. To obtain reliable expert trajectories from imperfect motion-capture references, a single tracking policy is trained using geometry-conditioned interaction rewards and relaxed reference tracking near hand-object contact. To guide interaction progress without prescribing a full-body kinematic reference, we factorize the controller into a task-level planner that predicts short-horizon object and humanoid-root trajectories, and an action generator that resolves whole-body motion and contacts in closed loop. After behavior cloning, we freeze the planner and post-tune the action generator on policy using the planner's predictions as stable supervision for intermediate task progression. In a controlled OMOMO evaluation, our tracker achieves 64.3% success compared with 53.2% for an InterMimic reimplementation, while a unified policy achieves 76.5% on the full OMOMO dataset. On the held-out split, LYRIC achieves 90.3% task success, compared with 74.2% for the strongest matched kinematic-planner baseline, with better semantic alignment and motion quality. Without retraining, the controller also supports test-time object-waypoint guidance. Qualitative results further demonstrate robust, natural contact-rich interactions and zero-shot transfer to novel object shapes. The webpage is available at https://neu-vi.github.io/LYRIC/

AI.tldr: LYRIC is a generative flow-matching controller that enables simulated humanoids to perform contact-rich whole-body object interactions from free-form language plus a sparse terminal object goal, using a factorized planner–generator design and policy post-tuning.
AI.motivation: Language-driven, physics-based contact-rich whole-body interaction is hard: motion-capture references are imperfect, and prescribing full-body kinematic references limits generalization. The authors aim to get reliable expert data and guide interaction progress without a full kinematic reference.
AI.method: A single tracking policy is trained using geometry-conditioned interaction rewards and relaxed reference tracking near hand-object contact. The controller is factorized into a task-level planner predicting short-horizon object and humanoid-root trajectories, and a closed-loop action generator resolving whole-body motion and contacts. After behavior cloning, the planner is frozen and the action generator is post-tuned on policy using planner predictions as stable supervision for intermediate task progression.
AI.result: On a controlled OMOMO evaluation, the tracker reaches 64.3% success vs. 53.2% for an InterMimic reimplementation; a unified policy reaches 76.5% on full OMOMO. On the held-out split, LYRIC achieves 90.3% task success vs. 74.2% for the strongest matched kinematic-planner baseline, with better semantic alignment and motion quality. It also supports test-time object-waypoint guidance without retraining and shows zero-shot transfer to novel object shapes.
AI.conclusion: LYRIC demonstrates that factorizing planning and control, combined with policy post-tuning, yields robust, natural, contact-rich whole-body interactions with strong success rates, improved semantics and motion quality, and generalization to new objects and test-time waypoints.

title: Neuro-Symbolic Agentic AI for Networked Low-Altitude UAVs
comment: Agentic AI, neuro-symbolic AI, unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), autonomous decision-making, networked UAV systems
summary: Networked low-altitude unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) need reliable and adaptive decision-making capabilities to operate under uncertain observations, dynamic environments, and intermittent connectivity, while many existing agentic systems remain limited by hallucination risks, data dependence, and weak generalization. This article investigates neuro-symbolic agentic AI (NSAAI) as a framework for combining neural grounding, symbolic reasoning, and closed-loop agentic interaction to support more reliable and adaptive UAV autonomy. We first examine its capability foundations in data efficiency, compositional generalization, continual learning, and zero-shot transfer, and then develop a reference architecture integrating task and goal management, neuro-symbolic planning, verification and metacognition, skill execution and network interaction, and shared knowledge and memory. An urban fire-inspection case implemented in LAESim illustrates how a UAV can coordinate sensing and cloud access under intermittent connectivity, reuse a verified image-delivery skill, and satisfy explicit evidence conditions before completing the mission. The results illustrate the potential of NSAAI to support reusable skills, evidence-grounded decision-making, and adaptive mission execution in networked UAV systems. We further discuss key research directions in uncertainty-aware reasoning, knowledge and skill expansion, adaptive self-monitoring, and standardized evaluation.

AI.tldr: This article examines neuro-symbolic agentic AI (NSAAI) as a framework to improve the reliability and adaptability of networked low-altitude UAV autonomy under uncertainty and intermittent connectivity, proposing a reference architecture and validating it with an urban fire-inspection case in LAESim.
AI.motivation: Networked low-altitude UAVs must make reliable, adaptive decisions under uncertain observations, dynamic environments, and intermittent connectivity, yet existing agentic systems suffer from hallucination risks, data dependence, and weak generalization. This motivates a neuro-symbolic agentic approach that can overcome these limitations.
AI.method: The paper analyzes NSAAI's capability foundations—data efficiency, compositional generalization, continual learning, and zero-shot transfer—and develops a reference architecture integrating task/goal management, neuro-symbolic planning, verification and metacognition, skill execution and network interaction, and shared knowledge and memory. It demonstrates the framework via an urban fire-inspection case implemented in LAESim.
AI.result: In the LAESim case, the UAV coordinates sensing and cloud access under intermittent connectivity, reuses a verified image-delivery skill, and satisfies explicit evidence conditions before completing its mission, illustrating reusable skills, evidence-grounded decision-making, and adaptive mission execution.
AI.conclusion: NSAAI shows promise for reliable and adaptive networked UAV autonomy, and the paper outlines key research directions in uncertainty-aware reasoning, knowledge and skill expansion, adaptive self-monitoring, and standardized evaluation.

title: UniExo: Unified Multi-Skill Policies for Musculoskeletal Locomotion and Co-Adaptive Exoskeleton Control
summary: Daily locomotion encompasses diverse activities and frequent transitions between them, yet most exoskeleton controllers are designed for a single activity or a narrow set of related movements. Changes in activity therefore typically require explicit mode switching and separately tuned or retrained controllers. Simulation-based learning reduces the need for hardware-based tuning but generally retains this limitation. Here we present UniExo, a framework that first constructs a multi-skill musculoskeletal human policy and then jointly trains an exoskeleton control policy with it. Four single-skill imitation experts for walking, turning, running and backward walking are distilled into a single network structured by a skill latent and subsequently fine-tuned through reinforcement learning on transition sequences. The resultant unified human policy achieves a mean tracking success rate of 94.7% on unseen clips of the four skills and exhibits greater robustness to perturbations than its constituent experts. A single hip exoskeleton controller (UniExo) is initialized from hip moment prediction of the human policy and co-adapted with it through multi-agent reinforcement learning across the four skills. This co-adaptation shifts the timing of the assistance torque and raises the fraction of positive work delivered to the hip. When deployed on a custom hip exoskeleton, the controller generalizes across four treadmill speeds in six participants and assists one participant through a continuous route of all four skills and their transitions, without skill labels or explicit mode switching. UniExo thus provides a step towards replacing activity-specific controllers with unified, user-specific controllers that support diverse locomotor activities and the transitions between them.

AI.tldr: UniExo builds a unified multi-skill musculoskeletal human policy from four imitation experts (walking, turning, running, backward walking) via skill-latent distillation and RL fine-tuning on transitions, then co-adapts a single hip exoskeleton controller with it through multi-agent RL, achieving label-free assistance across all four skills and their transitions.
AI.motivation: Daily locomotion involves diverse activities and frequent transitions, but most exoskeleton controllers target a single activity or a narrow set of related movements, requiring explicit mode switching and separately tuned or retrained controllers. Simulation-based learning reduces hardware tuning yet generally retains this limitation. The goal is to replace activity-specific controllers with unified, user-specific controllers supporting diverse locomotor activities and transitions without skill labels or mode switching.
AI.method: Four single-skill imitation experts for walking, turning, running, and backward walking are distilled into a single network structured by a skill latent, then fine-tuned via reinforcement learning on transition sequences to yield a unified human policy. A single hip exoskeleton controller (UniExo) is initialized from hip moment prediction of the human policy and co-adapted with it through multi-agent reinforcement learning across the four skills.
AI.result: The unified human policy reaches a mean tracking success rate of 94.7% on unseen clips of the four skills and shows greater robustness to perturbations than its constituent experts. Co-adaptation shifts the timing of the assistance torque and raises the fraction of positive work delivered to the hip. Deployed on a custom hip exoskeleton, the controller generalizes across four treadmill speeds in six participants and assists one participant through a continuous route of all four skills and their transitions, without skill labels or explicit mode switching.
AI.conclusion: UniExo provides a step towards replacing activity-specific controllers with unified, user-specific controllers that support diverse locomotor activities and the transitions between them.

title: Customizable and Jointly Optimized Route Planning: A Deep Architecture Enabling Differentiable Shortest-Path Search
summary: With the widespread use of online navigation and ride-hailing services, achieving optimal route planning for diverse user preferences has recently attracted increasing attention. Classic graph algorithms for pathfinding use heuristic cost functions to define edge weight, thus providing no optimality guarantee of route quality. Prior data-driven approaches equating ground truth of the optimal route with user trajectory, which is however moderately influenced by the navigation service, suffers from the feedback loop problem. To address these issues, we propose a deep architecture that is able to jointly optimize cost functions and route-ranking model towards any route preference. First, we run a multi-objective Dijkstra algorithm offline to collect the set of Pareto optimal routes, deeming it as the complete candidate set. Exploiting the property of such a set, we design a neural network structure that emulates shortest-path search and route ranking in an end-to-end differentiable manner. Second, we define route preference as a task of constrained optimization of route attributes, and propose a novel loss function that optimizes a single-objective variable, with other variables strictly under constraints. We conduct extensive experiments on real-world datasets. The results show that our architecture significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in route quality and customizability.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a deep architecture that jointly optimizes cost functions and a route-ranking model for diverse user route preferences, using Pareto-optimal routes as candidates and a constrained-optimization loss, outperforming state-of-the-art methods in route quality and customizability.
AI.motivation: Online navigation and ride-hailing demand optimal route planning for diverse user preferences. Classic graph pathfinding uses heuristic cost functions for edge weights, offering no optimality guarantee on route quality. Prior data-driven methods equate the ground-truth optimal route with user trajectories, which are influenced by the navigation service, causing a feedback loop problem.
AI.method: The authors run a multi-objective Dijkstra algorithm offline to collect the set of Pareto optimal routes as the complete candidate set. Leveraging this set, they design a neural network that emulates shortest-path search and route ranking in an end-to-end differentiable manner. Route preference is formulated as a constrained optimization over route attributes, with a novel loss optimizing a single-objective variable while strictly constraining others.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on real-world datasets show that the proposed architecture significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both route quality and customizability.
AI.conclusion: Jointly optimizing cost functions and a route-ranking model over a Pareto-optimal candidate set, trained with a constrained-optimization loss, yields superior and customizable route planning, addressing the optimality-guarantee and feedback-loop limitations of prior approaches.

title: Decoupling Physical Speed from Path Parameterization in Singularity-Free Guiding Vector Fields
summary: The existing singularity-free guiding vector field (SF-GVF) with an additional virtual coordinate can eliminate singular points (i.e., points where the vector field vanishes) inherent in conventional GVFs and guarantee global convergence of robot trajectories to closed and self-intersecting desired paths. However, the desired speed given by the GVF along the desired path in the original lower-dimensional space cannot be arbitrarily specified but depends on path parameterizations. One possible workaround is to partially normalize the physical projection of the SF-GVF and assign a user-designed speed. However, we show that this workaround may introduce new singularities since the normalization denominator can become zero. To address this issue, we propose a new SF-GVF with prescribed physical speed (PPS). The integral curves of the new SF-GVF converge exponentially to the desired path from any initial condition in the higher-dimensional space (including virtual dimension); more importantly, the robot's physical speed converges to the PPS, while the path-error dynamics remain invariant under regular reparameterizations of the desired path. We further develop a saturated acceleration control law for second-order kinematic models. Finally, comparative simulations and 3D path-following experiments with a quadrotor under different PPS profiles validate the theoretical results and demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a new singularity-free guiding vector field (SF-GVF) with prescribed physical speed (PPS) that guarantees exponential convergence to the desired path from any initial condition and allows arbitrary specification of the robot's physical speed, while preserving path-error dynamics invariance under regular reparameterizations.
AI.motivation: The existing SF-GVF with an additional virtual coordinate eliminates singular points and guarantees global convergence, but the desired speed along the desired path in the original lower-dimensional space cannot be arbitrarily specified—it depends on path parameterizations. A partial normalization workaround may introduce new singularities because the normalization denominator can become zero.
AI.method: The authors propose a new SF-GVF with prescribed physical speed (PPS), designed so that its integral curves converge exponentially to the desired path from any initial condition in the higher-dimensional space (including the virtual dimension). They also develop a saturated acceleration control law for second-order kinematic models.
AI.result: The integral curves of the new SF-GVF converge exponentially to the desired path from any initial condition. The robot's physical speed converges to the PPS, and the path-error dynamics remain invariant under regular reparameterizations of the desired path. Comparative simulations and 3D path-following experiments with a quadrotor under different PPS profiles validate the theoretical results.
AI.conclusion: The proposed SF-GVF with PPS resolves the singularity issue of the normalization workaround and enables arbitrary prescribed physical speed while maintaining convergence and reparameterization invariance, demonstrating effectiveness in simulations and quadrotor experiments.

title: E-AVI: Evidence-Grounded Multimodal Assessment for Automated Video Interviews
summary: Automated video interview assessment integrates verbal content, acoustic delivery, and visual behavior, yet numerical predictions alone provide limited inspectable support. We present E-AVI, an evidence-grounded framework that extracts timestamped multimodal evidence and integrates dimension-conditioned evidence attention with source-level embeddings for scoring. A shared evidence pool further supports natural-language feedback and follow-up question answering. On RecruitView and a private hospitality dataset, E-AVI consistently outperforms fine-tuned multimodal baselines in rank correlation. Ablation, evidence-deletion, bootstrap, human-audit, and QA analyses characterize the predictive contribution, grounding, and practical utility of the evidence pathway. Together, these results demonstrate that our proposed E-AVI framework improves predictive performance while providing inspectable support for assessment, feedback, and interactive analysis.

AI.tldr: E-AVI is an evidence-grounded automated video interview assessment framework that extracts timestamped multimodal evidence and uses dimension-conditioned evidence attention with source-level embeddings to improve scoring, feedback, and interactive QA.
AI.motivation: Automated video interview assessment integrates verbal, acoustic, and visual cues, but numerical predictions alone offer limited inspectable support; there is a need for grounded, interpretable evidence.
AI.method: E-AVI extracts timestamped multimodal evidence and integrates dimension-conditioned evidence attention with source-level embeddings for scoring. A shared evidence pool supports natural-language feedback and follow-up question answering.
AI.result: On RecruitView and a private hospitality dataset, E-AVI consistently outperforms fine-tuned multimodal baselines in rank correlation. Ablation, evidence-deletion, bootstrap, human-audit, and QA analyses characterize the predictive contribution, grounding, and practical utility of the evidence pathway.
AI.conclusion: E-AVI improves predictive performance while providing inspectable support for assessment, feedback, and interactive analysis.

title: Equivariant Filter Design for Acoustic and Depth Aided Inertial Navigation Systems
summary: Autonomous Underwater Vehicles (AUVs) navigating without GPS typically fuse inertial measurements with acoustic Doppler Velocity Log (DVL) velocities and pressure-derived depth. Posing the navigation state on a Lie group improves accuracy and consistency. However, state-of-the-art filters based on the Invariant Extended Kalman Filter (IEKF) append the Inertial Measurement Unit (IMU) biases as a Euclidean extension, which breaks the group-affine structure required for exact log-linear error dynamics, causing the reported covariance to degrade alongside the estimate. We apply the Tangent-Group (TG) symmetry, which carries the biases within the geometry of the state space, to derive an Equivariant Filter (EqF) for this system, leaving zero linearization error in the navigation states and second-order error only in the biases. We develop an equivariant output model for the DVL, whose update incurs only third-order linearization error, together with a direct pressure output. Monte Carlo simulations benchmark the TG-EqF against a Two-Frame-Group IEKF and a Multiplicative EKF. The TG-EqF reduces error by 18--25\% against both alternatives in each of attitude, velocity, and position. The main benefit is in the covariance it estimates: its Average Normalized Estimation Error Squared (ANEES) stays closer to its nominal value of one than that of the others. Offline analysis on AUV field data corroborates the findings of the simulations, demonstrating reduced position drift.

AI.tldr: This paper derives an Equivariant Filter (EqF) for AUV navigation using Tangent-Group symmetry, embedding IMU biases within the state-space geometry to eliminate linearization error, and benchmarks it against IEKF and MEKF variants.
AI.motivation: AUVs without GPS fuse IMU, DVL, and pressure data, and Lie-group-based filters improve accuracy and consistency. However, state-of-the-art IEKF formulations append IMU biases as a Euclidean extension, breaking the group-affine structure needed for exact log-linear error dynamics. This causes the reported covariance to degrade along with the estimate.
AI.method: Apply Tangent-Group (TG) symmetry, which carries the biases within the state-space geometry, to derive an Equivariant Filter (EqF). This yields zero linearization error in navigation states and only second-order error in biases. An equivariant output model for the DVL is developed, whose update incurs only third-order linearization error, together with a direct pressure output.
AI.result: Monte Carlo simulations benchmark the TG-EqF against a Two-Frame-Group IEKF and a Multiplicative EKF. The TG-EqF reduces error by 18-25% against both alternatives in attitude, velocity, and position. Its ANEES stays closer to the nominal value of one than the others. Offline analysis on AUV field data corroborates the simulations, showing reduced position drift.
AI.conclusion: The TG-EqF improves both estimation accuracy and covariance consistency over IEKF and MEKF baselines for AUV navigation, validated in simulation and on field data.

title: Geopolitical Divisions Across Languages in Large Language Models
summary: People increasingly turn to AI chatbots for news and explanations of world events. But do they receive the same political answers when they ask in different languages? Here we show that the language of a question can change how the same AI systems assess the war in Ukraine. We ask GPT, Claude and Gemini to evaluate twenty statements about the war in 112 languages, collecting 67,200 responses. The balance between Russia-leaning and Ukraine-leaning responses differs across languages. When we group responses by countries' official languages, they follow a pattern resembling worldwide political divisions: relatively more Russia-leaning answers correspond to more favourable public views of Russia, less support for Ukraine in United Nations votes, and less aid to Ukraine. The broad pattern recurs across all three models and remains when individual statement pairs are removed. Our findings suggest a possible route through which information warfare may shape the text used to train AI models, which may in turn spread geopolitical biases.

AI.tldr: The language of a question changes how GPT, Claude, and Gemini evaluate the war in Ukraine: across 112 languages and 67,200 responses, the Russia-leaning vs. Ukraine-leaning balance varies by language and mirrors real-world geopolitical divisions.
AI.motivation: People increasingly rely on AI chatbots for news and explanations of world events, yet it is unclear whether these systems give consistent political answers across languages. This raises concerns about whether linguistic variation encodes or amplifies geopolitical bias.
AI.method: The authors asked GPT, Claude, and Gemini to evaluate twenty statements about the war in Ukraine in 112 languages, collecting 67,200 responses. They compared the balance of Russia-leaning versus Ukraine-leaning responses across languages, grouped responses by countries' official languages, and tested robustness by removing individual statement pairs.
AI.result: The balance between Russia-leaning and Ukraine-leaning responses differs across languages. When grouped by countries' official languages, the pattern resembles worldwide political divisions: more Russia-leaning answers correspond to more favourable public views of Russia, less support for Ukraine in UN votes, and less aid to Ukraine. The pattern recurs across all three models and remains when individual statement pairs are removed.
AI.conclusion: The findings suggest a possible route through which information warfare may shape the text used to train AI models, which may in turn spread geopolitical biases.

title: LIFD: Anchored Diffusion for 3D-Aware Scene Memory in Robotic Manipulation
summary: Robotic manipulation under partial observability requires spatial information that extends beyond the current view. Geometry-aware RGB features describe visible structure, but previously observed regions may disappear as the robot or scene moves.
