Maintaining a useful scene representation therefore requires retaining observation history while inferring missing content without losing its connection to visible evidence. We introduce LIFD (Look, Imagine, Focus, and Do), a framework for persistent, 3D-aware scene memory. LIFD learns a scene-token representation from multi-view agreement and completes it from a single RGB view and recurrent memory. A rectified-flow model generates the tokens while Anchor-Guided Cross-Attention conditions completion on current geometric features. Compact slot features connect this representation to a manipulation policy. Multi-view and geometric supervision are used during representation learning; deployment requires one RGB camera, proprioception, and a task instruction. LIFD (Staged) reaches 91.6% average success on LIBERO and 79.8% on MetaWorld, improving LIBERO average success by 3.1 percentage points over Joint training. On four UR5e task families with ten demonstrations per family, it achieves 56.0% mean success, compared with 40.5% for OpenVLA-7B.

AI.tldr: LIFD is a framework for persistent, 3D-aware scene memory in robotic manipulation under partial observability, learning scene-token representations from multi-view agreement and completing them via rectified flow and anchor-guided cross-attention, achieving strong success rates on LIBERO, MetaWorld, and real UR5e tasks.
AI.motivation: Robotic manipulation under partial observability needs spatial information beyond the current view. Geometry-aware RGB features only capture visible structure, and previously observed regions vanish as the robot or scene moves, so a useful scene representation must retain observation history and infer missing content while staying tied to visible evidence.
AI.method: LIFD learns a scene-token representation from multi-view agreement and completes it from a single RGB view plus recurrent memory. A rectified-flow model generates the tokens, with Anchor-Guided Cross-Attention conditioning completion on current geometric features. Compact slot features link the representation to a manipulation policy. Multi-view and geometric supervision are used during representation learning; deployment needs only one RGB camera, proprioception, and a task instruction.
AI.result: LIFD (Staged) achieves 91.6% average success on LIBERO and 79.8% on MetaWorld, a 3.1 percentage-point gain over Joint training on LIBERO. On four UR5e task families with ten demonstrations each, it reaches 56.0% mean success versus 40.5% for OpenVLA-7B.
AI.conclusion: LIFD demonstrates that persistent, 3D-aware scene memory built from multi-view agreement and generative completion can support manipulation policies effectively, yielding consistent improvements in simulated and real-world robotic tasks.

title: FedeRICo: Federated Region-Influenced Coupling for Traffic Flow Prediction
summary: Urban traffic forecasting often relies on information distributed across stakeholders who may be unable to share raw data due to privacy or commercial constraints, motivating federated spatial-temporal approaches. In such federated settings, each client observes traffic over a distinct sensor subgraph with its own spatial topology and temporal dynamics, leading to significant heterogeneity across clients. Existing federated spatial-temporal methods typically rely on model parameter aggregation and provide limited mechanisms for recovering spatial dependencies across client boundaries. This introduces two key limitations. Specifically, parameter aggregation across heterogeneous graph domains tends to dilute client-specific representations, while road network partitioning breaks the propagation of traffic dynamics across client boundaries. To address these challenges, we propose FedeRICo, a federated traffic forecasting framework that combines gradient-level collaboration with boundary-aware residual communication. FedeRICo employs a dual-branch forecasting architecture in which a globally guided branch captures transferable forecasting structure, while a private residual branch preserves client-specific corrections and incorporates boundary residual signals. The global branch is coordinated through gradient alignment across all clients, enabling collaborative optimisation without destructive parameter interference. To recover cross-client spatial dependencies, boundary messages are extracted through a trend-residual decomposition that suppresses periodic structure and communicates only transient spatial-temporal residual signals between physically adjacent clients. Experiments across four real-world traffic forecasting benchmarks demonstrate that FedeRICo consistently outperforms state-of-the-art federated spatial-temporal baselines while maintaining competitive training runtime.

AI.tldr: FedeRICo is a federated traffic forecasting framework that uses gradient-level collaboration and boundary-aware residual communication to address client heterogeneity and cross-client spatial dependency loss.
AI.motivation: Urban traffic forecasting requires data distributed across stakeholders who cannot share raw data due to privacy or commercial constraints. In federated settings, each client observes a distinct sensor subgraph with unique spatial topology and temporal dynamics, causing heterogeneity. Existing federated spatial-temporal methods rely on model parameter aggregation and offer limited mechanisms to recover spatial dependencies across client boundaries, leading to two limitations: parameter aggregation across heterogeneous graph domains dilutes client-specific representations, and road network partitioning breaks propagation of traffic dynamics across client boundaries.
AI.method: FedeRICo combines gradient-level collaboration with boundary-aware residual communication. It uses a dual-branch forecasting architecture: a globally guided branch captures transferable forecasting structure, while a private residual branch preserves client-specific corrections and incorporates boundary residual signals. The global branch is coordinated through gradient alignment across all clients, enabling collaborative optimization without destructive parameter interference. Cross-client spatial dependencies are recovered by extracting boundary messages via trend-residual decomposition, which suppresses periodic structure and communicates only transient spatial-temporal residual signals between physically adjacent clients.
AI.result: Experiments on four real-world traffic forecasting benchmarks show that FedeRICo consistently outperforms state-of-the-art federated spatial-temporal baselines while maintaining competitive training runtime.
AI.conclusion: FedeRICo effectively addresses client heterogeneity and broken cross-client spatial dependencies in federated traffic forecasting, achieving superior accuracy over existing baselines with competitive runtime.

title: Affective Shared Autonomy: Temporal Affect Dynamics and Subjective Evaluation in Bimanual Teleoperation Tasks
summary: Physical teleoperation integrates human cognitive flexibility with robotic precision, yet demanding manipulation tasks frequently induce severe cognitive workload, acute frustration, and execution breakdown. Conventional shared autonomy paradigms rely primarily on task-based rules, such as spatial error boundaries, which disregard the operator's transient affective state and risk misaligned control interventions. To address this limitation, we propose an affect-aware shared autonomy teleoperation framework that dynamically modulates robotic assistance based on real-time operator state estimation. The system estimates operator affective states from synchronized facial video, cardiac signals, and bilateral arm kinematics, outputting a seven-state affective distribution and a three-category operational abstraction (neutral, productive, adverse). Affect-aware assistance is selectively triggered when the user is detected in a continuous adverse state, preserving task-positive engagement without unnecessary disruption. The empirical user study ($N = 30$) confirms that the proposed affective assistance increases the productive states by up to 39.7% without compromising user agency. The collected dataset represents the first multimodal dataset that provides continuous visual, physiological, and operator's bilateral motion tracking of temporal affective state shifts during bimanual teleoperation. Our multimodal fusion model outperforms zero-shot baselines (Qwen, MiniCPM-V) in tracking temporal state dynamics. This real-world deployment offers a new human-centric framework that integrates visual, physiological, and motion tracking for physical human-robot interaction.

AI.tldr: An affect-aware shared autonomy framework modulates robotic assistance in physical teleoperation based on real-time multimodal estimation of operator affective state, increasing productive states by up to 39.7% without reducing user agency.
AI.motivation: Demanding teleoperation tasks induce severe cognitive workload, frustration, and execution breakdown. Conventional shared autonomy relies on task-based rules (e.g., spatial error boundaries) that ignore the operator's transient affective state, risking misaligned control interventions.
AI.method: The system estimates operator affective states from synchronized facial video, cardiac signals, and bilateral arm kinematics, outputting a seven-state affective distribution and a three-category operational abstraction (neutral, productive, adverse). Affect-aware assistance is selectively triggered only when a continuous adverse state is detected, preserving task-positive engagement. Evaluation includes a user study (N = 30) and comparison against zero-shot baselines (Qwen, MiniCPM-V).
AI.result: Affective assistance increased productive states by up to 39.7% without compromising user agency. The multimodal fusion model outperformed zero-shot baselines in tracking temporal state dynamics. The collected dataset is the first multimodal dataset providing continuous visual, physiological, and bilateral motion tracking of temporal affective state shifts during bimanual teleoperation.
AI.conclusion: The real-world deployment offers a new human-centric framework integrating visual, physiological, and motion tracking for physical human-robot interaction, enabling affect-aware shared autonomy that aligns assistance with operator state.

title: Can Data Attribution Filter Out Subliminal Learning? Not Reliably
summary: Subliminal learning allows language models to transmit behavioral traits through training data with no obvious semantic relationship to those traits, undermining content-based data filtering as a safety intervention. Training data attribution offers an alternative: it identifies the training examples responsible for a given model behavior, independent of their semantic content, and so may apply in exactly the cases where semantic inspection fails. We evaluate three gradient-based attribution methods (GradCos, a contrastive GradCos variant, and EK-FAC) across three models, comparing them against divergence tokens, a strong baseline previously shown to localize subliminal learning (albeit one that requires access to counterfactual teacher models). Filtering at the token level, EK-FAC mitigates a significant part of the effect, the other methods provide little benefit, and all mostly fall short of divergence tokens. Filtering entire samples is less effective for every method, though EK-FAC often gives a stronger signal than divergence tokens in this setting. Success is inconsistent across methods and settings: variants that work well for some model-preference combinations fail for others, and we do not identify a consistent explanation for these differences. Our results suggest that gradient-based attribution can identify data responsible for subliminal learning in some settings, but that some approximations are more reliable than others.

AI.tldr: Gradient-based training data attribution can partially identify and filter data responsible for subliminal learning, with EK-FAC the most reliable method, though results are inconsistent and generally fall short of a counterfactual-teacher baseline.
AI.motivation: Subliminal learning transmits behavioral traits through training data with no obvious semantic relationship to those traits, which defeats content-based data filtering. Training data attribution is proposed as an alternative because it identifies responsible training examples independent of their semantic content, potentially covering exactly the cases where semantic inspection fails.
AI.method: The authors evaluate three gradient-based attribution methods (GradCos, a contrastive GradCos variant, and EK-FAC) across three models. They compare these against divergence tokens, a strong baseline that localizes subliminal learning but requires access to counterfactual teacher models. Attribution is applied both at the token level and the sample level for filtering.
AI.result: At token-level filtering, EK-FAC mitigates a significant part of the effect, while the other methods provide little benefit and all mostly fall short of divergence tokens. Sample-level filtering is less effective for every method, though EK-FAC often gives a stronger signal than divergence tokens in that setting. Success is inconsistent: variants that work well for some model-preference combinations fail for others, with no consistent explanation identified.
AI.conclusion: Gradient-based attribution can identify data responsible for subliminal learning in some settings, but some approximations (notably EK-FAC) are more reliable than others, and overall performance remains uneven and setting-dependent.

title: HEROIC: Heterogeneous Evidential Reasoning for Open-Vocabulary Identification and Cross-Robot Collaboration
summary: Multi-agent heterogeneous air-ground robot teams are attractive for open world search, with applications for reconnaissance, urban search and rescue missions (USAR), disaster response and recovery, and hazardous environments. These two platforms have different failure modes: aerial robots cover ground quickly but cannot resolve small or occluded targets from altitude, while ground robots can identify objects-of-interest, such as people or hazardous objects, at close range but cover less area. Existing language-tasked teams either have roles fixed prior, or have a language model assign them from hand-written capability tags, so the team is unable to know when within a mission an asset is no longer useful. We present HEROIC, a decentralized heterogeneous multi-agent open-vocabulary search coordination framework that requires agents to communicate in natural language only. HEROIC's initial agent role assignment is derived from sensor properties and a scale law to determine whether targets can be detected with a high confidence. From the mission's natural language prompt alone, this law assigns aerial flight altitudes and sweep spacing. When this calculated height falls below the altitude for safe flight, aerial agents re-task themselves from searcher to aerial triage, escort, and route guide for ground agents. Both robots maintain an evidential belief over the search area (bearing rays for positive evidence, a log-odds posterior for negative evidence) and gate any arrival on close-range verification. In full-stack experiments, HEROIC reaches the target 84% of the time across all 6 scenes, compares to 35-54% for vision-language frontier baselines, frontier-based search, lawnmower, and random-walk running the same perception, all while being 2-4x sooner to arrive at the target.

AI.tldr: HEROIC is a decentralized, open-vocabulary coordination framework for heterogeneous air-ground robot teams that communicates only in natural language, deriving initial roles and flight parameters from a sensor-based scale law and dynamically re-tasking aerial agents when safe flight altitude is exceeded.
AI.motivation: Heterogeneous air-ground teams are promising for open-world search, but the two platforms have complementary failure modes: aerial robots cover ground quickly yet cannot resolve small or occluded targets from altitude, while ground robots identify objects-of-interest at close range but cover less area. Existing language-tasked teams either fix roles in advance or assign them via handwritten capability tags, so they cannot recognize when an asset has become useless mid-mission.
AI.method: A decentralized heterogeneous multi-agent open-vocabulary search coordination framework requiring natural-language communication only. Initial agent role assignment is derived from sensor properties and a scale law that determines whether targets can be detected with high confidence; from the mission's natural-language prompt alone, this law sets aerial flight altitudes and sweep spacing. When the calculated height falls below the safe-flight altitude, aerial agents re-task themselves from searcher to aerial triage, escort, and route guide for ground agents. Both robots maintain an evidential belief over the search area—bearing rays for positive evidence and a log-odds posterior for negative evidence—and gate any arrival on close-range verification.
AI.result: In full-stack experiments, HEROIC reaches the target 84% of the time across all 6 scenes, compared to 35–54% for vision-language frontier baselines, frontier-based search, lawnmower, and random-walk using the same perception, while arriving at the target 2–4x sooner.
AI.conclusion: A scale-law-driven, natural-language-only coordination scheme with dynamic aerial re-tasking and evidential belief fusion substantially outperforms fixed-role and capability-tag baselines in open-vocabulary air-ground search, yielding higher success rates and faster target arrival.

title: DART: Distillation-Aware Reparameterization for Training-Free LoRA Reuse in Few-Step Video Diffusion Models
summary: Step distillation reduces the cost of video generation, but reusing a LoRA trained for a longer trajectory can alter its functional effect or degrade target quality. Static parameter compatibility offers one perspective on this problem; our observations show that similar measured geometry can coexist with different adapter behavior under a shortened denoising schedule. We propose DART, a training-free method that combines low-rank coordinate transport with target-schedule response calibration using forward evaluations and no source training videos. On a four-step Wan2.2 target, DART-F improves the joint quality score from 0.9029 to 0.9227 and changes macro functional retention from -0.4644 to +0.1349. Component analysis shows that calibration accounts for most of the quality improvement, while coordinate transport provides complementary gains when combined with calibration. Adapter-level results reveal positive functional effects for some adapters and strong attenuation with reduced negative functional effects for others. Evaluations on two additional targets show the same aggregate trend. These results motivate evaluating distilled-model LoRA reuse jointly through functional preservation and negative-transfer avoidance, without assuming recovery for every adapter.

AI.tldr: DART, a training-free method combining low-rank coordinate transport with target-schedule response calibration, improves LoRA reuse quality and functional retention when applying adapters to step-distilled video generation models.
AI.motivation: Step distillation lowers video generation cost, but reusing a LoRA trained for a longer denoising trajectory can shift its functional effect or degrade target quality. Static parameter compatibility is insufficient because similar measured geometry can coexist with different adapter behavior under a shortened denoising schedule.
AI.method: DART is a training-free approach that combines low-rank coordinate transport with target-schedule response calibration, using forward evaluations only and requiring no source training videos.
AI.result: On a four-step Wan2.2 target, DART-F raises the joint quality score from 0.9029 to 0.9227 and shifts macro functional retention from -0.4644 to +0.1349. Calibration drives most of the quality gain, while coordinate transport adds complementary benefit when combined. Adapter-level analysis shows positive effects for some adapters and strong attenuation of negative effects for others, with the same aggregate trend on two additional targets.
AI.conclusion: Distilled-model LoRA reuse should be evaluated jointly through functional preservation and negative-transfer avoidance, without assuming recovery for every adapter.

title: Vehicle Trajectory Prediction via Neural Fusion of Multiple EKF-Based Trajectory Candidates
summary: Predicting the future trajectories of surrounding vehicles in autonomous driving is important for collision risk assessment and safe ego-vehicle path planning. Conventional neural network-based trajectory predictors typically achieve strong prediction performance by exploiting agent history, dynamic scene graphs, and semantic maps. However, in specific motion regimes such as acceleration, deceleration, and turning, these predictors may fail to reflect physically feasible trajectories. To address this issue, this study proposes a framework that fuses the output of Trajectron++, a neural network-based trajectory predictor, with extended Kalman filter (EKF)-based multiple trajectory candidates at a late stage. On the nuScenes dataset, the proposed method reduces the average displacement error and final displacement error of the Trajectron++ robot baseline by 13.7% and 14.6%, respectively, without modifying the baseline architecture. These results indicate that EKF-based trajectory candidates can effectively complement neural trajectory prediction through learned fusion.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a late-fusion framework combining Trajectron++ with EKF-based multiple trajectory candidates to improve physically feasible vehicle trajectory prediction, reducing average and final displacement errors on nuScenes.
AI.motivation: Neural network-based trajectory predictors achieve strong performance using agent history, dynamic scene graphs, and semantic maps, but they may fail to produce physically feasible trajectories in specific motion regimes such as acceleration, deceleration, and turning. This limits their reliability for collision risk assessment and safe ego-vehicle path planning in autonomous driving.
AI.method: The study proposes a framework that fuses the output of Trajectron++, a neural network-based trajectory predictor, with extended Kalman filter (EKF)-based multiple trajectory candidates at a late stage. The fusion is learned and does not modify the baseline architecture.
AI.result: On the nuScenes dataset, the proposed method reduces the average displacement error and final displacement error of the Trajectron++ robot baseline by 13.7% and 14.6%, respectively.
AI.conclusion: EKF-based trajectory candidates can effectively complement neural trajectory prediction through learned late-stage fusion, improving physical feasibility and accuracy without altering the baseline architecture.

title: MAGMA-GEN: Validated Recovery Supervision from Ambiguous Failures via Counterfactual Re-Execution
summary: Hierarchical robotic systems executing long-horizon manipulation tasks must make high-level semantic decisions that orchestrate stochastic low-level skills. In this setting, failed rollouts are ambiguous: a poor downstream state may reflect an invalid high-level decision, partial observation, or a valid decision whose physical execution failed. Traditional supervised learning lacks data for such recovery states, while reinforcement learning struggles with sparse rewards and non-local credit assignment. We propose MAGMA-GEN, an on-policy data-generation pipeline that converts ambiguous failed rollouts into validated recovery supervision. MAGMA-GEN first uses a privileged coach to hypothesize an early decision-level error and propose localized correction or recovery actions. Because this diagnosis is fallible, candidates are retained only if re-execution from the same state under matched conditions improves downstream progress. This produces supervised examples from the agent's own failure distribution without per-step human demonstrations. Evaluated on interactive long-horizon manipulation tasks, MAGMA-GEN improves task success and recovery capabilities, against distillation and trajectory-repair baselines under evolving task constraints in both simulation and real-robot execution.

AI.tldr: MAGMA-GEN is an on-policy data-generation pipeline that turns ambiguous failed rollouts in hierarchical long-horizon manipulation into validated recovery supervision, using a privileged coach to hypothesize and then verify decision-level corrections before training.
AI.motivation: In hierarchical robotic systems, failed rollouts are ambiguous: a poor downstream state can stem from an invalid high-level decision, partial observation, or a valid decision whose physical execution failed. Supervised learning lacks data for such recovery states, and reinforcement learning suffers from sparse rewards and non-local credit assignment.
AI.method: MAGMA-GEN is an on-policy pipeline that: (1) uses a privileged coach to hypothesize an early decision-level error and propose localized correction or recovery actions; (2) since this diagnosis is fallible, retains candidates only if re-execution from the same state under matched conditions improves downstream progress; (3) thereby produces supervised examples drawn from the agent's own failure distribution without per-step human demonstrations.
AI.result: On interactive long-horizon manipulation tasks, MAGMA-GEN improves task success and recovery capabilities compared to distillation and trajectory-repair baselines, under evolving task constraints in both simulation and real-robot execution.
AI.conclusion: Validated, on-policy recovery supervision generated from the agent's own failures offers an effective alternative to human demonstrations and sparse-reward RL for hierarchical long-horizon manipulation.

title: RotateIt! Fast and Reliable Single-Arm Garment Unfolding via Online-Adaptive Dynamic Rotation
summary: Robotic garment unfolding is essential for downstream tasks, yet quasi-static methods require repeated actions, while existing dynamic approaches predominantly rely on bimanual flinging. We present RotateIt!, a single-arm framework that uses adaptive axial rotation for dynamic garment unfolding. To the best of our knowledge, it is the first unfolding framework to employ dynamic axial rotation as its primary manipulation primitive. From a randomly initialized tabletop configuration, the robot selects a rotation-effective grasp and rotates the lifted garment about an approximately fixed anchor, generating inertial tension that separates overlapping layers within a compact workspace. A grasp ranker selects the anchor, while an online residual policy adapts the rotation extent and speed, thereby determining the release timing. Across seen and unseen simulated garments and eight unseen real garments, RotateIt! improves success within three attempts by 44.0-61.0 percentage points over quasi-static pick-and-place. The simulation-trained policies transfer zero-shot to the real world, achieving 75.6% success, 41% higher first-attempt coverage, and 26% higher final coverage. The resulting states further enable autonomous robotic folding without manual rearrangement.

AI.tldr: RotateIt! is a single-arm framework that unfolds garments by dynamically rotating them about an approximately fixed anchor, using a grasp ranker and an online residual policy to adapt rotation and release timing, outperforming quasi-static baselines and transferring zero-shot to real garments.
AI.motivation: Robotic garment unfolding is essential for downstream tasks, but quasi-static methods require repeated actions and existing dynamic approaches predominantly rely on bimanual flinging (two arms). A single-arm dynamic alternative is needed.
AI.method: The framework selects a rotation-effective grasp, then rotates the lifted garment about an approximately fixed anchor, generating inertial tension that separates overlapping layers within a compact workspace. A grasp ranker selects the anchor, and an online residual policy adapts the rotation extent and speed, determining release timing.
AI.result: Across seen and unseen simulated garments and eight unseen real garments, RotateIt! improves success within three attempts by 44.0-61.0 percentage points over quasi-static pick-and-place. Simulation-trained policies transfer zero-shot to the real world, achieving 75.6% success, 41% higher first-attempt coverage, and 26% higher final coverage.
AI.conclusion: RotateIt! is the first unfolding framework to employ dynamic axial rotation as its primary manipulation primitive, achieving strong simulation and real-world performance and enabling autonomous robotic folding without manual rearrangement.

title: WiCleanData: Guaranteeing the Type Consistency of Wikidata by Taxonomy Refinement and Constraint Enforcement
summary: Because of its collaborative nature, Wikidata suffers from errors, in- consistencies, and excessive complexity, such as redundant classes, ambiguity between instances and classes, wrong taxonomic paths, and type constraint violations. The manual curation of these issues is infeasible at scale. To address these challenges, we introduce WiCleanData, a refined version of Wikidata with a consistent tax- onomy and free from type constraint violations. Specifically, we have designed an automated pipeline that first cleans the taxonomy with language model assistance, then simplifies type constraints by hierarchical aggregation, and finally filters facts accordingly. The resulting knowledge graph, free from any type violation, is made publicly available via a Web interface, enabling easy exploration and downstream applications.

AI.tldr: WiCleanData is an automated pipeline that produces a refined Wikidata with a consistent taxonomy and no type constraint violations, made publicly available via a Web interface.
AI.motivation: Wikidata's collaborative nature leads to errors, inconsistencies, and excessive complexity (redundant classes, instance-class ambiguity, wrong taxonomic paths, type constraint violations). Manual curation of these issues is infeasible at scale.
AI.method: An automated pipeline that (1) cleans the taxonomy with language model assistance, (2) simplifies type constraints via hierarchical aggregation, and (3) filters facts accordingly.
AI.result: A resulting knowledge graph free from any type violation, publicly available via a Web interface for easy exploration and downstream applications.
AI.conclusion: WiCleanData provides a scalable, refined version of Wikidata with a consistent taxonomy and no type constraint violations, enabling practical reuse.

title: TADreamer: Zero-Shot Language-Guided 3D Navigation for Terrestrial-Aerial Bimodal Robots via Video Imagination
summary: Language-guided navigation for terrestrial-aerial bimodal robots requires selecting routes and locomotion modes that match scene context and task intent. Generated videos can represent such motion sequences, but recovering metrically consistent navigation references from them is challenging because of scale ambiguity and axis-dependent geometric distortions. We present TADreamer, a zero-shot framework that grounds video-imagined navigation in measured geometry without task-specific training or fine-tuning. A vision-language model translates onboard observations and instructions into navigation prompts, selects valid generated videos, and provides corrective feedback when regeneration is needed. The selected video is reconstructed into 3D waypoints annotated with terrestrial or aerial modes. A two-stage calibration procedure uses field-of-view constraints to initialize scale estimation, then refines axis-dependent scales, rotation, and translation by registering the reconstructed point cloud to measured geometry. The calibrated waypoints and mode labels guide a planner that incorporates measured geometry for robot execution. Real-world experiments demonstrate navigation across seven indoor and outdoor scenarios. With five candidates per round, usable videos are obtained within two rounds in all seven scenarios. On the calibration observations, our method reduces mean absolute depth error by 87.7% and mean absolute relative depth error by 86.3% compared with NavDreamer.

AI.tldr: TADreamer is a zero-shot framework that grounds video-imagined navigation for terrestrial-aerial bimodal robots in measured geometry via vision-language prompting, 3D waypoint reconstruction, and two-stage scale/pose calibration, achieving robust real-world navigation across seven indoor and outdoor scenarios.
AI.motivation: Language-guided navigation for terrestrial-aerial bimodal robots requires selecting routes and locomotion modes matching scene context and task intent. Generated videos can represent such motion sequences, but recovering metrically consistent navigation references is hard due to scale ambiguity and axis-dependent geometric distortions.
AI.method: A vision-language model translates onboard observations and instructions into navigation prompts, selects valid generated videos, and provides corrective feedback for regeneration. The selected video is reconstructed into 3D waypoints annotated with terrestrial or aerial modes. A two-stage calibration first initializes scale using field-of-view constraints, then refines axis-dependent scales, rotation, and translation by registering the reconstructed point cloud to measured geometry. Calibrated waypoints and mode labels guide a planner incorporating measured geometry.
AI.result: Real-world experiments cover seven indoor and outdoor scenarios. With five candidates per round, usable videos are obtained within two rounds in all seven scenarios. On calibration observations, the method reduces mean absolute depth error by 87.7% and mean absolute relative depth error by 86.3% versus NavDreamer.
AI.conclusion: TADreamer enables zero-shot, training-free grounding of video-imagined navigation in measured geometry, yielding metrically consistent waypoints that support reliable terrestrial-aerial bimodal robot navigation.

title: FCA-Guided Counterfactual Explanations for Multi-Modal Breast Cancer Diagnosis: A Framework Achieving Perfect Validity with Emergent Sparsity
summary: Deep learning models for multi-modal breast cancer diagnosis achieve high predictive accuracy but remain clinically unacceptable without actionable, counterfactual explanations. Attribution-based methods (LIME, SHAP) are categorically inapplicable to this purpose, as they generate no alternative instances and thus cannot be evaluated on counterfactual quality metrics. This investigation provides empirical evidence that FCA-Guided Counterfactual (FCA-CF) framework that uses a Formal Concept Analysis (FCA) concept lattice as a hard structural constraint on counterfactual search, operating over a multi-modal TCGA-BRCA dataset. We benchmark against four genuine counterfactual methods: Wachter-style CF, DiCE, FACE, and NICE, evaluated on 60 benign-predicted TCGA-BRCA instances. The FCA-CF framework achieves Validity = 1.0000 (100% of counterfactuals successfully flip the prediction), Sparsity = 2.37 features changed (best among all valid methods), and Proximity = 0.900 (normalised L2-based, matching NICE as joint best). The classifier achieves Accuracy = 0.980, F1 = 0.976, ROC-AUC = 0.9947. Ablation analysis confirms that the FCA lattice constraint is the primary sparsity driver (removing it increases sparsity by +40%, p < 0.001, Cohen's d = 0.78), while Phase C greedy refinement accounts for the largest individual contribution (+113% sparsity increase when disabled, p < 0.001, d = 5.01). FCA-guided counterfactual generation achieves a clinically important Pareto-dominant outcome; it is simultaneously the sparsest and among the most proximate of all valid methods, with perfect validity. The emergent sparsity property arising from lattice topology rather than numerical penalty terms constitutes a structurally novel contribution to the counterfactual explanation literature.

Attribution-based methods such as LIME and SHAP are categorically inapplicable for this purpose because they generate no alternative instances and therefore cannot be evaluated on counterfactual quality metrics.

It is benchmarked against four genuine counterfactual methods: Wachter-style CF, DiCE, FACE, and NICE, evaluated on 60 benign-predicted TCGA-BRCA instances. An ablation analysis examines the contribution of the FCA lattice constraint and the Phase C greedy refinement.

title: Improving Cross-embodiment Transfer in Latent Action Models with Action-Similarity Supervision
summary: As generalist robot policies gain vision and language from web-scale pretraining, demonstrations remain costly to collect and tied to the robot that recorded them. Latent action models (LAMs) address both by learning latent actions from action-free videos that can be shared across embodiments, however, in practice, LAMs are sensitive to background visual noise, and the same motion from two different robots may be encoded with different latents. One solution to the background visual noise is to add an auxiliary loss predicting the robot action from the latent action, further associating the latent action space to the embodiment specific robot action space. We study a different use of the same labels, through action-similarity supervision. The similarity between any two latent actions is trained to match the similarity of the two ground-truth robot action sequences. The ground-truth actions are never predicted by the LAM, so the latent action does not need to encode embodiment specifics. We evaluate cross-embodiment transfer on RoboTwin 2.0 in a controlled setup, two bimanual robots demonstrate disjoint task sets, a policy is trained on all the demonstrations, and each robot is evaluated closed-loop on the tasks only the other demonstrated. With the policy architecture and its hyperparameters, the dataset, and the evaluation protocol fixed, predicting latent actions instead of ground-truth actions more than doubles cross-embodiment success. Given the same ground-truth actions, similarity supervision transfers better than an auxiliary loss that predicts the ground-truth action during the LAM training. Computing the similarities on end-effector motion rather than joint-space motion, and letting the loss compare latent actions across the two robots, gives the best approach of the study.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes action-similarity supervision for latent action models (LAMs) to improve cross-embodiment transfer. Instead of predicting ground-truth robot actions, latent actions are trained so that their pairwise similarity matches the similarity of ground-truth action sequences. On RoboTwin 2.0 with two bimanual robots, this approach more than doubles cross-embodiment success compared to predicting ground-truth actions, and outperforms an auxiliary action-prediction loss.
AI.motivation: Demonstrations for generalist robot policies are costly to collect and tied to the recording robot. Latent action models (LAMs) learn latent actions from action-free videos that can be shared across embodiments, but they remain sensitive to background visual noise, and identical motions from different robots may be encoded as different latents. An auxiliary loss that predicts robot actions from latent actions (associating the latent space to embodiment-specific action spaces) is one existing fix. This paper explores a different use of the same action labels to achieve better cross-embodiment transfer.
AI.method: A controlled setup on RoboTwin 2.0: two bimanual robots demonstrate disjoint task sets; a policy is trained on all demonstrations and each robot is evaluated closed-loop on tasks only the other robot demonstrated. The dataset, policy architecture, hyperparameters, and evaluation protocol are fixed. Similarity supervision is used: the similarity between any two latent actions is trained to match the similarity of the two corresponding ground-truth robot action sequences. Ground-truth actions are never predicted, so the latent action need not encode embodiment specifics. The approach also compares computing similarities on end-effector motion versus joint-space motion, and comparing latent actions across the two robots.
AI.result: With the policy architecture, hyperparameters, dataset, and evaluation protocol fixed, predicting latent actions instead of ground-truth actions more than doubles cross-embodiment success. Given the same ground-truth actions, similarity supervision transfers better than an auxiliary loss that predicts the ground-truth action during LAM training. Computing similarities on end-effector motion rather than joint-space motion, and letting the loss compare latent actions across the two robots, yields the best approach in the study.
AI.conclusion: Action-similarity supervision is a more effective use of ground-truth action labels for LAMs than action-prediction auxiliary losses, improving cross-embodiment transfer in a controlled bimanual robot setting. Best performance comes from end-effector-motion similarities and cross-robot latent action comparison.

title: Marginal utility, matrix factorization, and the Key-Value (KV) cache: a unified information-economic framework for sovereign geo-mining inference
comment: Version 11, 14 septembre 2026. 49 pages, 9 tables. Les valeurs de l'architecture souveraine sont projet{é}es et non mesur{é}es ; le calcul {à} grande {é}chelle est en cours. Soumission pr{é}vue {à} IEEE Transactions on Artificial Intelligence
summary: This paper builds a theoretical bridge between the economic notion of marginal utility and two machine-learning constructs, matrix factorization and the Key--Value cache of transformer language models. The singular value spectrum of a rating matrix is shown to be a diminishing marginal utility schedule for latent factors, the eigenvalue spectrum of the projected covariance operator to be the marginal utility schedule of a model's learned representation, and cache eviction and low-rank cache compression to be instances of constrained utility maximization under a memory budget. The three collapse into a single allocation rule: retain the top dimensions whose eigenvalue exceeds the shadow price of the binding constraint. The framework is applied to the automated extraction of structured information from geo-mining documents, where it motivates a multi-pass inference protocol, a layer-wise TIES model merging procedure, and a selection policy combining extraction quality, localization drift and energy, scalarized with a Conditional Value-at-Risk term on drift. Two empirical contributions are reported. An 11.2-million-parameter hierarchical classifier, trained in about five minutes on a single GPU, reaches 90.0 per cent level-1 accuracy on a held-out test set from a 973-document uranium-exploration corpus, against 92.0 per cent for a proprietary model on a fifty-document human audit of the same corpus, at a latency of 2.62 ms per card against approximately 2,000 ms for the API and at negligible cost. A diagnostic of uniform-density TIES merging exposes a reproducible degenerate mode in which the merged model returns token-identical outputs across five geographically distinct districts while declaring high confidence; re-executing the merge under layer-wise calibrated densities removes that signature on the diagnostic sample. The full-scale extraction benchmark, including LoRA fine-tuning, is reported as projected rather than measured and remains an empirical extension of this work.

AI.tldr: The paper unifies marginal utility with matrix factorization and transformer KV-cache, yielding one allocation rule (retain dimensions whose eigenvalue exceeds the shadow price); it applies this to geo-mining document extraction with a multi-pass protocol, layer-wise TIES merging, and a CVaR-scalarized policy, reporting a tiny hierarchical classifier that is fast, cheap, and near proprietary accuracy.
AI.motivation: To bridge economic marginal utility with machine-learning constructs (matrix factorization, transformer Key-Value cache) and to apply the resulting unified framework to automated structured information extraction from geo-mining documents.
AI.method: Theoretical unification: singular value spectrum of a rating matrix as a diminishing marginal utility schedule for latent factors; eigenvalue spectrum of the projected covariance operator as the marginal utility schedule of learned representations; cache eviction and low-rank cache compression as constrained utility maximization under a memory budget; collapse into one allocation rule. Applied via a multi-pass inference protocol, a layer-wise TIES model merging procedure, and a selection policy combining extraction quality, localization drift, and energy, scalarized with a Conditional Value-at-Risk term on drift.
AI.result: An 11.2M-parameter hierarchical classifier trained in ~5 minutes on one GPU reaches 90.0% level-1 accuracy on a held-out test set from a 973-document uranium-exploration corpus, vs 92.0% for a proprietary model on a fifty-document human audit, at 2.62 ms per card latency vs ~2,000 ms for the API and negligible cost. A diagnostic of uniform-density TIES merging exposes a reproducible degenerate mode (token-identical outputs across five geographically distinct districts with high confidence); layer-wise calibrated densities remove that signature on the diagnostic sample.
AI.conclusion: The three constructs reduce to a single constrained utility-maximization allocation rule. The framework motivates practical protocols and merging procedures, and the light classifier offers near-proprietary accuracy at vastly lower latency and cost. The full-scale extraction benchmark, including LoRA fine-tuning, is reported as projected rather than measured and remains an empirical extension.

title: GR2PO: Group Relative Return Policy Optimization for Continuous Robot Control
summary: Actor-critic architecture has been widely used in continuous robot control. However, they rely on learning a value network, introducing additional computational overhead during training. Moreover, policy learning may also be affected by the approximation error of value estimation. Critic-free group relative policy optimization methods provide a simpler training approach by removing the need for a critic. However, they fail to learn long-term action outcomes when directly applying immediate rewards to policy optimization in dense-reward environments. To address these problems, we propose Group Relative Return Policy Optimization (GR2PO), a critic-free reinforcement learning framework for continuous robot control. GR2PO estimates the discounted returns from the parallelly collected trajectories, performs group normalization at each rollout time index, and uses relative advantages and clipped targets to update the policy. To evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed framework, we instantiate it on robot control simulation environments and deploy the model to a real-world edge device. The results show that GR2PO significantly outperforms critic-free baselines that use immediate rewards and performs competitively against state-of-the-art actor-critic methods. Furthermore, GR2PO demonstrates competitive training efficiency. Inference tests on NVIDIA Jetson TX2 demonstrate the feasibility of deploying the learned policies on edge platforms. Further ablation experiments analyze the effects of parallel group size, return estimation methods, and target clipping ratio on learning performance. To support follow-up research, we will make the complete code publicly available after the paper is accepted, including the framework implementation, experimental configuration, and training and evaluation scripts.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes GR2PO, a critic-free reinforcement learning framework for continuous robot control that uses group-normalized discounted returns and relative advantages with clipped targets, outperforming critic-free baselines and matching state-of-the-art actor-critic methods while remaining deployable on edge devices.
AI.motivation: Actor-critic methods for continuous robot control rely on a learned value network, which adds computational overhead during training and can degrade policy learning due to value estimation approximation error. Critic-free group relative policy optimization offers a simpler alternative but, in dense-reward environments, fails to capture long-term action outcomes when immediate rewards are directly used for policy optimization.
AI.method: GR2PO is a critic-free RL framework. It estimates discounted returns from parallelly collected trajectories, performs group normalization at each rollout time index, and updates the policy using relative advantages and clipped targets.
AI.result: On robot control simulation environments and a real-world edge deployment, GR2PO significantly outperforms critic-free baselines using immediate rewards and performs competitively against state-of-the-art actor-critic methods. It also shows competitive training efficiency, and inference tests on NVIDIA Jetson TX2 confirm the feasibility of deploying learned policies on edge platforms. Ablation experiments analyze the effects of parallel group size, return estimation methods, and target clipping ratio.
AI.conclusion: GR2PO provides an effective critic-free reinforcement learning solution for continuous robot control, achieving strong performance and training efficiency without a value network, with demonstrated edge deployability, and code will be released upon acceptance to support follow-up research.

title: Tailored to you: longitudinal effects of personalising language models
summary: Interest in developing personalised language models is rapidly growing. While personalisation is often viewed as a mechanism to better serve diverse user needs, the effects of sustained interactions with personalised models on people's perception of and behaviour toward AI remain poorly understood. Most critically, downstream consequences outside the immediate human--AI interaction loop, such as effects on users' self-perceptions and interpersonal relationships, remain largely unexamined. In this study, we recruited 992 participants to complete daily advice-seeking interactions with language models over the course of five days, comparing outcomes from a non-personalised baseline against two personalisation approaches: memory-based (conditioned on prior conversational history) and survey-based (conditioned on information collected through a pre-study intake survey). We find that several changes in human-AI interaction over time are driven primarily by repeated exposure rather than personalisation itself. However, participants interacting with personalised models experienced differences in advice-seeking and information-sharing attitudes and behaviours: participants in the memory-based condition engaged in greater self-disclosure and rated the model as less creepy, while participants in the survey-based condition reported higher regret about having shared personal information with the AI. We conclude by highlighting the nuanced effects of different personalisation approaches on interaction outcomes, and discussing the implications of these findings for the responsible design and deployment of personalised AI systems.

AI.tldr: A 5-day, 992-participant study compares non-personalised, memory-based, and survey-based personalisation of language models. Many interaction changes are driven by repeated exposure rather than personalisation, but personalisation type differentially affects self-disclosure, perceived creepiness, and regret over sharing personal information.
AI.motivation: Personalised language models are growing rapidly and are often framed as better serving diverse user needs, yet the effects of sustained interaction with them on users' perceptions and behaviours are poorly understood. Crucially, consequences beyond the immediate human–AI interaction loop—such as impacts on users' self-perceptions and interpersonal relationships—remain largely unexamined.
AI.method: 992 participants completed daily advice-seeking interactions with language models over five days. Three conditions were compared: a non-personalised baseline, memory-based personalisation (conditioned on prior conversational history), and survey-based personalisation (conditioned on a pre-study intake survey).
AI.result: Several changes in human–AI interaction over time were driven primarily by repeated exposure rather than personalisation. Nonetheless, personalised conditions differed: the memory-based condition showed greater self-disclosure and lower ratings of the model as creepy, while the survey-based condition reported higher regret about having shared personal information with the AI. Both conditions differed from baseline in advice-seeking and information-sharing attitudes and behaviours.
AI.conclusion: Different personalisation approaches produce nuanced, distinct effects on interaction outcomes. These findings carry implications for the responsible design and deployment of personalised AI systems.

title: Feeling Terrain Before Crossing: World Models for Off-Road Navigation
summary: Navigation world models plan by foresight, predicting the future that each candidate action sequence produces and selecting the best, rather than mapping observations to actions directly. Unlike urban settings where a predicted scene is a sufficient proxy, off-road navigation hinges on the robot--terrain interaction, so the prediction must cover not only what the camera will see but what the robot will feel. However, existing scene-focused models do not predict how much the robot will slip, tilt or shake along a planned trajectory. Proprioception captures these dynamics directly and, when used as input, improves the prediction of the physical future. We present Feel-WM, the first off-road navigation world model that conditions on proprioception and predicts what the robot will feel alongside what the camera will see. The physical future takes the form of a future proprioceptive state and a failure risk, both learned from the robot's own experience without human labels. The planner rolls out the physical future alongside the scene and weighs the predicted failure risk against goal similarity in a separable score. Experiments on real off-road data and in simulation demonstrate that Feel-WM outperforms visual-only navigation world models in open-loop planning and closed-loop rough-terrain navigation across wheeled and legged platforms. Deployed on a Husky on mountain trails, Feel-WM plans onboard, predicts rough ground ahead and steers around it, completing courses that an end-to-end policy fails.

AI.tldr: Feel-WM is the first off-road navigation world model that conditions on proprioception and predicts both future proprioceptive states and failure risk alongside visual scene predictions, improving open-loop planning and closed-loop rough-terrain navigation on wheeled and legged robots.
AI.motivation: Navigation world models plan via foresight, predicting the outcome of candidate action sequences. Unlike urban settings where a predicted camera scene suffices, off-road navigation depends on robot-terrain interaction: prediction must capture not only what the camera will see but what the robot will feel (e.g., slip, tilt, shake). Existing scene-focused world models fail to predict these dynamics, since proprioception, which directly captures them, is not used as input.
AI.method: Feel-WM conditions on proprioception and jointly predicts a physical future (a future proprioceptive state and a failure risk, learned from the robot's own experience without human labels) and the visual future. The planner rolls out the physical future together with the scene and combines predicted failure risk and goal similarity in a separable score.
AI.result: Experiments on real off-road data and in simulation show Feel-WM outperforms visual-only navigation world models in open-loop planning and closed-loop rough-terrain navigation across wheeled and legged platforms. Deployed onboard a Husky on mountain trails, it predicts rough ground ahead, steers around it, and completes courses that an end-to-end policy fails.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating proprioception into an off-road navigation world model enables prediction of the robot's physical future, yielding superior planning and rough-terrain navigation, and successful real-world onboard deployment.

authors: Henrique Curi de Miranda e Lourenço Alves Pereira
title: A Proposal for an Agentic AI Architecture to Support Multi-Domain Decision-Making in the Brazilian Armed Forces
comment: This paper was accepted for publication in the XXVIII SIGE (Simpósio de Aplicações Operacionais em Áreas de Defesa)
summary: The growing complexity of multi-domain operational environments (land, aerospace, naval, cyber, and electromagnetic spectrum) has increased the volume and velocity of data reaching command-and-control (C2) centers, straining the observe-orient-decide-act (OODA) decision cycle. Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems currently employed in defense are, in general, reactive and isolated tools that still rely heavily on human operators to integrate information, assess scenarios, and formulate courses of action. This paper proposes a conceptual Agentic AI architecture for AI systems that can plan, access data sources, execute tools, and act autonomously and audibly, aimed at supporting decision-making across the three Brazilian Armed Forces (Navy, Army, and Air Force). Four application fronts are discussed (decision support, situational analysis, feasibility studies, and countermeasure suggestion), as well as the data and sensor access requirements and the security and permission safeguards necessary for responsible employment across administrative, strategic, operational, and tactical contexts.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a conceptual Agentic AI architecture to support command-and-control decision-making across the three Brazilian Armed Forces, addressing data overload in multi-domain operations. It outlines four application fronts—decision support, situational analysis, feasibility studies, and countermeasure suggestion—along with data/sensor access requirements and security safeguards across administrative, strategic, operational, and tactical levels.
AI.motivation: Multi-domain operational environments (land, aerospace, naval, cyber, and electromagnetic spectrum) generate increasing data volume and velocity that strain the OODA decision cycle at C2 centers. Current defense AI systems are largely reactive, isolated, and depend heavily on human operators to integrate information, assess scenarios, and formulate courses of action, leaving a gap for more autonomous, integrated support.
AI.method: The paper proposes a conceptual Agentic AI architecture enabling systems to plan, access data sources, execute tools, and act autonomously and audibly. It analyzes four application fronts (decision support, situational analysis, feasibility studies, and countermeasure suggestion) and specifies the data and sensor access requirements, plus security and permission safeguards needed for responsible use across administrative, strategic, operational, and tactical contexts.
AI.result: As a conceptual proposal, the paper presents an architectural design and identifies application fronts, data/sensor access needs, and safeguard requirements rather than reporting empirical or experimental outcomes.
AI.conclusion: An Agentic AI architecture can support decision-making across the three Brazilian Armed Forces (Navy, Army, and Air Force) by moving beyond reactive, isolated tools toward autonomous, integrated agents. Responsible employment depends on defined data/sensor access and robust security and permission safeguards spanning administrative, strategic, operational, and tactical contexts.

title: Learning Reliable Parking Policies via Offline Reinforcement Learning with Quantized Action Representations
summary: Parking is a routine yet safety-critical task for autonomous vehicles operating in urban environments. However, cluttered and weakly structured parking spaces, compounded by the interactive uncertainty from surrounding vehicles, hinder reliable maneuver generation. To address these challenges, we develop a waypoint-level offline reinforcement learning framework for interaction-aware autonomous parking. Specifically, a dedicated parking dataset is constructed from hierarchical expert rollouts with rotational waypoint augmentation, covering both non-interactive scenarios and interactive ones. The policy is then conditioned on a compact state representation, in which LiDAR-based obstacle features are adapted to the target pose via feature-wise linear modulation. A state-conditioned tokenizer further quantizes continuous waypoint sequences into discrete action tokens, over which conservative Q-learning is performed to suppress value overestimation on poorly supported actions. Extensive closed-loop experiments are conducted in the high-fidelity CARLA simulator. The proposed framework attains the highest parking success rate among all baselines and transfers reliably to unseen parking slots.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a waypoint-level offline RL framework for interaction-aware autonomous parking, using a dedicated dataset, pose-adapted LiDAR features, and a state-conditioned tokenizer with conservative Q-learning, achieving top success rates in CARLA.
AI.motivation: Parking is safety-critical for autonomous vehicles in urban settings, but cluttered, weakly structured parking spaces and interactive uncertainty from surrounding vehicles hinder reliable maneuver generation.
AI.method: A parking dataset is built from hierarchical expert rollouts with rotational waypoint augmentation, covering non-interactive and interactive scenarios. The policy uses a compact state representation where LiDAR obstacle features are adapted to the target pose via feature-wise linear modulation. A state-conditioned tokenizer quantizes continuous waypoint sequences into discrete action tokens, and conservative Q-learning suppresses value overestimation on poorly supported actions.
AI.result: In closed-loop experiments in the high-fidelity CARLA simulator, the framework achieves the highest parking success rate among all baselines and transfers reliably to unseen parking slots.
AI.conclusion: The waypoint-level offline RL framework with pose-adapted features, discrete action tokenization, and conservative Q-learning enables interaction-aware autonomous parking with strong success and generalization.

title: UnifiedPlayers: Enhance Tool-Integrated Reasoning in Agentic Reinforcement Learning
summary: Self-evolving methods reduce the need for human-annotated trajectories by allowing tool-using agents to generate their own training data. Yet existing methods typically separate trajectory generation from evaluation, relying on static verifiers that cannot adapt to emerging failure modes or self-consistency signals that may reinforce errors shared across trajectories. Jointly adapting planning, execution, and evaluation offers a promising alternative, but introduces a fundamental coordination challenge: each component continuously changes the data or feedback used to train the others. We address this challenge with \textbf{UnifiedPlayers}, a cooperative framework comprising a Planning Player that generates tasks, an Execution Player that produces multi-turn trajectories with Python tool calls, and an Evaluation Player that constructs executable verifiers. We design role-specific rewards that coordinate the three players toward a shared learning objective under GRPO. Across two model backbones and twelve reasoning benchmarks, UnifiedPlayers outperforms the strongest prior baseline by at least 3.5\% on mathematical reasoning and 3.9\% on general reasoning tasks. Moreover, the learned verifier achieves 84.2\% adversarial detection accuracy, while its reward signal exhibits 2.03$\times$ higher per-question variance than a self-consistency baseline, providing more discriminative verifications. These results highlight cooperation among specialized players as a promising path toward self-enhanced tool-integrated agents.

AI.tldr: UnifiedPlayers is a cooperative self-evolving framework with role-specialized planner, executor, and evaluator players jointly trained under GRPO with role-specific rewards, improving reasoning performance and producing discriminative executable verifiers.
AI.motivation: Self-evolving tool-using agents reduce reliance on human-annotated trajectories by generating their own training data, but existing methods decouple trajectory generation from evaluation. They use static verifiers that cannot adapt to emerging failure modes or self-consistency signals that may reinforce shared errors. Jointly adapting planning, execution, and evaluation is promising but creates a coordination challenge, since each component continuously alters the data or feedback used to train the others.
AI.method: The authors propose UnifiedPlayers, a cooperative framework of three players: a Planning Player that generates tasks, an Execution Player that produces multi-turn trajectories with Python tool calls, and an Evaluation Player that constructs executable verifiers. Role-specific rewards are designed to coordinate the three players toward a shared learning objective under GRPO.
AI.result: Across two model backbones and twelve reasoning benchmarks, UnifiedPlayers exceeds the strongest prior baseline by at least 3.5% on mathematical reasoning and 3.9% on general reasoning tasks. The learned verifier reaches 84.2% adversarial detection accuracy, and its reward signal shows 2.03x higher per-question variance than a self-consistency baseline, yielding more discriminative verifications.
AI.conclusion: Cooperation among specialized players is a promising direction for building self-enhanced, tool-integrated agents.

title: Learning and Transferring Closed-Loop Robot Software
summary: Closed-loop robot policies require observation processing, state management, and situation-dependent branching, making them costly to design and tune manually. Although coding agents increasingly support control-code generation and optimization, it remains unclear whether implementations improved on source tasks also support policy acquisition for new tasks. We study this question by treating complete closed-loop implementations as reusable execution experience. For each source task, a coding agent generates policy code from a few successful demonstrations and iteratively improves it using simulation feedback. The validation-selected implementations are retained in a software archive. For new tasks, the agent generates and improves policies using archived implementations, target demonstrations, and execution feedback. The resulting policy is then frozen and executes without further model calls. Across four source tasks in RoboCasa, iterative optimization increases mean success from 28.3% to 64.2%. Across nine target tasks and three independent runs, mean success is 45.2% without references, 41.5% with initial source code, and 57.0% with optimized source code. Optimized references outperform initial references in all three runs on the nine-task average, with a mean gain of 15.6 percentage points. These results demonstrate the value of execution-improved software as a resource for acquiring new policies in this setting, although initial references remain better on two target tasks when averaged across runs.

AI.tldr: A coding agent iteratively improves closed-loop robot policy code on source tasks, archives the optimized implementations, and reuses them as references to acquire policies for new tasks, improving mean success over no-reference and initial-reference baselines.
AI.motivation: Closed-loop robot policies require observation processing, state management, and situation-dependent branching, making manual design and tuning costly. Coding agents can generate and optimize control code, but it is unclear whether improvements found on source tasks transfer as useful experience for acquiring policies on new tasks.
AI.method: Complete closed-loop implementations are treated as reusable execution experience. For each source task, a coding agent generates policy code from a few successful demonstrations and iteratively improves it using simulation feedback; validation-selected implementations are stored in a software archive. For each new task, the agent generates and improves policies using archived implementations, target demonstrations, and execution feedback. The final policy is frozen and executes without further model calls. Evaluated on four RoboCasa source tasks and nine target tasks over three independent runs.
AI.result: Iterative optimization on source tasks raises mean success from 28.3% to 64.2%. On the nine target tasks over three runs, mean success is 45.2% without references, 41.5% with initial source code, and 57.0% with optimized source code. Optimized references beat initial references in all three runs on the nine-task average, with a mean gain of 15.6 percentage points, though initial references remain better on two target tasks when averaged across runs.
AI.conclusion: Execution-improved software serves as a valuable resource for acquiring new closed-loop robot policies, outperforming both no-reference and initial-reference conditions on average, with task-specific exceptions where initial references are preferable.

title: Solving Minimum Span Antibandwidth and Cyclic Antibandwidth Labeling Problems
summary: The Antibandwidth and Cyclic Antibandwidth problems are NP-hard graph labeling problems that aim to maximize the minimum (cyclic) distance between labels assigned to adjacent vertices. Extensive research on these problems has resulted in a variety of mathematical formulations and computational approaches. However, their minimum span perspective, in which a prescribed minimum (cyclic) distance is fixed and the objective is to minimize the label span, has received comparatively little attention. In this paper, we consider this complementary perspective by introducing the Minimum Span Antibandwidth/Cyclic Antibandwidth Labeling (MSABL/MSCABL) problems and developing a unified Boolean Satisfiability (SAT)-based framework for solving them. The SAT-based framework formulates MSABL/MSCABL as a sequence of decision problems and exploits their monotonicity to accelerate the search process. We also consider two SAT solving strategies, parallel and incremental SAT solving: the former examines multiple candidate spans concurrently, while the latter reuses a single SAT instance while progressively restricting the label domain. The proposed approaches are evaluated on benchmark instances from the Harwell-Boeing Sparse Matrix Collection and compared with CPLEXCP, CPLEXMIP, and Gurobi. The results show that SAT-based approaches are highly competitive in solution quality, with the parallel approach performing best overall for MSCABL and the incremental approach for MSABL. With the no-hole constraint, they remain competitive with CPLEXCP and significantly outperform CPLEXMIP and Gurobi, particularly for MSCABL. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of SAT solving as an exact approach for MSABL and MSCABL.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the Minimum Span Antibandwidth/Cyclic Antibandwidth Labeling (MSABL/MSCABL) problems and proposes a unified SAT-based framework, using parallel and incremental SAT solving strategies, that is competitive with CPLEX and Gurobi on Harwell-Boeing benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Antibandwidth and Cyclic Antibandwidth are NP-hard graph labeling problems, but existing research focuses mostly on the maximum minimum-distance perspective. Their complementary minimum span perspective, where a prescribed minimum (cyclic) distance is fixed and the label span is minimized, has received little attention.
AI.method: The authors formulate MSABL/MSCABL as a sequence of decision problems and exploit monotonicity to accelerate search within a unified Boolean Satisfiability (SAT)-based framework. Two SAT solving strategies are considered: parallel SAT solving, which examines multiple candidate spans concurrently, and incremental SAT solving, which reuses a single SAT instance while progressively restricting the label domain.
AI.result: Evaluated on benchmark instances from the Harwell-Boeing Sparse Matrix Collection and compared against CPLEXCP, CPLEXMIP, and Gurobi, the SAT-based approaches are highly competitive in solution quality. The parallel approach performs best overall for MSCABL and the incremental approach for MSABL. With the no-hole constraint, they remain competitive with CPLEXCP and significantly outperform CPLEXMIP and Gurobi, especially for MSCABL.
AI.conclusion: The results demonstrate the effectiveness of SAT solving as an exact approach for the MSABL and MSCABL problems.

title: Distributed Model Predictive Control with Connectivity-based Contracts
summary: Teams of mobile robots rely on continuous communication with their neighbors for coordination, yet most distributed model predictive control (DMPC) schemes assume the communication network stays connected rather than actively enforcing it. Adding such a guarantee is hard since the usual mathematical condition for connectivity is nonconvex and links every agent to every other, which is incompatible with a scalable distributed real-time controller. We propose a DMPC framework in which each agent is assigned a connectivity contract: a local region prescribing where its predicted positions may lie over the prediction horizon. The contracts are designed so that, as long as every agent stays within its own contract, the team is guaranteed to remain connected. Given the maintained contract graph, an agent builds its contract from a single exchange with its immediate neighbors, after which every agent solves its own optimization problem independently. We prove that the resulting closed-loop system maintains connectivity, avoids collisions, and respects local state and input constraints. Simulation and hardware experiments on miniature autonomous car-like robots demonstrate the approach.

AI.tldr: A DMPC framework uses local "connectivity contracts" so each agent can independently guarantee team connectivity with only neighbor-to-neighbor information exchange.
AI.motivation: Most distributed model predictive control (DMPC) schemes for mobile robot teams assume the communication network remains connected instead of actively enforcing it. Enforcing connectivity is difficult because the standard mathematical condition is nonconvex and couples every agent to every other, which is incompatible with a scalable distributed real-time controller.
AI.method: Each agent is assigned a connectivity contract: a local region prescribing where its predicted positions may lie over the prediction horizon. Contracts are designed so that if every agent stays within its own contract, the team remains connected. Given the maintained contract graph, each agent builds its contract from a single exchange with its immediate neighbors, then solves its own optimization problem independently.
AI.result: The closed-loop system is proven to maintain connectivity, avoid collisions, and respect local state and input constraints. The approach is demonstrated in simulation and hardware experiments on miniature autonomous car-like robots.
AI.conclusion: Connectivity contracts enable scalable, distributed real-time DMPC that actively guarantees network connectivity without the nonconvex all-to-all coupling of standard connectivity conditions.

title: Perception, Layout, and Validation: Calibrated Confidence for Reliable Straight-Through Processing of Financial Documents
summary: Straight-through processing (STP) on extracted key-value fields from financial documents without human review requires a calibrated probability together with a bounded guarantee on the residual error of the auto-approved tier. The emergence of modern Vision Language Models (VLMs) provides an out-of-the-box capability for extracting the key-values, but their verbalized confidence signals are unreliable and weakly track field correctness. This paper introduces a decomposed confidence layer along three interpretable channels, including perception, layout, and validation. Together with a final conformal risk control, the score can be used for reliable STP of financial documents. The method is validated on three public datasets covering real invoices, synthetic invoices, and ad-buy forms, using two different VLM families (Qwen3.6-27B and Gemini-3.1-Flash-Lite). Our decomposed score consistently improves the separation of correct from incorrect extractions, substantially raising the AUROC from 0.54-0.74 for VLM verbalized signals to 0.90-0.99 with contributions from all three designed channels. Crucially for industrial deployment, this enables usable STP. The native VLM confidence signals could clear only 0.1%-7.0% of fields under risk control at a target error of <10%. In contrast, the proposed method auto-approves 49-72% of fields while holding the empirical error of the accepted tier at or below the target.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a decomposed confidence layer with perception, layout, and validation channels plus conformal risk control to enable reliable straight-through processing of key-value fields extracted from financial documents by VLMs, raising AUROC to 0.90-0.99 and auto-approving 49-72% of fields at <10% error.
AI.motivation: STP on extracted key-value fields from financial documents without human review requires a calibrated probability together with a bounded guarantee on the residual error of the auto-approved tier. Although modern VLMs can extract key-values out of the box, their verbalized confidence signals are unreliable and only weakly track field correctness, limiting their industrial deployment.
AI.method: A decomposed confidence layer along three interpretable channels-perception, layout, and validation-is introduced, combined with a final conformal risk control to produce a score usable for reliable STP of financial documents.
AI.result: Validated on three public datasets (real invoices, synthetic invoices, ad-buy forms) with two VLM families (Qwen3.6-27B and Gemini-3.1-Flash-Lite), the decomposed score consistently improves separation of correct from incorrect extractions, raising AUROC from 0.54-0.74 for VLM verbalized signals to 0.90-0.99, with contributions from all three channels. Native VLM confidence signals could clear only 0.1%-7.0% of fields under risk control at a target error of <10%, whereas the proposed method auto-approves 49-72% of fields while holding empirical error of the accepted tier at or below target.
AI.conclusion: The decomposed confidence score with conformal risk control enables usable STP in industrial deployment, substantially improving correctness discrimination and auto-approval rates over native VLM confidence signals while respecting bounded error guarantees.

title: Co-VLA: Consensus-based Federated Training for Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Vision-language-action models (VLAs) have emerged as a promising paradigm for general-purpose robot learning, with performance improving as models and datasets scale.
