Scaling robot data collection, however, remains challenging because data are naturally distributed across robots, tasks, and locations, making centralization costly or impractical. Federated learning offers a way to train on decentralized robot data, but applying it to VLAs requires accounting for heterogeneous robot client data distributions. We present Co-VLA, which applies consensus optimization using the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers~(ADMM) to federated VLA training. We show that the same algorithm supports both full-model training and parameter-efficient fine-tuning with both fixed-rank and rank-adaptive adapters. The name Co-VLA reflects both consensus and collaboration: clients with different local robot datasets collaboratively train a shared model without sharing their data. Our experiments demonstrate that Co-VLA achieves performance comparable to centralized training in both full-model training and parameter-efficient fine-tuning settings.

AI.tldr: Co-VLA applies ADMM-based consensus optimization to federated vision-language-action model training, supporting full-model training and parameter-efficient fine-tuning with fixed-rank and rank-adaptive adapters, achieving performance comparable to centralized training while keeping robot data decentralized.
AI.motivation: Vision-language-action models improve with scale, but scaling robot data collection is hard because data are naturally distributed across robots, tasks, and locations, making centralization costly or impractical. Federated learning can train on decentralized data, yet applying it to VLAs must handle heterogeneous robot client data distributions.
AI.method: Co-VLA formulates federated VLA training as consensus optimization solved via the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM). Clients with different local robot datasets collaboratively train a shared model without sharing data. The same algorithm supports both full-model training and parameter-efficient fine-tuning, including fixed-rank and rank-adaptive adapters.
AI.result: Experiments show that Co-VLA achieves performance comparable to centralized training in both full-model training and parameter-efficient fine-tuning settings.
AI.conclusion: Co-VLA offers a practical federated approach for training VLAs on decentralized, heterogeneous robot data, spanning full-model and parameter-efficient regimes, matching centralized performance while preserving data privacy.

title: MTVA-Bench: Evaluating the Language Model Inside Cascaded Voice Agents
summary: Generally, most voice agents are cascaded systems, i.e., an ASR model transcribes the caller's audio, a language model reads the transcript and decides what to say and which backend tools to call, and a TTS model speaks the reply. Nearly all of the decision making happens in the language model, but existing evaluations measure it either too broadly or too narrowly. End-to-end voice benchmarks score the full pipeline, so recognition errors and model errors mix into a single number. LLM benchmarks isolate the model but they do not evaluate what makes real phone calls hard, such as transcription issues, caller's voice being split across messages and the requirement that replies follow the language and script specified. We introduce the Multi-Turn Voice Agent Benchmark (MTVA-Bench), which evaluates the language model on the same conditions it faces inside a cascaded system. The caller is played by an LLM following a set of rubrics and tool calls are answered by a mock backend which responds to the arguments the model actually sent. The benchmark contains 49 agents working across 490 reviewed scenarios and supports 7 languages. Scoring is a combination of deterministic checks on tool calls with two LLM judges, one that scores scenario specific rules and one that grades conversation quality without access to the task. Both judges must cite specific messages from the transcript. Task and conversation scores are weighted equally, since a call can complete its task and still go badly for the caller. In a seven-model study, six of the models select the correct tool within 6.4 points of one another, but their overall scores span 24.4 points. Most of the gap comes from argument values, action ordering, rule compliance, and what the model says around its tool calls.

AI.tldr: MTVA-Bench evaluates the language model of cascaded voice agents under realistic phone-call conditions, using LLM callers, a mock tool backend, deterministic tool-call checks, and two citation-grounded LLM judges across 49 agents, 490 scenarios, and 7 languages.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations of the decision-making component in cascaded voice agents are mismatched: end-to-end voice benchmarks conflate ASR errors with model errors into one score, while LLM benchmarks ignore the actual difficulties of phone calls, such as transcription issues, caller turns split across messages, and language/script constraints on replies.
AI.method: MTVA-Bench places the language model in the same conditions it faces inside a cascaded system. An LLM caller follows rubrics, and a mock backend answers tool calls based on the arguments actually sent. It covers 49 agents, 490 reviewed scenarios, and 7 languages. Scoring combines deterministic tool-call checks with two LLM judges: one scores scenario-specific rules, the other grades conversation quality without task access; both must cite specific transcript messages. Task and conversation scores are weighted equally.
AI.result: In a seven-model study, six models select the correct tool within 6.4 points of each other, yet overall scores span 24.4 points. Most of the gap stems from argument values, action ordering, rule compliance, and the model's utterances around tool calls.
AI.conclusion: Tool selection alone is a weak discriminator of voice-agent language models; meaningful differences lie in argument correctness, action ordering, rule adherence, and conversational behavior surrounding tool calls, which MTVA-Bench captures by weighting task and conversation quality equally.

title: Execution-Aware Pre-Execution Ranking for Grasp-Conditioned Robotic Placement
summary: A geometrically valid placement can still be difficult to execute because the selected grasp changes the required end-effector pose, collision geometry, and transport motion. Placement is formulated as a pre-execution ranking problem in which supplied grasp-placement candidates are scored before planning. The model combines a typed target-conditioned point cloud with three pose descriptors and hierarchical heads for planning success and execution success conditioned on planning. On a 30-object, 1,235-scene dataset with scene-group-held-out splits, three-seed top-1 success on covered test groups reaches 85.63 +/- 1.08% for joint selection and 79.84 +/- 0.16% for fixed-target ranking. For the designated frozen seed-42 checkpoint, top-1 success improves from 72.84% to 85.78% over full-pool cuMotion for joint ranking and from 59.65% to 79.67% for fixed-target ranking. Frozen transfer to xArm7/MoveIt requires no xArm-specific retraining. Across 27 locked cases, 13 complete end to end (48.15%). Of the 16 cases that pass Top-5 preflight and begin execution, 13 succeed (81.25%). Candidate-level deployment-feasibility prediction reaches 81.25% recall, 85.20% specificity, and 83.23% balanced accuracy.

AI.tldr: The paper formulates robot placement as a pre-execution ranking problem, scoring supplied grasp-placement candidates before planning using a hierarchical model that predicts planning success and subsequent execution success.
AI.motivation: A geometrically valid placement can still be hard to execute because the chosen grasp alters the required end-effector pose, collision geometry, and transport motion, so validity alone is insufficient for reliable execution.
AI.method: The model combines a typed target-conditioned point cloud with three pose descriptors and hierarchical heads that predict planning success and execution success conditioned on planning. Evaluation uses a 30-object, 1,235-scene dataset with scene-group-held-out splits and frozen transfer to xArm7/MoveIt without xArm-specific retraining.
AI.result: Three-seed top-1 success on covered test groups reaches 85.63 +/- 1.08% for joint selection and 79.84 +/- 0.16% for fixed-target ranking. For the frozen seed-42 checkpoint, top-1 success improves from 72.84% to 85.78% over full-pool cuMotion for joint ranking and from 59.65% to 79.67% for fixed-target ranking. Across 27 locked cases, 13 succeed end to end (48.15%); of 16 cases passing Top-5 preflight, 13 succeed (81.25%). Candidate-level deployment-feasibility prediction achieves 81.25% recall, 85.20% specificity, and 83.23% balanced accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Pre-execution hierarchical ranking of grasp-placement candidates substantially improves placement success and transfers across robot and planning stacks without retraining.

title: PaGNet: A Panel-Aware GBDT--Neural Network for Multi-Target Corporate Tax Avoidance Proxy Forecasting
summary: Forecasting corporate tax avoidance proxies from firm--year panel data is challenging because predictive signals are distributed across short firm histories and related targets, while screening-oriented use requires transparent model behavior. We propose PaGNet (Panel-Aware GBDT--Neural Network), a two-branch hybrid that combines a LightGBM branch using panel-temporal summaries with a Panel-MLP branch using attention-pooled temporal aggregation and shared-trunk multi-task learning. A per-target validation-optimal blender produces both the final prediction and a compact branch-reliance diagnostic without trainable fusion parameters. On the KoTaP panel of 1{,}754 Korean listed firms from 2011--2024, PaGNet is evaluated under a leakage-free, shared-hyperparameter protocol across four feature regimes. In the direct-proxy-lag-excluded FS1 regime and the tax-history-augmented FS2 regime, accrual targets (TSTA, TSDA) route stably to the LightGBM branch, where PaGNet raises explained variance over the strongest of six baselines by roughly $0.08$--$0.11$ on the primary split. GETR often leans toward the neural branch, while CETR exposes a validation--test branch-selection mismatch rather than a stable branch assignment. A panel-flatten control shows that most accrual gains come from observed multi-year base-panel values, with PaGNet's panel-aware representation adding a smaller but directionally consistent refinement. Rolling-origin analysis confirms stable accrual routing, bounds ETR diagnostics to split-specific behavior, and identifies a far-horizon split where supervised models underperform naive persistence. PaGNet is therefore best viewed not as a universally superior tabular learner, but as a proxy-aware panel model that combines competitive forecasting with explicit per-target branch-reliance reporting.

AI.tldr: PaGNet, a two-branch panel-aware GBDT-neural hybrid, forecasts corporate tax avoidance proxies with competitive accuracy and transparent per-target branch-reliance diagnostics.
AI.motivation: Forecasting corporate tax avoidance proxies from firm-year panel data is difficult: predictive signals are spread across short firm histories and related targets, and screening-oriented use demands transparent model behavior.
AI.method: A two-branch hybrid combines a LightGBM branch on panel-temporal summaries with a Panel-MLP branch using attention-pooled temporal aggregation and shared-trunk multi-task learning. A per-target validation-optimal blender yields predictions and a branch-reliance diagnostic without trainable fusion parameters. Evaluated on the KoTaP panel (1,754 Korean listed firms, 2011-2024) under a leakage-free, shared-hyperparameter protocol across four feature regimes.
AI.result: In FS1 and FS2 regimes, accrual targets (TSTA, TSDA) route to LightGBM, raising explained variance over the strongest of six baselines by ~0.08-0.11. GETR leans neural; CETR shows a validation-test branch-selection mismatch. A panel-flatten control shows most accrual gains come from observed multi-year base-panel values. Rolling-origin analysis confirms stable accrual routing, bounds ETR diagnostics to split-specific behavior, and finds a far-horizon split where supervised models underperform naive persistence.
AI.conclusion: PaGNet is best viewed not as a universally superior tabular learner but as a proxy-aware panel model coupling competitive forecasting with explicit per-target branch-reliance reporting.

title: LapaTrack-3D: 6 DoF pre-operative shape tracking for laparoscopic surgery
comment: This paper has been accepted by IEEE Transactions on Medical Robotics and Bionics (T-MRB)
summary: This work proposes a real-time 6 Degree-of-Freedom (6 DoF) tracking algorithm for monocular laparoscopic surgery. It provides alignment between intra-operative video and pre-operative data (e.g., CT). The 6 DoF tracking offers a solution for accurately locating the internal anatomy of the target organ despite the lack of tactile feedback and transparency. The ORB-SLAM2 framework is adopted and modified for prior-based 3D tracking with four major modifications. First, the primitive 3D shape is used for fast initialization of the ORB-SLAM2 monocular mode. Second, a pseudo-segmentation strategy is employed to separate the target organ from the background for tracking. Third, the 3D shape is incorporated as a geometric prior in its pose graph optimization. Fourth, the Multi-Scale Retinex with Chromaticity Preservation (MSRCP) algorithm is leveraged and modified for image enhancement in challenging illumination scenarios. In-vivo and ex-vivo experiments validate that LapaTrack-3D provides robust 3D tracking and effectively handles typical challenges such as poor illumination, fast motion, out-of-field-of-view scenarios, partial visibility, and ``organ-background'' relative motion. LapaTrack-3D achieves a processing rate of 13 Hz for 1280*720 pixel video.

AI.tldr: LapaTrack-3D: a real-time 6 DoF monocular laparoscopic surgery tracking algorithm based on a modified ORB-SLAM2, achieving 13 Hz on 1280×720 video and validated in in-vivo and ex-vivo experiments.
AI.motivation: Monocular laparoscopic surgery lacks tactile feedback and transparency, making it difficult to accurately locate internal anatomy of a target organ. Aligning intra-operative video with pre-operative data (e.g., CT) via 6 DoF tracking addresses this need.
AI.method: Adopts and modifies ORB-SLAM2 for prior-based 3D tracking with four key changes: (1) primitive 3D shape for fast initialization of the monocular mode; (2) pseudo-segmentation to separate target organ from background; (3) 3D shape used as a geometric prior in pose graph optimization; (4) modified Multi-Scale Retinex with Chromaticity Preservation (MSRCP) for image enhancement under challenging illumination.
AI.result: In-vivo and ex-vivo experiments show robust 3D tracking, handling poor illumination, fast motion, out-of-field-of-view, partial visibility, and organ-background relative motion. Processing rate of 13 Hz for 1280×720 pixel video.
AI.conclusion: LapaTrack-3D provides a robust, real-time 6 DoF monocular laparoscopic tracking solution enabling intra-operative video to pre-operative CT alignment under challenging surgical conditions.

title: Sequential Contextual Fit Predicts Human Behavioural and Neural Dynamics Across Domains
summary: Human perception, action and decision making unfold in sequences, but computational predictors are often domain-specific. This study computes and tests sequential contextual fit (SCF), an embedding-based measure of how well a current information state matches its recent context. The metric uses a simple recency-weighted similarity kernel and can be applied to words, sounds, visual scenes, affective states, choices, actions and neural representations. Across language processing, music-evoked emotion, a subset of audiovisual emotion EEG data, gambling decisions, human activity recognition and decision-related EEG, lower contextual fit predicted longer processing times, larger affective or behavioural transitions and stronger neural-state changes. These effects remained after controlling for established predictors including surprisal, reinforcement-learning prediction error, acoustic change, visual change and sensor change. SCF therefore provides a computational measurement layer for relating contextual compatibility to behavioural processing and cognitive/neural state-transition dynamics.

AI.tldr: Sequential contextual fit (SCF) is proposed as a domain-general, embedding-based measure of how well a current information state matches its recent context, and it consistently predicts processing difficulty, behavioural shifts, and neural-state transitions across multiple domains.
AI.motivation: Human perception, action, and decision making unfold sequentially, yet existing computational predictors tend to be domain-specific. There is a need for a general measurement layer that links contextual compatibility to behavioural processing and cognitive/neural state-transition dynamics.
AI.method: The authors compute SCF using a simple recency-weighted similarity kernel over embeddings, assessing how well a current information state fits its recent context. They apply this single metric across diverse domains: language processing, music-evoked emotion, a subset of audiovisual emotion EEG data, gambling decisions, human activity recognition, and decision-related EEG. They test whether lower SCF predicts longer processing times, larger affective or behavioural transitions, and stronger neural-state changes, while controlling for established predictors such as surprisal, reinforcement-learning prediction error, acoustic change, visual change, and sensor change.
AI.result: Across all tested domains, lower contextual fit predicted longer processing times, larger affective or behavioural transitions, and stronger neural-state changes. These effects survived controls for established predictors including surprisal, reinforcement-learning prediction error, acoustic change, visual change, and sensor change.
AI.conclusion: SCF offers a domain-general computational measurement layer for relating contextual compatibility to behavioural processing and cognitive/neural state-transition dynamics.

title: Hybrid Residual Reinforcement Learning for Contact-Rich Robotic Book Insertion
summary: Placing a grasped book into a tight shelf is a compact but difficult contact-rich control problem: millimetre-scale pose error can turn a geometrically valid approach into jamming, failed release, or incomplete seating. We study this final phase after grasp acquisition and global approach, and ask how control authority should be divided between known geometry and learned behaviour. Our method retains a nominal task-space controller for structured insertion and seating, while residual PPO supplies bounded local corrections and decides when to release. Only the brief open-retreat-reclose transition is scripted. For the final policy used on hardware, a deployment-matched simulation evaluation over 512 fixed conditions yields 98.50 percent mean success (0.23 percentage-point sample SD) across three independent training runs, compared with 37.89 percent for nominal control. On the physical xArm7, 60 trials over 30 matched conditions show the same qualitative advantage: residual control raises success from 26.7 percent to 63.3 percent, reduces failures from 22 to 11, and wins 13 of the 15 matched conditions in which the two controllers differ. Robustness tests show that performance remains above 87 percent under initialization perturbations up to 1.5x, while very tight clearances expose the geometric limit of local correction. These results support a hybrid design in which geometry preserves reliable task structure and learning is concentrated on the contact-sensitive behaviour that fixed rules handle poorly.

AI.tldr: A hybrid controller keeps a nominal task-space controller for structured book insertion into tight shelves and adds bounded residual PPO corrections plus a learned release decision; it reaches 98.5% simulated success vs 37.9% nominal, and 63.3% vs 26.7% on a physical xArm7.
AI.motivation: Placing a grasped book into a tight shelf is a compact, contact-rich control problem where millimetre-scale pose error can cause jamming, failed release, or incomplete seating. The paper studies the final phase after grasp acquisition and global approach and asks how control authority should be divided between known geometry and learned behaviour.
AI.method: A nominal task-space controller handles structured insertion and seating, while residual PPO supplies bounded local corrections and decides when to release. Only the brief open-retreat-reclose transition is scripted. The final policy is evaluated in deployment-matched simulation over 512 fixed conditions across three independent training runs, and on a physical xArm7 in 60 trials over 30 matched conditions, with robustness tests on initialization perturbations and tight clearances.
AI.result: Simulation yields 98.50% mean success (0.23 percentage-point sample SD) versus 37.89% for nominal control. On hardware, residual control raises success from 26.7% to 63.3%, reduces failures from 22 to 11, and wins 13 of the 15 matched conditions where the controllers differ. Performance stays above 87% under initialization perturbations up to 1.5x, while very tight clearances expose the geometric limit of local correction.
AI.conclusion: The results support a hybrid design in which geometry preserves reliable task structure and learning is concentrated on the contact-sensitive behaviour that fixed rules handle poorly.

title: JointMatch: A Unified Heterogeneous Graph Neural Solver for Large-Scale Ride-Sharing Matching
summary: Ride-sharing platforms must continuously decide which open requests to bundle into shared trips and which idle vehicles should serve them. The dominant academic approach decomposes this into two sequential matching problems -- request pairing first, then vehicle assignment -- and applies a separate solver to each. This decomposition is convenient computationally but loses revenue and scales poorly because the first stage commits to ride bundles before the available vehicles are known. We propose JointMatch, a learning-based framework that handles request pairing and vehicle assignment together on a single graph. The graph is sparsified by spatial proximity so that its size grows linearly rather than quadratically with the number of vehicles and requests, and a graph neural network scores all candidate decisions in one forward pass. On the New York City Yellow Taxi data, the framework already exceeds both the classical Blossom heuristic and a faithfully-trained two-stage GNN baseline -- often by a wide margin -- and at city scale (fleet 10000) it runs more than $20\times$ faster per dispatch epoch than either. A supervised training stage closes most of the remaining revenue gap, and a policy-gradient fine-tune aligns the trained model with realised revenue.

AI.tldr: JointMatch is a learning-based framework that jointly handles ride-request pairing and vehicle assignment on a single sparsified graph with a GNN, eliminating the errors of the dominant two-stage decomposition. It outperforms Blossom and a two-stage GNN baseline in revenue and runs >20x faster at city scale.
AI.motivation: The dominant academic approach decomposes ride-sharing dispatch into two sequential matching problems (request pairing first, then vehicle assignment), each solved separately. This decomposition is computationally convenient but loses revenue and scales poorly, because the first stage commits to ride bundles before the available vehicles are known.
AI.method: JointMatch handles request pairing and vehicle assignment together on a single graph. The graph is sparsified by spatial proximity so its size grows linearly (not quadratically) with the number of vehicles and requests, and a graph neural network scores all candidate decisions in one forward pass. Training uses a supervised stage followed by a policy-gradient fine-tune to align the model with realised revenue.
AI.result: On New York City Yellow Taxi data, JointMatch exceeds both the classical Blossom heuristic and a faithfully-trained two-stage GNN baseline, often by a wide margin. At city scale (fleet of 10000) it runs more than 20x faster per dispatch epoch than either baseline. The supervised training stage closes most of the remaining revenue gap, and policy-gradient fine-tuning aligns the model with realised revenue.
AI.conclusion: Jointly solving request pairing and vehicle assignment on a sparsified graph with a GNN yields higher revenue and far better scalability than the standard two-stage decomposed approach, with supervised and policy-gradient training further improving alignment to realised revenue.

title: MaskHarness-WAM: Instance-Grounded Harnessing for Long-Horizon Robot Manipulation
summary: Long-horizon robot manipulation requires not only stable local visuomotor control, but also continuous target tracking and reliable task progress assessment throughout execution. This challenge becomes particularly critical when multiple objects share identical appearances and must be manipulated in a prescribed order. In such scenarios, relying solely on a limited-horizon manipulation policy is often insufficient to determine which instance should be operated on and when the task should transition to the next stage. To address this challenge, we propose MaskHarness-WAM, an instance-grounded harness for long-horizon manipulation. The proposed system connects high-level task planning with low-level manipulation policies through target masks, while leveraging visual feedback for subtask scheduling and continuous execution. Since each subtask corresponds to a different target instance, the low-level policy requires a newly established initial target mask under the updated scene at each subtask transition. The harness continuously re-observes the environment, generates, and verifies the target mask at subtask boundaries, thereby updating the instance-level spatial condition provided to the low-level policy. Furthermore, the system advances the manipulation process by switching target instances according to the verified completion status of each subtask. Experiments on a real robot platform demonstrate that MaskHarness-WAM substantially outperforms limited-horizon policies on sequential multi-object manipulation, showing its effectiveness in extending local manipulation skills to reliable long-horizon execution.

AI.tldr: MaskHarness-WAM is an instance-grounded harness that connects high-level task planning with low-level manipulation policies via target masks, enabling reliable long-horizon sequential manipulation of visually identical objects on a real robot.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon robot manipulation requires stable visuomotor control plus continuous target tracking and reliable progress assessment. This is critical when multiple identical-looking objects must be manipulated in a prescribed order, where limited-horizon policies cannot decide which instance to operate on or when to transition to the next stage.
AI.method: The system links high-level planning with low-level policies through target masks and uses visual feedback for subtask scheduling. At each subtask boundary, it re-observes the environment, generates and verifies a new instance-level target mask under the updated scene, updating the spatial condition given to the low-level policy, then switches target instances based on verified subtask completion.
AI.result: Experiments on a real robot platform show that MaskHarness-WAM substantially outperforms limited-horizon policies on sequential multi-object manipulation.
AI.conclusion: MaskHarness-WAM effectively extends local manipulation skills into reliable long-horizon execution by grounding subtasks in verified target instances.

title: When AI Agents Commit: Cognitive Serializability Across Data, Evidence, Policy, and Authority
summary: Autonomous agents derive concrete mutations from database reads, retrieved evidence, policy, beliefs, and delegated authority. Those inputs may change while reasoning is in progress. Database isolation orders the submitted transaction; agentic transaction processing determines whether a proposal satisfies an executable contract. Neither guarantee establishes a common valid point for the mutation and its derivation inputs unless the contract represents the relevant predicates. Typed dependency tokens distinguish content integrity from applicability, and trusted mediation captures the values exposed to reasoning. Under strict Cognitive Serializability, committed effects admit a serial order and a logical event at which every value exposed to derivation is unchanged. The fences last until the runtime event that realizes the sealed durability domain. The weaker Effect-Compatible Cognitive Admission recertifies an effect against a simultaneously held current dependency vector and current policy without claiming to serialize the original stochastic derivation. TCT combines immutable versioned executable definitions, registry-derived authority plans, sealed envelopes, guard-first commit transactions, post-seal envelope- and witness-bound grants, co-committed receipts, idempotent grant finalization, and receipt-driven epistemic reconciliation. Complete registered footprints and a single growing phase induce an acyclic lock-point order over local guards and incompatible external reservations. The corresponding results give serializability conditions and an observational-equivalence boundary for zero-error soundness and positive progress. A falsification suite tests the implementation obligations: the prototype prevented all injected anomalies and added 3.22 ms mean commit overhead.

AI.tldr: Autonomous agents derive concrete mutations from inputs (database reads, retrieved evidence, policy, beliefs, delegated authority) that may change mid-reasoning. Neither DB isolation nor transactional processing alone establishes a common valid point for a mutation and its derivation inputs unless the contract encodes the relevant predicates. The paper introduces Typed Cognitive Transactions (TCT), built on typed dependency tokens, trusted mediation, strict Cognitive Serializability, and the weaker Effect-Compatible Cognitive Admission, to provide zero-error soundness with positive progress.
AI.motivation: Reasoning is stochastic and its derivation inputs can shift while it is in progress. Database isolation only orders the submitted transaction, and agentic transaction processing only checks whether a proposal satisfies an executable contract. Neither guarantees that the values exposed to derivation are unchanged at the point a mutation commits, so the validity premise of a mutation—its derivation inputs—can be silently invalidated. The paper targets this gap: providing a common valid point between a mutation and its derivation inputs via contracts that represent the relevant predicates.
AI.method: The work distinguishes content integrity from applicability via typed dependency tokens and captures reasoning-exposed values through trusted mediation. It defines Strict Cognitive Serializability (committed effects admit a serial order and a logical event at which every derivations-exposed value is unchanged, with fences persisting until the runtime event realizing the sealed durability domain) and Effect-Compatible Cognitive Admission (recertifies an effect against a simultaneously held current dependency vector and current policy, without claiming to serialize the original stochastic derivation). TCT composes immutable versioned executable definitions, registry-derived authority plans, sealed envelopes, guard-first commit transactions, post-seal envelope- and witness-bound grants, co-committed receipts, idempotent grant finalization, and receipt-driven epistemic reconciliation. Complete registered footprints plus a single growing phase induce an acyclic lock-point order over local guards and incompatible external reservations.
AI.result: Serializability conditions and an observational-equivalence boundary are established, yielding zero-error soundness and positive progress. A falsification suite exercises the implementation obligations; the prototype prevented all injected anomalies at a mean commit overhead of 3.22 ms.
AI.conclusion: Contract-mediated validity—not isolation or transaction admission alone—is required to align autonomous-agent mutations with their derivation inputs. TCT supplies this via typed dependency tokens, trusted mediation, and the twin notions of Strict Cognitive Serializability and Effect-Compatible Cognitive Admission, achieving zero-error soundness with positive progress at modest commit overhead.

title: Compliance for Free: Learning Identifiable Impedance via Bilateral Teleoperation
summary: Vision-language-action models tell a robot where to move, but not how hard to push. Contact-rich tasks depend on that second quantity, compliance, yet no widely used demonstration interface records it. The obstacle is identifiability as realized pose and measured force cannot separate the operator's intended equilibrium from their stiffness, so VR controllers, SpaceMouse and handheld grippers cannot supply compliance supervision even in principle. Prior compliance-output policies work around this with hand-specified task structure, privileged simulation contact state, or dedicated force and tactile hardware. Four-channel bilateral teleoperation removes the ambiguity directly by using the leader arm as a separate measurement of the intended equilibrium, making per-axis stiffness identifiable by regression using only the joint-torque sensing already on the manipulator. This yields per-timestep, direction-dependent compliance labels at zero annotation cost, which we use to fine-tune a VLA to emit stiffness alongside pose. On a Franka Research 3 wiping task, ours is the only policy of five whose contact force changes when the instruction asks for a firm wipe rather than a normal one (6.4N (normal) to 9.1N (firm) RMS, Cohen's d = 0.89, p = 0.023

AI.tldr: A four-channel bilateral teleoperation interface makes per-axis stiffness identifiable from existing joint-torque sensing, producing zero-cost compliance labels that let a VLA emit stiffness alongside pose; the resulting policy is the only one of five that adjusts contact force to instruction verbosity—6.4N to 9.1N RMS when asked for a firm wipe.
AI.motivation: Vision-language-action (VLA) models specify where a robot should move but not how hard to push, which contact-rich tasks require. No widely used demonstration interface records compliance because realized pose and measured force are confounded: the operator's intended equilibrium cannot be separated from their stiffness, so VR controllers, SpaceMouse, and handheld grippers cannot provide compliance supervision even in principle. Prior compliance-output policies sidestep this via hand-specified task structure, privileged simulation contact state, or dedicated force/tactile hardware.
AI.method: Four-channel bilateral teleoperation directly resolves the identifiability problem: the leader arm serves as an independent measurement of the intended equilibrium, making per-axis stiffness identifiable by regression using only the joint-torque sensing already present on the manipulator. This yields per-timestep, direction-dependent compliance labels at zero annotation cost, which are used to fine-tune a VLA to output stiffness alongside pose.
AI.result: On a Franka Research 3 wiping task, the proposed approach is the only policy among five whose contact force changes when the instruction requests a firm wipe rather than a normal one: 6.4N (normal) to 9.1N (firm) RMS, with Cohen's d = 0.89 and p = 0.023.
AI.conclusion: Compliance supervision for VLAs is achievable without extra hardware or annotation by exploiting four-channel bilateral teleoperation's leader arm as an equilibrium reference, enabling instruction-conditioned stiffness control on contact-rich tasks.

title: AI-Driven Real-Time Relay Optimisation in Smart Urban NR-V2X Networks via Learning-to-Optimise Graph Neural Networks
summary: Reliable and low-latency communication is a fundamental requirement for smart city services and Industry 4.0 applications enabled by NR-V2X networks. However, limited Road-Side Unit (RSU) deployment and complex urban propagation conditions often prevent Connected and Automated Vehicles (CAVs) from maintaining stable connectivity. This paper proposes an AI-driven Learning-to-Optimise (L2O) framework based on Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) for real-time multi-hop relay selection in NR-V2X systems. The vehicular network is modelled as a graph, where nodes represent CAVs and RSUs, and edges encode radio-link characteristics. An offline Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) formulation provides optimal relay decisions used as supervision for training an edge-aware Graph Isomorphism Network with Edge Features (GINE). Extensive experiments on realistic urban datasets demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves near-optimal connectivity performance, recovering up to 11.3% connectivity gain, while reducing execution time by orders of magnitude (up to 100 x speed-up) compared to MILP. The framework enables scalable and real-time network control, making it suitable for smart city and Industry 4.0 deployments.

AI.tldr: A GNN-based Learning-to-Optimise framework (edge-aware GINE) performs real-time multi-hop relay selection in NR-V2X, approximating MILP-optimal connectivity with up to 100x speed-up.
AI.motivation: Reliable, low-latency communication is essential for smart city services and Industry 4.0 applications in NR-V2X networks, but limited RSU deployment and complex urban propagation conditions prevent CAVs from maintaining stable connectivity. Real-time multi-hop relay selection is needed, yet exact optimisation is too slow for online control.
AI.method: The vehicular network is modelled as a graph with CAVs and RSUs as nodes and radio-link characteristics as edges. An offline MILP formulation generates optimal relay decisions, which supervise training of an edge-aware Graph Isomorphism Network with Edge Features (GINE) within an AI-driven Learning-to-Optimise (L2O) framework for real-time multi-hop relay selection.
AI.result: Experiments on realistic urban datasets show near-optimal connectivity performance, recovering up to 11.3% connectivity gain and achieving up to 100x speed-up in execution time compared with MILP.
AI.conclusion: The framework enables scalable, real-time network control, making it suitable for smart city and Industry 4.0 NR-V2X deployments.

title: DR-MPC: Fast and Feasible Dynamics-Relaxed Model-Predictive Control for Legged Locomotion
summary: This paper presents dynamics-relaxed model predictive control (DR-MPC), a novel MPC formulation for legged locomotion, and a tailored interior-point method (IPM) solver. The formulation combines online optimization feasibility by construction with a contact-aware input parameterization. DR-MPC moves the dynamics equality and affine input constraints into quadratic penalties and retains only nonempty box constraints. The resulting box-constrained quadratic program (QP) has a block-arrow Hessian that enables the state and affine-output directions to be eliminated through a Schur complement. The solver factors only the reduced control system after swing-force elimination and contact-aligned move blocking. For the evaluated implementations using the same DR-MPC formulation, our method achieves median end-to-end MPC speedups of $16.0\times$ over HPIPM and $4.4\times$ over OSQP, with comparable locomotion performance in simulation. DR-MPC achieves a median onboard MPC end-to-end time of $4.4$ ms and is validated on a Unitree Go1 quadruped. Open-source code will be made available after publication.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces DR-MPC, a relaxed model predictive control formulation for legged locomotion, paired with a custom interior-point solver that exploits problem structure for substantial speedups.
AI.motivation: Legged locomotion requires fast, feasible online MPC, but standard formulations involving dynamics equality and affine input constraints are computationally costly to solve onboard in real time.
AI.method: DR-MPC moves dynamics equality and affine input constraints into quadratic penalties, leaving only nonempty box constraints. This yields a box-constrained QP with a block-arrow Hessian, enabling elimination of state and affine-output directions via a Schur complement. The tailored IPM solver factors only the reduced control system after swing-force elimination and contact-aligned move blocking.
AI.result: Using the same DR-MPC formulation, the method achieves median end-to-end MPC speedups of 16.0x over HPIPM and 4.4x over OSQP, with comparable locomotion performance in simulation, and a median onboard MPC end-to-end time of 4.4 ms on a Unitree Go1 quadruped.
AI.conclusion: DR-MPC, combined with the tailored IPM solver, delivers a fast and onboard-feasible MPC for legged locomotion, validated in hardware, with open-source code to be released after publication.

title: JEPA-WAM: Connecting Generated Visual Instructions to World Action Models through JEPA Latent Representations
summary: World Action Models (WAMs) have demonstrated strong robotic manipulation capabilities by augmenting pretrained video generative models with action experts. However, current WAMs still show limited instruction-following ability when conditioned solely on text instructions. We argue that this limitation stems in part from a structural imbalance in robot-learning data: rich visual-action trajectories are often paired with sparse and repetitive language annotations, allowing policies to identify tasks from visual context and motion regularities rather than grounding the instruction itself. To address this limitation, we introduce JEPA-WAM, which augments each text instruction with a bank of stochastically generated visual instructions, providing diverse visual cues for instruction following. Specifically, JEPA-WAM uses an off-the-shelf text-to-image generator to sample multiple task-completion images conditioned on the text instruction, without training the generator. Although these generated images may differ from the current visual scene in appearance and layout, they remain semantically aligned with the instruction and serve as visual goal references. To focus on task-level semantics beyond appearance, we encode these references with a frozen V-JEPA 2.1 encoder. The resulting dense goal representations are compressed into compact goal tokens that condition both the video and action experts through cross-attention. We further construct a real-robot instruction-following benchmark covering in-distribution, out-of-distribution scene, and out-of-distribution instruction settings. On this benchmark, JEPA-WAM achieves success rates of 87.3%, 74.5%, and 80.9% in these three settings, outperforming π0 and Fast-WAM by at least 10.0, 27.3, and 14.5 percentage points, respectively.

AI.tldr: JEPA-WAM augments text instructions with stochastically generated, semantically aligned visual goal references encoded by a frozen V-JEPA 2.1 encoder to improve instruction-following in World Action Models.
AI.motivation: Current World Action Models (WAMs) show limited instruction-following when conditioned solely on text, argued to stem partly from a structural imbalance in robot-learning data: rich visual-action trajectories are paired with sparse, repetitive language, letting policies identify tasks from visual context and motion regularities instead of grounding the instruction.
AI.method: JEPA-WAM augments each text instruction with a bank of stochastically generated visual instructions. It uses an off-the-shelf (untrained/frozen) text-to-image generator to sample multiple task-completion images conditioned on the text instruction. Though these may differ in appearance/layout from the current scene, they stay semantically aligned as goal references. A frozen V-JEPA 2.1 encoder encodes them to capture task-level semantics beyond appearance; the resulting dense goal representations are compressed into compact goal tokens that condition both the video and action experts via cross-attention.
AI.result: On a newly constructed real-robot instruction-following benchmark covering in-distribution, out-of-distribution scene, and out-of-distribution instruction settings, JEPA-WAM achieves success rates of 87.3%, 74.5%, and 80.9%, respectively. It outperforms π0 and Fast-WAM by at least 10.0, 27.3, and 14.5 percentage points in the three settings.
AI.conclusion: Providing diverse, semantically aligned visual goal references—rather than relying on text alone—substantially improves instruction grounding and generalization in robotic manipulation policies.

title: Mechanical Precision Weeding with a Quadruped Robot
summary: Herbicide-based weed control is increasingly unsustainable due to rising weed resistance and the adverse environmental impacts of chemical use. While mechanical weed control avoids these drawbacks, it is typically implemented using large machines that cause soil compaction. We propose a novel alternative based on small mobile robots for mechanical weeding. Compared with existing automated mechanical weeding approaches, the proposed method offers reduced soil compaction, simpler automation, and improved scalability. Our solution involves a Boston Dynamics Spot quadruped robot equipped with a custom weed removal tool featuring a milling bit at its end. The tool is rigidly attached to the robot and uses the degrees of freedom of the robot base by actuating the legs, while keeping the feet stationary. We develop a software architecture that enables autonomous weed removal and integrate this system with all other required components. We analyze the accuracy and efficiency of the current proof of concept both in an indoor and outdoor environment and provide recommendations for future work to make the system more accurate and efficient.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a small mobile robot system for mechanical weeding to overcome herbicide unsustainability and soil compaction from large machines, using a Spot quadruped robot with a custom milling-bit tool and autonomous software architecture, evaluated indoors and outdoors.
AI.motivation: Herbicide-based weeding is unsustainable due to rising weed resistance and environmental harm; mechanical weeding avoids these issues but relies on large machines that cause soil compaction. Small mobile robots are proposed as an alternative.
AI.method: A Boston Dynamics Spot quadruped robot equipped with a custom weed removal tool featuring a milling bit at its end. The tool is rigidly attached, and the robot manipulates it by actuating its legs while keeping its feet stationary, leveraging the robot base's degrees of freedom. A software architecture is developed for autonomous weed removal, integrated with other required components.
AI.result: The accuracy and efficiency of the current proof of concept were analyzed in both indoor and outdoor environments. Recommendations for future work are provided to improve system accuracy and efficiency.
AI.conclusion: The proposed small mobile robot approach reduces soil compaction, simplifies automation, and improves scalability compared with existing automated mechanical weeding approaches, though further work is needed for improved accuracy and efficiency.

title: AgentPProf: Semantic Profiler for Long Horizon AI Agents
summary: AI agents increasingly orchestrate long-running activities with users, tools, and system resources for days and weeks. To improve agent quality, safety, and cost efficiency, developers need to determine where failures happen, what triggers unsafe effects, and which tasks consume the most budget, then optimize those tasks. In systems software, profiling answers similar questions by aggregating resource consumption and attributing it to responsible code paths to identify hotspots. Yet existing agent observability tools focus on per-execution debugging and tracing rather than cross-run, long term profiling, making these questions difficult to answer at scale. Agent observability needs profiling, not only debugging, but profiling agents is challenging: the responsible entities are task intent like diagnose authentication, compare branches rather than code paths, and lack stable identifiers for aggregation. We propose a semantic operation stack model that adapts profiling to agent trajectories. Uniform operations represent all activities, and operation stacks replace the runtime call stack, enabling hierarchical attribution at different granularities. We observe that an agent's task occupies a contiguous span and decomposes into subtasks, so we introduce recursive operation segmentation, which recursively splits trajectories at task boundaries. AgentPProf is a profiler that aggregates agent trajectories into pprof-compatible profiles, enabling flame graph visualization and analysis. AgentPProf reaches 0.764 $B^3$ F1 against human annotations on CodeTraceBench. On three problem-localization benchmarks, the profile raises MAP by up to 56%, demonstrating that it effectively attributes resources, locates problems, and helps optimize token cost at practical profiling cost. AgentPProf is available at https://github.com/eunomia-bpf/agentsight.

AI.tldr: AgentPProf adapts classic software profiling to AI agents via a semantic operation stack model, aggregating agent trajectories into pprof-compatible profiles for hierarchical resource attribution and flame-graph analysis across long-running runs.
AI.motivation: AI agents run long, expensive, multi-tool activities over days or weeks, so developers must identify where failures occur, what triggers unsafe effects, and which tasks consume the most budget. Existing agent observability tools focus on per-execution debugging and tracing rather than cross-run, long-term profiling, leaving these questions hard to answer at scale. Profiling agents is difficult because the responsible entities are task intents (e.g., diagnose authentication) rather than code paths and lack stable identifiers for aggregation.
AI.method: The paper proposes a semantic operation stack model: uniform operations represent all agent activities, and operation stacks replace the runtime call stack, enabling hierarchical attribution at multiple granularities. Exploiting the observation that an agent's task occupies a contiguous span and decomposes into subtasks, it introduces recursive operation segmentation that recursively splits trajectories at task boundaries. The resulting profiler, AgentPProf, aggregates agent trajectories into pprof-compatible profiles for flame graph visualization and analysis.
AI.result: AgentPProf achieves 0.764 B^3 F1 against human annotations on CodeTraceBench. On three problem-localization benchmarks, the generated profile raises MAP by up to 56%, showing it effectively attributes resources, locates problems, and helps optimize token cost at practical profiling overhead.
AI.conclusion: Agent observability needs profiling, not just debugging. By recasting profiling around semantic operations and recursive task segmentation, AgentPProf brings scalable, cross-run, hierarchical resource attribution to agent trajectories. It is publicly available at https://github.com/eunomia-bpf/agentsight.

title: FlipToSee: A Probabilistic Stable Placement Prior for Active Visual Exploration via Regrasping
summary: Active visual exploration of tabletop objects often requires reorienting an unknown resting object onto a different stable support face to expose occluded surfaces. To identify such placements without exhaustive physical search, we learn a probabilistic placement prior from a single-view point cloud. Stable placement prediction is inherently multimodal, and conventional 6-DoF regression introduces further ambiguity by modeling translation and in-plane yaw. We therefore propose FlipToSee, a probabilistic framework that removes this representational ambiguity by parameterizing placements as unit support normals on $S^2$ while modeling their multimodal conditional distribution via a von Mises--Fisher mixture density network. To decouple mode diversity from physical robustness, FlipToSee deterministically extracts a compact candidate set from the mixture components and applies robustness-aware reranking using an auxiliary head trained with candidate-aligned supervision. In simulation, FlipToSee achieves $98.4\%$ first-proposal success on in-distribution objects, $95.3\%$ on out-of-distribution shapes, and $90.0\%$ under zero-shot transfer to household YCB objects. We further demonstrate the learned placement prior on a physical robot by integrating it with grasp and motion planning for exploratory regrasping.

AI.tldr: FlipToSee learns a probabilistic multimodal placement prior from a single-view point cloud, parameterizing placements as unit support normals on S^2 with a von Mises-Fisher mixture density network, and uses deterministic candidate extraction plus robustness-aware reranking for exploratory regrasping.
AI.motivation: Active visual exploration of tabletop objects often requires reorienting an unknown resting object onto a different stable support face to expose occluded surfaces. Identifying such placements without exhaustive physical search requires a learned prior, since stable placement prediction is inherently multimodal and conventional 6-DoF regression adds ambiguity by modeling translation and in-plane yaw.
AI.method: FlipToSee is a probabilistic framework that removes representational ambiguity by parameterizing placements as unit support normals on S^2 and modeling their multimodal conditional distribution via a von Mises-Fisher mixture density network. It deterministically extracts a compact candidate set from mixture components and applies robustness-aware reranking with an auxiliary head trained under candidate-aligned supervision.
AI.result: In simulation, FlipToSee achieves 98.4% first-proposal success on in-distribution objects, 95.3% on out-of-distribution shapes, and 90.0% under zero-shot transfer to household YCB objects. The learned placement prior is further demonstrated on a physical robot integrated with grasp and motion planning for exploratory regrasping.
AI.conclusion: FlipToSee provides an ambiguity-free, multimodal placement prior that generalizes across in-distribution, out-of-distribution, and zero-shot YCB objects, and successfully supports physical robot exploratory regrasping when integrated with grasp and motion planning.

title: Diagnose, Recover, Certify: Task Readiness under Hidden Dynamics Changes
summary: A deployed control policy can conceal consequential dynamics changes: an actuator may lose effectiveness without affecting the current task when the policy rarely excites it, despite being critical for a future task that has not yet been specified. We introduce task readiness under dormant dynamics drift, a decision problem that unifies active change diagnosis and post-change control recovery under a limited, task-agnostic interaction budget. An agent must identify whether and where local dynamics have changed, use a small number of informative interactions to characterize the change before downstream task identity is revealed, and subsequently provide each candidate task with either a recovered policy and a calibrated lower bound on its achievable return or an abstention decision to a safe fallback. We propose Evidence-Gated Matched-Pulse Transport, an intervention-based Bayesian procedure that couples fault localization with estimation of actuator effectiveness through a shared matched-response representation, thereby preserving diagnostic reliability while converting localized evidence into recovery-relevant uncertainty. This uncertainty is propagated to task-conditioned policy selection and readiness certification, enabling deployment decisions that explicitly trade off expected performance, confidence, and fallback use. We evaluate the resulting framework on a diverse suite of dormant-actuator benchmarks spanning multiple simulators, under a protocol that separates diagnosis from capability recovery, scores deployment by readiness coverage, selective risk, and interaction cost as well as return, and identifies the fault regimes in which transported evidence is decisive.

AI.tldr: The paper formalizes "task readiness under dormant dynamics drift," a decision problem combining active fault diagnosis and post-change control recovery under a limited, task-agnostic interaction budget, and proposes Evidence-Gated Matched-Pulse Transport (EG-MPT), an intervention-based Bayesian procedure that localizes actuator faults and estimates effectiveness via a shared matched-response representation, propagating that uncertainty into task-conditioned policy selection and readiness certification.
AI.motivation: A deployed control policy can mask consequential dynamics changes: an actuator may lose effectiveness without affecting the current task if the policy rarely excites it, yet remain critical for an as-yet-unspecified future task. Existing work treats fault diagnosis and control recovery separately and typically assumes the task is known, so it cannot decide how to spend limited interactions to become ready for unknown downstream tasks.
AI.method: The authors define task readiness under dormant dynamics drift, requiring an agent to (i) detect whether and where local dynamics have changed, (ii) characterize the change with a few informative interactions before task identity is revealed, and (iii) for each candidate task either supply a recovered policy with a calibrated lower bound on achievable return or abstain to a safe fallback. They propose Evidence-Gated Matched-Pulse Transport, an intervention-based Bayesian procedure that couples fault localization with actuator-effectiveness estimation through a shared matched-response representation, preserving diagnostic reliability while converting localized evidence into recovery-relevant uncertainty. This uncertainty is propagated to task-conditioned policy selection and readiness certification, yielding deployment decisions that trade off expected performance, confidence, and fallback use.
AI.result: Evaluation on a diverse suite of dormant-actuator benchmarks spanning multiple simulators, under a protocol separating diagnosis from capability recovery, scores deployment by readiness coverage, selective risk, and interaction cost in addition to return, and identifies the fault regimes in which transported evidence is decisive.
AI.conclusion: The framework unifies active change diagnosis and post-change control recovery under a shared interaction budget, and its evidence-transport mechanism enables principled readiness certification and deployment decisions that explicitly balance performance, confidence, and fallback usage.

title: Graph-Based Design of Soft Grippers with Multi-Objective Quality-Diversity Optimisation
summary:
Effective manipulation across diverse objects is critical for applications ranging from agricultural harvesting to laboratory and domestic automation. While the inherent compliance of soft robotics is well suited to this challenge, designing grippers that generalize across tasks remains difficult due to the vast design space of continuum mechanics and the risk of overfitting to specific scenarios.
  We propose a graph-based design space for representing soft structures and mechanisms, coupled with a multi-objective, diversity-driven genetic optimization framework that explicitly promotes solution variety throughout the design process. Using multiple grasping scenarios during optimization, we study how task diversity influences the emergence of generalization to unseen objects and contact conditions.
  Our results show that optimization over a sufficiently diverse set of grasping cases leads to designs with emergent generalization, exhibiting improved robustness compared to task-specific solutions on novel scenarios. These findings suggest that diversity-driven optimization offers a principled pathway toward general-purpose soft grippers, aligned with the adaptable nature of soft robotics.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a graph-based design space for soft gripper structures and mechanisms, combined with a multi-objective, diversity-driven genetic optimization framework, to study how task diversity during optimization promotes emergent generalization to unseen grasping scenarios.
AI.motivation: Manipulating diverse objects is essential for applications like agricultural harvesting and laboratory/domestic automation. Although soft robotics' inherent compliance suits this task, designing grippers that generalize across tasks is hard due to the vast continuum-mechanics design space and the risk of overfitting to specific scenarios.
AI.method: The authors propose a graph-based design space to represent soft structures and mechanisms, coupled with a multi-objective, diversity-driven genetic optimization framework that explicitly encourages solution variety throughout the design process. Multiple grasping scenarios are used during optimization to examine how task diversity affects generalization to unseen objects and contact conditions.
AI.result: Optimization over a sufficiently diverse set of grasping cases yields designs with emergent generalization, showing improved robustness on novel scenarios compared to task-specific solutions.
AI.conclusion: Diversity-driven optimization offers a principled pathway toward general-purpose soft grippers, consistent with the adaptable nature of soft robotics.

title: NeuSOGA3D: A Neuro-Symbolic Framework for Explainable 3D Geometric Reconstruction
comment: Preprint. Community feedback and comments are welcome
summary:
Three-dimensional reconstruction from unorganized point clouds remains a challenging problem in computer vision, geometric modeling, and computer-aided design. While neural implicit methods achieve impressive reconstruction accuracy, geometry is typically encoded in latent representations that limit interpretability and reuse within engineering workflows.
  We present NeuSOGA3D (Neuro-Symbolic Geometric Abstraction in 3D), a hybrid framework that combines learned perceptual priors inherited from NeuSOGA with explicit symbolic geometric reasoning. The method projects point clouds onto principal orthographic planes, constructs symbolic implicit spline representations from the resulting observations, and fuses them through shape-preserving constructive solid geometry operations to generate a coarse visual hull. Additional geometric detail is recovered through cross-sectional decomposition and volumetric reconstruction using Partial Shape-Preserving Splines.
  Unlike conventional neural implicit approaches, NeuSOGA3D progressively transforms observations into explicit symbolic entities, including control polygons, implicit spline fields, cross-sections, and volumetric lofts. Experiments on all forty categories of the ModelNet40 benchmark demonstrate the ability of the framework to recover structurally meaningful and CAD-compatible geometric representations from diverse point-cloud observations. The results highlight the potential of combining learned perception with symbolic geometric reasoning for explainable geometric intelligence.

AI.tldr: NeuSOGA3D is a hybrid neuro-symbolic framework that reconstructs CAD-compatible geometry from unorganized point clouds by projecting them onto orthographic planes, building symbolic implicit spline representations, and fusing them via shape-preserving CSG operations into an explicit visual hull refined by cross-sectional decomposition and Partial Shape-Preserving Splines.
AI.motivation: 3D reconstruction from unorganized point clouds is a persistent challenge in computer vision, geometric modeling, and CAD. Neural implicit methods are accurate but encode geometry in latent representations that are hard to interpret and reuse in engineering workflows, motivating a shift toward explicit, symbolic, and reusable geometric abstractions.
AI.method: NeuSOGA3D combines learned perceptual priors (inherited from NeuSOGA) with explicit symbolic geometric reasoning. It projects point clouds onto principal orthographic planes, constructs symbolic implicit spline representations from these observations, and fuses them through shape-preserving constructive solid geometry (CSG) operations to form a coarse visual hull. Geometric detail is then recovered via cross-sectional decomposition and volumetric reconstruction using Partial Shape-Preserving Splines. The pipeline progressively converts observations into explicit symbolic entities: control polygons, implicit spline fields, cross-sections, and volumetric lofts.
AI.result: Experiments across all forty categories of the ModelNet40 benchmark show that the framework recovers structurally meaningful and CAD-compatible geometric representations from diverse point-cloud observations.
AI.conclusion: NeuSOGA3D demonstrates the potential of combining learned perception with symbolic geometric reasoning to achieve explainable geometric intelligence, producing interpretable, reusable geometric abstractions rather than opaque latent encodings.

title: Safety-Critical Scenanrio Emerges from Initial Scene
summary: Safety-critical driving scenario generation has largely focused on manipulating the behavior of surrounding agents while starting from an initial scene from driving data. This assumption can limit the space of discoverable failures, since driving data can provide little opportunity for meaningful interaction. For example, in the Waymo Open Motion Dataset, 20.44% of recorded slices feature a stationary ego vehicle that never moves, and 30.39% of initial frames contain no nearby traffic participants within 10 meters. We instead study safety-critical scenario generation as an initialization problem: given agnostic black-box driving policies, we learn to generate realistic initial scenes that are more likely to evolve into critical interactions. We propose AdvScene, a conditional latent diffusion model that is trained in two stages. Starting from pretraining on naturalistic driving data, we post-train the adversarial-agent generation branch using reinforcement learning with feedback from closed-loop simulator rollouts. Conditioning on ego driving displacement prevents the ego from remaining static, and RL finetuning induces criticality directly with non-differentiable safety-critical metrics. Experiments on the Waymo dataset across 12 combinations of ego and traffic policies show that our AdvScene substantially increases the rate of ego-fault collision events and TTC<3s events.

AI.tldr: AdvScene reformulates safety-critical driving scenario generation as an initialization problem, using a two-stage conditional latent diffusion model to generate realistic initial scenes that evolve into critical interactions for black-box ego policies.
AI.motivation: Prior work manipulates surrounding agent behavior starting from driving-data initial scenes, which limits discoverable failures. Driving data offers few meaningful interactions: 20.44% of Waymo Open Motion Dataset slices have a stationary ego, and 30.39% of initial frames have no traffic participant within 10 meters.
AI.method: AdvScene is a conditional latent diffusion model trained in two stages: pretraining on naturalistic driving data, then post-training the adversarial-agent generation branch with reinforcement learning using feedback from closed-loop simulator rollouts. Conditioning on ego driving displacement prevents a static ego, and RL finetuning induces criticality directly using non-differentiable safety-critical metrics.
AI.result: Experiments on the Waymo dataset across 12 combinations of ego and traffic policies show that AdvScene substantially increases the rate of ego-fault collision events and TTC<3s events.
AI.conclusion: Generating safety-critical scenarios as realistic initializations, rather than only perturbing agent behavior, yields markedly more critical interactions under agnostic black-box driving policies.

title: Structured Four-Stage Legal Translation: From Natural-Language Traffic Rules to PROLOG
comment: In Proceedings of the International Workshop on Translating Natural Legal Language into Formal Representations (NLL2FR 2025)
summary: Traffic regulations are written for human interpretation and therefore rely on shared background knowledge and flexible phrasing, which inherently introduce ambiguity, context dependence, and semantic underspecification. These linguistic characteristics conflict with the precision required by computational reasoning engines such as Prolog, which demand explicit logical structure. This study evaluates two baseline translation approaches, Natural Language to Prolog ($NL\rightarrow Prolog$) and Logical English to Prolog ($LE\rightarrow Prolog$), and introduces a new reasoning-guided translation framework called Structured Four-Stage Legal Translation ($S4L\rightarrow Prolog$). The proposed S4L framework performs semantic role extraction, scene completion, logical mapping, and Prolog rule generation within a single guided prompt, enabling direct translation of raw traffic rules into executable logic without human intervention. A benchmark consisting of twenty real-world traffic rules was used to evaluate each approach in terms of syntactic validity, semantic correctness, and logical completeness. $S4L\rightarrow Prolog$ achieves the highest accuracy, correctly formalizing 75 percent of the rules, while $NL\rightarrow Prolog$ reaches 60 percent and $LE\rightarrow Prolog$ reaches 55 percent. Qualitative analysis further shows that S4L captures implicit causal relations, deontic modality, and exception structure more reliably than the baselines. These results demonstrate that structured reasoning prompts can substantially improve the reliability of natural-language-to-logic translation for legal and safety-critical applications.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces S4L, a reasoning-guided framework that translates raw traffic rules into executable Prolog, outperforming NL→Prolog and LE→Prolog baselines on a 20-rule benchmark.
AI.motivation: Traffic regulations rely on shared background knowledge and flexible phrasing, introducing ambiguity, context dependence, and semantic underspecification. These traits conflict with the precision required by computational reasoning engines like Prolog, which demand explicit logical structure. Prior translation approaches are inadequate for this gap.
AI.method: The study evaluates two baselines, Natural Language to Prolog (NL→Prolog) and Logical English to Prolog (LE→Prolog), and introduces a new reasoning-guided framework: Structured Four-Stage Legal Translation (S4L→Prolog). S4L performs semantic role extraction, scene completion, logical mapping, and Prolog rule generation within a single guided prompt, enabling direct translation of raw traffic rules into executable logic without human intervention.
AI.result: Using a benchmark of twenty real-world traffic rules, evaluated on syntactic validity, semantic correctness, and logical completeness, S4L→Prolog achieves the highest accuracy (75% correctly formalized), versus NL→Prolog at 60% and LE→Prolog at 55%. Qualitative analysis shows S4L captures implicit causal relations, deontic modality, and exception structure more reliably than baselines.
AI.conclusion: Structured reasoning prompts substantially improve the reliability of natural-language-to-logic translation, making the approach promising for legal and safety-critical applications.

title: AnyViewDex: View-Invariant Dexterous Manipulation from RGB Observations
summary: Visuomotor policies for multi-fingered dexterous manipulation are highly sensitive to camera viewpoint shifts. To achieve view invariance, recent methods increasingly rely on explicit 3D modalities like RGB-D or point clouds, which can introduce hardware dependencies, calibration requirements, and vulnerability to sensor noise during real-world deployment. In this work, we show that view-invariant control can be achieved without explicit test-time 3D sensing by encoding geometric knowledge into the visual representation during simulation. We present AnyViewDex, an asymmetric training pipeline that combines multi-view contrastive alignment with privileged 3D geometric supervision. By regressing absolute 3D object coordinates during simulated training, this auxiliary objective provides a geometric grounding signal that mitigates the spatial collapse of the globally pooled contrastive embedding. At deployment, the policy operates zero-shot using only uncalibrated monocular RGB and proprioception. We validate this approach across both reinforcement learning and student-teacher distillation. In hardware evaluation on an xArm7 with a 16-DoF LEAP Hand, AnyViewDex reaches 76.7% grasping success across eight unseen objects and six uncalibrated viewpoints (480 trials; 2,400 across all ablation conditions), indicating that geometrically grounded monocular policies transfer zero-shot without test-time depth. Project Page: https://anyviewdex.github.io/

AI.tldr: AnyViewDex is an asymmetric training pipeline that achieves view-invariant dexterous manipulation using only uncalibrated monocular RGB and proprioception at deployment, by encoding 3D geometry into the visual representation through multi-view contrastive alignment and privileged 3D supervision during simulation.
AI.motivation: Multi-fingered visuomotor policies are highly sensitive to camera viewpoint shifts. Existing view-invariance approaches rely on explicit 3D modalities (RGB-D, point clouds), which introduce hardware dependencies, calibration requirements, and sensor noise vulnerability in real-world deployment. The authors aim to obtain view-invariant control without explicit test-time 3D sensing.
AI.method: An asymmetric training pipeline combining multi-view contrastive alignment with privileged 3D geometric supervision. An auxiliary objective regresses absolute 3D object coordinates during simulated training, providing a geometric grounding signal that mitigates spatial collapse of the globally pooled contrastive embedding. The policy is validated across reinforcement learning and student-teacher distillation, and deploys zero-shot with uncalibrated monocular RGB plus proprioception.
AI.result: On an xArm7 with a 16-DoF LEAP Hand, AnyViewDex achieves 76.7% grasping success across eight unseen objects and six uncalibrated viewpoints (480 trials; 2,400 across all ablation conditions).
AI.conclusion: Geometrically grounded monocular policies transfer zero-shot to real hardware without test-time depth, showing that explicit test-time 3D sensing is unnecessary for view-invariant dexterous control.

title: A Qualitative Model for Reasoning about Path and Support
comment: Workshop on Qualitative Reasoning 2026 at IJCAI (35th International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence)
summary: Spatial reasoning abilities correlate strongly with performance in STEM fields. Games offer a compelling medium for training these critical skills in developing children who have a natural proclivity for play. However, to facilitate human-like tutoring and player guidance, these games require an AI agent capable of making commonsense inferences from spatial events. Qualitative reasoning (QR) models appear to be a suitable framework for these application domains. As these models reason in symbolic representations, they can seamlessly translate game states into interpretable feedback for human-like player guidance. This paper introduces a hybrid qualitative model designed for Camelot Jr., a block-puzzle game that requires constructing multi-level bridges to connect two avatars stationed on separate towers. The game poses a challenge for the player, who must make platforms stable, plan their path, and ensure they use all the provided blocks. To handle the precise physics required by the domain, we integrate a mathematical center-of-mass stability logic to guide our qualitative solver. Our work facilitates spatial skill training in Camelot Jr. and contributes to the development of human-centric, explainable game-playing agents.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a hybrid qualitative reasoning model for Camelot Jr., a block-puzzle game, integrating a mathematical center-of-mass stability logic to enable commonsense spatial inference and interpretable player guidance for spatial skill training.
AI.motivation: Spatial reasoning correlates strongly with STEM performance, and games are effective for training these skills in children. However, games need an AI agent capable of commonsense inference from spatial events to provide human-like tutoring and guidance. Qualitative reasoning (QR) models are suitable for this because they reason in symbolic representations, allowing game states to be translated into interpretable feedback. Camelot Jr. presents challenges: players must stabilize platforms, plan paths, and use all provided blocks.
AI.method: The authors introduce a hybrid qualitative model for Camelot Jr., a block-puzzle game requiring construction of multi-level bridges connecting two avatars on separate towers. To handle the precise physics of the domain, they integrate a mathematical center-of-mass stability logic to guide the qualitative solver.
AI.result: The hybrid model facilitates spatial skill training in Camelot Jr. by combining qualitative reasoning with center-of-mass stability logic, enabling the solver to handle the domain's precise physics.
AI.conclusion: The work supports spatial skill training in Camelot Jr. and contributes to the development of human-centric, explainable game-playing agents.

title: Universal Navigation Interface: Robot-Free Data for Wheeled Robot Navigation
comment: 8 pages, 4 figures, 7 tables. Project page: https://universal-nav.github.io/
summary: Collecting real-world navigation data for mobile robots typically requires platform-specific teleoperation, making large-scale collection expensive and difficult to scale. We introduce Universal Navigation Interface (UNI), a robot-free data collection paradigm that uses a four-wheeled rollator walker (rollator) and smartphone to collect physically constrained human demonstrations. Because the rollator cannot climb stairs, negotiate uncut curbs, or pass through narrow gaps, demonstrations are naturally biased toward wheeled-feasible routes. Using UNI, we collect 37.2 km of real-world navigation data and recover metric trajectories that directly supervise goal-conditioned navigation models. Fine-tuning visual-navigation models on UNI reduces trajectory prediction error by 17.4-24.8% on held-out UNI demonstrations. Evaluation on other navigation datasets shows benefits that vary by dataset and metric. We further demonstrate closed-loop transfer to a powered wheelchair in curb, staircase, and curb-cut scenarios. These results support low-cost physical proxies as a practical source of navigation supervision collected without the target robot.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces UNI, a robot-free data collection paradigm using a rollator walker and smartphone to gather physically constrained human navigation demonstrations that directly supervise goal-conditioned navigation models, enabling low-cost, scalable real-world data collection.
