AI.motivation: Collecting real-world navigation data for mobile robots typically requires platform-specific teleoperation, which makes large-scale collection expensive and difficult to scale. There is a need for a low-cost, robot-free approach to obtain navigation supervision data.
AI.method: UNI uses a four-wheeled rollator walker and a smartphone to collect physically constrained human demonstrations. Because the rollator cannot climb stairs, negotiate uncut curbs, or pass through narrow gaps, the demonstrations are naturally biased toward wheeled-feasible routes. Metric trajectories are recovered and used to directly supervise goal-conditioned navigation models.
AI.result: Using UNI, 37.2 km of real-world navigation data was collected. Fine-tuning visual-navigation models on UNI reduces trajectory prediction error by 17.4–24.8% on held-out UNI demonstrations. Evaluation on other navigation datasets shows benefits that vary by dataset and metric. Closed-loop transfer to a powered wheelchair was demonstrated in curb, staircase, and curb-cut scenarios.
AI.conclusion: These results support low-cost physical proxies as a practical source of navigation supervision collected without the target robot.

title: Generating Heterogeneous 3D Geological Microstructures from 2D Images via a Stable Diffusion-Adversarial Model
summary:
Characterizing the physical properties of clay and cementitious materials matters across many fields, from materials science to geological waste disposal. Property simulation typically calls for 3D imaging, which is expensive, not always accessible, and technically limited for certain materials. Recent progress in deep generative models offers a way around this, reconstructing 3D volumes from the more easily acquired 2D images.
  Among GAN-based methods for 3D microstructure generation, SliceGAN has shown strong results for homogeneous isotropic and anisotropic systems. It struggles, however, to capture the finer detail of more complex heterogeneous microstructures, which motivates alternative generative frameworks.
  We introduce a hybrid approach that draws on the stability and generation quality of denoising diffusion models. Since no 3D ground truth is available, we replace the standard denoising loss with an adversarial loss, which yields a stable training process in our experiments. We show that the resulting model generates microstructures of varying complexity with minimal slice artefacts and close agreement with ground-truth phase fractions and structural descriptors.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a hybrid diffusion-based generative model that reconstructs 3D microstructures of clay and cementitious materials from 2D images, using an adversarial loss instead of the standard denoising loss, achieving stable training and high-quality generation without 3D ground truth.
AI.motivation: Characterizing the physical properties of clay and cementitious materials requires 3D imaging, which is expensive, not always accessible, and technically limited for certain materials. Deep generative models offer a route to reconstruct 3D volumes from more easily acquired 2D images. However, existing GAN-based methods such as SliceGAN, though effective for homogeneous isotropic and anisotropic systems, struggle to capture fine detail in complex heterogeneous microstructures, motivating alternative generative frameworks.
AI.method: The authors introduce a hybrid approach leveraging the stability and generation quality of denoising diffusion models. Because no 3D ground truth is available, they replace the standard denoising loss with an adversarial loss, which yields stable training in their experiments.
AI.result: The resulting model generates microstructures of varying complexity with minimal slice artefacts and close agreement with ground-truth phase fractions and structural descriptors.
AI.conclusion: The hybrid diffusion-based framework overcomes the limitations of SliceGAN for complex heterogeneous microstructures, enabling accurate 3D reconstruction from 2D images without 3D ground truth supervision.

title: GPT-6-Astra in a Navigation Workflow: Behavioral Analysis in Zero-Shot Vision-and-Language Navigation in Continuous Environments
summary: We study GPT-6-Astra in a zero-shot Vision-and-Language Navigation in Continuous Environments (VLN-CE) system, where it interprets instructions, assesses its surroundings, and proposes actions. The system uses a common observation--decision--execution workflow with direct model API calls, without a packaged agent harness or navigation-specific fine-tuning. In this workflow, each request receives selected observations, execution feedback, and retained progress records. Evaluation covers the complete system, including context management and action control. We evaluate the system on 50 of the 100 R2R-CE val-unseen episodes used by Open-Nav. It achieves a success rate of 52.0\%, an SPL of 48.9\%, and an nDTW of 70.8\%. Our analysis highlights three findings. First, recorded responses link landmarks and earlier actions to instructions using observations and supplied history. Second, reviews include requests for additional views and revisions of uncertain judgments. Third, the results suggest a gap between task understanding and autonomous completion: an unfinished crossing is recognized while rotation continues. At termination, 36.0\% of episodes succeed with a workflow-accepted STOP, while another 16.0\% meet the distance criterion at the step limit. These results highlight a central challenge: translating correct local judgments into sustained progress and appropriate stopping.

AI.tldr: A zero-shot GPT-6-Astra system for VLN-CE achieves 52.0% success, 48.9% SPL, and 70.8% nDTW on 50 R2R-CE val-unseen episodes, revealing a gap between task understanding and autonomous completion.
AI.motivation: To test whether a general-purpose model can handle VLN-CE (interpreting instructions, assessing surroundings, proposing actions) in a zero-shot manner, without a packaged agent harness or navigation-specific fine-tuning.
AI.method: A common observation–decision–execution workflow using direct model API calls. Each request receives selected observations, execution feedback, and retained progress records; evaluation covers the complete system, including context management and action control. Tested on 50 of the 100 R2R-CE val-unseen episodes used by Open-Nav.
AI.result: 52.0% success rate, 48.9% SPL, and 70.8% nDTW. Recorded responses link landmarks and earlier actions to instructions via observations and history; reviews request additional views and revise uncertain judgments; an unfinished crossing is recognized while rotation continues. At termination, 36.0% of episodes succeed with a workflow-accepted STOP, and another 16.0% meet the distance criterion at the step limit.
AI.conclusion: The central challenge is translating correct local judgments into sustained progress and appropriate stopping, exposing a gap between task understanding and autonomous completion.

title: The Organization of Inference: Information, Resource Constraints, and AI Production
summary: The economic value of inference depends on how capacity and task information are distributed across stages of AI production. We study these organizational margins using controlled workflow experiments on externally verified software-engineering tasks. In two matched resource panels, direct execution records the same success rate of 59.6 percent at logical-token ceilings of 12,000 and 24,000, while success under information-constrained planning rises from 36.2 to 51.2 percent. The planning disadvantage narrows by 15.0 percentage points (95 percent task-cluster bootstrap interval: 4.2 to 25.8). A strict read-only planning campaign varies whether the planner sees the task issue. At 12,000 tokens, issue access raises success by about 16 percentage points over issue-hidden planning. Compared with direct execution, task-informed planning is about 10 points lower at 12,000 tokens; at 24,000 tokens, it shows a 29.6-point advantage. In the resource panels, direct execution uses substantially less than either ceiling, while the planning workflow's binding rate falls from 46.2 to 0.8 percent and downstream execution accounts for 89.9 percent of the increase in total use. Scale determines the capacity available to a system; workflow and information structure shape the productive value

AI.tldr: Using controlled software-engineering workflow experiments, this paper shows that the economic value of inference depends on how capacity and task information are distributed across AI production stages: planning's disadvantage relative to direct execution shrinks as capacity grows, and information access (seeing the task issue) materially raises planning success, while binding resource constraints and downstream execution drive most capacity use.
AI.motivation: The economic value of inference is argued to depend not only on raw capacity (scale) but on organizational margins—how capacity and task information are distributed across stages of AI production. The paper motivates studying these workflow and information-structure margins, which are typically overlooked relative to scale alone.
AI.method: Controlled workflow experiments on externally verified software-engineering tasks. Two matched resource panels compare direct execution against information-constrained planning at logical-token ceilings of 12,000 and 24,000, with task-cluster bootstrap intervals. A strict read-only planning campaign varies whether the planner sees the task issue. Resource-use diagnostics measure binding rates and the downstream share of total token use.
AI.result: Direct execution holds a constant 59.6% success rate at both 12,000 and 24,000-token ceilings, while information-constrained planning rises from 36.2% to 51.2%, narrowing the planning gap by 15.0 points (95% bootstrap interval: 4.2–25.8). Issue access raises planning success by ~16 points over issue-hidden planning at 12,000 tokens. Versus direct execution, task-informed planning is ~10 points lower at 12,000 tokens but gains a 29.6-point advantage at 24,000. Direct execution uses well below either ceiling; planning's binding rate falls from 46.2% to 0.8%, and downstream execution accounts for 89.9% of the increase in total use.
AI.conclusion: Scale determines the capacity available to a system, whereas workflow and information structure shape its productive value. Organizational choices—where capacity sits and who sees task information—are first-order determinants of inference economics, not mere implementation details.

title: VLN on the Fly: An Onboard Vision-Language Navigation Stack for Aerial Robots
summary: Running vision-language navigation fully onboard an aerial robot is hard, since grounding, planning, and control must share limited compute and a single-stage error is difficult to isolate in flight. End-to-end aerial policies fuse these stages into one network, giving up the observability and safety checks a modular stack keeps available. We propose VLN on the Fly, an onboard stack that keeps grounding, planning, and control as separate, inspectable stages. A quantized VLM grounds an instruction to a coarse image cell, depth lifts it to a 3D goal, a fast B-spline planner returns a feasible trajectory, and a pretrained reinforcement learning policy tracks it to motor commands across quadrotors. Across 15 onboard flights over three everyday referents in a controlled indoor volume, the stack reaches the target in 13 of 15 trials with 5.72 cm mean goal error and 39.3% average GPU utilization. In 6 additional cluttered-environment trials, the stack tracks collision-free trajectories under onboard perception gating.

AI.tldr: VLN on the Fly is a modular, fully onboard vision-language navigation stack for aerial robots that keeps grounding, planning, and control as separate inspectable stages, achieving 13/15 successful indoor flights with 5.72 cm mean goal error at 39.3% average GPU utilization.
AI.motivation: Running vision-language navigation fully onboard an aerial robot is difficult because grounding, planning, and control must share limited compute, and a single-stage error is hard to isolate in flight. End-to-end aerial policies fuse these stages into one network, sacrificing the observability and safety checks that a modular stack provides.
AI.method: The proposed onboard stack separates grounding, planning, and control into distinct inspectable stages: a quantized VLM grounds the instruction to a coarse image cell, depth lifts it to a 3D goal, a fast B-spline planner returns a feasible trajectory, and a pretrained reinforcement learning policy tracks it to motor commands across quadrotors.
AI.result: Across 15 onboard flights over three everyday referents in a controlled indoor volume, the stack reached the target in 13 of 15 trials with 5.72 cm mean goal error and 39.3% average GPU utilization. In 6 additional cluttered-environment trials, the stack tracked collision-free trajectories under onboard perception gating.
AI.conclusion: A modular, fully onboard vision-language navigation stack can reliably ground language instructions, plan feasible trajectories, and control quadrotors within tight compute budgets, while preserving stage-wise observability and enabling onboard perception gating for safe flight in cluttered environments.

title: SkillAA: Attribution-Guided Skill-Graph Updating with Targeted Validation and Rollback
summary: External skills provide domain procedures without parameter updates, but existing methods often edit skills directly from failed rollouts without structured routing from an observed failure to an editable location; existing skill graphs also underuse semantic boundaries, object addresses, and topological dependencies for skill retrieval, targeted updating, and scoped validation. We introduce SkillAA (Skill Abductive Attribution), a structured skill-optimization framework for frozen language models. It represents skill applicability, execution, and composition in a unified graph, allowing the same structure to support skill selection, attribution-guided repair, and update validation. SkillAA contrasts successful and failed executions to route candidate repairs to specific graph objects, updates only the selected local structure, and uses Local and Big Gates to screen candidate changes before commitment. With gpt-5.6-sol, SkillAA reaches 81.5%, 66.7%, and 91.2% on SearchQA, LiveMath, and DocVQA, respectively, and attains the highest observed mean in every main setting. These results support the utility of attribution-guided graph editing and graph-scoped validation.

AI.tldr: SkillAA is a structured skill-optimization framework for frozen LLMs that uses a unified skill graph and attribution-guided repair with gated validation, achieving 81.5%/66.7%/91.2% on SearchQA/LiveMath/DocVQA.
AI.motivation: External skills provide domain procedures without parameter updates, but existing methods edit skills directly from failed rollouts without structured routing from an observed failure to an editable location; existing skill graphs underuse semantic boundaries, object addresses, and topological dependencies for skill retrieval, targeted updating, and scoped validation.
AI.method: SkillAA (Skill Abductive Attribution) represents skill applicability, execution, and composition in a unified graph supporting skill selection, attribution-guided repair, and update validation. It contrasts successful and failed executions to route candidate repairs to specific graph objects, updates only the selected local structure, and uses Local and Big Gates to screen candidate changes before commitment.
AI.result: With gpt-5.6-sol, SkillAA reaches 81.5%, 66.7%, and 91.2% on SearchQA, LiveMath, and DocVQA, respectively, and attains the highest observed mean in every main setting.
AI.conclusion: Results support the utility of attribution-guided graph editing and graph-scoped validation for skill optimization in frozen language models.

title: Strategic Transformer for Resource-Constrained Multi-Object Navigation in Ultra-Large-Scale Environments
summary: Resource-constrained multi-object navigation in vast indoor environments ($>2,000\text{ m}^2$) poses significant challenges for efficiency and strategic planning. To tackle this, we reformulate the task as a Set Orienteering Problem (SOP), providing an optimization framework under resource constraints where exploitation is governed by the SOP model and exploration is managed by a separate heuristic switcher. Conventional baselines suffer from either rigid planning or myopic behaviors. To overcome these limitations and resolve the NP-hard computational challenges of SOP for real-time navigation, we develop the Strategic Transformer. This lightweight architecture functions as a priority planner that internalizes expert combinatorial logic into a predictable $41.03\text{ ms}$ forward pass while reducing teacher-student information asymmetry. Incorporating geometric attention biases allows the network to effectively model long-range structural dependencies. By coupling the Transformer's macro-plan with a bounded iterative 2-opt local refinement on a capped candidate graph, our framework achieves a $94\times$ speedup compared to heavy meta-heuristics, ensuring bounded-latency inference suitable for onboard deployment. Experiments on ProcTHOR validate that our method successfully bridges the gap between exploration and exploitation, outperforming carefully re-implemented baselines under Progress weighted by Path Length (PPL) and establishing a new benchmark for scalable, resource-constrained navigation.

AI.tldr: This paper reformulates resource-constrained multi-object navigation in large indoor environments as a Set Orienteering Problem and proposes a Strategic Transformer priority planner with local 2-opt refinement, achieving large speedups over meta-heuristics and a new benchmark on ProcTHOR.
AI.motivation: Navigating vast indoor spaces (>2,000 m²) to reach multiple objects under resource constraints is difficult: efficiency and strategic planning are required, but conventional baselines are either rigidly planned or myopic. The problem is also NP-hard (SOP), making real-time onboard computation challenging.
AI.method: The task is recast as a Set Orienteering Problem (SOP), where exploitation is modeled by SOP and exploration controlled by a separate heuristic switcher. A lightweight Strategic Transformer serves as a priority planner, internalizing expert combinatorial logic into a single forward pass (41.03 ms) while reducing teacher-student information asymmetry. Geometric attention biases enable long-range structural dependency modeling. The Transformer's macro-plan is coupled with bounded iterative 2-opt local refinement on a capped candidate graph.
AI.result: The framework achieves a 94× speedup versus heavy meta-heuristics with bounded-latency inference suitable for onboard deployment. On ProcTHOR, it outperforms carefully re-implemented baselines under Progress weighted by Path Length (PPL), bridging exploration and exploitation.
AI.conclusion: The proposed SOP-based Strategic Transformer plus local refinement provides a scalable, resource-constrained navigation solution, establishing a new benchmark for efficient multi-object navigation in large indoor environments.

title: How Do Agent Harnesses Create Value? Planning Information and Release Control in Stateful LLM Agents
summary: Agent harnesses supply planning guidance, organize execution, and check completion. We study how these components affect success, erroneous acceptance, and cost in two Retail experiments and an Airline pilot in $τ^2$-bench. The primary comparison pairs prewritten task-specific plans (Fixed) with shuffled policy text matched in word count (Sham), isolating the contribution of guidance content. Across 265 matched cells, Fixed improves oracle-verified success by 7.17 percentage points (90\% task-clustered bootstrap interval, 1.15--13.36 points), with gains concentrated in higher-complexity tasks. A read-only terminal verifier rejects 61\% of Retail oracle-invalid episodes while withholding 17\% of correct ones, at less than one cent of additional cost per episode. Which component matters more depends on the loss assigned to erroneous acceptance: at low liability the planning gain dominates; at high liability the verifier's avoided false passes dominate---and a standalone verifier captures nearly all the false-pass benefit of the full planning-plus-verification stack at a fraction of its cost.

AI.tldr: Agent harness planning guidance (Fixed vs. Sham plans) improves task success by 7.17 points across 265 task cells in τ²-bench, with gains concentrated on complex tasks. A cheap read-only terminal verifier rejects 61% of invalid episodes at <1 cent each. The optimal component—planning versus verification—depends on the cost assigned to erroneous acceptance: planning wins at low liability, verification at high liability, and a standalone verifier nearly matches the full stack's false-pass reduction at much lower cost.
AI.motivation: Agent harnesses bundle planning guidance, execution organization, and completion checking, but it is unclear how each component individually contributes to success, erroneous acceptance, and cost. The paper aims to isolate the effect of guidance content and verification, and to determine which component matters more under different loss assumptions for erroneous acceptance.
AI.method: Two Retail experiments and an Airline pilot within τ²-bench. The primary comparison pairs prewritten task-specific plans (Fixed) against word-count-matched shuffled policy text (Sham) to isolate guidance content. 265 matched cells are analyzed using oracle-verified success with a 90% task-clustered bootstrap interval. A read-only terminal verifier is also evaluated for its rejection rate of oracle-invalid episodes and its effect on correct episodes and cost.
AI.result: Fixed plans improve oracle-verified success by 7.17 percentage points (90% task-clustered bootstrap interval 1.15–13.36 points), with gains concentrated in higher-complexity tasks. The read-only terminal verifier rejects 61% of Retail oracle-invalid episodes while withholding 17% of correct ones, costing less than one cent per episode. At low liability for erroneous acceptance, the planning gain dominates; at high liability, the verifier's avoided false passes dominate, and a standalone verifier captures nearly all the false-pass benefit of the full planning-plus-verification stack at a fraction of its cost.
AI.conclusion: Guidance content and verification make distinct, measurable contributions to agent harness performance. Which component matters more is contingent on the loss assigned to erroneous acceptance: planning dominates at low liability, verification dominates at high liability. A standalone verifier can capture nearly all false-pass benefits of the full stack far more cheaply, suggesting verification may be the more cost-effective intervention when erroneous acceptance is costly.

title: LLM-Guided Transformation of Non-Critical Driving Scenes into Safety-Critical Scenarios Using Augmented Reality
summary: Testing Autonomous Driving Systems (ADS) requires realistic safety-critical scenarios, but collecting such data from real-world driving is costly and unsafe. This paper presents an automated pipeline that transforms safe driving scenes into safety-critical scenarios by combining computer vision, Large Language Models (LLMs), and Augmented Reality (AR). The system detects and tracks road users, extracts safety features including distance, velocity, motion direction, and Time-to-Collision (TTC), and assesses scene criticality. Safe scenes are modified by an LLM, which generates realistic collision-inducing objects and behaviors that are integrated into the original scene using AR. The proposed pipeline was evaluated on the nuScenes dataset, achieving 97.52% safety classification accuracy and successfully generating realistic scenarios such as pedestrian crossings, rear overtaking vehicles, and sudden-stop events. The results demonstrate an effective and flexible approach for automated generation of safety-critical scenarios to support the testing and validation of autonomous driving systems.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an automated pipeline combining CV, LLMs, and AR to transform safe driving scenes into safety-critical scenarios for ADS testing, achieving 97.52% safety classification accuracy on nuScenes.
AI.motivation: Testing Autonomous Driving Systems (ADS) requires realistic safety-critical scenarios, but collecting such data from real-world driving is costly and unsafe.
AI.method: The pipeline detects and tracks road users, extracts safety features (distance, velocity, motion direction, TTC), assesses scene criticality, and uses an LLM to generate realistic collision-inducing objects and behaviors that are integrated into the original scene via AR.
AI.result: Evaluated on nuScenes, the pipeline achieved 97.52% safety classification accuracy and successfully generated realistic scenarios such as pedestrian crossings, rear overtaking vehicles, and sudden-stop events.
AI.conclusion: The results demonstrate an effective and flexible approach for automated generation of safety-critical scenarios to support ADS testing and validation.

title: SoL-Pi: Recursively Scaling Auto-Research Loops for Efficient Agent Harness
comment: 15 pages, 8 figures, 4 tables. Code: https://github.com/NVlabs/SoL-Pi . Project page: https://nvlabs.github.io/SoL-Pi/
summary: As coding agents move from supervised code completion to unattended, around-the-clock exploration, their work expands from isolated predictions into long trajectories of reasoning, tool use, and feedback. Token efficiency therefore becomes important for scaling recursive self-improvement. We take an RSI-inspired approach at the harness layer, scaling auto-research loops across increasingly numerous and diverse environments for harness rollouts. At this scale, the process yields reusable improvements that transfer beyond their development setting, moving automated harness discovery toward production-level outcomes. Four mechanisms survive selection and form SoL-Pi, spanning action execution, context compaction, observation handling, and delegated reading. On the 51-task EdgeBench evaluation, SoL-Pi achieves performance comparable to Pi across GPT-5.6 Sol and Opus 5 while reducing recorded token traffic by 44.7-49.0% and API cost by about one third. In other words, estimated hourly savings are \$8.75-\$13.50 relative to native Codex and Claude Code harnesses, and \$4.36-\$5.71 relative to Pi.

AI.tldr: SoL-Pi is a harness-layer, RSI-inspired system that scales auto-research loops across many diverse environments to discover token-efficient coding-agent harness improvements, yielding four transferable mechanisms that cut token traffic and cost while matching Pi's performance on EdgeBench.
AI.motivation: Coding agents are shifting from supervised code completion to unattended, around-the-clock exploration, so their work becomes long trajectories of reasoning, tool use, and feedback rather than isolated predictions. Token efficiency thus becomes critical for scaling recursive self-improvement.
AI.method: An RSI-inspired approach at the harness layer: scaling auto-research loops across increasingly numerous and diverse environments for harness rollouts. Four mechanisms survive selection and form SoL-Pi, spanning action execution, context compaction, observation handling, and delegated reading.
AI.result: On the 51-task EdgeBench evaluation, SoL-Pi matches Pi's performance across GPT-5.6 Sol and Opus 5 while reducing recorded token traffic by 44.7-49.0% and API cost by about one third. Estimated hourly savings are \$8.75-\$13.50 versus native Codex and Claude Code harnesses, and \$4.36-\$5.71 versus Pi.
AI.conclusion: At sufficient scale, the auto-research process yields reusable harness improvements that transfer beyond their development setting, moving automated harness discovery toward production-level outcomes.

title: Implementation of Tightly-Coupled SLAM Fusion of GPS, IMU, and LiDAR for Autonomous Vehicles
summary: Autonomous vehicles depend entirely on Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) to navigate safely in unknown environments. However, relying on a single sensory modality introduces critical failure points: LiDAR systems degrade in featureless corridors, Inertial Measurement Units (IMUs) accumulate mathematical drift, and GPS drops frequently in urban canyons. This paper presents the implementation of a tightly-coupled SLAM fusion architecture that integrates a Velodyne 3D LiDAR, a high-frequency IMU, and GPS to achieve continuous spatial awareness. Utilizing a phased development methodology, we establish a 2D baseline to validate hardware synchronization and transform geometries before upgrading to a full 3D architecture driven by FAST-LIO2. This advanced approach uses an Iterated Error-State Kalman Filter (IESKF) to process dense 3D laser points alongside continuous inertial data, eliminating motion blur at high speeds. To eradicate long-term drift, a GTSAM pose-graph optimization back-end executes multi-modal loop closures. Evaluated across simulated environments and physical deployments, the results demonstrate that tightly-coupled 3D fusion effectively overcomes individual sensor blind spots to generate highly detailed point clouds, providing the foundational High-Definition (HD) maps required for advanced downstream autonomous planners.

AI.tldr: This paper implements a tightly-coupled multi-sensor SLAM architecture fusing a Velodyne 3D LiDAR, high-frequency IMU, and GPS using FAST-LIO2's IESKF and a GTSAM pose-graph back-end, validated in simulation and physical deployments to produce HD maps for autonomous planners.
AI.motivation: Single-modality SLAM suffers critical failure points: LiDAR degrades in featureless corridors, IMUs accumulate mathematical drift, and GPS drops in urban canyons, so continuous spatial awareness for autonomous navigation requires sensor fusion.
AI.method: A phased development methodology: first a 2D baseline validating hardware synchronization and transform geometries, then a full 3D tightly-coupled architecture driven by FAST-LIO2. An Iterated Error-State Kalman Filter (IESKF) processes dense 3D laser points with continuous inertial data, and a GTSAM pose-graph optimization back-end performs multi-modal loop closures.
AI.result: Evaluated across simulated environments and physical deployments, the tightly-coupled 3D fusion overcomes individual sensor blind spots, eliminates motion blur at high speeds, eradicates long-term drift, and generates highly detailed point clouds.
AI.conclusion: Tightly-coupled LiDAR-IMU-GPS fusion provides the foundational High-Definition (HD) maps required for advanced downstream autonomous planners.

title: FreqCondNorm: Towards Cross-domain Predictive Maintenance through a Frequency-Conditioned Transformer Foundation Model
summary: Deep learning predictive maintenance models suffer from poor transferability across machines and operating conditions, especially when labelled data are scarce and signals span five orders of magnitude in sampling frequency (1 Hz to ~100 kHz). We propose FreqCondNorm, a Transformer-based architecture that introduces a FiLM-style frequency-conditioned normalization layer to unify heterogeneous time-series within a single model. The architecture is pretrained on five public predictive maintenance datasets (CWRU, MFPT, UOC18, PRONOSTIA, CMAPSS) using masked auto-encoding and contrastive learning with balanced domain sampling. On fault diagnosis, the model achieves 99.2% accuracy on CWRU (+6.4 pp over CNN) and 82.1% zero-shot accuracy on MFPT, demonstrating strong transfer across sampling frequencies. However, the approach does not improve remaining useful life prediction, suggesting a mismatch between pretraining and RUL objectives that warrants future investigation.

AI.tldr: FreqCondNorm, a Transformer with a FiLM-style frequency-conditioned normalization layer, unifies heterogeneous time-series across sampling frequencies for predictive maintenance; it excels at fault diagnosis transfer but does not improve RUL prediction.
AI.motivation: Existing deep learning predictive maintenance models transfer poorly across machines and operating conditions, particularly under scarce labelled data and when signals span five orders of magnitude in sampling frequency (1 Hz to ~100 kHz).
AI.method: A Transformer-based architecture with a FiLM-style frequency-conditioned normalization layer to unify heterogeneous time-series in a single model. It is pretrained on five public datasets (CWRU, MFPT, UOC18, PRONOSTIA, CMAPSS) using masked auto-encoding and contrastive learning with balanced domain sampling.
AI.result: On fault diagnosis, 99.2% accuracy on CWRU (+6.4 pp over CNN) and 82.1% zero-shot accuracy on MFPT, showing strong cross-sampling-frequency transfer. However, no improvement in remaining useful life (RUL) prediction.
AI.conclusion: Frequency-conditioned normalization enables effective unification and transfer for fault diagnosis, but the pretraining objective appears mismatched with RUL prediction, warranting future investigation.

title: RoboFind: Multi-Agent Personalized Object Search for People Who Are Blind or Have Low Vision
summary: Blind and low-vision users often need to locate a specific personal object rather than an arbitrary instance of the same category. The task calls for a robot that can move through the space and reach viewpoints the user cannot, and for an accessible interface where the user says which object is meant and learns whether the right one was found. We present RoboFind, a multi-agent framework in which a smartphone teaches the target and a quadruped robot carries out the search. A Target Teaching Agent converts guided smartphone recordings into a semantic target profile and a reusable multi-view reference bank through an accessible capture flow with AR guidance, speech and haptic feedback, and screen-reader support, so later missions refer to a stored object without repeating the teaching process. At runtime, a Navigation Agent explores the environment and proposes candidate targets, a Verification Agent checks each candidate against the stored references, and a Coordination and Recovery Agent completes the mission or triggers recovery and continued search. Across 32 real-robot missions, RoboFind reaches 85.0% success against 25.0% for a reconstructed sequential first-stop baseline over 20 trials with ten targets, and reduces false success from 75.0% to 5.0%. On six shared targets it succeeds in 10/12 trials, against 5/12 for 12 independently executed GPT-6 Astra-only trials. These results show that the multi-agent design fits the demands of personalized object search, where verifying object identity before declaring completion is what makes the outcome something a user can rely on.

AI.tldr: RoboFind is a multi-agent framework where a smartphone teaches a specific personal object and a quadruped robot searches for it, reaching 85.0% success versus 25.0% for a sequential first-stop baseline and cutting false success from 75.0% to 5.0%.
AI.motivation: Blind and low-vision users often need to find a specific personal object, not any instance of a category. This requires a robot that can reach viewpoints the user cannot and an accessible interface for specifying and confirming the intended object.
AI.method: RoboFind uses three agents: a Target Teaching Agent that converts guided smartphone recordings into a semantic target profile and multi-view reference bank via AR guidance, speech/haptic feedback, and screen-reader support; a Navigation Agent that explores and proposes candidates; and a Verification Agent that checks candidates against stored references, with a Coordination and Recovery Agent completing or retrying the mission.
AI.result: Over 32 real-robot missions, RoboFind achieves 85.0% success versus 25.0% for a reconstructed sequential first-stop baseline (20 trials, ten targets), and reduces false success from 75.0% to 5.0%. On six shared targets it succeeds in 10/12 trials versus 5/12 for 12 independently executed GPT-6 Astra-only trials.
AI.conclusion: The multi-agent design suits personalized object search: verifying object identity before declaring completion is what makes the outcome reliable for users.

title: Refuse, Decompose, Refresh: A Claim-Safe Protocol for Closed-Loop AI Evaluation
comment: 8 pages, 0 figures, 3 tables. The reproducibility artifact is linked in the paper
summary: An AI evaluation can be perfectly reproducible and still support the wrong claim. This risk is acute in closed-loop systems: policy determines visited states, observable components, and which failures leave a measurable trace. We propose a claim-safe protocol with three actions. Refuse: abstain when a clean reference stream or matched runtime comparison lacks support. Decompose: report protocol execution, operational false admission, and structural hypotheses separately rather than as one PASS/FAIL label. Refresh: treat distribution-shift alarms as requests to invalidate and recompute a reference map, not as fault evidence. We instantiate the protocol in an aggregate-only simulator with 24 policy components, three demand regimes, two fault-mask families, and independent development and heldout seeds. The preregistered heldout contains 1,440 cases and 21,600 partition rows. Only 55/72 regime-component units were reference-admitted and 54/55 remained runtime-admitted, making abstention part of the result. Stable false admission was 0/20 represented components, with a one-sided exact 95% upper bound of 0.1391 under a frozen 0.20 rule. Within admitted units, affected clean traffic outpredicted nominal fault-cell fraction: across 540 unit-arm rows nested in 20 component clusters, the cell-minus-traffic negative-log-likelihood difference was 0.1264 nats per row, with a 95% component-cluster interval of [0.0593, 0.1918]. A drift log shows why "null" must be reference-relative: clean fault-null streams triggered 15/15, 0/15, and 14/15 alarms across three regimes, while only the middle regime matched the frozen detector reference. Rather than a universal threshold, we contribute an executable contract linking observable support, statistical calibration, and justified claims.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a "claim-safe" protocol (Refuse, Decompose, Refresh) for AI evaluation in closed-loop systems, arguing that reproducibility alone does not guarantee valid claims. It instantiates this in a simulator and reports results emphasizing abstention, reference-relative nulls, and an executable contract.
AI.motivation: In closed-loop systems, policy determines visited states, observable components, and which failures leave a measurable trace, so an evaluation can be perfectly reproducible yet still support the wrong claim. The work aims to prevent such unsupported claims.
AI.method: They propose a claim-safe protocol with three actions: Refuse (abstain when a clean reference stream or matched runtime comparison lacks support), Decompose (report protocol execution, operational false admission, and structural hypotheses separately rather than as a single PASS/FAIL label), and Refresh (treat distribution-shift alarms as requests to invalidate and recompute a reference map, not as fault evidence). They instantiate it in an aggregate-only simulator with 24 policy components, three demand regimes, two fault-mask families, and independent development and heldout seeds; the preregistered heldout contains 1,440 cases and 21,600 partition rows.
AI.result: Only 55/72 regime-component units were reference-admitted and 54/55 remained runtime-admitted, making abstention part of the result. Stable false admission was 0/20 represented components with a one-sided exact 95% upper bound of 0.1391 under a frozen 0.20 rule. Within admitted units, affected clean traffic outpredicted nominal fault-cell fraction: across 540 unit-arm rows nested in 20 component clusters, the cell-minus-traffic negative-log-likelihood difference was 0.1264 nats per row with a 95% component-cluster interval of [0.0593, 0.1918]. A drift log showed clean fault-null streams triggered 15/15, 0/15, and 14/15 alarms across three regimes, and only the middle regime matched the frozen detector reference.
AI.conclusion: Rather than advocating a universal threshold, the authors contribute an executable contract that links observable support, statistical calibration, and justified claims, with abstention and reference-relative nulls treated as integral to the evaluation result.

title: Navi-Agent: Unlocalized Monocular Navigation Agent
comment: 8 pages, 7 figures. Submitted to 2027 IEEE International Conference on Robotics & Automation (ICRA)
summary: Vision-Language Navigation in Continuous Environments (VLN-CE) requires an embodied agent to execute long-horizon instructions in unknown environments. Existing zero-shot VLN-CE systems typically maintain spatial states through geometric localization or coordinate-based representations. Recent geometry-constrained navigation removes depth and globally consistent coordinates, but maintaining persistent spatial awareness for place confirmation, progress verification, and recovery remains challenging. We present Navi-Agent, a zero-shot VLN-CE agent that constructs a coordinate-free spatial state from visual observations and executed motion histories. Navi-Agent organizes this state as a navigation topology, where nodes represent visual places and edges represent motion transitions. This representation enables observation-based approximate self-localization, task progress verification, and visual revisitation-based recovery. Navi-Agent performs closed-loop navigation by decomposing instructions into sub-goals, executing local visual navigation, and verifying visited places through the constructed spatial state. Experiments on zero-shot VLN-CE benchmark and real-world robot platforms show that Navi-Agent achieves state-of-the-art performance among geometry-constrained methods while remaining competitive with approaches relying on geometric localization.

AI.tldr: Navi-Agent is a zero-shot VLN-CE agent that builds a coordinate-free spatial state as a navigation topology (visual places as nodes, motion transitions as edges), enabling self-localization, progress verification, and visual revisitation-based recovery without depth or global coordinates.
AI.motivation: Existing zero-shot VLN-CE systems rely on geometric localization or coordinate-based representations. Recent geometry-constrained navigation removes depth and globally consistent coordinates to reduce sensor dependence, but then struggles to maintain persistent spatial awareness needed for place confirmation, progress verification, and recovery.
AI.method: Navi-Agent constructs a coordinate-free spatial state from visual observations and executed motion histories, organized as a navigation topology with nodes as visual places and edges as motion transitions. This supports observation-based approximate self-localization, task progress verification, and visual revisitation-based recovery. It performs closed-loop navigation by decomposing instructions into sub-goals, executing local visual navigation, and verifying visited places via the constructed spatial state.
AI.result: On the zero-shot VLN-CE benchmark and real-world robot platforms, Navi-Agent achieves state-of-the-art performance among geometry-constrained methods and remains competitive with approaches relying on geometric localization.
AI.conclusion: A coordinate-free topology-based spatial state can serve as an effective alternative to geometric localization for zero-shot VLN-CE, delivering strong benchmark and real-world performance while avoiding depth and globally consistent coordinate dependencies.

title: Language-model groups overstate consensus when replaying human deliberation on a reasoning task
comment: 37 pages, 4 figures. Preregistration: https://osf.io/5jp7s . Code and data: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21318346
summary: Full-consensus rates are often treated as indicators of collective cognition, yet depend on how participation and final states are operationalized. We replayed 100 held-out human Wason groups with matched large language model (LLM) agent groups, seeding one belief-anchored agent per participant's pre-discussion answer and scoring agents and people with the same code. Across human scoring definitions, estimates ranged from 24.0% to 57.0%; about one fifth of participants never posted, whereas agents almost always did. Agent groups remained more consensual in two post-unblinding sensitivity analyses: the submit-based comparison (n = 98) yielded gaps of 34.0 and 43.9 percentage points for chat and reasoning modes, and the participation-matched comparison (n = 45) yielded gaps of 34.1 and 44.4 points. These complementary routes reduced different measurement asymmetries yet converged within 0.5 percentage points. The gap persisted without early stopping and under a reparameterization removing the memorizable answer; reasoning-mode groups then agreed nearly unanimously, mostly on incorrect answers. Simulated consensus did not track collective accuracy, and belief-anchored agent groups were biased estimators of the human group-outcome distribution in this setting. These analyses provide a scoring-explicit basis for assessing simulated-group estimates of human deliberative outcomes.

AI.tldr: LLM agent groups seeded with human pre-discussion beliefs appear more consensual than real human deliberative groups, but this gap is sensitive to how consensus and participation are operationalized; simulated consensus does not track collective accuracy.
AI.motivation: Full-consensus rates are commonly used as indicators of collective cognition, yet they depend heavily on how participation and final states are defined. The authors aim to test whether LLM agent groups reproduce human deliberative outcomes and to make explicit how scoring choices shape such comparisons.
AI.method: One hundred held-out human Wason groups were replayed with matched LLM agent groups. Each agent was seeded with one participant's pre-discussion answer as a belief anchor, and both agents and humans were scored with identical code. Human scoring definitions were varied, and two post-unblinding sensitivity analyses were run: a submit-based comparison (n = 98) and a participation-matched comparison (n = 45). Additional checks removed early stopping and reparameterized the task to eliminate the memorizable answer.
AI.result: Human consensus estimates ranged from 24.0% to 57.0% depending on scoring definitions. Roughly one fifth of participants never posted, whereas agents almost always did. Agent groups were more consensual in both sensitivity analyses, with gaps of 34.0 and 43.9 percentage points (chat vs. reasoning) in the submit-based comparison and 34.1 and 44.4 points in the participation-matched comparison; the two routes converged within 0.5 percentage points. The gap persisted without early stopping and under the reparameterization, where reasoning-mode groups agreed nearly unanimously, mostly on incorrect answers. Simulated consensus did not track collective accuracy, and belief-anchored agent groups were biased estimators of the human group-outcome distribution.
AI.conclusion: LLM agent groups overestimate human consensus, and simulated consensus is not a valid proxy for collective accuracy in this setting. The findings provide a scoring-explicit basis for evaluating simulated-group estimates of human deliberative outcomes.

title: Imagine-TAMP: Imagination-Guided Task and Motion Planning in Partial Observability
summary: Robots operating in cluttered environments must often manipulate objects whose locations are only partially observable. A central challenge is deciding whether to acquire another observation or to first manipulate objects that may occlude the target. Conventional task and motion planning (TAMP) approaches typically make this decision using symbolic action costs or expensive geometric planning, neither of which adequately captures how likely an observation is to reveal an occluded target. We introduce Imagine-TAMP, an interleaved planning and execution framework that uses semantic and geometric imagination to compare alternative task-level strategies under partial observability before committing to expensive motion planning. A vision-language model shapes a particle belief over target locations using commonsense relationships between the target and visible objects, while a generative scene model estimates plausible geometry in unobserved regions. Given a target hypothesis and imagined scene, Imagine-TAMP generates multiple symbolic plan skeletons and assigns non-unit costs that approximate both manipulation effort and target visibility from sensing actions, distinguishing a short but poorly informative observation strategy from a longer strategy that first manipulates an occluder to better expose the target. The selected skeleton is then refined into a feasible continuous plan and executed, with new observations updating the belief and triggering replanning when necessary. Experiments show that imagination-guided evaluation improves observation-versus-manipulation decisions: in viewpoint-constrained shelf scenes, non-unit geometric evaluation increases success from 46.0% to 84.0%, while semantic belief shaping further reduces manipulation and replanning. On a real robot, the complete system reduces planning time by 32% relative to a geometry-only ablation.

AI.tldr: Imagine-TAMP is an interleaved planning and execution framework that uses semantic and geometric imagination to compare task-level strategies under partial observability before committing to expensive motion planning.
AI.motivation: Robots in cluttered environments must manipulate objects with only partially observable locations. The key challenge is deciding whether to acquire another observation or to first manipulate occluding objects. Conventional TAMP approaches rely on symbolic action costs or expensive geometric planning, neither of which adequately captures how likely an observation is to reveal an occluded target.
AI.method: The framework employs a vision-language model to shape a particle belief over target locations using commonsense relationships between the target and visible objects, while a generative scene model estimates plausible geometry in unobserved regions. Given a target hypothesis and imagined scene, it generates multiple symbolic plan skeletons and assigns non-unit costs approximating both manipulation effort and target visibility from sensing actions, distinguishing short but uninformative observation strategies from longer strategies that manipulate occluders to expose the target. The selected skeleton is refined into a feasible continuous plan and executed, with new observations updating the belief and triggering replanning when necessary.
AI.result: In viewpoint-constrained shelf scenes, non-unit geometric evaluation increases success from 46.0% to 84.0%, while semantic belief shaping further reduces manipulation and replanning. On a real robot, the complete system reduces planning time by 32% relative to a geometry-only ablation.
AI.conclusion: Imagination-guided evaluation improves observation-versus-manipulation decisions, and combining semantic belief shaping with geometric imagination yields more effective and efficient task and motion planning under partial observability.

title: Limits of Confidence in Diffusion
summary: Discrete diffusion, including remasking and uniform-state samplers, generate a sequence by writing multiple token positions per step, drawing each from a per-position distribution and choosing which positions to write from those same distributions. For domains of general interest (pixels, phonemes, or words) there are inherent dependencies between tokens. We show that a step matches the training distribution only when the positions it writes are conditionally independent given the tokens already fixed, that no product of per-position distributions can match a dependent group, and that per-position distributions do not determine whether a group is dependent: two joint distributions can have identical per-position marginals while differing in which combinations of values occur. On ScanAndAdd, a synthetic task whose joint distribution is available in closed form, we verify that every group of two or more undetermined positions a confidence ranking writes is dependent, and measure the generated distribution to be $29\times$ the sampling-noise floor total variation while per-sample metrics are $1.0$.

AI.tldr: Discrete diffusion samplers write multiple positions per step using per-position distributions, but this fails for inherently dependent tokens: such a step only matches the training distribution when written positions are conditionally independent, and per-position marginals cannot detect dependence. On ScanAndAdd, confidence-ranked writing groups are always dependent and yield 29x the noise-floor total variation.
AI.motivation: Discrete diffusion (remasking and uniform-state samplers) writes multiple token positions per step, selecting values and positions from per-position distributions. For real domains (pixels, phonemes, words) tokens exhibit inherent dependencies, so the question is whether this per-position, multi-position-per-step generation can match the true training distribution.
AI.method: Theoretical analysis showing that (1) a step matches the training distribution only when the positions it writes are conditionally independent given already-fixed tokens, (2) no product of per-position distributions can match a dependent group, and (3) per-position distributions do not determine dependence, since two joint distributions can share identical marginals yet differ in which value combinations occur. Empirical test on ScanAndAdd, a synthetic task with a closed-form joint distribution, checking whether groups of two or more undetermined positions written by confidence ranking are dependent and measuring the generated distribution against the sampling-noise floor in total variation.
AI.result: Every group of two or more undetermined positions written by the confidence ranking is dependent. The generated distribution measures 29x the sampling-noise floor in total variation, while per-sample metrics report 1.0.
AI.conclusion: Multi-position-per-step discrete diffusion samplers cannot faithfully match dependent training distributions; dependence is pervasive in the written groups yet invisible to per-position marginals and per-sample metrics, which can appear perfect (1.0) even as the distribution deviates 29x from the noise floor.

title: Resilient Motion Planning for Free-Flying Space Robots under Actuator Failures
summary: Free-flying robots rely on multiple thrusters to maneuver in space. If one or more of these thrusters fail, the robot may lose control authority and risk mission failure. At the same time, their free-flying nature implies that, even in the absence of actuation, they continue along (locally) straight-line trajectories. In this work we present a probabilistic, proactive, motion planning framework that explicitly accounts for actuator failures in space. We model actuator failure modes as a Markov chain and propagate the probability of successfully reaching the goal along the planning horizon. Precomputed reachable sets evaluate the robot's capabilities of reaching waypoints under potential failures and an RRT$^*$-based planner concatenates these waypoints. The resulting algorithm maximizes the overall target-reaching probability, providing maximally resilient motion plans utilizing free-flying properties. We validate our approach experimentally on a physical free-flyer platform with injected actuator failures.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a probabilistic, proactive motion planning framework for free-flying robots that explicitly accounts for actuator failures, modeling failure modes as a Markov chain and maximizing goal-reaching probability using precomputed reachable sets and an RRT*-based planner, validated on a physical free-flyer platform.
AI.motivation: Free-flying robots depend on multiple thrusters for maneuvering. If one or more thrusters fail, the robot may lose control authority and risk mission failure. However, their free-flying nature means that even without actuation they continue along locally straight-line trajectories, a property that can be exploited for resilience.
AI.method: The authors model actuator failure modes as a Markov chain and propagate the probability of successfully reaching the goal along the planning horizon. Precomputed reachable sets evaluate the robot's capability of reaching waypoints under potential failures, and an RRT*-based planner concatenates these waypoints.
AI.result: The resulting algorithm maximizes the overall target-reaching probability, yielding maximally resilient motion plans that utilize free-flying properties. The approach was validated experimentally on a physical free-flyer platform with injected actuator failures.
AI.conclusion: A probabilistic, proactive motion planning framework that explicitly accounts for actuator failures enables maximally resilient motion plans for free-flying robots, as demonstrated through physical experiments with injected actuator failures.

title: PAA: The Probabilistic Allen Algebra: A Generative and Complete Probabilistic Extension of Allen's Interval Relations
summary: Allen's interval algebra is a qualitative calculus for temporal relations, but its thirteen base relations are crisp predicates over exact interval boundaries. This is inadequate for temporal information from language, perception, databases, or uncertain histories, where times, durations, and boundaries are uncertain and expressions such as "just before" or "roughly during" have graded meaning. We develop the probabilistic Allen algebra (PAA): a generative and complete extension in which relation probabilities are derived from distributions over interval boundaries rather than assigned as scores. Time points are Gaussian; intervals have Gaussian midpoints and truncated-Gaussian durations. Every relation is a boundary-ordering predicate in one common probability space: point-point relations reduce to error functions, and point-interval and interval-interval relations to multivariate Gaussian orthant probabilities induced by linear inequalities. Contact relations (meets, starts, finishes, equals) receive positive measure through a tolerance band, and under a single tolerance the thirteen relations form a true partition that recovers crisp Allen as the tolerance vanishes. The construction derives Allen's taxonomy rather than positing it: coarse predicates such as precedence, overlap, and containment are unions of leaves whose probabilities are leaf sums, and this hierarchy is preserved as intervals collapse to points and thirteen relations reduce to five and then three. Each relation further decomposes into correlation-aware temporal primitives in the spirit of CIDOC CRM. The algebra is scale-invariant and separates graded expressions such as "shortly before" from contact relations. All results are Monte-Carlo validated and shipped as an open, tested Python package.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the Probabilistic Allen Algebra (PAA), a generative extension of Allen's interval algebra where temporal relation probabilities are derived from Gaussian distributions over interval boundaries, forming a true partition of the 13 relations under a tolerance band.
AI.motivation: Allen's interval algebra uses crisp predicates over exact interval boundaries, which is inadequate for uncertain temporal information from language, perception, databases, or uncertain histories, where times, durations, and boundaries are uncertain and expressions like "just before" or "roughly during" carry graded meaning.
AI.method: Time points are modeled as Gaussian; intervals have Gaussian midpoints and truncated-Gaussian durations. Every relation becomes a boundary-ordering predicate in one common probability space: point-point relations reduce to error functions, while point-interval and interval-interval relations reduce to multivariate Gaussian orthant probabilities induced by linear inequalities. Contact relations (meets, starts, finishes, equals) get positive measure via a tolerance band. Each relation decomposes into correlation-aware temporal primitives in the spirit of CIDOC CRM.
AI.result: Under a single tolerance the 13 relations form a true partition that recovers crisp Allen as the tolerance vanishes. The construction derives Allen's taxonomy rather than positing it: coarse predicates (precedence, overlap, containment) are unions of leaves with probabilities as leaf sums, and this hierarchy is preserved as intervals collapse to points, with 13 relations reducing to 5 and then 3. The algebra is scale-invariant and separates graded expressions like "shortly before" from contact relations. All results are Monte-Carlo validated and released as an open, tested Python package.
AI.conclusion: PAA provides a generative, complete probabilistic extension of Allen's interval algebra that recovers crisp Allen as a limiting case, preserves the relational hierarchy, supports graded temporal expressions, and is validated and shipped as open-source software.

title: Time-Efficient Iterative Learning Planning for Safety-Critical Dynamic Obstacle Avoidance
summary: Autonomous mobile robots require timeefficient planning and safety-critical dynamic obstacle avoidance under constrained onboard computation. While Iterative Learning Planning (ILP) offers lightweight and efficient traversal planning, it lacks explicit mechanisms for dynamic obstacle perception and avoidance. This article extends ILP to safety-critical navigation in dynamic environments by integrating an anticipatory risk-blended control barrier function (ARB-CBF). The extended ILP learns traversal-speed and steering-bias profiles via a fractionalpower update based on local obstacle risk, generating nominal control commands that ARB-CBF modifies at runtime for real-time safety guarantees. Algorithmic analysis demonstrates that the ILP replanning stage scales at O(kN) for k iterations and N waypoints, while ARB-CBF executes with linear complexity. Comprehensive simulations and real-world experiments validate the framework, demonstrating superior temporal efficiency and safety with lower computational overhead compared to optimizationbased baselines, making it highly suitable for resourceconstrained platforms.

AI.tldr: This paper extends Iterative Learning Planning (ILP) with an anticipatory risk-blended control barrier function (ARB-CBF) to achieve time-efficient, safety-critical dynamic obstacle avoidance on computationally constrained mobile robots, validated in simulation and real-world experiments.
AI.motivation: Autonomous mobile robots must plan efficiently and avoid dynamic obstacles safely under limited onboard computation. ILP is lightweight and efficient for traversal planning but lacks explicit dynamic obstacle perception and avoidance mechanisms.
AI.method: The authors integrate ARB-CBF into ILP. The extended ILP learns traversal-speed and steering-bias profiles via a fractional-power update based on local obstacle risk, producing nominal control commands. ARB-CBF modifies these commands at runtime to provide real-time safety guarantees.
AI.result: Algorithmic analysis shows ILP replanning scales as O(kN) for k iterations and N waypoints, while ARB-CBF runs with linear complexity. Simulations and real-world experiments show superior temporal efficiency and safety with lower computational overhead than optimization-based baselines, suitable for resource-constrained platforms.
AI.conclusion: Integrating ARB-CBF with ILP yields a computationally efficient and safety-guaranteed navigation framework for dynamic environments, well suited to resource-constrained robotic platforms.

title: Ownership in AI-Assisted Everyday Tasks
summary: When does work done with AI still feel like ours? As AI becomes woven into everyday tasks, we must examine what happens to our sense of ownership and contribution when a machine shares in producing what we make. We report an exploratory qualitative survey in which participants were asked to describe two recent, self-selected tasks completed with AI: one that felt like their own and one that did not. We find that felt ownership depends on the process of collaboration: people disown work when they merely approve AI's suggestions, but retain ownership when they lead, iterate, or rewrite. Ownership can also extend to settings where people own the vision for a project but not the execution; respondents reported high ownership on tasks they could not have completed without AI. Loss of personal voice and a lack of comprehension of the output both erode ownership. Finally, willingness to disclose AI use is often decoupled from actual pride or ownership, and instead shaped by community norms and fear of credit erasure. We propose several research directions as a result of these findings to promote AI development that supports people's sense of authorship over their own lives.

AI.tldr: An exploratory qualitative survey of self-selected AI-assisted tasks shows that felt ownership depends on the collaboration process: people disown work they merely approve, but retain ownership when they lead, iterate, or rewrite, even for tasks they could not have done without AI.
AI.motivation: As AI becomes woven into everyday tasks, it is unclear what happens to people's sense of ownership and contribution when a machine shares in producing what they make. The paper aims to understand when AI-assisted work still feels like one's own.
AI.method: An exploratory qualitative survey in which participants described two recent, self-selected tasks completed with AI: one that felt like their own and one that did not. The analysis examines the collaboration process, sources of ownership loss, and disclosure attitudes.
AI.result: Felt ownership depends on the collaboration process. People disown work when they merely approve AI suggestions, but retain ownership when they lead, iterate, or rewrite. Ownership extends to settings where people own the vision but not the execution, with high ownership reported on tasks they could not have completed without AI. Loss of personal voice and lack of comprehension of the output both erode ownership. Willingness to disclose AI use is often decoupled from actual pride or ownership, shaped instead by community norms and fear of credit erasure.
AI.conclusion: The authors propose several research directions to promote AI development that supports people's sense of authorship over their own lives.

title: Spatial-Semantic Uncertainty in VLM-Based Target Search: Balancing Exploration and Identification
comment: Accepted for presentation at IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS 2026) WorkshopRethinking Uncertainty for Modern Robotics Paradigms
summary: Robots searching for a target from a natural-language description must determine not only where to search, but also which observed candidate is the desired target. These decisions reflect two distinct sources of uncertainty - spatial uncertainty over candidate locations and semantic uncertainty over target identity - that are often conflated in VLM-based search systems. We introduce a spatial-semantic uncertainty formulation that maintains separate beliefs over each component and integrates probabilistic VLM evidence into a global target-identity posterior, including probability mass for undiscovered targets. This decomposition allows an information-theoretic planner to independently value candidate discovery and target disambiguation through spatial and semantic expected information gain (EIG), providing an explicit mechanism for trading broader exploration against earlier identification. We evaluate six VLM uncertainty-elicitation interfaces on 500 synthetic targets and show that similar recognition accuracy can conceal substantial differences in calibration and false confidence. In degraded-observation search-and-identify experiments, EIG-based planners reach confident decisions in 75.0%-92.5% of trials, compared with 20.0% for Random search, while different spatial-semantic weightings achieve comparable identification accuracy once confidence is attained. Increasing semantic emphasis reduces unnecessary exploration and VLM queries, demonstrating that explicitly planning over semantic uncertainty can accelerate target resolution without sacrificing decision quality. These results highlight the distinct roles of uncertainty representation and uncertainty-driven planning in embodied VLM systems.

AI.tldr: This paper decomposes robot target search into spatial and semantic uncertainty, using probabilistic VLM evidence and information-theoretic planning to reach confident identifications far more often than random search (75.0%-92.5% vs 20.0%).
AI.motivation: Robots searching for a target from a natural-language description must decide both where to search and which observed candidate matches. VLM-based search systems often conflate two distinct uncertainty sources: spatial uncertainty over candidate locations and semantic uncertainty over target identity. The paper aims to disentangle these to enable principled exploration-exploitation trade-offs.
AI.method: A spatial-semantic uncertainty formulation maintains separate beliefs over location and identity, integrating probabilistic VLM evidence into a global target-identity posterior with probability mass for undiscovered targets. An information-theoretic planner independently values candidate discovery (spatial EIG) and target disambiguation (semantic EIG), explicitly trading broader exploration against earlier identification. Six VLM uncertainty-elicitation interfaces are evaluated on 500 synthetic targets, followed by degraded-observation search-and-identify experiments.
AI.result: Similar recognition accuracy across VLM interfaces can conceal substantial differences in calibration and false confidence. EIG-based planners reach confident decisions in 75.0%-92.5% of trials versus 20.0% for Random search. Different spatial-semantic weightings yield comparable identification accuracy once confidence is attained; increasing semantic emphasis reduces unnecessary exploration and VLM queries.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly planning over semantic uncertainty can accelerate target resolution without sacrificing decision quality, highlighting the distinct roles of uncertainty representation and uncertainty-driven planning in embodied VLM systems.

title: Deep Noir: Autonomous Steering Discovery via Architectural Chronometry in Transformer Models
summary: Activation steering modifies LLM behavior at inference time, but identifying where and how strongly to steer remains manual. We introduce Deep Noir, a framework that uses Logit Lens convergence and causal head-level attribution to autonomously discover optimal steering parameters. Across three scales (1B x 3, 2-3B x 2, and 7-9B x 4), our engine achieves 16.7 percentage-point improvement on spam at 1B (standard deviation 4.7; 39 runs), with gains increasing to 21 to 42 percentage points at 7-9B across four architectures. On SST-2 sentiment, it achieves a 13.1 percentage-point improvement with zero code changes. Mechanistic grounding enables automated discovery of intervention points that generalize across tasks and architectures. On sentiment, RepE without head masking fails to improve over baseline, while Deep Noir improves all models (p less than 0.01). We further show that steering creates a predictable prompt-injection attack surface whose vulnerability increases monotonically with steering magnitude. This finding is relevant to agent systems deploying steered classifiers.

AI.tldr: Deep Noir autonomously discovers activation-steering parameters via Logit Lens convergence and causal head-level attribution, yielding 16.7–42 pp spam gains and 13.1 pp SST-2 gains, while revealing a steering-magnitude-dependent prompt-injection vulnerability.
AI.motivation: Activation steering alters LLM behavior at inference but requires manual selection of where and how strongly to steer, limiting scalability and generalization.
AI.method: A framework combining Logit Lens convergence with causal head-level attribution to autonomously identify optimal steering parameters, tested across three model scales (1B, 2–3B, 7–9B) and multiple architectures without code changes.
AI.result: 16.7 pp spam improvement at 1B (SD 4.7; 39 runs), scaling to 21–42 pp at 7–9B across four architectures; 13.1 pp SST-2 gain; RepE without head masking fails on sentiment while Deep Noir improves all models (p < 0.01); vulnerability to prompt injection increases monotonically with steering magnitude.
AI.conclusion: Mechanistic grounding enables automated, generalizable discovery of intervention points; steered classifiers in agent systems introduce a predictable, magnitude-dependent prompt-injection attack surface.

title: Visual Sim-to-Real Learning for Robotic Insertion under Geometric Variations: Application to Rebar Installation
summary: Rebar insertion is among the most repetitive and physically demanding tasks on construction sites, and a contact-rich problem at 1.4 mm clearance. The parts, however, vary at two levels: a nominal design per structural member, and fabrication tolerance around each nominal design. Real-world data therefore has to be re-collected as designs and batches change. We present RebarSim, a visual sim-to-real system trained entirely in simulation. A privileged state-based teacher is trained with reinforcement learning over procedurally generated rebar geometries, then distilled into a multi-view student that maps raw RGB and proprioception directly to actions under extensive domain randomization. The student transfers to the real world zero-shot, seating rebars taken from a real factory production run in 91.3% of real-robot rollouts. Underlying that result, geometry diversity and pretraining both bring benefits. Training across a diverse set of nominal designs rather than one lifts the zero-shot success of both the teacher and the student on unseen designs, and the student policy outperforms a single-design specialist on that specialist's own design. A pretrained student then adapts to a new design with 4--6x fewer distillation samples than one trained from scratch. Visual sim-to-real transfer depends on appearance randomization and the DAgger mixture: removing either one sharply lowers success. Videos, code, and task assets are available at https://rebarsim.github.io.

AI.tldr: RebarSim trains a visual sim-to-real policy entirely in simulation—distilling a privileged RL teacher over procedurally generated rebar geometries into a multi-view RGB student—achieving 91.3% zero-shot real-robot rebar insertion success.
AI.motivation: Rebar insertion is highly repetitive, physically demanding, and contact-rich at 1.4 mm clearance. Real-world variation occurs at two levels—nominal design per structural member and fabrication tolerance per batch—so data must be re-collected whenever designs or batches change. This makes real-data-driven learning impractical and motivates a simulation-trained, zero-shot transferable policy.
AI.method: A privileged state-based teacher is trained with reinforcement learning over procedurally generated rebar geometries. It is then distilled into a multi-view student that maps raw RGB and proprioception directly to actions under extensive domain randomization, using a DAgger mixture for data aggregation.
AI.result: The student transfers zero-shot to the real world, seating rebars from a real factory production run in 91.3% of real-robot rollouts. Geometry diversity and pretraining both help: training across diverse nominal designs improves zero-shot success on unseen designs for both teacher and student, and the student outperforms a single-design specialist on that specialist's own design. A pretrained student adapts to a new design with 4–6x fewer distillation samples. Removing appearance randomization or the DAgger mixture sharply lowers success, showing both are essential to visual sim-to-real transfer.
AI.conclusion: Training entirely in simulation with procedural geometry generation, privileged-to-visual distillation, and domain randomization enables zero-shot real-world rebar insertion despite tight tolerances and design variability. Geometry diversity and pretraining yield generalization and sample-efficient adaptation, while appearance randomization and DAgger mixing are critical for visual sim-to-real transfer. Videos, code, and task assets are released.

title: Q&A on Any Spreadsheet Requires Interpreting Its Grid Structure
summary: Semantic cell annotation improves chunking interpretability for spreadsheets in LLM-driven RAG systems, aiding answer generation through enriched context rather than improved retrieval accuracy. We propose a novel framework of splitting any spreadsheet into interpretable chunks using cell role annotation. Our framework beats the state of the art, yet it faces a hard ceiling. Spreadsheets are fundamentally two-dimensional unstructured data with continuous relationships and infinite potential cell roles. Because classification models are restricted to finite, pre-defined classes, they cannot perfectly capture this structural nuance, even with human-level annotation. We show that addressing the spreadsheet-to-LLM bottleneck requires moving beyond discrete cell classification. Instead, the field must develop dimensionality-reduction techniques to directly flatten 2D unstructured spreadsheets into 1D unstructured text. Text chunks would be easier for downstream RAG to interpret and generate from.

AI.tldr: Semantic cell annotation improves interpretability of spreadsheet chunks in LLM-driven RAG, but discrete cell classification hits a fundamental ceiling. The authors argue the field must develop dimensionality-reduction methods to flatten 2D spreadsheets directly into 1D text.
AI.motivation: Spreadsheets are two-dimensional unstructured data with continuous relationships and infinite potential cell roles. Existing classification models are limited to finite, pre-defined classes, so even human-level annotation cannot capture this structural nuance. This motivates the need to rethink how spreadsheets are processed for LLM-driven RAG systems.
AI.method: The authors propose a framework that splits any spreadsheet into interpretable chunks using cell role annotation, providing enriched context for answer generation. They further analyze the limitations of this discrete classification approach.
AI.result: The proposed framework surpasses the state of the art, yet it encounters a hard performance ceiling due to the finite nature of classification models. Cell annotation primarily aids answer generation via enriched context rather than improving retrieval accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Overcoming the spreadsheet-to-LLM bottleneck requires moving beyond discrete cell classification toward dimensionality-reduction techniques that directly flatten 2D spreadsheets into 1D unstructured text, yielding chunks that downstream RAG can more easily interpret and generate from.

title: Worst-Case Hidden-Vehicle Trajectory Search in Spatiotemporal Occlusion Regions
