comment: 16 pages, 3 figures. Accepted at the ECCV 2026 Workshop on Safe and Defensive Autonomous Driving (SDAD) as an Oral Presentation; Best Paper Award. Workshop website: https://sdad.cc/papers.html
summary: Occlusion creates fundamental uncertainty in autonomous driving. Existing methods often propagate frame-wise hypotheses or optimize ego behavior against prescribed hidden-agent predictions, leaving the worst history-consistent interaction unexplored. We introduce History-Conditioned Minimax Trajectory Search (HC-MTS), which combines temporal occlusion reasoning with response-aware search. First, HC-MTS constructs finite hidden-state modes, each certified by a backward witness satisfying multi-frame visibility, occupancy, semantic-map support, and class-specific kinematic constraints. It then solves a bilevel minimax problem: an inner finite oracle maximizes the ego driving score over destination attainment and ride comfort, while the outer search selects the legal hidden-vehicle trajectory that minimizes this best-response value. Across eight Waymo Open Motion Dataset scenarios, increasing the visibility-memory horizon from K=1 to K=20 reduces the mean per-scenario vehicle, pedestrian, and total retained hidden-seed counts by 18.12%, 21.67%, and 18.45%, respectively. HC-MTS identifies six avoidable counterexamples, while no legal collision-producing attacker is found in the remaining two scenes within the finite search budget.

AI.tldr: HC-MTS combines temporal occlusion reasoning with response-aware bilevel minimax search to find worst-case, history-consistent hidden-agent interactions in autonomous driving, pruning hidden-state modes via visibility-memory certification.
AI.motivation: Occlusion creates fundamental uncertainty in autonomous driving. Existing methods typically propagate frame-wise hypotheses or optimize ego behavior against prescribed hidden-agent predictions, leaving the worst history-consistent interaction unexplored—i.e., they fail to search for adversarial yet physically and historically legitimate hidden trajectories.
AI.method: HC-MTS has two components. (1) It constructs finite hidden-state modes, each certified by a backward witness that satisfies multi-frame visibility, occupancy, semantic-map support, and class-specific kinematic constraints. (2) It solves a bilevel minimax problem: an inner finite oracle maximizes the ego driving score (destination attainment and ride comfort), while the outer search selects the legal hidden-vehicle trajectory minimizing this best-response value.
AI.result: On eight Waymo Open Motion Dataset scenarios, increasing the visibility-memory horizon from K=1 to K=20 reduces mean per-scenario retained hidden-seed counts for vehicle, pedestrian, and total by 18.12%, 21.67%, and 18.45%, respectively. HC-MTS identifies six avoidable counterexamples, while no legal collision-producing attacker is found in the remaining two scenes within the finite search budget.
AI.conclusion: History-conditioned certification effectively prunes the hidden-state space as the visibility-memory horizon grows, and the minimax search surfaces concrete avoidable failure cases, demonstrating the value of exploring worst-case history-consistent interactions for occlusion-aware planning.

title: RAFT: A Stateful Retrieval-Augmented Framework for Troubleshooting Agents
comment: Accepted to the EMNLP 2026 Industry Track
summary: Effective troubleshooting agents in enterprise customer support depend on retrieving actionable guidance from similar historical cases, yet existing retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems treat support cases as static documents and overlook their multi-stage, stateful nature. We introduce RAFT (Retrieval-Augmented Framework for Troubleshooting Agents), a stateful RAG framework that abstracts each closed historical case into a directed chain of timeline entries and retrieves at the entry level, surfacing cases whose intermediate states match the active case and returning the parent-case trajectory anchored at the matched state; an optional case-level graph links cases through a configurable similarity representation. We evaluate this retrieval layer directly, which, unlike evaluating a full agent system, requires no production deployment. Because public multi-stage troubleshooting data is extremely rare, we pair a synthetic benchmark built from Microsoft Learn Windows Server documentation with real Apache Jira issues carrying human-created duplicate labels. RAFT improves Case Hit over vanilla RAG and GraphRAG baselines at every stage of case progress, with statistically significant gains over the strongest baseline; the Jira results provide directional evidence that the advantage transfers to real case histories. We release our benchmark, implementation, and the Apache Jira evaluation set.

AI.tldr: RAFT is a stateful RAG framework for enterprise troubleshooting agents that abstracts closed cases into directed chains of timeline entries, retrieves at the entry level to surface cases with matching intermediate states, and returns the parent-case trajectory anchored at the matched state.
AI.motivation: Existing RAG systems treat support cases as static documents and overlook their multi-stage, stateful nature, limiting the retrieval of actionable guidance from similar historical cases in enterprise customer support.
AI.method: RAFT abstracts each closed historical case into a directed chain of timeline entries and performs entry-level retrieval, returning the parent-case trajectory anchored at the matched state. An optional case-level graph links cases via a configurable similarity representation. Evaluation focuses directly on the retrieval layer, avoiding production deployment. A synthetic benchmark from Microsoft Learn Windows Server documentation is paired with real Apache Jira issues containing human-created duplicate labels.
AI.result: RAFT improves Case Hit over vanilla RAG and GraphRAG baselines at every stage of case progress, with statistically significant gains over the strongest baseline. Jira results show directional evidence that the advantage transfers to real case histories.
AI.conclusion: Stateful, entry-level retrieval grounded in case timelines outperforms static-document RAG approaches for troubleshooting agents. The benchmark, implementation, and Apache Jira evaluation set are released.

title: Towards AI-enhanced control: a numerical technique for trajectory smoothing of a parallel robot for pancreatic surgery
summary: The paper presents a numerical approach for the end-effector trajectory smoothing of a parallel robot designed for minimally invasive pancreatic surgery. The approach is tailored for real-time master-slave control architecture and uses a 3D space mouse for command input for velocity control. The trajectory smoothing is achieved by generating S-curves in the end-effector velocity fields, thus controlling the accelerations, which in turn reduces tissue trauma in the minimally invasive procedures. Real-time control is enabled by segmenting the S-curves based on the command inputs from the 3D space mouse. A special case is considered where the acceleration time is constant for all command inputs. Numeric results demonstrate stable transitions (without abrupt changes) in both the end-effector parameter space and in the active joints parameters, thereby validating the proposed approach. Further work aims to test the approach on an experimental model and integrate it into AI-based training modules.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an S-curve-based end-effector trajectory smoothing method for a minimally invasive pancreatic surgery parallel robot, enabling real-time master-slave velocity control via a 3D space mouse to reduce tissue trauma.
AI.motivation: Reducing tissue trauma in minimally invasive robotic surgery by controlling accelerations, and enabling real-time slave-side control within a master-slave architecture.
AI.method: Trajectory smoothing is achieved by generating S-curves in the end-effector velocity fields to control accelerations. Real-time control is enabled by segmenting the S-curves according to command inputs from a 3D space mouse used for velocity command input. A special case with constant acceleration time across all command inputs is considered.
AI.result: Numeric results demonstrate stable transitions without abrupt changes in both the end-effector parameter space and the active joint parameters, validating the proposed approach.
AI.conclusion: The proposed S-curve smoothing approach is validated numerically. Future work aims to test it on an experimental model and integrate it into AI-based training modules.

title: An Empirical Study of Harness Design for Coding Agents
summary: Coding harnesses shape how autonomous coding agents translate model capabilities into long-horizon software-engineering performance, yet existing work typically evaluates harnesses as monolithic systems, leaving the effectiveness of individual components unclear. To enable component-level comparisons, we study this question with a lightweight coding harness whose execution loop is fixed while three components are varied: planning, action space, and context management. Across four models evaluated on SWE-Bench Verified and Terminal-Bench 2.1, we evaluate 176 matched settings spanning five context-management strategies, four context-window budgets, and targeted ablations of planning and action space. We find that: (1) Context management becomes increasingly valuable as the context-window budget tightens, with most of its benefit coming from preventing context-overflow failures. (2) Staging rule-based elision before LLM-based summarization provides the strongest overall efficiency among the context-management strategies, whereas making elided content recoverable adds machinery that models rarely use and yields no accuracy gain. (3) Planning shifts from an accuracy scaffold for weaker models to a cost saver for stronger models, with little change in accuracy. (4) Predefined tools improve performance for models with weaker bash proficiency, whereas bash-capable models can operate effectively with a bash-only interface and achieve substantially lower cost, especially on command-line-centric tasks. Trajectory-level analysis explains these effects: context management extends execution trajectories without substantially altering agent behavior, planning changes where trajectories stop, and the action space changes the granularity at which code is written. These findings inform model- and budget-aware harness design and provide a modular framework for evaluating future harness components.

AI.tldr: The paper performs a component-level study of coding harnesses for autonomous coding agents, fixing the execution loop while varying planning, action space, and context management across 176 matched settings, and shows that context management, planning, and tool design each affect performance/cost in model- and budget-dependent ways.
AI.motivation: Prior work evaluates coding harnesses as monolithic systems, so the effectiveness of individual harness components remains unclear. Component-level comparison is needed to guide model- and budget-aware harness design.
AI.method: A lightweight coding harness with a fixed execution loop is used to isolate three varied components: planning, action space, and context management. Four models are evaluated on SWE-Bench Verified and Terminal-Bench 2.1 across 176 matched settings covering five context-management strategies, four context-window budgets, and targeted ablations of planning and action space. Trajectory-level analysis is used to explain observed effects.
AI.result: Context management becomes more valuable as the context-window budget tightens, mainly by preventing context-overflow failures. Staging rule-based elision before LLM-based summarization yields the strongest overall efficiency; recoverable elided content adds rarely used machinery with no accuracy gain. Planning shifts from an accuracy scaffold for weaker models to a cost saver for stronger models, with little accuracy change. Predefined tools help models with weaker bash proficiency, while bash-capable models remain effective with a bash-only interface at substantially lower cost, especially on command-line-centric tasks. Trajectories show context management extends execution trajectories without substantially altering agent behavior, planning changes where trajectories stop, and action space changes code-writing granularity.
AI.conclusion: Harness components should be designed in a model- and budget-aware manner rather than as a monolithic system. The modular framework enables component-level evaluation of future coding-harness designs.

title: Integrated Guidance and Control of a Mother-Child UAV-UGV System for Cooperative Missions
summary: Autonomous recovery of a small multirotor onto a hovering multirotor carrier differs from recovery onto ground or shipborne platforms because the recovery surface is itself an actively controlled, thrust-limited aerial vehicle. This paper presents a field-validated autonomy framework for a heterogeneous rover-mothership-child system executing rover supervision, mothership transit, child deployment and sortie, autonomous return, aerial recovery, and synchronized descent. The recovery stack combines jerk-bounded reference generation, disturbance-observer-augmented planar tracking, feasibility-aware vertical control, a discrete-time barrier-based safety filter for relative vertical geometry, and communication-aware carrier-state prediction. The contribution is the coordinated system-level integration of these methods for recovery onto a hovering multirotor and its full-scale outdoor validation. The framework is implemented on a PX4-ROS 2 architecture using RTK-enabled GNSS, IMU, and barometric fusion, with mothership-side 1D lidar used only as an auxiliary near-contact cue. RTK-fixed positioning was maintained throughout testing. Across 20 outdoor cooperative missions, 17 successfully completed deployment, sortie, and recovery, giving an observed mission success rate of 85%. For successful recoveries, mean terminal-alignment time was 6.3 s, mean planar alignment error at acceptance was 0.18 m, maximum terminal planar deviation was 0.32 m within a 0.40 m capture radius, and minimum logged relative vertical separation during coupled descent was 0.41 m. Mothership planar station-keeping RMS error was 0.25 m. The three unsuccessful trials occurred at different mission stages and are analyzed separately. Results demonstrate practical autonomous aerial recovery within the tested outdoor operating envelope.

AI.tldr: A field-validated autonomy framework enables a child multirotor to autonomously recover onto a hovering multirotor mothership, achieving an 85% mission success rate over 20 outdoor cooperative missions.
AI.motivation: Recovery onto a hovering multirotor carrier differs fundamentally from ground or shipborne recovery because the landing surface is itself an actively controlled, thrust-limited aerial vehicle, introducing coupled dynamics and relative-motion challenges that conventional recovery methods do not address.
AI.method: The recovery stack integrates jerk-bounded reference generation, disturbance-observer-augmented planar tracking, feasibility-aware vertical control, a discrete-time barrier-based safety filter for relative vertical geometry, and communication-aware carrier-state prediction. It is implemented on a PX4-ROS 2 architecture using RTK-enabled GNSS, IMU, and barometric fusion, with mothership-side 1D lidar as an auxiliary near-contact cue.
AI.result: RTK-fixed positioning was maintained throughout. Across 20 outdoor cooperative missions, 17 completed deployment, sortie, and recovery (85% success). Successful recoveries showed 6.3 s mean terminal-alignment time, 0.18 m mean planar alignment error at acceptance, 0.32 m maximum terminal planar deviation within a 0.40 m capture radius, and 0.41 m minimum relative vertical separation during coupled descent; mothership planar station-keeping RMS error was 0.25 m. The three failures occurred at different mission stages.
AI.conclusion: The results demonstrate practical autonomous aerial recovery within the tested outdoor operating envelope, with the key contribution being the coordinated system-level integration of these methods and its full-scale outdoor validation.

title: Learning Slope-Adaptive Whole-Body Locomotion for Humanoid Robots in Roofing Construction
summary: Roofing requires workers to coordinate locomotion, balance, and work-related body motions on pitched surfaces, creating a challenging application for humanoid robots. Directly retargeted human demonstrations, however, may preserve motion appearance while placing the robot's feet or hands incorrectly relative to the roof. This study presents a task-semantic scene-grounded framework for learning roofer-style whole-body motions on a Unitree G1. Human demonstrations are captured using a tracking system and retargeted to the robot, while a metric roof model supplies the spatial reference unavailable from the tracking system. A trajectory-level optimization grounds inferred support contacts and annotated work relations to the roof, and execution-aware reinforcement learning encourages the resulting policy to preserve these relations under dynamic tracking errors. The framework is evaluated through a multi-motion tracking study, a roof-pitch coverage matrix, a five-way nailgun ablation, cross-task experiments on hammering and lateral pushing, and comparisons with pure reinforcement learning and zero-shot teleoperation. Our method enables the robot to satisfy support, work-clearance, and nonpenetration criteria across all evaluated seeds. Across nailgun, hammering, and pushing, it achieves work-clearance errors between 0.256 and 0.531 cm and 3/3 successful evaluations per task. Physical experiments reproduce uphill walking, nailgun, hammering, and bending motions with mean base-frame motion errors below 80 mm. These findings establish scene-grounded human motion learning as a promising basis for construction-oriented humanoid motion primitives.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a task-semantic, scene-grounded framework that learns roofer-style whole-body motions on a Unitree G1 humanoid by grounding retargeted human demonstrations to a metric roof model and refining them with execution-aware reinforcement learning.
AI.motivation: Roofing demands coordinated locomotion, balance, and work-related body motions on pitched surfaces, making it hard for humanoid robots. Directly retargeted human demonstrations may preserve motion appearance but place the robot's feet or hands incorrectly relative to the roof, because tracking systems lack the spatial reference of the roof. There is a need to ground learned motions in the task scene rather than only in kinematic mimicry.
AI.method: Human demonstrations are captured with a tracking system and retargeted to the Unitree G1, while a metric roof model provides the spatial reference the tracking system lacks. A trajectory-level optimization grounds inferred support contacts and annotated work relations to the roof. Execution-aware reinforcement learning then encourages the resulting policy to preserve these relations under dynamic tracking errors.
AI.result: Evaluated via a multi-motion tracking study, a roof-pitch coverage matrix, a five-way nailgun ablation, cross-task experiments (hammering, lateral pushing), and comparisons with pure RL and zero-shot teleoperation. The robot satisfies support, work-clearance, and nonpenetration criteria across all seeds. Work-clearance errors range from 0.256 to 0.531 cm with 3/3 successful evaluations per task. Physical experiments reproduce uphill walking, nailgun, hammering, and bending with mean base-frame motion errors below 80 mm.
AI.conclusion: Scene-grounded human motion learning is a promising basis for construction-oriented humanoid motion primitives, enabling task-semantic, roof-consistent whole-body behaviors.

title: OmniMimic: Dynamics-completed Motion Augmentation for Multi-style Omnidirectional Quadruped Locomotion
comment: The project page is at https://OmniMimic.github.io
summary: Animal demonstrations provide quadruped robots with natural and distinctive gait styles that are difficult to specify through hand-crafted rewards. However, their narrow directional coverage leaves little style-consistent supervision for backward, lateral, and turning commands. We present OmniMimic, a training framework that turns directionally limited animal demonstrations into a single multi-gait policy over target per-axis velocity ranges. OmniMimic first combines temporal reversal, constrained dynamics completion, and sagittal reflection to construct robot-specific kinematic and physical supervision beyond the observed directions. It then expands commands progressively from the demonstrated velocity distribution toward the target per-axis bounds, and uses a shared actor with soft-gated, gait-specialized residual experts to balance reusable locomotion skills with gait-specific corrections. Across four gaits in simulation, OmniMimic reduces mean foot-position RMSE at forward and backward reference velocities by 12.9% and velocity-tracking RMSE on a uniform Cartesian command grid by 63.1%, compared with the matched APEX baseline. The project page is at https://OmniMimic.github.io.

AI.tldr: OmniMimic is a training framework that expands directionally limited animal motion demonstrations into a single multi-gait quadruped policy covering full per-axis velocity commands, combining data augmentation with progressive command expansion and a soft-gated mixture-of-experts actor.
AI.motivation: Animal demonstrations give quadruped robots natural, distinctive gaits that are hard to obtain via hand-crafted rewards, but the demonstrations cover only narrow direction ranges, leaving little style-consistent supervision for backward, lateral, and turning commands. A method is needed to extrapolate the demonstrated style to the full target velocity space.
AI.method: OmniMimic (1) constructs robot-specific kinematic and physical supervision beyond observed directions via temporal reversal, constrained dynamics completion, and sagittal reflection; (2) progressively expands commands from the demonstrated velocity distribution toward target per-axis bounds; (3) uses a shared actor with soft-gated, gait-specialized residual experts to balance reusable locomotion skills and gait-specific corrections.
AI.result: Across four gaits in simulation, OmniMimic lowers mean foot-position RMSE at forward and backward reference velocities by 12.9% and velocity-tracking RMSE on a uniform Cartesian command grid by 63.1%, relative to the matched APEX baseline.
AI.conclusion: Directionally limited animal demonstrations can be systematically transformed into a single policy that imitates natural gait styles while tracking velocity commands over target per-axis ranges, outperforming the matched baseline in both style fidelity and velocity tracking.

title: Walking on the Slope: Stable Bipedal Gaits with Genetic-Algorithm-Optimized Trajectories
summary: This paper presents the kinematic and dynamic modeling, trajectory generation, and stability analysis of an 8-degree-of-freedom (DOF) biped robot walking on flat and inclined terrain. Denavit-Hartenberg (DH) parameters and homogeneous transformations are used to derive the forward kinematics, while closed-form inverse kinematics maps the desired hip and swing-foot Cartesian trajectories, generated with cubic splines, to joint angles. Joint torques are computed using the Newton-Euler iterative algorithm, and dynamic stability is evaluated using the zero moment point (ZMP) criterion. A genetic algorithm (GA) optimizes the hip height, maximum swing-foot lift, and frontal-plane tilt angle by minimizing the work done by the joints subject to a ZMP feasibility penalty. Simulation results in MATLAB show that the nominal 8-DOF model remains ZMP-stable for step completion times down to 0.5 s and for slope inclinations up to 22.5 degrees with the given foot geometry. Beyond these limits, the ZMP leaves the support polygon, and either the foot dimensions or the trajectory parameters must be modified. The results also show that ZMP stability is governed by the mass distribution among the links rather than the total mass of the robot.

AI.tldr: Kinematic and dynamic modeling, trajectory generation, and ZMP-based stability analysis of an 8-DOF biped robot on flat and inclined terrain, with GA optimization of trajectory parameters.
AI.motivation: To enable stable bipedal walking on flat and inclined terrain by integrating kinematics, dynamics, trajectory generation, and stability analysis, and to identify the design/control limits (step time, slope) under which the robot remains ZMP-stable.
AI.method: DH parameters and homogeneous transformations for forward kinematics; closed-form inverse kinematics mapping hip and swing-foot Cartesian trajectories (cubic splines) to joint angles; Newton-Euler iterative algorithm for joint torques; ZMP criterion for dynamic stability; GA optimizing hip height, maximum swing-foot lift, and frontal-plane tilt angle by minimizing joint work with a ZMP feasibility penalty.
AI.result: MATLAB simulations show the nominal 8-DOF model stays ZMP-stable for step completion times down to 0.5 s and slope inclinations up to 22.5 degrees given the foot geometry. Beyond these limits the ZMP exits the support polygon, requiring modification of foot dimensions or trajectory parameters. ZMP stability depends on mass distribution among links rather than total robot mass.
AI.conclusion: The integrated modeling and optimization framework yields a ZMP-stable 8-DOF biped gait within defined step-time and slope limits; stability is governed by inter-link mass distribution, not total mass, and exceeding the limits demands changes to foot geometry or trajectory parameters.

title: Accelerating Visual Policy Learning with Sampling-Based Model Predictive Control
summary: Learning visual policies for locomotion and manipulation requires coordinating contact with the environment and can incur substantial computation and GPU memory costs. First-order policy gradients (FoPG) reduce training cost through differentiable simulation, but local optimization can converge to unintended contact patterns. To address this shortfall, we propose Sampling-Guided Policy Search (SGPS), which couples recurring action-target refinement by sampling-based model-predictive control with first-order policy optimization. Behavior cloning initializes the policy from sampled actions; training then alternates sampling-based refinement with short-horizon FoPG updates under perturbed initial states and randomized dynamics. For visual policy training, we use a decoupled FoPG formulation that excludes rendering from the computation graph, enabling direct learning from depth observations without a state-policy teacher. On a single GPU, SGPS learns policies for locomotion, obstacle traversal, crate pushing, and bimanual carrying on simulated Unitree Go2 and G1 robots. Our experiments further show that refinement improves policy learning beyond initialization and tracking alone. For hardware deployment, the distilled policy transfers zero-shot to a real Go2 and uses onboard depth to autonomously trot, crawl, clear hurdles, and switch between these behaviors.

AI.tldr: SGPS couples sampling-based MPC refinement with first-order policy gradients to train visual locomotion and manipulation policies efficiently on a single GPU, achieving zero-shot sim-to-real transfer.
AI.motivation: Learning visual policies for contact-rich locomotion and manipulation is computationally and memory intensive. First-order policy gradients (FoPG) via differentiable simulation cut training cost but suffer from local optima, converging to unintended contact patterns.
AI.method: SGPS alternates sampling-based model-predictive control for recurring action-target refinement with short-horizon FoPG updates under perturbed initial states and randomized dynamics. Behavior cloning initializes the policy from sampled actions. A decoupled FoPG formulation excludes rendering from the computation graph, enabling direct learning from depth observations without a state-policy teacher.
AI.result: On a single GPU, SGPS learns policies for locomotion, obstacle traversal, crate pushing, and bimanual carrying on simulated Unitree Go2 and G1 robots. Refinement improves learning beyond initialization and tracking alone. The distilled policy transfers zero-shot to a real Go2, using onboard depth to trot, crawl, clear hurdles, and switch behaviors autonomously.
AI.conclusion: Combining sampling-based refinement with FoPG overcomes local-optima limitations, yielding efficient visual policy training and effective zero-shot sim-to-real deployment on legged hardware.

title: V2-STRep: VLM-Grounded Structured Task Representations for Reusable Robot Skills Acquired from Generated Videos
summary: Human manipulation videos provide rich motion and interaction cues for acquiring robot skills without robot demonstrations. Video generation models synthesize such demonstrations from an initial scene image and task instruction, avoiding the need to record demonstrations for each task. However, the recovered motion captures only one scene-specific realization, leaving task structure, geometric relations, and constraints implicit. We present V2-STRep, a zero-shot framework that converts generated video motion into reusable robot skills through VLM-grounded structured task representations. The representation specifies motion phases, references, and task-relevant constraints, with targets described by minimal geometric structures: points, point-normals, axes, planes, and full 6D poses. VLM-provided 2D image-space cues are lifted into 3D using RGB-D observations to reconstruct task geometry and candidate grasp poses. Geometry-specific rules transfer motion to new scenes, while task-constrained trajectory optimization couples grasp selection with complete robot motion planning. It preserves task requirements while using remaining rotational freedom to accommodate joint limits. Updating deployment grounding and constraints enables reuse under new compatible instructions without generating another video. Experiments on six real-world manipulation tasks demonstrate improved execution success over baselines, reliable cross-scene transfer of successfully acquired skills, and adaptation to changed deployment instructions.

AI.tldr: V2-STRep is a zero-shot framework that converts motion from generated human manipulation videos into reusable robot skills via VLM-grounded structured task representations using minimal geometric primitives and task-constrained trajectory optimization.
AI.motivation: Human manipulation videos offer rich motion and interaction cues for learning robot skills without robot demonstrations, and video generation models can synthesize such demonstrations from an initial image and task instruction. However, the recovered motion only captures one scene-specific realization, leaving task structure, geometric relations, and constraints implicit—limiting reuse and transfer.
AI.method: V2-STRep builds a VLM-grounded structured task representation specifying motion phases, references, and task-relevant constraints, with targets described by minimal geometric structures (points, point-normals, axes, planes, full 6D poses). VLM-provided 2D image-space cues are lifted into 3D using RGB-D observations to reconstruct task geometry and candidate grasp poses. Geometry-specific rules transfer motion to new scenes, and task-constrained trajectory optimization couples grasp selection with complete robot motion planning, using remaining rotational freedom to accommodate joint limits. Updating deployment grounding and constraints enables reuse under new compatible instructions without generating another video.
AI.result: Experiments on six real-world manipulation tasks show improved execution success over baselines, reliable cross-scene transfer of successfully acquired skills, and adaptation to changed deployment instructions.
AI.conclusion: V2-STRep enables zero-shot conversion of generated human video motion into reusable, transferable robot skills via structured representations, achieving better success and cross-scene and instruction adaptation.

title: CoRef-GS: Cooperative Referring Gaussian Splatting for Multi-Agent Scene Understanding
comment: The established benchmark and source code will be publicly released at https://github.com/ruojiruoli17/CoRef-GS.git
summary: Referring scene understanding for embodied robots requires grounding object- and relation-centric language queries from a designated viewpoint. While a local semantic Gaussian map can support such grounding within one agent's observations, cooperative settings require this ability to remain effective after independently reconstructed maps are aligned and fused. In this setting, the referred target or its contextual landmark may come from another agent's observations, while spatial relations must still be interpreted from the querying robot's viewpoint. We formulate this problem as cooperative referring Gaussian grounding over fused maps, which requires geometric alignability, instance-level semantic comparability, and view-conditioned relation reasoning. Existing language-aware Gaussian methods mainly focus on single-map querying, whereas Gaussian registration methods optimize geometric or photometric alignment without preserving language-grounding-oriented semantic compatibility. We propose CoRef-GS, a cooperative referring Gaussian splatting framework. CoRef-GS constructs local open-vocabulary instance-aware Gaussian maps, then aligns partially overlapping maps with a cross-agent alignment module by geometric and semantic consistency, and grounds queries using a view-conditioned mask relation graph. We further introduce CoQuad-Ref, a dual-quadruped benchmark spanning both real-world and simulated indoor scenes. Experiments show that, on simulated scenes, CoRef-GS reduces the rotation error from 2.58° after coarse initialization to 0.15° after refinement, and improves real-world referring mIoU over ReferSplat from 52.6% to 68.8%. The established benchmark and source code will be publicly released at https://github.com/ruojiruoli17/CoRef-GS.git.

AI.tldr: CoRef-GS is a cooperative referring Gaussian splatting framework for multi-robot scene understanding, enabling viewpoint-conditioned language grounding over independently built, aligned, and fused 3D Gaussian maps, supported by the new CoQuad-Ref dual-quadruped benchmark.
AI.motivation: Embodied robots need to ground object- and relation-centric language queries from a specific viewpoint. A single agent's local semantic Gaussian map supports this, but cooperative settings require grounding to remain effective after independently reconstructed maps are aligned and fused, where the referred target or its landmark may originate from another agent while spatial relations must still be interpreted from the querying robot's viewpoint. Existing language-aware Gaussian methods handle only single-map querying, and Gaussian registration methods optimize geometric or photometric alignment without preserving language-grounding-oriented semantic compatibility.
AI.method: The authors formulate the task as cooperative referring Gaussian grounding over fused maps, requiring geometric alignability, instance-level semantic comparability, and view-conditioned relation reasoning. They propose CoRef-GS, which (1) builds local open-vocabulary instance-aware Gaussian maps, (2) aligns partially overlapping maps via a cross-agent alignment module using geometric and semantic consistency, and (3) grounds queries with a view-conditioned mask relation graph. They also introduce CoQuad-Ref, a dual-quadruped benchmark covering both real-world and simulated indoor scenes.
AI.result: On simulated scenes, CoRef-GS reduces rotation error from 2.58° after coarse initialization to 0.15° after refinement. On real-world data, it improves referring mIoU over ReferSplat from 52.6% to 68.8%. The benchmark and source code will be released at https://github.com/ruojiruoli17/CoRef-GS.git.
AI.conclusion: CoRef-GS enables cooperative, viewpoint-conditioned referring grounding over fused Gaussian maps with strong alignment accuracy and grounding performance, and the accompanying CoQuad-Ref benchmark establishes a foundation for multi-robot cooperative referring scene understanding.

title: Semantic SLAM in Precision Agriculture using Bayesian Inference
summary: This paper presents a real-time semantic world modeling framework specialized for precision agriculture using autonomous robots. The framework combines probabilistic mapping of objects and their semantic attributes, updated through Bayesian inference, with a graph-based Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) approach implemented using $g^2o$, a general framework for graph optimization. This integration enables accurate mapping and localization without relying solely on GPS. By leveraging semantic information such as plant type, size, and health, the robot can perform tasks while mapping and localizing itself within a field of crops. The proposed framework was validated through Gazebo simulations and physical experiments on an indoor field with artificial plants using Boston Dynamics' robot dog Spot. A YOLOv8n object detection model was trained to extract object and semantic data from depth camera observations. These simulations and experiments demonstrate that the system can successfully perform real-time mapping of up to at least 400 plants.

AI.tldr: A real-time semantic world modeling framework for precision agriculture combines Bayesian probabilistic mapping with graph-based SLAM (g²o), enabling GPS-independent localization and mapping of crops, validated on Spot with YOLOv8n detection for up to 400 plants.
AI.motivation: Precision agriculture robots need accurate mapping and localization in crop fields, but cannot rely solely on GPS. Semantic information (plant type, size, health) is also needed for task execution, motivating an integrated semantic-synchronous localization and mapping approach.
AI.method: The framework integrates probabilistic mapping of objects and their semantic attributes, updated via Bayesian inference, with graph-based SLAM implemented using g²o. Semantic attributes are extracted from depth camera observations by a trained YOLOv8n object detection model. The robot performs tasks while simultaneously mapping and localizing within the crop field.
AI.result: Validation through Gazebo simulations and physical experiments on an indoor field with artificial plants using Boston Dynamics' Spot robot dog showed successful real-time mapping of up to at least 400 plants.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework enables accurate, GPS-independent semantic world modeling and localization for precision agriculture, demonstrated to scale to at least 400 plants in real-time.

title: Bayesian Continuum Robot Dynamics and State Estimation
summary: Recent factor graph approaches to continuum robot state estimation have been successful for quasi-static applications and spatiotemporal estimation using white-noise kinematic motion priors. However, when inertial effects are significant, these approximations may fail to capture the underlying physics, limiting accuracy during dynamic motions. In contrast, our approach approximates the Cosserat rod dynamics of continuum robots. We write inertia and damping as equivalent applied loads, so that the dynamic balance retains the algebraic form of the static one from prior work with quasi-static robots. Without backbone observations, the framework reduces to a stochastic forward simulation of the robot's motion. Given observations, it jointly refines kinematic and dynamic states and infers external loads, among other states. We validate the approach through simulation and experiments, demonstrating stochastic forward simulation as well as state estimation on tendon-driven continuum robots.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a factor graph approach for continuum robot state estimation that approximates Cosserat rod dynamics by treating inertia and damping as equivalent applied loads, retaining the algebraic form of static equilibrium while enabling dynamic state estimation and external load inference.
AI.motivation: Prior factor graph approaches for continuum robot state estimation succeed only in quasi-static regimes or with white-noise kinematic motion priors. When inertial effects become significant, these approximations fail to capture the underlying physics, degrading accuracy during dynamic motions.
AI.method: The authors approximate Cosserat rod dynamics of continuum robots. Inertia and damping are written as equivalent applied loads, so the dynamic balance retains the same algebraic form as the static one from prior quasi-static work. Without backbone observations, the framework reduces to a stochastic forward simulation of robot motion; with observations, it jointly refines kinematic and dynamic states and infers external loads and other states.
AI.result: The approach is validated through both simulation and experiments, demonstrating stochastic forward simulation and state estimation on tendon-driven continuum robots.
AI.conclusion: By reformulating dynamics as equivalent loads, the method unifies static and dynamic estimation within a single factor graph formulation, extending continuum robot state estimation to dynamic regimes.

title: INSPECT: Learning Robot View Selection from Assistant Use
summary: Robots inspecting an assembly must determine which parts are present and whether they are correctly installed. During egocentric assembly assistance, head motion and workpiece handling reveal evidence for these checks, while spoken state confirmations link observations to procedural outcomes. We introduce INSPECT, which learns robot view preferences from records of a smart-glasses assistant that answers part queries and provides next-step guidance. Presence-Invariant TwinSwap (PI-TwinSwap) calibrates object evidence through paired identity interventions. Claim-indexed supervision separates evidence requirements from camera-reproducible observation changes. Object-centered calibration adapts relative view preferences to robot poses, while clause-level screening checks predicted evidence. The robot selects views using only its current observation and known poses, without candidate images. Evaluation uses annotated assistant-video replay to simulate state feedback, without target-domain view labels for policy training. On images of physical gearbox assemblies, INSPECT achieves the highest view utility among the compared non-oracle policies and raises human-rated full verifiability from 34.8% to 41.7% compared with keeping the current view. On commercial angle-grinder recordings in IMPACT, the transferred relative-view selector increases the correct decision rate from 50.6% to 54.3% with a frozen perception head. The source code is available at https://github.com/Kratos-Wen/INSPECT.

AI.tldr: INSPECT learns robot view preferences from smart-glasses assistant records, using Presence-Invariant TwinSwap calibration, claim-indexed supervision, object-centered calibration, and clause-level screening to select informative views for assembly inspection.
AI.motivation: Robots inspecting assemblies must determine part presence and correct installation; during egocentric assistance, head motion, workpiece handling, and spoken confirmations carry evidence. Training a view-selection policy is hard because target-domain view labels are unavailable.
AI.method: INSPECT learns view preferences from records of a smart-glasses assistant answering part queries and giving next-step guidance. Components: Presence-Invariant TwinSwap (PI-TwinSwap) calibrating object evidence via paired identity interventions; claim-indexed supervision isolating evidence requirements from camera-reproducible observation changes; object-centered calibration adapting relative view preferences to robot poses; clause-level screening checking predicted evidence. The robot selects views from only its current observation and known poses, with no candidate images. Evaluation replays annotated assistant video to simulate state feedback.
AI.result: On physical gearbox assembly images, INSPECT attains the highest view utility among compared non-oracle policies and raises human-rated full verifiability from 34.8% to 41.7% versus keeping the current view. On commercial angle-grinder recordings in IMPACT, the transferred relative-view selector lifts the correct decision rate from 50.6% to 54.3% with a frozen perception head.
AI.conclusion: INSPECT transfers assistant-derived relative view preferences to robot inspection, improving verifiability and decision accuracy without target-domain view labels; code is publicly available.

title: A Simulation Platform for AUV Fault Recovery: Exploring LLM-Based Diagnostic Strategies
comment: 6 pages, 3 figures, 2 tables. Accepted for presentation at the 2026 IEEE/OES Autonomous Underwater Vehicles Symposium (AUV 2026), Southampton, UK. This is the author-accepted manuscript
summary: Autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs) operating beyond reliable communications must recover from failures without human intervention. We investigate an architecture in which conventional deterministic layered control autonomy manages normal operations, while an invokable large language model (LLM) serves as a diagnostic and recovery planner when onboard anomaly detection identifies performance outside expected limits. Because language models are stochastic, rigorous evaluation requires ensemble testing rather than individual demonstrations. We present a closed-loop simulation architecture that couples real-time C vehicle software with a higher-level orchestration layer for physics-based fault injection, structured prompting, language-model interaction, mission file generation, validation, execution, and LLM-judge scoring. The framework, which we call SPAR (Simulation Platform for AUV Recovery), supports evaluation across fault realizations, prompt structures, reasoning models, and mission conditions. We vary these for a mass-shift fault over 480 SPAR trials, evaluating a frontier model and three off-the-shelf locally deployable LLMs. Model choice dominates diagnosis: the frontier model places the CG-shift mechanism in its top three hypotheses in 85-90% of trials, versus 60-78% for the best local model. Reasoning analysis indicates that local-model success is associated with following the complete diagnostic procedure, whereas weaker models often commit prematurely to elevator failure even though the actuator tracks its command. Diagnosis and operational decision performance do not appear to be coupled in this dataset. The contributions are an architecture extending unanticipated-fault recovery from detection to mitigation and an ensemble methodology for evaluating LLM-assisted mission management on low-power AUVs.

AI.tldr: SPAR is a closed-loop simulation platform that pairs deterministic layered AUV autonomy with an invokable LLM diagnostic/recovery planner, evaluated via ensemble testing (480 trials) on a mass-shift fault across a frontier model and three local LLMs.
AI.motivation: AUVs operating beyond reliable communications cannot rely on human intervention, so they must autonomously recover from unanticipated faults. Deterministic layered control handles nominal operations but lacks adaptive diagnostic/recovery capability, while LLMs offer flexible reasoning but are stochastic and need rigorous ensemble-based evaluation rather than single demonstrations.
AI.method: A closed-loop simulation architecture (SPAR) coupling real-time C vehicle software with a higher-level orchestration layer for physics-based fault injection, structured prompting, LLM interaction, mission file generation, validation, execution, and LLM-judge scoring. Evaluation varies fault realizations, prompt structures, reasoning models, and mission conditions, running 480 trials for a mass-shift (CG-shift) fault on one frontier model and three off-the-shelf locally deployable LLMs.
AI.result: Model choice dominates diagnosis: the frontier model placed the CG-shift mechanism in its top three hypotheses in 85–90% of trials versus 60–78% for the best local model. Local-model success correlated with following the complete diagnostic procedure, while weaker models often committed prematurely to elevator failure despite the actuator tracking its command. Diagnosis and operational decision performance were not coupled in this dataset.
AI.conclusion: The work contributes an architecture extending unanticipated-fault recovery from detection to mitigation, and an ensemble methodology for evaluating LLM-assisted mission management on low-power AUVs.

title: SmellDiffusion: Diffusion-Based Quadruped Navigation with Olfactory Scene Graphs
comment: 8 pages, 5 figures, 7 tables, submitted to IEEE ICRA 2027
summary: A robot sent to a named gas leak must preserve gas identity, estimate the source, and navigate to the resulting goal. We present SmellDiffusion, a simulation pipeline that represents species-specific gas zones in an open-vocabulary olfactory scene graph and shares the selected goal between classical and diffusion planners. Its key components are a peak-local geometric gate for selective source correction and diffusion-based, gas-guided trajectory generation. Among 424 unique source-wind configurations in solved flow, 28 have a concentration peak displaced more than 0.5m from the source. A source-independent geometric gate, calibrated only on the training split and evaluated at the observed peak, detects 9 of 10 held-out displacements at 0.64 precision. Gating a precomputed forward-matching correction reduces mean error on the displaced cases from 1.468m to 0.592m (60%), using matching for only 14/204 cases. All-case mean error falls from 0.205m to 0.180m. All planners receive the same scene-graph source estimate as their goal. In a controlled comparison, best-of-ten diffusion achieves mean gas exposure comparable to gas-guided A* (0.0476 versus 0.0455). A single diffusion proposal takes 41.7ms, compared with 72.3ms for gas-guided A*, although best-of-ten sequential sampling increases total runtime. Plain A* also reaches the same goal and remains the fastest and shortest-path method. Six matched Gazebo runs give mean robot-to-source errors of 0.39m for A* and 0.31m for diffusion.

AI.tldr: SmellDiffusion is a simulation pipeline for odor-source localization and navigation that encodes species-specific gas zones in an open-vocabulary olfactory scene graph, shares goals across classical and diffusion planners, and uses a geometric peak gate to selectively correct displaced concentration peaks—reducing displaced-case error by 60% while matching gas-guided A* exposure.
AI.motivation: A robot tasked with reaching a named gas leak must preserve gas identity, estimate the source location, and navigate to the inferred goal. Concentration peaks can be displaced from the true source, so naive goal assignment introduces error. The work targets robust source estimation and gas-guided navigation in a unified pipeline.
AI.method: Open-vocabulary olfactory scene graph representing species-specific gas zones; shared goal between classical (A*) and diffusion planners; a peak-local geometric gate for selective source correction, calibrated on the training split only and evaluated at the observed peak; gated forward-matching correction; diffusion-based gas-guided trajectory generation; evaluation on 424 unique source-wind configurations.
AI.result: Of 424 configurations, 28 have peaks displaced >0.5m from the source. The geometric gate detects 9/10 held-out displacements at 0.64 precision, using matching for only 14/204 cases. Displaced-case mean error drops from 1.468m to 0.592m (60%); all-case error falls from 0.205m to 0.180m. Best-of-ten diffusion achieves exposure 0.0476 vs 0.0455 for gas-guided A*; one diffusion proposal takes 41.7ms vs 72.3ms for A*. Plain A* is fastest and shortest. Gazebo runs: 0.39m (A*) and 0.31m (diffusion) robot-to-source error.
AI.conclusion: A selective, peak-local geometric gate combined with forward-matching correction and diffusion planning yields accurate named-gas source estimation and competitive gas-guided navigation, matching classical A* on exposure while offering faster single proposals but higher total cost under best-of-ten sequential sampling.

title: RTK-Vision PPO for Autonomous Micro UAV Recovery on an Airborne Carrier
summary: Autonomous recovery of a micro unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) onto a moving airborne carrier enables reusable deploy-mission-recover operation, but couples long-range rendezvous, close-range perception, carrier motion, aerodynamic interaction, and a discontinuous contact event. This paper presents an RTK-vision-guided reinforcement-learning framework in which a child UAV is physically transported by a larger carrier, takes off from the carrier while airborne, executes an independent sortie, returns to the carrier's current position, redocks, and subsequently descends with the carrier. Both vehicles carry RTK-GNSS, and the carrier continuously shares its navigation state with the child. Near the recovery deck, RTK remains active while a downward-facing camera with a fiducial marker detector provides marker-relative alignment cues. A proximal policy optimization (PPO) policy governing the terminal recovery phase is trained in a physics-based MuJoCo simulation environment with explicit sensor noise models, an aerodynamic disturbance surrogate, and marker-latency randomization, then transferred to hardware. PX4 retains low-level stabilization, and a deterministic safety gate authorizes descent independently of the learned policy. The PPO checkpoint achieves 99.55% success over 2,000 held-out randomized terminal episodes, compared with 78.4% for a tuned PD baseline under identical conditions, with a median planar terminal error of 6.62 cm. Across 14 outdoor trials, the full mission succeeds in 13 trials (92.9%), spanning both near-region recovery and recovery after the carrier translates away from the release point. The results demonstrate a complete autonomous aerial deployment-and-recovery cycle rather than an isolated landing maneuver, establishing a practical basis for reusable carrier-child operation in inspection, surveillance, and mobile-logistics applications.

AI.tldr: An RTK-vision-guided PPO framework enables a child UAV to be launched from, redocked onto, and recovered by a moving airborne carrier, achieving 92.9% success across 14 outdoor full-mission trials.
AI.motivation: Autonomous recovery onto a moving airborne carrier enables reusable deploy-mission-recover operation, but it couples long-range rendezvous, close-range perception, carrier motion, aerodynamic interaction, and a discontinuous contact event, making the full cycle challenging to realize.
AI.method: The child UAV is physically transported and launched by a larger carrier, executes an independent sortie, returns to the carrier's current position, redocks, and descends with it. Both vehicles carry RTK-GNSS, and the carrier continuously shares its navigation state. Near the recovery deck, RTK stays active while a downward-facing camera with a fiducial marker detector supplies marker-relative alignment cues. A PPO policy governs the terminal recovery phase, trained in a physics-based MuJoCo simulation with explicit sensor noise models, an aerodynamic disturbance surrogate, and marker-latency randomization, then transferred to hardware. PX4 retains low-level stabilization, and a deterministic safety gate authorizes descent independently of the learned policy.
AI.result: The PPO checkpoint achieves 99.55% success over 2,000 held-out randomized terminal episodes versus 78.4% for a tuned PD baseline under identical conditions, with a median planar terminal error of 6.62 cm. Across 14 outdoor trials, the full mission succeeds in 13 trials (92.9%), covering both near-region recovery and recovery after the carrier translates away from the release point.
AI.conclusion: The work demonstrates a complete autonomous aerial deployment-and-recovery cycle rather than an isolated landing maneuver, establishing a practical basis for reusable carrier-child operation in inspection, surveillance, and mobile-logistics applications.

title: TraceFlow: Guiding Frozen Flow-Matching Robot Policies with Success and Failure Traces
summary: A vision-language-action (VLA) policy with a flow-matching action expert generates each action chunk (a short command sequence) by integrating a learned velocity field; once its weights are fixed, the success or failure of an earlier rollout cannot change the chunk generated now. Concurrent test-time methods give a frozen policy such an input from retrieved successes, a learned critic, a verifier, or a dynamics model, but none uses the robot's own failed rollouts as negative evidence with nothing but a terminal outcome bit. We introduce TraceFlow, a progress-aligned guidance field that turns the action densities of retrieved successful and failed rollouts into a bounded correction to a frozen flow-matching action expert, using one terminal outcome bit per rollout and no other label. Its TraceBank stores traces, time-ordered state-action records with a terminal label, starts from the target-task training traces, and later admits the deployed robot's own rollouts. On an ordered real-robot packing task the base completes 21 of 50 trials in order, TraceFlow 39, and one stacking round without any weight update 47, with wrong-sequence episodes falling from 20 to 0. In simulation the gain is selective: with per-suite selected settings, TraceFlow raises RoboMemArena Sequence from 78.92\% to 91.50\% task success and Transferring from 54.41\% to 62.00\% at stacking round 2, leaves the 26-task aggregate unchanged, lowers Counting and Occlusion by 1.12 and 1.42 points, and changes LIBERO-Plus (Long) by +1.27 points (p = 0.0733). Stacking gains are finite, every branch peaking before round ten, and the bank's success-to-failure ratio predicts no retrieval allocation.

AI.tldr: TraceFlow is a test-time guidance method that converts retrieved successful and failed rollouts, labeled only by a terminal outcome bit, into a bounded correction field for a frozen flow-matching vision-language-action policy, improving sequential real-robot packing and selective simulation benchmarks without any weight update.
AI.motivation: Frozen VLA policies generate each action chunk independently of prior rollout outcomes, so earlier failures cannot inform later chunk generation. Existing test-time approaches supply guidance from successes, critics, verifiers, or dynamics models, but none exploits the robot's own failed rollouts as negative evidence under a minimal terminal-outcome-bit supervision.
AI.method: TraceFlow builds a progress-aligned guidance field that maps action densities of retrieved successful and failed rollouts into a bounded correction to a frozen flow-matching action expert, using one terminal outcome bit per rollout and no other labels. Its TraceBank stores time-ordered state-action traces with terminal labels, initialized from target-task training traces and later admitting the deployed robot's own rollouts.
AI.result: On an ordered real-robot packing task, base success is 21/50 versus 39 for TraceFlow, reaching 47 within one stacking round with no weight update, and wrong-sequence episodes drop from 20 to 0. In simulation, gains are selective: with per-suite tuned settings, RoboMemArena Sequence rises from 78.92% to 91.50% and Transferring from 54.41% to 62.00% at stacking round 2; the 26-task aggregate is unchanged, Counting and Occlusion drop by 1.12 and 1.42 points, and LIBERO-Plus (Long) changes by +1.27 points (p = 0.0733). Stacking gains are finite, peaking before round ten, and the bank's success-to-failure ratio does not predict retrieval allocation.
AI.conclusion: Failed rollouts can serve as effective negative evidence for guiding a frozen flow-matching VLA policy at test time using only a terminal outcome bit, yielding strong sequential-task improvements and eliminating sequence errors, though benefits are finite, task-selective, and not governed by the success-to-failure ratio in the trace bank.

title: SkipVLA: Skipping VLA Steps with Classical Planning for Fast Robot Manipulation
comment: This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are a class of generalist robot policies that map camera images and language instructions directly to robot actions. While promising, these models remain slow at test time, particularly for long-horizon tasks that require many queries to the policy. Recent efforts reduce VLA latency by distilling smaller models, overlapping asynchronous action chunks, or pairing the VLA with a fast low-level policy, but still run a learned policy for the entire task. In contrast to VLA, classical motion planners quickly find collision-free motions, but require an explicit goal and have no semantic understanding of the task. In this work, we present SkipVLA, a hybrid policy that combines a pretrained VLA with a classical motion planner, using the planner for free-space motion and querying the VLA only for contact-rich skills such as grasping and placing. SkipVLA reuses the frozen vision-language backbone of the VLA to predict a target pose for each planned motion, and learns this predictor without additional demonstrations introduced into the system by using what was already learnt by the large VLA. We evaluate SkipVLA with three VLAs on 13 LIBERO tasks in simulation and three pick-and-place tasks on a physical 6-DoF YAM arm, demonstrating up to 2.5x faster task completion and significantly lower energy consumption while achieving the same task success rate.

AI.tldr: SkipVLA is a hybrid robot policy that combines a pretrained VLA with a classical motion planner, using the planner for free-space motion and querying the VLA only for contact-rich skills, achieving up to 2.5x faster task completion with equal success rate.
AI.motivation: VLA models are generalist robot policies but are slow at test time, especially for long-horizon tasks requiring many policy queries. Existing latency-reduction efforts (distillation, asynchronous action chunks, fast low-level policies) still run a learned policy for the entire task. Classical motion planners are fast and collision-free but need explicit goals and lack semantic understanding.
AI.method: SkipVLA is a hybrid policy pairing a pretrained VLA with a classical motion planner. The planner handles free-space motion, while the VLA is queried only for contact-rich skills such as grasping and placing. It reuses the frozen VLA vision-language backbone to predict a target pose for each planned motion, training this predictor without extra demonstrations by leveraging the VLA's existing knowledge.
AI.result: Evaluated with three VLAs on 13 LIBERO tasks in simulation and three pick-and-place tasks on a physical 6-DoF YAM arm, SkipVLA achieves up to 2.5x faster task completion and significantly lower energy consumption while maintaining the same task success rate.
AI.conclusion: Combining a classical motion planner with a VLA—querying the VLA only for contact-rich skills—reduces latency and energy without sacrificing success, offering an effective hybrid approach for long-horizon robot tasks.

title: DexTouch-WM: Learning Action-Conditioned Tactile World Models from Human Touch for Dexterous Robot Manipulation
comment: Accept to IROS 2026 Workshop RoBoWoMo (Lightning Talk)
summary: Learning predictive models of contact-rich dexterous manipulation requires dense tactile interaction, but such data are costly to scale on real robots and remain tied to embodiment-specific sensors. We introduce DexTouch-WM, an action-conditioned world model that learns from scalable human touch to jointly predict future RGB observations and bilateral tactile dynamics. Our insight is that human and robot manipulation share transferable contact dynamics when their tactile observations and action spaces are made compatible. We deploy flexible piezoresistive arrays with a shared sensing layout on both human and dexterous robot hands, and retarget human motion into the robot action space so that human interaction can supervise the same dynamics model used for real-robot prediction. DexTouch-WM couples a pretrained video expert with a lightweight tactile expert using anatomy-aware tactile tokens and aligned action conditioning. In human-to-robot scaling experiments, we keep five hours of real-robot supervision fixed while increasing human interaction from 0 to 100 hours, and observe substantial improvements in held-out robot-domain visual, geometric, and contact prediction despite disjoint human and robot task sets. Beyond prediction, we evaluate the world models as surrogate environments for policy evaluation and as generators of synthetic trajectories for real-robot policy learning, showing that scalable human interaction provides a complementary data axis for learning dexterous robot world models.

AI.tldr: DexTouch-WM is an action-conditioned world model that leverages scalable human touch data to jointly predict future RGB observations and bilateral tactile dynamics for dexterous robot manipulation.
AI.motivation: Learning predictive models for contact-rich dexterous manipulation requires dense tactile interaction data, but collecting such data on real robots is costly to scale and remains tied to embodiment-specific sensors. A scalable, transferable data source is needed.
AI.method: The authors exploit shared transferable contact dynamics between human and robot manipulation by making tactile observations and action spaces compatible. They deploy flexible piezoresistive arrays with a shared sensing layout on both human and dexterous robot hands, and retarget human motion into the robot action space so human interaction supervises the same dynamics model used for real-robot prediction. DexTouch-WM couples a pretrained video expert with a lightweight tactile expert via anatomy-aware tactile tokens and aligned action conditioning.
AI.result: In human-to-robot scaling experiments with five hours of fixed real-robot supervision and human interaction increased from 0 to 100 hours, the model shows substantial improvements in held-out robot-domain visual, geometric, and contact prediction, despite disjoint human and robot task sets. The world models also serve as surrogate environments for policy evaluation and as generators of synthetic trajectories for real-robot policy learning.
AI.conclusion: Scalable human interaction provides a complementary data axis for learning dexterous robot world models, enabling improved contact-rich manipulation prediction and downstream policy evaluation and learning.

title: HIL-UMI: Bringing Human-in-the-Loop Post-Training of Vision-Language-Action Models to Universal Manipulation Interface
summary: Large-scale vision-language-action (VLA) models provide powerful priors for robot manipulation, yet adapting them to a specific deployment remains challenging. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on task-specific demonstrations provides a step toward deployment, but faces two persistent limitations: static data provide limited coverage of out-of-distribution states, and standard imitation objectives do not distinguish progressing behavior from less useful data. Interactive post-training can address these limitations, but typically requires repeated policy execution and human intervention on a physical robot. We introduce HIL-UMI, a policy-guided Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI) framework for robot-free human-in-the-loop VLA post-training. During handheld UMI demonstrations, HIL-UMI queries the current policy on the same observation stream without executing its predictions. The Energy Score compares the human action trajectory with policy inference and triggers collection when their discrepancy indicates an out-of-distribution region. In a separate feedback loop, low online advantage predictions identify essential segments for refining a progress-based advantage estimator. The updated estimator then guides advantage-conditioned behavioral cloning using a balanced mixture of base demonstrations and new policy data. This design preserves the iterative and policy-aware nature of human-in-the-loop learning while decoupling data collection from robot deployment. Experiments on four real-world tasks spanning long-horizon and precise manipulation show that HIL-UMI achieves consistent improvement over SFT and benefits from both targeted collection and advantage refinement. Moreover, HIL-UMI outperforms HG-DAgger on Clean Up Table with lower per-frame collection time, suggesting a scalable path for VLA post-training across operators and locations.

AI.tldr: HIL-UMI is a robot-free human-in-the-loop framework that post-trains VLA policies using handheld UMI demonstrations, guided by an Energy Score for targeted data collection and an online advantage estimator for refining progress-based advantage-conditioned behavioral cloning.
AI.motivation: Adapting large-scale VLA models to specific deployments via SFT is limited by static demonstration coverage of out-of-distribution states and imitation objectives that fail to distinguish progressing behavior from less useful data. Existing interactive post-training methods address this but require repeated policy execution and human intervention on a physical robot, which is costly and impractical.
AI.method: HIL-UMI queries the current policy on the same observation stream during handheld UMI demonstrations without executing its predictions. An Energy Score compares human action trajectories with policy inference and triggers collection when discrepancy indicates out-of-distribution regions. A separate feedback loop uses low online advantage predictions to identify essential segments for refining a progress-based advantage estimator, which then guides advantage-conditioned behavioral cloning with a balanced mixture of base demonstrations and new policy data.
AI.result: Across four real-world tasks spanning long-horizon and precise manipulation, HIL-UMI consistently improves over SFT and benefits from both targeted collection and advantage refinement. It also outperforms HG-DAgger on Clean Up Table with lower per-frame collection time.
AI.conclusion: HIL-UMI preserves the iterative, policy-aware nature of human-in-the-loop learning while decoupling data collection from robot deployment, offering a scalable path for VLA post-training across operators and locations.

title: GeoAAC: Geometry-Based Adaptive Action Chunking from Denoising Trajectories in VLA Policies
comment: 9 pages, 6 figures. Submitted to the IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA) 2027
summary: Action chunking is widely used for action generation and execution in Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies, yet existing approaches commonly use a fixed action horizon. During a rollout, different task stages may require different levels of action continuity, control precision, and closed-loop feedback, making a fixed horizon unable to accommodate changing control requirements. We propose \textbf{GeoAAC}, a geometry-based adaptive action chunking method for flow-based VLA policies that adjusts the action horizon according to the reliability of the current action prediction. We show that the geometry of Flow Matching denoising trajectories provides process-level information for characterizing prediction reliability, with geometric variation across action prefixes remaining positively correlated with predictive uncertainty. GeoAAC uses this prefix-wise geometry to construct a horizon-wise geometric profile and adaptively determine the action horizon from a single generation without additional training. Experiments with GR00T N1.5 and π0.5 on LIBERO, LIBERO-Pro, RoboCasa365, and real-world manipulation tasks show consistent improvements over fixed-action-horizon baselines and existing adaptive methods, including up to 8.7 percentage points in simulation and an increase in average real-world success rate from 53.3\% to 74.4\%.

AI.tldr: GeoAAC is a training-free, geometry-based adaptive action chunking method for flow-based VLA policies. It adjusts the action horizon by exploiting the geometry of Flow Matching denoising trajectories (prefix-wise geometric variation correlates with predictive uncertainty), determining the horizon from a single generation and consistently outperforming fixed-horizon and existing adaptive baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing VLA action chunking uses a fixed action horizon, but different task stages demand varying action continuity, control precision, and closed-loop feedback. A fixed horizon cannot accommodate these changing control requirements.
AI.method: GeoAAC leverages the geometry of Flow Matching denoising trajectories as a process-level signal of prediction reliability. Since geometric variation across action prefixes is positively correlated with predictive uncertainty, GeoAAC builds a horizon-wise geometric profile from prefix-wise geometry and adaptively selects the action horizon from a single generation, without additional training.
AI.result: With GR00T N1.5 and π0.5 on LIBERO, LIBERO-Pro, RoboCasa365, and real-world manipulation tasks, GeoAAC consistently improves over fixed-action-horizon baselines and existing adaptive methods, achieving up to +8.7 percentage points in simulation and raising average real-world success rate from 53.3% to 74.4%.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive action chunking driven by denoising-trajectory geometry offers an effective, training-free way to match action horizons to task-stage control needs, yielding consistent gains across simulation benchmarks and real-world manipulation.

title: Learning Foresight without Explicit Trajectories for 3D Diffusion Policies
summary: 3D diffusion policies are strong at generating geometrically grounded actions from current observations, but successful manipulation requires not only knowing what motion is feasible now, but also anticipating where the interaction is heading. Existing policies largely leave such foresight to emerge implicitly from action learning. We introduce Movement Trend Guidance, a simple but effective way to provide this foresight without introducing an explicit plan. From a short observation history, the policy learns a compact latent representation of interaction evolution. During training, sparse future gripper states supervise this representation; at inference, only the latent is retained as future-oriented conditioning alongside the current observation. The latent provides global conditioning for action generation, while an additional gated FiLM branch is used only at the UNet bottleneck. Despite adding only 3.52% more parameters to DP3, our method preserves the original dense-action and receding-horizon formulation and consistently improves upon DP3 across RoboTwin2.0, LIBERO-40, and DexArt. It reaches 62.8% vs. 56.1% in 50-task RoboTwin2.0 mixed training, 71.93% vs. 37.08% on LIBERO-40, and 72.0% vs. 49.0% on five real-robot tasks. These results show that a diffusion policy can benefit substantially from knowing where an interaction is heading, without being told exactly where to move.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Movement Trend Guidance, a lightweight method that gives 3D diffusion policies foresight about interaction evolution via a learned latent from short observation history, improving DP3 across multiple benchmarks with minimal parameter overhead.
AI.motivation: 3D diffusion policies generate geometrically grounded actions but lack foresight about where an interaction is heading; existing policies leave this anticipation to emerge implicitly from action learning, which is insufficient for successful manipulation.
AI.method: Learn a compact latent representation of interaction evolution from a short observation history. During training, sparse future gripper states supervise this latent. At inference, only the latent is retained as future-oriented conditioning alongside the current observation. The latent provides global conditioning for action generation, with an additional gated FiLM branch applied only at the UNet bottleneck.
AI.result: Adds only 3.52% more parameters to DP3 while preserving the dense-action and receding-horizon formulation. Achieves 62.8% vs. 56.1% on 50-task RoboTwin2.0 mixed training, 71.93% vs. 37.08% on LIBERO-40, and 72.0% vs. 49.0% on five real-robot tasks.
AI.conclusion: A diffusion policy can benefit substantially from anticipating where an interaction is heading, without being explicitly told where to move, and the proposed guidance yields consistent improvements over DP3 across simulation and real-robot benchmarks.

title: Workspace Models: Lightweight Robotic Memory via Saliency-Driven Supervision
summary: Complex robotic manipulation tasks frequently require a long-term memory of past events and actions. As conditioning on full histories renders policies prone to spurious correlations and degrades performance, many approaches to policy memory involve compressing historical information through expensive VLM queries in-the-loop to process only task-salient information. In this paper, we propose an alternative approach in which computationally intensive VLM queries are made during train-time to learn a lightweight latent memory that can be efficiently queried at deployment time. Our representation, which we call the \textbf{workspace token}, is trained by (1) using a VLM to identify current and historical information necessary for completing a task, then (2) distilling these into the workspace token using a set-reconstruction decoder loss. In both simulation and hardware, we show that the workspace token can be used as a drop-in replacement for observations during deployment, enabling policies to solve memory-intensive tasks without the need for VLM reasoning in-the-loop. Interestingly, we found that workspace tokens are not only more lightweight but also lead to better policy performance.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes "workspace token," a lightweight latent memory for robotic manipulation policies. Instead of running expensive VLM queries in-the-loop at deployment, VLM queries are used only at train-time to distill task-salient current and historical information into the token via a set-reconstruction decoder loss.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon robotic manipulation tasks need memory of past events and actions. Conditioning on full histories causes spurious correlations and degraded performance, while existing memory approaches that compress history via in-the-loop VLM queries are computationally expensive. The authors aim for an efficient alternative that retains task-relevant memory without deployment-time VLM reasoning.
AI.method: Train-time VLM usage: (1) a VLM identifies current and historical information necessary for the task; (2) this information is distilled into a compact latent "workspace token" using a set-reconstruction decoder loss. At deployment, the workspace token serves as a drop-in replacement for observations, avoiding in-the-loop VLM queries.
