AI.result: Evaluated in both simulation and on hardware. The workspace token enables policies to solve memory-intensive tasks without in-the-loop VLM reasoning. Notably, it is both more lightweight and yields better policy performance than baselines.
AI.conclusion: Lightweight latent memory learned via train-time VLM distillation offers an efficient and effective substitute for observation-based memory in long-horizon robotic manipulation, improving both efficiency and task performance.

title: MAGNETAR: Multipath-Guided Spatial Posteriors for Transmitter Pose Inference in the Upper Mid-Band
summary: Robots that localize a radio transmitter need more than a point estimate: in cluttered rooms, one measurement is often consistent with several transmitter locations and, because upper-mid-band antennas are directional, several headings. We present MAGNETAR, which infers a joint posterior over planar transmitter position and heading from a single asynchronous radio-frequency (RF) multipath snapshot, represented by angle-of-arrival and signal-to-noise-ratio estimates, given the room layout and receiver pose. Among our five neural scorers, MAGNETAR adopts a shared 2D U-Net conditioned on each candidate heading, jointly normalizing scores over a discretized position-heading grid. Training uses real-to-sim-calibrated 10 GHz simulations and a small measured subset. Grid-based joint posteriors outperform parametric ones on held-out simulations, the heading-conditioned scorer transfers best to robotic measurements, and fusing joint posteriors improves on fusing position-only marginals.

AI.tldr: MAGNETAR infers a joint posterior over planar transmitter position and heading from a single asynchronous RF multipath snapshot (AoA and SNR estimates), given room layout and receiver pose, using a heading-conditioned 2D U-Net over a discretized position-heading grid.
AI.motivation: Point estimates are insufficient for radio-transmitter localization: in cluttered rooms a single measurement is often consistent with multiple transmitter locations and, due to directional upper-mid-band antennas, multiple headings. A joint posterior is therefore needed.
AI.method: MAGNETAR represents the snapshot as angle-of-arrival and SNR estimates and conditions on room layout and receiver pose. Among five neural scorers, it adopts a shared 2D U-Net conditioned on each candidate heading, jointly normalizing scores over a discretized position-heading grid. Training uses real-to-sim-calibrated 10 GHz simulations plus a small measured subset.
AI.result: Grid-based joint posteriors outperform parametric ones on held-out simulations. The heading-conditioned scorer transfers best to robotic measurements, and fusing joint posteriors improves on fusing position-only marginals.
AI.conclusion: Joint position-heading posterior inference from a single RF snapshot is feasible and beneficial, with grid-based, heading-conditioned scoring giving the best simulated accuracy and sim-to-real transfer, and joint-posterior fusion outperforming marginal fusion.

title: Coding Agents with an Obstacle-Aware Harness for Safe Robot Manipulation
summary: Coding agents have emerged as a promising paradigm for robot manipulation: a language model writes the robot controller as a program, and agents built in this way now operate robots without robot-specific training.Whether this paradigm is also safe, however, has not been asked. We evaluate coding agent under a safety constraint, where each task pairs a manipulation goal with an obstacle the robot must not touch. The agent pursues the goal but collides with the obstacle in most cases, treating task completion as its sole objective while neglecting safety. The agent reasons about the obstacle in its traces, and the prompt already forbids touching it, so neither perception nor instruction is at fault; the fault lies in the planning, where the stated constraint never becomes a priority. By decomposing manipulation into a route phase and a contact-rich moment, we locate the source of the failure. Along the route, the model cannot prioritize the safety constraint, having no notion of a clearing route and none of replanning once a chosen route becomes infeasible. At the contact, it is unaware that contact execution is bounded by the same constraint. To close this gap, we present SafeHarness, which equips the model with two obstacle-aware harnesses that enable it to prioritize the safety constraint. Obstacle-aware route planning grounds the objects as bounding boxes and draws candidate routes over them as sequences of waypoints. The agent then plans a route in advance, verifies it, replans when necessary, and only then executes it. Obstacle-aware contact execution instead selects the contact position so that the contact itself avoids the obstacle. SafeHarness attains 71.9% task success and 87.5% collision avoidance, surpassing the previous SOTA by 6.5% and 27.0%, respectively. These results are $2.3\times$ and $1.5\times$ those of the same agent without harnesses.

AI.tldr: Coding agents for robot manipulation are unsafe: given a goal plus a no-touch obstacle constraint, they collide in most cases because the constraint never becomes a planning priority. SafeHarness adds obstacle-aware route planning and contact execution to enforce it, reaching 71.9% task success and 87.5% collision avoidance.
AI.motivation: Coding agents that write robot controllers now operate robots without robot-specific training, but their safety has not been examined. The paper asks whether this paradigm holds under a safety constraint where each task pairs a manipulation goal with an obstacle that must not be touched.
AI.method: The failure is decomposed into a route phase and a contact-rich moment. SafeHarness provides two obstacle-aware harnesses: (1) obstacle-aware route planning, which grounds objects as bounding boxes and draws candidate routes as waypoint sequences, so the agent plans a route in advance, verifies it, replans when infeasible, and then executes; and (2) obstacle-aware contact execution, which selects the contact position so the contact itself avoids the obstacle.
AI.result: SafeHarness attains 71.9% task success and 87.5% collision avoidance, surpassing the previous SOTA by 6.5% and 27.0%, respectively, i.e., 2.3x and 1.5x the same agent without harnesses.
AI.conclusion: The failures are not perceptual or instructional but planning-related: the stated constraint never becomes a priority. Equipping the model with obstacle-aware harnesses for both route planning and contact execution closes the safety gap.

title: Towards Scaling Marine Perception with Synthetic Data
summary: Scalable machine learning in challenging underwater environments is strongly limited by the lack of labeled real-world training data. This data is often expensive and laborious to gather, making large-scale real-world data challenging to gather and curate. However, simulated data can help close the gap, enabling many learning-based tasks for underwater perception. In this work, we extend OceanSim, an IsaacSim-based underwater perception simulator, with a Synthetic Data Generation (SDG) pipeline for training models to be used in underwater scenarios. The proposed pipeline enables users to generate large, automatically labeled, photorealistic datasets with configurable scene appearance, structure, and sensor settings. We evaluate the pipeline on a real-world sea urchin detection task and study how different forms of synthetic scene variation affect sim-to-real performance. Based on these experiments, we discuss findings on our results, main limitations of the current pipeline and identify future directions for improving underwater rendering fidelity, scene diversity, and the evaluation of sim-to-real generalization. The open-source code can be found at https://github.com/umfieldrobotics/OceanSim.

AI.tldr: The paper extends OceanSim, an IsaacSim-based underwater perception simulator, with a Synthetic Data Generation pipeline that produces large, automatically labeled, photorealistic datasets with configurable scene appearance, structure, and sensor settings, evaluated on a real-world sea urchin detection task to study how synthetic scene variation affects sim-to-real performance.
AI.motivation: Scalable machine learning in underwater environments is limited by the lack of labeled real-world training data, which is expensive and laborious to collect and curate. Simulated data can help close this gap, but requires tooling to generate useful, varied synthetic datasets.
AI.method: The authors extend OceanSim, an IsaacSim-based underwater perception simulator, with a Synthetic Data Generation (SDG) pipeline. The pipeline enables generation of large, automatically labeled, photorealistic datasets with configurable scene appearance, structure, and sensor settings. They evaluate the pipeline on a real-world sea urchin detection task and conduct experiments studying how different forms of synthetic scene variation affect sim-to-real performance.
AI.result: The pipeline successfully generates large, automatically labeled, photorealistic synthetic datasets with configurable variation, and the experiments on the sea urchin detection task reveal how different forms of synthetic scene variation affect sim-to-real transfer performance.
AI.conclusion: The paper presents findings from the experiments, discusses the main limitations of the current pipeline, and identifies future directions for improving underwater rendering fidelity, scene diversity, and the evaluation of sim-to-real generalization. The code is open-source.

title: Custom PX4 firmware for autonomous hybrid aerial-marine missions
comment: Accepted to I-RIM 3D 2026 and it will be published in SPAR series
summary: Mapping and monitoring aquatic environments can benefit from hybrid aerial-amphibious drones able to combine flight and water-surface navigation within the same mission. This paper presents a PX4 firmware extension for such platforms, introducing manual and autonomous marine navigation modes integrated with the standard PX4 mission pipeline and QGroundControl interface. The proposed framework preserves existing flight functionalities and safety mechanisms while enabling unified planning and execution of hybrid aerial-marine missions with differentiated aerial and marine waypoints. Simulated case studies validate the implementation and demonstrate stable surface navigation under calm and wavy conditions.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a PX4 firmware extension enabling hybrid aerial-amphibious drones to perform both flight and marine-surface navigation within a unified mission, validated through simulated case studies.
AI.motivation: Mapping and monitoring aquatic environments stand to benefit from hybrid aerial-amphibious drones that combine flight and water-surface navigation in a single mission, yet existing autopilot frameworks lack integrated support for such dual-domain operation.
AI.method: The authors extend the PX4 firmware by adding manual and autonomous marine navigation modes, integrating them into the standard PX4 mission pipeline and QGroundControl interface, while preserving existing flight functionalities and safety mechanisms. Unified planning and execution of hybrid missions is enabled through differentiated aerial and marine waypoints.
AI.result: Simulated case studies validate the implementation and demonstrate stable surface navigation under both calm and wavy conditions.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework successfully enables unified planning and execution of hybrid aerial-marine missions within PX4, supporting amphibious drone operation without compromising flight capabilities or safety.

title: HOPHY: A Hierarchical Hypergraph Representation for Off-Road Path and Mission Planning
summary: Mission-level autonomy for disaster response, search and rescue, and tactical UGV operations requires repeated path and mission planning as terrain conditions, agent types, and objectives change. Pixel-grid search is costly for repeated kilometer-scale queries, while semantic abstractions must maintain valid costs and connectivity as conditions change. We present HOPHY (Hierarchical Off-Road Planning using Hypergraphs), a reusable hierarchical terrain representation that organizes map-scale terrain into geometrically connected semantic regions (GSNodes), connectivity-preserving critical regions (Coarse Regions), and typed hyperedges for terrain, agent, and weather context. Hyperedge intersections select affected regions and incident edges for state updates without rebuilding the hierarchy. Across real off-road maps spanning kilometer-scale areas, HOPHY achieves 100% planning success and less than 0.01% median cost deviation from the oracle (pixel A*), with substantially lower query and replanning latency than the evaluated pixel and abstraction baselines. Applied to a multi-robot task-allocation (MRTA) problem, these gains reduce total computation by 79x over pixel A* and 7.2x over the fastest abstraction baseline, with mission makespan comparable to pixel A*. Finally, we demonstrate HOPHY on a physical Clearpath Jackal that successfully executes a 1.5-km, eight-task mission across mixed-surface outdoor terrain and a blockage-triggered replanned route.

AI.tldr: HOPHY is a reusable hierarchical terrain representation using hypergraphs that organizes terrain into semantic regions and typed hyperedges, enabling fast, accurate repeated off-road path and mission planning with 100% success and near-oracle cost fidelity at much lower latency.
AI.motivation: Disaster response, search-and-rescue, and tactical UGV operations demand repeated path and mission planning as terrain, agent types, and objectives change. Pixel-grid search is expensive for repeated kilometer-scale queries, whereas semantic abstractions struggle to preserve valid costs and connectivity under changing conditions.
AI.method: HOPHY builds a reusable hierarchical representation with geometrically connected semantic regions (GSNodes), connectivity-preserving critical regions (Coarse Regions), and typed hyperedges encoding terrain, agent, and weather context. Hyperedge intersections localize affected regions and incident edges so state updates are applied without rebuilding the hierarchy.
AI.result: On real kilometer-scale off-road maps, HOPHY achieves 100% planning success with under 0.01% median cost deviation from pixel A* oracle, and lower query/replanning latency than pixel and abstraction baselines. In multi-robot task allocation it cuts computation 79x versus pixel A* and 7.2x versus the fastest abstraction baseline, with comparable makespan. A physical Clearpath Jackal executed a 1.5-km, eight-task mission with blockage-triggered replanning.
AI.conclusion: HOPHY provides a reusable, connectivity-preserving hierarchical terrain abstraction that enables fast, cost-accurate repeated planning and replanning for large-scale off-road multi-robot missions, validated in both benchmarks and a field deployment.

title: MoWAM: Explicit Future Motion Prediction for Efficient World Action Models
summary: World Action Models (WAMs) improve robot policy learning by incorporating future dynamics, yet explicitly generating future videos at inference introduces substantial computational overhead. Removing future generation improves efficiency, but leaves future dynamics only implicitly encoded in observation features, which can limit robustness under distribution shifts. We propose MoWAM, an efficient WAM that replaces future video generation with explicit future motion prediction. Instead of reconstructing the complete future scene, MoWAM models structured robot motion as a compact abstraction of the future, capturing how the robot is expected to evolve under the current scene and interaction constraints. A Mixture-of-Transformer architecture learns future visual dynamics during training while jointly predicting motion and action, allowing video generation to be removed entirely at inference while retaining an explicit representation of the future. The compact motion representation further enables efficient inference-time scaling by sampling multiple candidates of motion and action pairs and selecting among them with a motion-aware task-progress verifier. Experiments on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and real-world manipulation tasks demonstrate that MoWAM achieves strong in-distribution performance, improved out-of-distribution robustness, and higher average real-world success than representative WAM baselines. In addition, performance improves as more candidates are explored, demonstrating that explicit future motion provides an effective and efficient basis for inference-time scaling.

AI.tldr: MoWAM is an efficient World Action Model that replaces explicit future video generation with compact future motion prediction, retaining an explicit future representation at reduced inference cost while enabling verifier-based inference-time scaling.
AI.motivation: World Action Models improve robot policy learning by incorporating future dynamics, but explicitly generating future videos at inference incurs substantial computational overhead. Removing this generation improves efficiency but leaves future dynamics only implicitly encoded in observation features, limiting robustness under distribution shifts.
AI.method: MoWAM replaces future video generation with explicit future motion prediction, modeling structured robot motion as a compact abstraction of the future that captures how the robot should evolve under current scene and interaction constraints. A Mixture-of-Transformer architecture learns future visual dynamics during training while jointly predicting motion and action, allowing video generation to be removed entirely at inference. The compact motion representation supports efficient inference-time scaling by sampling multiple motion-action candidate pairs, selected via a motion-aware task-progress verifier.
AI.result: On LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and real-world manipulation tasks, MoWAM achieves strong in-distribution performance, improved out-of-distribution robustness, and higher average real-world success than representative WAM baselines. Performance further improves as more candidates are explored.
AI.conclusion: Explicit future motion provides an effective and efficient basis for inference-time scaling, enabling robust robot policy learning without the cost of future video generation.

title: Underwater Visual Target Tracking with Target-Specific Depth Estimation and Adaptive Model-Fusion Predictive Control
summary: Vision-based underwater target tracking is challenged by unreliable depth measurements and unknown target motion. This paper proposes a stereo visual-servoing framework for an autonomous underwater vehicle (AUV). For perception, the framework derives a stable 3D relative state from stereo images through target-specific depth extraction and Kalman filtering. It constructs a target-depth mask from color, disparity, and temporal cues to select reliable target pixels, and then filters the resulting depth measurement and detected image center separately. For control, the framework decouples yaw regulation from translational control, avoiding computationally expensive coupled multi-DOF optimization and enabling real-time translational MPC. The translational controller employs adaptive model-fusion predictive control, combining constant-velocity and zero-velocity target models to accommodate different target-motion patterns. It updates the model weights using historical prediction errors and computes translational commands subject to actuation, following-distance, and field-of-view constraints. Through simulations and real-world experiments, we validate the effectiveness of the proposed framework and show it has better performance than existing frameworks.

AI.tldr: Vision-based underwater target tracking is hindered by unreliable depth measurements and unknown target motion. This paper proposes a stereo visual-servoing framework for an AUV that combines robust stereo-based 3D state estimation with a decoupled, adaptive MPC controller, validated in simulation and real-world experiments.
AI.motivation: Underwater vision-based target tracking suffers from unreliable depth measurements and unknown/uncertain target motion, which degrade tracking robustness and precision. Existing frameworks struggle to provide stable 3D relative state estimates and to handle varying target-motion patterns in real time.
AI.method: A stereo visual-servoing framework with two parts. Perception: derives a stable 3D relative state from stereo images via target-specific depth extraction and Kalman filtering; builds a target-depth mask from color, disparity, and temporal cues to select reliable pixels, then filters depth measurement and detected image center separately. Control: decouples yaw regulation from translational control to avoid costly coupled multi-DOF optimization, enabling real-time translational MPC; uses adaptive model-fusion predictive control combining constant-velocity and zero-velocity target models, updating model weights from historical prediction errors, and computes commands under actuation, following-distance, and field-of-view constraints.
AI.result: Simulations and real-world experiments validate the effectiveness of the proposed framework and demonstrate better performance than existing frameworks.
AI.conclusion: The proposed stereo visual-servoing framework provides robust depth/target-state estimation and efficient, adaptive translational control, enabling improved real-time AUV target tracking over prior frameworks.

title: MILER: Semantic Mid-Level Representation for Sim-to-Real Reinforcement Learning in Unstructured Autonomous Driving
summary: Reinforcement learning constitutes a promising approach owing to its potential for superhuman performance and self-learned policies. However, its application to real-world autonomous driving remains scarce, particularly in unstructured environments, because of the challenges associated with sim-to-real transfer for unstructured environments. In this work, we present MILER, an end-to-end policy framework with zero-shot sim-to-real transfer. During offline training, we employ a custom semantic mid-level representation (MLR) simulator and train the policy network using reinforcement learning, with its control outputs applied directly to a bicycle model. During deployment on the real vehicle, camera and LiDAR data are processed by BEVFusion to generate a semantic bird's-eye-view representation consistent with that of the MLR simulator. The actions generated by the policy network are not applied directly to the real vehicle. Instead, we employ a trajectory-alignment strategy that enables zero-shot sim-to-real transfer of both perception and control. We extensively evaluate the proposed framework on a diverse test track comprising numerous challenges, including various obstacles, hairpin curves, velocities of up to 33.6 km/h, and off-road sections. In total, we drove 17.3 km with two different vehicles on a 3.0 km test track without human intervention, thereby demonstrating the effectiveness of our approach. Furthermore, the entire software stack runs on a Jetson AGX Orin.

AI.tldr: MILER is an end-to-end policy framework that achieves zero-shot sim-to-real transfer for autonomous driving in unstructured environments by combining a mid-level representation simulator, RL-trained policy, BEVFusion perception, and a trajectory-alignment control strategy.
AI.motivation: Reinforcement learning promises superhuman performance and self-learned policies, but its real-world application to autonomous driving is scarce, especially in unstructured environments, due to the difficulty of sim-to-real transfer.
AI.method: During offline training, a custom semantic mid-level representation (MLR) simulator is used to train the policy network with RL, with control outputs applied directly to a bicycle model. At deployment, camera and LiDAR are processed by BEVFusion to produce a semantic bird's-eye-view representation consistent with the MLR simulator. Policy actions are not applied directly; a trajectory-alignment strategy enables zero-shot transfer of both perception and control. The stack runs on a Jetson AGX Orin.
AI.result: Evaluation on a diverse 3.0 km test track with obstacles, hairpin curves, speeds up to 33.6 km/h, and off-road sections. A total of 17.3 km was driven with two different vehicles without human intervention, demonstrating effectiveness.
AI.conclusion: The proposed MILER framework achieves effective zero-shot sim-to-real transfer for autonomous driving in unstructured environments, validated by extensive real-world driving with no human intervention.

title: OPTED: On-Policy Fine-Tuning for End-to-End Driving using a Render-Free Teacher
summary: As scaling pre-training data alone yields diminishing returns, post-training is becoming increasingly important across physical AI domains such as autonomous driving. End-to-end driving policies are pre-trained in open loop with behavior cloning on human demonstrations. However, compounding errors during closed-loop deployment can take the vehicle outside the training data distribution, increasing the risk of safety-critical incidents. Closed-loop post-training can mitigate this risk but requires costly simulation for sensor-based policies. We propose OPTED (on-policy fine-tuning for end-to-end driving) which decouples reinforcement learning from the post-training of the end-to-end policy: a privileged teacher is trained using RL on vectorized inputs (HD-map and bounding boxes). This teacher then provides supervision to the pre-trained student during closed-loop post-training. We apply OPTED to two camera-based models, TransFuser and VaVAM, and fine-tune them in AlpaSim, using neural reconstructions (3DGS) of real driving logs. Driving scores increase by factors of 1.6$\times$ and 9.5$\times$, respectively. In controlled experiments OPTED matches closed-loop performance with approximately three orders of magnitude fewer simulator interactions than direct RL post-training, while staying closer to the human prior. Project page: https://01dami23.github.io/opted/

AI.tldr: OPTED decouples RL from end-to-end driving policy post-training by first training a privileged teacher (RL on vectorized inputs) that then supervises a pre-trained camera-based student in closed-loop post-training, improving driving scores 1.6x and 9.5x with ~1000x fewer simulator interactions than direct RL.
AI.motivation: Scaling pre-training data yields diminishing returns, making post-training increasingly important for physical AI domains like autonomous driving. End-to-end driving policies are pre-trained in open loop via behavior cloning on human demonstrations, but compounding errors during closed-loop deployment push the vehicle out of the training distribution, raising the risk of safety-critical incidents. Closed-loop post-training can mitigate this, yet it is costly because it requires simulation for sensor-based policies.
AI.method: OPTED (on-policy fine-tuning for end-to-end driving) decouples reinforcement learning from the post-training of the end-to-end policy. A privileged teacher is trained with RL on vectorized inputs (HD-map and bounding boxes). This teacher then provides supervision to the pre-trained student during closed-loop post-training. The method is applied to two camera-based models, TransFuser and VaVAM, fine-tuned in AlpaSim using neural reconstructions (3D Gaussian Splatting) of real driving logs.
AI.result: Driving scores increase by factors of 1.6x and 9.5x for TransFuser and VaVAM, respectively. In controlled experiments, OPTED matches closed-loop performance with approximately three orders of magnitude fewer simulator interactions than direct RL post-training, while staying closer to the human prior.
AI.conclusion: OPTED offers an efficient closed-loop post-training approach for end-to-end driving policies, achieving strong performance gains at dramatically reduced simulation cost and preserving fidelity to human demonstrations. Project page: https://01dami23.github.io/opted/

title: Agile-WAM: An Agile Tactile World Action Model for Contact-Rich Robot Control
summary: World Action Models (WAMs) advance beyond conventional visuomotor policies by jointly predicting future world states and robot actions, enabling the policy to learn physical dynamics that support effective control. However, recent tactile WAMs often rely on large-scale pretrained generative backbones to capture contact-rich physical dynamics, which limit their inference efficiency and flexible deployment. In this paper, we present \ABBR{}, an agile tactile World Action Model for contact-rich robot control. \ABBR{} encodes visual and tactile observations into a shared latent that serves as the source of a direct vision-tactile-to-action flow-matching process, which can jointly generate latent representations of action chunks and future visual/tactile latents. A key observation is that vision and tactile signals evolve at inherently different timescales: adjacent visual frames are often highly similar, whereas tactile signals can change abruptly upon contact. We therefore introduce multi-horizon multimodal prediction in \ABBR{}, which provides supervision for visual latent at a larger temporal offset while predicting the tactile latent in the next frame to capture fine-grained contact dynamics. Across nine simulated and five real-world contact-rich manipulation tasks, \ABBR{} demonstrates strong and robust performance, outperforming the strongest baseline in success rate while maintaining low inference latency. In particular, in five real-world experiments, \ABBR{} yields a relative gain of $\textbf{29.4\%}$ in overall success rates while achieving inference latency of $\textbf{11.9 ms}$. These results demonstrate that multimodal WAM can be achieved with an agile architecture suitable for precise and high-frequency robot control. More details are available on our project page: https://hanchuzhou.github.io/TARO_project_page/.

AI.tldr: TARO is an agile tactile World Action Model that jointly generates action chunks and future visual/tactile latents via a shared vision-tactile latent and flow matching, using multi-horizon multimodal prediction to handle differing timescales of vision and touch, achieving strong success rates with 11.9 ms inference latency.
AI.motivation: Conventional visuomotor policies lack physical dynamics learning, while recent tactile World Action Models depend on large-scale pretrained generative backbones to capture contact-rich dynamics, limiting inference efficiency and deployment flexibility. An agile architecture is needed for precise, high-frequency contact-rich control.
AI.method: TARO encodes visual and tactile observations into a shared latent serving as the source of a direct vision-tactile-to-action flow-matching process that jointly generates latent action chunks and future visual/tactile latents. It introduces multi-horizon multimodal prediction, supervising visual latents at a larger temporal offset while predicting tactile latents at the next frame, reflecting the different evolution timescales of vision and touch.
AI.result: Across nine simulated and five real-world contact-rich manipulation tasks, TARO outperforms the strongest baseline in success rate with low inference latency. In five real-world experiments it achieves a 29.4% relative gain in overall success rate and 11.9 ms inference latency.
AI.conclusion: Multimodal World Action Models can be realized with an agile architecture suitable for precise and high-frequency robot control.

title: StageGuard: Learning Stage Transitions for Long-Horizon Robot Tasks via Agentic Distillation
summary: Hierarchical planning frameworks combine skills from multiple robot control policies for long-horizon task execution, where determining when to terminate the current skill and advance to the next subtask is essential. Existing approaches often rely on pre-designed completion signal checkers that are hard to obtain in real-world execution. Large-scale vision-language models (VLMs) offer strong reasoning capabilities, but their decision boundaries are not inherently aligned with task completion criteria, while cloud deployment and lengthy reasoning introduce substantial latency, limiting real-time monitoring. We propose StageGuard, an agentic distillation framework for accurate and efficient stage-transition decisions. StageGuard combines teacher-model reasoning with demonstration trajectories to generate structured explanations of subtask completion and policy switching. A lightweight student VLM uses these explanations to generate compact self-explanations, which are used for supervised fine-tuning. We evaluate stage-transition prediction on trajectories from two benchmarks and assess closed-loop task success through integration into hierarchical robot control on BEHAVIOR-1K, with further validation on real robots. Results show substantial improvements in stage-transition prediction while supporting efficient online monitoring.

AI.tldr: StageGuard is an agentic distillation framework that produces accurate and efficient stage-transition decisions for hierarchical robot planning by distilling teacher-model reasoning into a lightweight student VLM for real-time online monitoring.
AI.motivation: Hierarchical planning frameworks combine skills from multiple robot control policies for long-horizon tasks, and deciding when to terminate the current skill and advance to the next subtask is essential. Existing approaches rely on pre-designed completion signal checkers that are hard to obtain in real-world execution. Large-scale VLMs offer strong reasoning but their decision boundaries are not aligned with task completion criteria; cloud deployment and lengthy reasoning also introduce substantial latency that limits real-time monitoring.
AI.method: StageGuard uses an agentic distillation framework. Teacher-model reasoning is combined with demonstration trajectories to generate structured explanations of subtask completion and policy switching. A lightweight student VLM uses these explanations to produce compact self-explanations, which are then used for supervised fine-tuning.

Results show substantial improvements in stage-transition prediction while supporting efficient online monitoring.
